Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 1 (part 1 of 2):

Surat al-Tawbah (9) is Madani, as related from Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿAbdullah ibn al-Zubayr, Qatadah and a great many others, and some have reported a consensus on this.

Ibn al-Faras said: it is so, except for two verses of it, ﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves﴾ etc. This is problematic, based on what is in al-Mustadrak from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, and Abu al-Shaykh reported in his Tafsir from ʿAli ibn Zayd, from Yusuf al-Makki, from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the last verse revealed was ﴿There has certainly come to you﴾ etc. And what they said regarding the way of reconciling the differing reports about the last thing revealed does not apply here. Others excepted ﴿It is not for the Prophet﴾ (the verse), based on what is reported, that it was revealed concerning the words of the Prophet (ﷺ) to Abu Talib: "I will certainly ask forgiveness for you as long as I am not forbidden from you." It was revealed, as Ibn Kaysan said, in the ninth year after the Hijrah. It has several names: al-Tawbah (Repentance), because of His words in it: ﴿Allah has certainly turned in forgiveness to the Prophet and the Emigrants and the Helpers﴾ up to His words: ﴿and to the three who were left behind﴾. Al-Fadihah (The Exposer): Abu ʿUbayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and others reported from Ibn Jubayr who said: I said to Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "Surat al-Tawbah?" He said: "Rather, it is al-Fadihah; it kept descending, [mentioning] of them and of them, until we thought that none of us would be left without being mentioned in it." Surat al-ʿAdhab (The Punishment): al-Hakim reported in his Mustadrak from Hudhayfah who said: "The one they call Surat al-Tawbah is Surat al-ʿAdhab."

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn Jubayr who said: When Surat Bara'ah was mentioned to ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, and it was said "Surat al-Tawbah," he said: "It is closer to punishment; it did not cease from the people until it hardly left anyone." Al-Muqashqishah (The Absolving): Ibn Mardawayh and others reported from Zayd ibn Aslam that a man said to ʿAbdullah: "Surat al-Tawbah," and Ibn ʿUmar said: "Which of them is Surat al-Tawbah?" He said: "Bara'ah." He, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Did it not do to the people the deeds except it? We did not call it except al-Muqashqishah," i.e., the one that absolves [from hypocrisy]; and perhaps he meant "from hypocrisy." Al-Munaqqirah (The Probing): Abu al-Shaykh reported from ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr who said: "Bara'ah was called al-Munaqqirah; it probed what was in the hearts of the polytheists." Al-Bahuth, with a fatha on the ba', is an intensive form from al-bahth (investigation), in the sense of the active participle, as al-Hakim related that from al-Miqdad. Al-Mubaʿthirah: Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Muhammad ibn Ishaq who said: "Bara'ah was called, in the time of the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, and after him, al-Mubaʿthirah, because it uncovered the secrets of the people." It was thought that it was a corruption of al-Munaqqirah, after a suspicion.

Ibn al-Faras mentioned that it is also called al-Hafirah, because it dug out the hearts of the hypocrites; this is related from al-Hasan. Al-Muthirah, as related from Qatadah, because it stirred up disgraceful and ugly things. Al-Mudamdimah, as related from Sufyan ibn ʿUyaynah. Al-Mukhziyah, al-Munakkilah and al-Mushharridah, as al-Sakhawi and others mentioned. And Surat Bara'ah. Sa'id ibn Mansur, al-Bayhaqi in al-Shuʿab and others reported from Abu ʿAtiyyah al-Hamdani who said: ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, wrote: "Teach Surat Bara'ah and teach your women Surat al-Nur." It has one hundred and twenty-nine verses according to the Kufans, and one hundred and thirty according to the rest.

The way its connection to al-Anfal lies is that in the first [surah] is the division of the spoils, and its fifth was placed for five categories, as you know; and in this [surah] is the value of the alms (al-sadaqat), which were assigned to eight categories, as you will know, God willing. Also in the first he mentioned covenants, and here he rejected them. And He, exalted is He, commanded in the first preparation, saying, glorified is He: ﴿And prepare against them whatever you can of power﴾; and here He reproached the hypocrites for not preparing, with His words, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And if they had intended the departure, they would have prepared for it provision﴾. And He, glorified is He, concluded the first with the obligation that the believers should be allies of one another and that they should be wholly cut off from the disbelievers; and He, exalted is His majesty, expressed this meaning in this [surah] with His words, blessed and exalted is He: ﴿A declaration of immunity from Allah and His Messenger﴾ etc., and other aspects of connection.

It is related from Qatadah and others that it and al-Anfal are one surah, and for this reason the basmalah was not written between them. It has also been said that the reason for not writing it is that the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, differed over whether it is a surah or part of a surah; so they separated it from al-Anfal out of consideration for those who say they are two surahs, and did not write the basmalah out of consideration for those who say they are one surah. The truth is that they are two surahs, but the basmalah was not written between them due to what Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, from ʿAli, may Allah honor his face: that the basmalah is a security, and Bara'ah was revealed with the sword. Similar is reported from Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah and Sufyan ibn ʿUyaynah. This goes back to the fact that it was not revealed in this surah like its sisters, for the reason mentioned; and the adoption of its independence is supported by the names given to it, mentioned above.

Shaykh al-Akbar, may his secret be sanctified, in his Futuhat chose that they are one surah, and that the omission is for this reason. He said in the three-hundred-and-first chapter, after a discourse: "As for Surat al-Tawbah, people differed about it: is it an independent surah like the rest of the surahs, or is it and Surat al-Anfal one surah? For the completeness of a surah is not known except by separation by the basmalah, and it did not come here. This indicates that it is from Surat al-Anfal, and this is the more likely, although there is a reason for its omission, namely the lack of connection between mercy and disavowal; but that reason does not have that force; rather it is a weak reason."

The cause of its weakness is that in the Name Allah there is what the basmalah requires, whereas disavowal is only from a partner, not from a polytheist; for how could the Creator disavow the created, and if one disavowed him who was preserving his existence, while the partner is non-existent, disavowal from him would be valid, so it is an attribute of transcendence (tanzih); and the transcendence of Allah from a partner and of the Messenger, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, is from the belief of ignorance. And another aspect of the weakness of this interpretation that we mentioned is that the basmalah is present at the beginning of Surat ﴿Woe to every slanderer﴾ and Surat ﴿Woe to the defrauders﴾; where is mercy in woe?" End of quote.

It may be said: that disavowal from a partner is not apparent from its verse at all, and you will know, God willing, what is meant by it. What he, may his secret be sanctified, mentioned as the other weakness may be answered by saying: no surah resembles this surah, for it does not leave anyone, as Hudhayfah said, without touching him, overpowering him and going to extremes regarding his case. As for the hypocrites and disbelievers, this is clear; and as for the believers, it is in His words, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, do not take your fathers﴾ up to ﴿the defiantly disobedient﴾, and this is among the most severe things by which an opponent is addressed, so how about one who agrees? Neither Surat Woe nor Surat "Perish" (Tabbat) nor [others] contains this. Even if it is granted that a surah includes some type of what this one includes, the distinction by quantity and quality is something whose denial has no path; and for this reason the basmalah was omitted in it, according to what I say. The Mighty Name, though it includes the subjugation that suits what the surah contains, also includes other things besides that, together with its being explicitly joined to what included only mercy; and the aim here is only to manifest the attribute of subjugation, and this cannot be achieved with the opening by the basmalah, even if the exclusive dedication of the Mighty Name to it is granted. Yes, He, glorified is He, did not entirely abandon His custom of opening surahs here, since He opened this surah with the letter ba' as He opened others with it within the basmalah, although the ba' of the basmalah is a word and the ba' of this surah is part of a word; and that is for a subtle secret known to its people. This is what [I say].

It is related from al-Sakhawi that he said in Jamal al-Qurra': The omission of the basmalah at the beginning of Bara'ah is well known, but it is reported from ʿAsim that the basmalah is at its beginning, and this is the analogical position. The omission is either because it was revealed with the sword, or because they did not definitively decide it was an independent surah but rather part of al-Anfal. The first does not hold, because it is specific to the one concerning whom it was revealed; and we only say the basmalah for blessing. Do you not see that it is permitted by consensus to say "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Ever-Merciful" before ﴿Fight the polytheists﴾ and similar? And even if the omission is because it is not independent, then the basmalah at the beginning of parts is permitted. It is also reported that it is established in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him.

Ibn Minadir went to reciting it, and in al-Iqna' its permissibility is stated. The correct position is that omitting it is recommended, since it was not written in the Imam (the standard codex), and one should not follow other than it. As for the claim that it is forbidden and obligatory to omit it, as some Shafiʿi shaykhs said, the apparent position is contrary to that; and I see no harm in reciting it for one who begins reciting from the middle of the surah. And Allah knows best.

﴿A declaration of immunity from Allah and His Messenger﴾: that is, this is a declaration of immunity; the tanwin is for magnification. The "min" (from) is ibtida'iyyah (indicating origin), as is indicated by its contrast with "ila" (to). It is connected to an omitted element that falls as an attribute of the predicate, because connecting it directly to the predicate is unsound; that is, "arriving from Allah." They estimated it thus, rather than its result, to minimize the estimation, since "ila" which comes later also connects to it. It is also permitted that it be a subject, since it is specified by its description, and its predicate is His words, exalted is He: ﴿to those with whom you made covenant among the polytheists﴾.

ʿIsa ibn ʿAmr read "bara'atan" with the accusative, and it is then governed by "isma'u" (listen) or "ilzamu" (adhere), as an exhortation. The people of Najran read "min Allah" with a kasra on the nun, on the basis that the original for the vowelling of a sakin is kasra; but the preferred reading is fatha together with the definite article, to avoid the succession of two kasras. The thing to which the disavowal is connected is not mentioned, as it is in His words: ﴿that Allah is disassociated from the polytheists﴾, being content with what is in the relative clause, since it clearly indicates it, and to avoid repeating the word "min." The covenant (al-ʿahd) is a binding contract confirmed by oath. The address in "ʿahadtum" (you made covenant) is to the Muslims; and they had made covenant with the polytheists of the Arabs, from the people of Makkah and others, with Allah's permission and the agreement of the Messenger, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him; then they broke it, except the Banu Damrah and the Banu Kinanah. The Muslims were commanded to renounce the covenant with those who broke it, and were given a respite of four months to travel wherever they wished.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 1 (part 2 of 2):

The disavowal (al-bara'ah) is attributed to Allah the Exalted and His Messenger (ﷺ), even though it also includes the Muslims in sharing its ruling and in the obligation to act upon its requirements. The treaty (al-mu'ahadah) is attached to the Muslims specifically, even though it is by the permission of Allah the Exalted and the agreement of the Messenger, peace be upon him. This is to indicate that its execution and binding force are immediate, without depending on the opinion of those addressed. This is because it is an expression of ending the ruling of safe-conduct (al-aman) and lifting the danger that resulted from the earlier covenant of non-aggression toward the disbelievers. That lies with the side of Allah the Exalted, without depending on anything at all. The participation of the Muslims is only by way of compliance (al-imtithal) and nothing more. As for the treaty, since it is a contract like other legal contracts, it is not realized, and its rulings do not take effect, except through the direct action of the two contracting parties, in a manner that cannot be conceived of as proceeding from Him, may He be exalted. What proceeds from Him, glorified is He, is only the permission for that, and the one who actually carries it out is the Muslims. It is not hidden that the disavowal is only connected to the covenant and not to the permission regarding it. So each of the two was attributed to the one who is its origin. Moreover, in this there is an exaltation of the status of the disavowal, an emphasis on its gravity, a recording against the disbelievers of utmost humiliation and disgrace and ultimate shame and abandonment, and a declaring of the sanctity of the Majesty free from anything that might suggest a flaw or a change of mind, exalted is Allah far above that, greatly exalted. The inclusion of him (ﷺ) in the first attribution and his exclusion from the second is to honour his lofty status, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, in both situations. So did some of the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun) write it down, and it is a sound explanation. But some claimed that since the treaty was not obligatory but permissible and permitted, it was attributed to him, unlike the disavowal, which is obligatory by the command of Allah the Exalted, and therefore it was attributed to the Lawgiver. But this, as you see, is not right.

Ibn al-Munayyir mentioned, regarding the secret of this, that attributing the covenant to Allah the Exalted and His Messenger (ﷺ) in a context where the rejection (al-nabdh) by the polytheists is attributed does not show good manners.

Page 43

Do you not see the instruction of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to the commanders of the expeditions, where he says to them: «When you come down upon a fortress and they ask to come down under the judgment of Allah, the Exalted, then do not bring them down under your judgment, for you do not know whether you have hit upon the judgment of Allah concerning them or not. And if they ask for the protection (dhimmah) of Allah, the Exalted, then bring them down under your protection, for your protection being violated is better than the protection of Allah, the Exalted, being violated». Look at his command, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, to honour the protection of Allah, the Exalted, out of fear that it might be violated, even though that anticipated matter had not yet occurred. So honouring the covenant of Allah, the Exalted, when the polytheists have already been proven to break it, and when Allah the Exalted and His Messenger, peace be upon him, have disavowed it, is more appropriate and more fitting, by not attributing the rejected covenant to Him, glorified is He. Therefore the covenant was attributed to the Muslims and not the disavowal from it. This is not devoid of good sense, except that it is not fully adequate to what has already been mentioned. It has also been said: the mention of Allah the Exalted is for preparation (al-tamhid), as in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Do not put yourselves forward before Allah and His Messenger﴾ (49:1), in exaltation of his status, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him. Had the purpose not been preparation, the preposition (min) would have been repeated, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿How can there be a covenant for the polytheists with Allah and with His Messenger?﴾ (9:7). The disavowal was attributed to the Messenger, peace be upon him, and the treaty to them, because they share in the second but not in the first. This was criticised, on the grounds that it is not hidden what is in it, for whoever the Messenger, peace be upon him, disavows, the believers also disavow. What was mentioned about repeating the preposition is not necessary. And what he mentioned about preparation does not suit the context, since the effect of intimidation is weakened in that case. It has also been said: you may say that he attributed the covenant to the Muslims because Allah the Exalted knew that they had no covenant, and informed His Messenger, peace be upon him, of it. Therefore He did not attribute the covenant to Himself, due to His disavowal of them and of their covenant from eternity. This is the subtle point of the expression in the form of a nominal, declarative sentence (jumlah ismiyyah khabariyyah). And it has been said that it is performative (inshaiyyah), expressing the disavowal of them, and for this reason it indicates renewal and continuity.

But there is an objection: the notion of eternity does not apply in the case of the Messenger, peace be upon him, literally, and with interpretation it is not far-fetched to consider the Muslims as well. The subtle point of the nominal sentence, which is indicating permanence and continuity, does not depend on that hadith. Indeed, whoever did not mention it, mentioned it along with the added subtle point of seeking a means to intimidation through the magnifying indefiniteness (al-tankir al-tafkhimi).

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 2:**

﴿So travel freely in the land﴾, meaning: travel in it wherever you wish. The root of *siyaha* (wandering, touring) is the flowing and spreading of water, and then it was used for travel according to what one wills. From this is the poet's saying:

*Had I feared this from you, you would not have reached me until you saw horses before me wandering freely.*

In this phrasing there is an indication of complete ease and freedom that is absent from "travel" (*siru*) and similar words. The addition of ﴿in the land﴾ is an addition for generality. The speech may be read with an implied verb, meaning: "So say to them, travel freely," or without it, and this is the *iltifat* (shift) from the third person to the second person. The purpose is permission and notification that safety from killing and fighting is granted for the stipulated period. This is so that they may reflect, take precautions, prepare as they wish, and know that they have nothing left after this except Islam or the sword. Perhaps this will lead them to Islam. Also, if the Muslims fought them immediately after the declaration of breach, they might be accused of treachery, so they were given respite to close the door of suspicion, to show the strength of their power, their indifference to the disbelievers, and their readiness. For emphasis on this, the imperative form was chosen instead of "you are free to travel." The *fa'* (so) indicates the ordering of the command to travel and what follows from it, on the basis of the mentioned disavowal of war, which implies that the first is consequent upon itself for the second, with both its connections, under the description that it is from God the Mighty, may His majesty be exalted. It is as if it were said: "This is a disavowal requiring your fighting, so strive to secure what will save you and prepare what will benefit you."

﴿four months﴾: these are Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah and Muharram, according to al-Zuhri, because the verse was revealed in the first month. It was also said that although it was revealed then, its recitation to the disbelievers and its delivery to them took place on the Day of the Greater Pilgrimage. So the beginning of the period is the tenth of Dhu al-Hijjah, to the end of the ten days of Rabi' al-Akhir. This was narrated from Abu 'Abd Allah (may Allah be pleased with him), Mujahid, and Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi.

It was also said: the beginning of that period is the day of sacrifice, the tenth of Dhu al-Qa'dah, until the end of ten days of Rabi' al-Awwal. This is because the pilgrimage in that year took place at that time due to the *nasi'* (intercalation) practised among them. Then in the second year it fell in Dhu al-Hijjah, and this was the Farewell Pilgrimage, in which the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, time has returned to its form on the day Allah created the heavens and the earth." To this view al-Jubba'i went. Some virtuous scholars preferred the second view and claimed that most scholars held it. It was related from several overlapping reports, some of which are in the two Sahihs: that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made a covenant with the Quraysh in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah that they would lay down war for ten years, during which people would be safe. The Khuza'ah entered into the covenant of the Prophet (ﷺ), and the Bani Bakr entered into the covenant of the Quraysh. Then the Bani Bakr attacked the Khuza'ah, harmed them, and the Quraysh aided them with weapons. When the Bani Bakr and the Quraysh united against the Khuza'ah and broke their covenant, 'Amr al-Khuza'i went out until he stood before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and recited:

*O Allah, I appeal to Muhammad, the covenant of our ancient father and his father.*

*You were a child and we were a parent; then we embraced Islam and did not withdraw our hand.*

*So help the Messenger of Allah with a mighty help, and call the servants of Allah, that they may come with reinforcement.*

*In it is the Messenger of Allah, who has stripped himself bare; if his face is humiliated, it turns dark.*

*In a host like a sea that comes foaming. Indeed the Quraysh have broken their promise to you.*

*And they broke your firm covenant, and they set up watchers for me at Kada'.*

*And they claimed that I would not call upon anyone, while they are the most humiliated and fewest in number.*

*They attacked us by night at al-Hatim, and killed us while we were bowing and prostrating.*

Then the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "I shall not be helped if I do not help you." Then he prepared to go to Makkah and conquered it in the eighth year of the Hijrah. When the ninth year came, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wished to perform the pilgrimage, but he said: "The polytheists will attend, and they will circumambulate naked." So in that year he (peace be upon him) sent Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) as commander over the people to conduct the pilgrimage for them, and he wrote down its *sunan* (practices) for him. Then he sent 'Ali (may Allah ennoble his face) after him on his she-camel al-'Adba' to recite the beginning of *Bara'ah* to the people of the gathering. When 'Ali (may Allah ennoble his face) approached, Abu Bakr heard the sound of the camel and stopped and said: "This is the sound of the she-camel of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." When he reached him he said: "Are you a commander or one commanded?" He said: "One commanded." When it was before the *tarwiyah* (eighth of Dhu al-Hijjah), Abu Bakr delivered a sermon and taught them about their rites. 'Ali (may Allah ennoble his face) stood on the day of sacrifice at the Jamrat al-'Aqabah and said: "O people, I am the messenger of Allah to you." They said: "With what?" So he recited to them thirty or forty verses of the surah. Then he said: "I have been commanded with four things: that no polytheist should approach the House after this year, that no naked person should circumambulate the House, that none shall enter Paradise except every believing soul, and that he should fulfil to every person of covenant his covenant."

The reports differ as to whether Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) was commanded to recite or not. Most hold that he was commanded, and that when 'Ali (may Allah ennoble his face) caught up with him, he (Ali) took from him what he had been commanded to recite. In a report of Ibn Hibban and Ibn Mardawayh from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, it came that Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), when that was taken from him, went to the Prophet (ﷺ), and fear had entered him that something had been revealed concerning him. When he came to him he said: "What is wrong with me, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "You are good, my brother and my companion in the cave, and you will be with me at the Pool, except that no one delivers on my behalf except me or a man from me."

It also came from the narration of Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it good), Abu al-Shaykh and others, from Anas, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) sent *Bara'ah* with Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him). Then he called him and said: 'It is not fitting for anyone to deliver this except a man from my family.' So he called 'Ali (may Allah ennoble his face) and gave it to him."

This is apparent that 'Ali did not take it from Abu Bakr on the road, and most reports are contrary to this. In some of them there is what is apparent that Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) was not removed from the command, but rather 'Ali (may Allah ennoble his face) was joined to him. Al-Tirmidhi (who graded it good), al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il*, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim (who authenticated it) reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent Abu Bakr and commanded him to proclaim these words, then followed him with 'Ali and commanded him to proclaim these words. They performed the pilgrimage, and 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) stood during the days of *tashriq* and proclaimed that Allah is free of the polytheists and His Messenger: "Travel freely in the land for four months; no polytheist shall make the pilgrimage after this year; no naked person shall circumambulate the House; and none shall enter Paradise except a believer." 'Ali (may Allah ennoble his face) kept proclaiming, and when he grew tired, Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) stood and proclaimed them.

In any case, there is nothing in any of the reports indicating that 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) was the caliph after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in preference to Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him). His (ﷺ) saying: "No one delivers on my behalf except me or a man from me," whether by revelation or not, follows the custom of the Arabs that only a man of the close kin would confirm or annul a covenant, so that the proof is entirely cut off. Thus the negated "delivery" is not general, as the hadith of Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi indicates.

How could generality be intended when many legal rulings were conveyed on his behalf (ﷺ) during his life and after his death by many who were not of his close kin, such as 'Ali (may Allah ennoble his face), and among them Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him)? For in that year he performed the pilgrimage with the people and taught them, on the authority of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), the practices of the pilgrimage and what it requires, and it is one of the five pillars upon which Islam is built. Moreover, whoever is fair to himself knows that in appointing Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) to establish such a great pillar of the religion, there is an indication, as His saying, glory be to Him, ﴿And due to Allah from the people is pilgrimage to the House﴾ suggests, that he was the caliph after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in establishing the rites of his religion. Especially since this was confirmed by his standing in his place (ﷺ) to lead the people in prayer at the end of his affair (ﷺ), and prayer is the greatest pillar and the most upright support of his religion (ﷺ). As for the claim that he (may Allah be pleased with him) was dismissed in both matters, as some Shi'ah assert, it has no basis, and the one who claims must provide proof, and beyond it are the mighty mountains.

In sum, the implication of "it is not fitting" and so on for the caliphate is something one should not claim. The most that the report indicates is the excellence of the Commander (may Allah ennoble his face) and his nearness to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the believer does not deny this, but it is far from requiring his precedence in the caliphate over the Truthful One (may Allah be pleased with him). Some Sunni scholars have mentioned a subtle point regarding the appointment of Abu Bakr as commander of the people in their pilgrimage, and the appointment of the Commander (may Allah ennoble his face) to deliver the breaking of the covenant at that gathering. It is that the Truthful One (may Allah be pleased with him), since he manifested the attribute of mercy and beauty, as what preceded in the hadith of the Night Journey indicates, and as the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) indicates: "The most merciful of my community towards my community is Abu Bakr." He (ﷺ) entrusted to him the affair of the Muslims, who are the locus of mercy. And since 'Ali (may Allah ennoble his face), who is the Lion of Allah, is the manifestation of His majesty, he was entrusted with the breaking of the covenant of the disbelievers, which is among the effects of majesty and the attributes of subjugation. Thus they were like two gushing springs: from one of them flows the attribute of beauty, and from the other the attribute of majesty, at that great assembly which was a model of the Gathering and a place of arrival for the Muslim and the disbeliever. End of quotation. Its goodness is not hidden, were it not for the Prophet's (ﷺ) reasoning being present in the matter.

And the period was made four months. It was said that this is because it is a third of the year, and a third is considerable. The number is put in the adverbial position relative to *siyahu* (travel freely), meaning: so travel freely in the regions of the land within four months. ﴿And know that you﴾, in your touring that, ﴿are not able to escape Allah﴾, you cannot elude Him, glory be to Him, by flight or fortification. ﴿And that Allah will disgrace the disbelievers﴾ in this world by killing and capture, and in the Hereafter by a humiliating punishment. The noble name is made explicit to cultivate awe and to magnify the matter of disgrace, which is humiliation with what entails shame and disgrace. The intended meaning of "the disbelievers" is either the polytheists addressed in what preceded, and the shift from "will disgrace you" to this is to censure them for disbelief after describing them as polytheists, and to indicate that the cause of the disgrace is their disbelief. Or it is the genus that includes them and others, and the addressees enter it as a primary inclusion.

﴿And a proclamation from Allah and His Messenger﴾: that is, an announcement (إعْلام). It is on the pattern of فَعال with the meaning of الإفْعال, i.e., إيذان, like أمان and عَطاء. Al-Tabarsi (al-Tabarsi) reported that its origin is from the call (النداء) that is heard by the ear, in the sense of أذنته: I made it reach his ear. Its nominative case is like that of بَراءَة, and the sentence is conjoined (عطف) to a similar sentence.

Al-Zajjaj (al-Zajjaj) claimed that it is conjoined to بَراءَةٌ. This was criticised on the grounds that there is no basis for it, since one does not say: "That ʿAmr is conjoined to Zayd in your saying: Zayd is standing and ʿAmr is sitting." Al-Allama al-Tibi (al-Tibi) mentioned that someone may say: why is it not permissible to conjoin it to "بَراءَةٌ" on the basis that it is the conjoining of an predicate to a predicate, as if it were said: "This sura is a disavowal (بَراءَةٌ) from Allah and His Messenger to those with whom you made covenants specifically, and a proclamation from Allah and His Messenger (﴿to the people﴾) generally." Yes, the more correct view is that it is the conjoining of sentences, so that no unrelated sentences intervene between the two predicates, and so that the agreement between the subject and predicate in gender (masculine and feminine) is not lost. Some also examined this: they permitted "في الدار زيدٌ والحجرةِ عمروٌ" and counted that among the conjoining to the objects (معمولَيْ) of two governing words, and they stated explicitly that a form like "زيدٌ قائمٌ وعمرٌو" admits both possibilities. It was answered that what is meant is conjoining the proclamation alone to the disavowal, without addressing the conjoining of predicate to predicate, as in "أُريدُ أنْ يَضْرِبَ زيدٌ عمرًا ويُهينَ بَكرٌ خالدًا", where the conjoining is only between the two verbs and not their objects. This is what prevented those who prevented it.

As for the intended meaning of ﴿the people﴾ as general, this is what most scholars held, because this proclamation is not like the disavowal that is specific to the covenant-breakers; rather it includes the disbelievers and all the believers as well. Some said that what is meant by them are the people of the covenant. His words, glorified is He: ﴿on the day of the greatest Hajj﴾ are in the accusative by what is governed by ﴿to the people﴾, not by "أذان", because a verbal noun that has been qualified does not govern, according to the well-known view. What is meant by it is the day of ʿId (the festival of sacrifice), because the completion of Hajj and most of its rites are on it, and because the announcement was made on it.

Al-Bukhari (al-Bukhari) reported it as a suspended narration (تعليقًا, i.e., a report without its full chain), and Abu Dawud, Ibn Majah, and a group related from Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood on the day of sacrifice between the jamarat in the Hajj he performed, and said: 'What day is this?' They said: 'The day of sacrifice.' He said: 'This is the day of the greatest Hajj.'" This was also related from ʿAli, may Allah honour his face, Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Jubayr, Ibn Zayd, Mujahid, and others. It was also said that it is the day of ʿArafah, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Hajj is ʿArafah." This is also attributed to Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him. Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Miswar, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Ibn Jarir related from Abu al-Sahba', that he asked ʿAli, may Allah honour his face, about this day, and he said: "It is the day of ʿArafah." From Mujahid and Sufyan, it is that it means all the days of Hajj, as one says: "the Day of the Camel" and "the Day of Siffin," where "day" means a period and time. The first view is stronger in transmission and in understanding.

It is described as "the greatest" Hajj because ʿUmrah is called "the lesser Hajj." Or because what is meant by Hajj is what occurred on that day of its acts, for it is greater than the rest of the acts; so the superlative is relative and not restricted to the Hajj of that year. From al-Hasan it is that it was described thus because the Muslims and the polytheists gathered on it, and its festival coincided with the festivals of the People of the Book. It was also said: because the might of the Muslims and the humiliation of the polytheists became manifest on it. Then the superlative is restricted to that year. As for calling the Hajj that coincides with the day of ʿArafah on a Friday "the greatest," they did not mention it, even though the reward of that Hajj is greater than others, as al-Jalal al-Suyuti (al-Suyuti) reported in some of his treatises.

﴿that Allah is free of the polytheists﴾: that is, from their covenants. Al-Hasan and al-A'raj read ﴿inna﴾ with a kasrah, because the proclamation contains the meaning of speech. It was also said that a verb of saying is to be understood. On the reading with a fatḥah, it is by the supposition of a preposition, and this is regular with inna and anna. The prepositional phrase may be a predicate of "أذان", or may be related to it, or may be related to a deleted element which functions as a qualifier of it.

His words, glorified is He: ﴿and His Messenger﴾ are conjoined to the pronoun concealed in "بريء" (free). It is also permissible that it be a subject whose predicate is deleted, or that it be a conjunction to the place of the noun of inna on the reading with a kasrah. Since the kasrah does not change the meaning, it may be treated as if absent, so that what it governs is conjoined to its place. That is, to the place that it had before the particle entered, for it was then a subject (مبتدأ). The place of anna with its noun occurs in their speech, and the matter in it is easy. The scholars did not permit this according to the well-known view with the fatḥah, because the fatḥah has a position other than the subject. Ibn al-Hajib (Ibn al-Hajib) permitted here the conjunction to the place even in the reading of the majority, on the basis that the fatḥah is of two types: one that admits conjunction to the place and one that does not. If it has the meaning of the kasrah of inna, as the one after verbs of the heart, such as "علمتُ أنَّ زيدًا قائمٌ وعمرٌو", conjunction is permitted, because it is specific to entering upon sentences, and the meaning with it is "that Zayd is standing and ʿAmr in my knowledge." That is why the kasrah is obligatory in "علمتُ إنَّ زيدًا لقائمٌ." If it is not like this, it is not permitted, as in "أعجبني أنَّ زيدًا كريمٌ وعمرٌو," where the accusative is required, because then it is neither kasrah nor in its rule. The basis of permissibility on this is that the proclamation has the meaning of knowledge, so it enters upon sentences as well, like ʿalima.

Ya'qub, by the transmission of Rawh, and Zayd read ﴿wa rasūlahu﴾ with the accusative. This is the reading of al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and ʿIsa ibn ʿAmr. On it, the conjunction is to the noun of inna, which is the apparent reading. It is also permissible that the waw means "with," and the accusative of "rasūlahu" is an object of accompaniment, i.e., "free together with him from them."

It is related from al-Hasan that he read it with the genitive, taking the waw as an oath particle. It is like an oath by the life of the Prophet (ﷺ) in His words, glorified is He: ﴿By your life (laʿamruka)﴾. It was also said that the genitive may be by proximity (الجِوار), but this is nothing. This reading "la-ʿamrī" is highly misleading, and it is extremely anomalous. Clearly, it is not authentic.

It is reported that a Bedouin heard a man reciting it, and said: "If Allah is free of His Messenger, then I am free of him." The man seized him by the collar and brought him to ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, and the Bedouin related his recitation. Thereupon ʿUmar ordered the teaching of Arabic grammar. It is also reported that Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali heard this and referred the matter to ʿAli, may Allah honour his face, and that this was the cause of the codification of grammar. And Allah knows best.

Al-Zamakhshari (al-Zamakhshari) distinguished between the meaning of the first sentence and this sentence: the former is an informing of the establishment of the disavowal, while this one is an informing of the obligation of announcing what has been established. In al-Kashshaf it is stated that this is clear on the assumption that both are read as predicates, but in his saying "an informing of the obligation of announcing" there is a figurative usage. He wished to show that the intent is not merely an informing about announcing; rather, He, glorified is He, informed that He is free [of them] so that they would inform the people of it. On the second assumption, its explanation is that the meaning of the first sentence is that the disavowal, which is from Allah, is established and reaches those of the polytheists with whom covenant was made. So it is an informing of the establishment of the disavowal, as you say of "Zayd exists": it is an informing of the existence of Zayd. In the second, it is the informing of the addressees that the disavowal which comes from Allah is established and reaches the people. So it is an explicit informing of the establishment of the specific announcement, and implicitly of the obligation that the addressees inform the people. Since the intended meaning is the implied meaning, it was stated that it is an informing of the obligation to announce. Some held, to avoid repetition, that the first disavowal is for the breaking of the covenant, and the second disavowal is for severing friendship and kindness. But this is not the case.

﴿So if you repent﴾ from disbelief and treachery by breaking the covenant, ﴿it is better for you﴾, that is, the repentance is better for you in both abodes. The shift from the third person to the second person is for added intimidation and emphasis. The first "fa" (then) indicates the ordering of the conditional clause's antecedent over the proclamation, which is concluded with a severe threat that indicates the softening of their stubbornness and the breaking of the intensity of their obstinacy. ﴿But if you turn away﴾ from repentance, or persist in turning away from Islam and fidelity, ﴿then know that you cannot escape Allah﴾: you cannot outrun Him, glorified is He, nor can you get beyond Him. ﴿And give good tidings to those who disbelieve of a painful punishment﴾: that is, in the Hereafter, according to the apparent meaning.

From here some restricted "you cannot escape Allah" with the phrase "in this world." The expression of good tidings is sarcasm. Turning the address away from them to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is said to be because good tidings befit only one who stands upon the divine secrets. It may be said: it is not far that the address is to everyone who has a share in it. In this there is an exaggeration that is not hidden.

[Page 49 of the original is marked in the text as "صفحة 49"]

﴿إلا الَّذِينَ عاهَدْتُمْ مِنَ المُشْرِكِينَ﴾ ("except those of the polytheists with whom you made a covenant") is an exception (istithna'), according to what al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari's commentary) has in mind regarding the implied element in His saying: ﴿فَسِيحُوا في الأرْضِ﴾ ("So travel freely in the land") etc., because the discourse is addressed to the Muslims, on the basis that the meaning is: a declaration of freedom from Allah and His Messenger to those of the polytheists with whom you made a covenant. So say to them: "Travel freely," except those of them with whom you made a covenant and who have not diminished anything for you; then fulfil their covenant to them. It has the sense of a correction (istidrak), as if it were said: "So do not give the covenant-breakers more than four months, but those who did not break their covenant, fulfil their covenant to them and do not treat them as the covenant-breakers."

It has been objected: how can the exception be valid when a foreign sentence has intervened between the exception and what it excepts from, namely His saying, glorified is He: ﴿وأذانٌ مِنَ اللَّهِ﴾ ("and a proclamation from Allah"), for it, as established, is coordinated with ﴿بَراءَةٌ﴾ ("a declaration of freedom")? It is answered that this sentence is not foreign in every respect, because it has the sense of a command to inform, as if it were said: "So say to them: Travel freely, and know that Allah, exalted is He, is free of them, but those with whom you made a covenant etc." Some of them made it a correction of the earlier rejection (nabdh), in which fighting was deferred for four months, and the outcome is one. It was also said that it is an exception from the first "polytheists," and al-Farra' went to this view. It was rejected on the grounds that retaining the generality in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿أنَّ اللَّهَ بَرِيءٌ مِنَ المُشْرِكِينَ﴾ ("that Allah is free of the polytheists") contradicts it. It was also said that it is an exception from the second "polytheists," and this was rejected on the grounds that retaining the generality in the first contradicts it. The view that it refers back to both, with the excepted item and what is excepted from in the two sentences not being in one structure, is not good. Some made the second a known group, namely the polytheists from whom these are excepted. It was said: the occurrence of the exception makes its adoption in the inimitable composition unlikely. And His saying, glorified is He: ﴿فَأتِمُّوا إلَيْهِمْ﴾ ("then complete for them") then necessarily has to be made the apodosis of an elided conditional, which is also contrary to the apparent meaning; the apparent meaning is that it is a declarative statement, and the "fa'" is because the subject contains the sense of a condition. That the intended referents are specific people, so it is not a general formula and therefore resembles a condition, so the "fa'" enters its predicate, is not harmful on the assumption that this is granted. Al-Akhfash went to the view that "fa'" may be added to the predicate of a relative construction (mawsul) without the condition of generality.

Al-Qutb argued for what al-Kashshaf has said by saying: here there are two sentences to which the exception may be attached, the sentence of the declaration of freedom and the sentence of the respite. But attaching the exception to the sentence of the declaration of freedom would entail that there is no freedom from some of the polytheists, so it is determined that it attaches to the sentence of the respite of four months. In this there is a failure to notice that what is meant is freedom from the covenants of the polytheists, not freedom from themselves. There is no dispute that the covenant-keeping parties who did not break their covenant, Allah and His Messenger, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, are not free of their covenants, even if they are free of themselves in some way of interpretation, so understand.

Ibn al-Munayyir said: it is possible that His saying, glorified is He: ﴿فَسِيحُوا﴾ is an address to the polytheists without the word "say" being implied before it, and in this case the exception is from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿إلى الَّذِينَ عاهَدْتُمْ﴾ ("to those with whom you made a covenant"), as if it were said: a declaration of freedom from Allah, exalted is He, and His Messenger, to the covenanting parties except those who remain upon the covenant; so fulfil their covenant to them, O Muslims. In this there is a shift from address to the Muslims in ﴿إلا الَّذِينَ عاهَدْتُمْ﴾ to address to the polytheists in ﴿فَسِيحُوا﴾, then a shift from the first person to the third person in ﴿واعْلَمُوا أنَّكم غَيْرُ مُعْجِزِي اللَّهِ وأنَّ اللَّهِ﴾

[Page 49]

and the original would be "غَيْرُ مُعْجِزِيَّ وإنِّي" ("you cannot escape Me, and indeed I"). In this shift, after the first shift, there is an elaboration of the methods of eloquence, an exaltation of the matter and a magnification of the affair. Then this shift is followed by a return to address in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿إلا الَّذِينَ عاهَدْتُمْ﴾ etc. All this is among the beauties of eloquence, end of quotation. The problems in it from excessive strained interpretation are not hidden.

"Min" ("of") is said to be explanatory (bayaniyya), and it was said to be partitive (tab'idiyya). "Thumma" ("then") in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿ثُمَّ لَمْ يَنْقُصُوكم شَيْئًا﴾ ("then they have not fallen short of you in anything") is to indicate their steadfastness in their covenant despite the lengthening of the period. The verb "yanquṣūkum" with the letter ṣād unpointed (with the unmarked ṣ), as the majority read it, may be transitive to one object, so "shay'an" is in the accusative of the verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: they did not fall short of you in any shortfall, neither a little nor a lot. It may also be transitive to two objects, so "shay'an" is its second object, meaning: they did not fall short of you in any of the conditions of the covenant, and they fulfilled them for you in full. ʿIkrima and ʿAṭāʾ read "yanquḍūkum" with the dotted ḍād, and the sentence then has an elided genitive construction (muḍāf), meaning: they did not break your covenants in any breaking. This reading suits the covenant, but the majority's reading is more fitting because it corresponds to "full" (tamām), and it avoids the need to posit the elision.

﴿شَيْئًا ولَمْ يُظاهِرُوا﴾ ("in anything, nor have they supported") means: they did not assist ﴿عَلَيْكم أحَدًا﴾ ("anyone against you") of your enemies, as the Banu Bakr transgressed against Khuza'a, and Quraysh supported them with weapons, as has preceded. ﴿فَأتِمُّوا إلَيْهِمْ عَهْدَهُمْ﴾ ("then fulfil their covenant to them") means: discharge it to them in full. ﴿إلى مُدَّتِهِمْ﴾ ("until their term") means: until its expiry. "And do not treat them as the covenant-breakers." It was said: there remained for Banu Damra and Banu Mudlij, two tribes of Kinana, nine months of their covenant, so He completed their covenant to them. Ibn Abi Hatim related that he said: these are Quraysh, who made a covenant with the Prophet of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, at the time of al-Hudaybiyya, and there remained of their term four months after the day of sacrifice, so Allah, whose affair is exalted, commanded His Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, to fulfil that covenant to them until their term. This contradicts what the reports have unanimously transmitted, that Quraysh broke the covenant, as you have known, and the relied-upon view is the first.

﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ يُحِبُّ المُتَّقِينَ﴾ ("Indeed Allah loves the righteous") is a reason for the obligation of compliance, and an alert that observing the covenant is part of piety, and that equating the treacherous with the faithful is incompatible with that, even if the covenanting party is a polytheist.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 5 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Then when the sacred months have passed﴾: that is, have come to an end. Its root is from *salkh* (stripping off), in the sense of *kashṭ* (flaying): one says, "I stripped (*salakhtu*) the hide (*ihab*) from the sheep," meaning I peeled it off and removed it from her. It also comes in the sense of extraction, as one says, "I stripped the sheep from its hide" when you draw it out of it. Abu al-Haytham mentioned that one says, "We began (*ahlalna*) the month of such-and-such," meaning we entered into it. So we add a garment to ourselves every night until it reaches its midpoint, and then we strip it from ourselves a part at a time until it ends. He recited:

"When I strip the month, I begin its like; enough for a killer is my stripping of the months and my beginning (of them)."

The *insilakh* (stripping away) in what we are discussing is a fine metaphor. The explanation of this is that time encompasses what is in it of temporal things and contains them the way a hide contains an animal. Likewise, every part of its extended divisions, such as days, months and years, when it passes, it is as if it has been stripped away from what is in it. In this there is additional subtlety, because it contains an allusion that those months were a protection for those covenanted (*mu'ahidin*) against the perils of the hands of the Muslims, so their fighting was tied to their passing. From here it is known that taking it as a metaphor from the first meaning of *salkh* is preferable to taking it from the second meaning, on the basis that once it has ended, it is as if it has been drawn out from the existing things. This allusion does not appear on it as clearly as it appears on the first.

The definite article (*al*) in "the months" is for a previously mentioned referent (*'ahd*). Thus what is meant by them is the four months mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿So travel freely in the land for four months﴾. This is what is related from Mujahid and others. In *al-Durr al-Masun* it is stated that when the Arabs mention an indefinite noun and then want to mention it again, they use a pronoun or the word in its definite form with *al*, and they may not then describe it with an attribute that indicates difference.

صفحة 50

So if one says, "I saw a man, and I honored the tall man," you do not mean by the second the first. But if you describe it with something that does not require difference, it is permitted, as in your saying, "So I honored the aforementioned man." The verse is of this kind, since *al-Huram* (the sacred) is an attribute understood from the import of the speech, and so it does not require difference. The point of turning away from the pronoun and placing the apparent noun in its place seems to be bringing this attribute, to serve as emphasis for what the permission to travel indicates, namely the inviolability of harming them, together with the additional care given to the matter of the one described.

On this basis, what is meant by "the polytheists" in His saying ﴿then kill the polytheists﴾ are those who broke their covenants. The intended meaning is then to state their ruling after alerting to the completion of the term of those who did not break covenant. The ruling of the rest is not understood from the explicit wording of the text but from its implication. It is also permitted that what is meant by them is those same four months, along with what is understood from His saying ﴿then fulfill their covenant to them until their term﴾, as being the completion of a period that remains for those who did not break covenant. On this view, the ruling of the rest is understood from the expression, since "the polytheists" here includes them and the covenant-breakers, except that the stripping away and the fighting tied to it occur gradually, not all at once. So it is as if it were said: "When the appointed time of each group is complete, then kill them."

It was also said that what is meant by them are the well-known months that recur each year: Rajab, Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah and al-Muharram. This disrupts the noble arrangement of the text, because the sequence marked by *fa* (then) rejects it, and it contradicts the context, which requires that these months be consecutive. It was also said that it contradicts the *ijma'* (scholarly consensus), because the consensus holds that these months are lawful for fighting and that their sanctity was abrogated (*nusikhat*). On interpreting it as referring to them, it would require that their sanctity remains, since no abrogating text had yet been revealed. It was answered that it does not necessarily follow that the Book is abrogated by the Book; it may be abrogated by the Sunnah, as is established in the principles of jurisprudence (*usul*). Even if it were necessary, as is the view of some, it is possible that its abrogating text is from the Book but with abrogated recitation (*mansukh al-tilawa*). This was rejected: this is a possibility that yields nothing and is not accepted, because if it were so it would have been transmitted, and abrogation cannot be established by mere possibility.

It was also said that if the consensus holds that they are abrogated, that suffices without any need to transmit a chain of narration (*sanad*) to us. It is sound that the Prophet (ﷺ) besieged Ta'if ten nights before the end of al-Muharram. Just as this suffices for their abrogation, it suffices for abrogating what occurred in the sound hadith, which is: "Indeed time has returned to its form on the day that Allah created the heavens and the earth. The year is twelve months, of which four are sacred: Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, al-Muharram, and Rajab." So it should not be said that this poses a difficulty for us because we do not know what abrogates it, as it was imagined.

Some of our scholars held that the Book may be abrogated by consensus. In *al-Nihaya Sharh al-Hidaya*: "Addition to the Book is permitted by consensus; this was explicitly stated by Imam al-Sarakhsi." Fakhr al-Islam said: "Abrogation by consensus was permitted by some of our companions on the basis that consensus necessitates certain knowledge like the text itself, so abrogation may be established by it. Consensus is stronger as a proof than a well-known report (*khabar mashhur*), and abrogation by it is permissible; so by consensus it is more appropriate." As for the condition that the Prophet (ﷺ) be alive for abrogation to be permitted, it is not a condition according to the view of that group of companions. End of quote.

You know that the matter is disputed among us. Moreover, there is discussion regarding the consensus. It has been said that the prohibition of fighting Muslims in them remains, except if they fight; this is related from Ata', but it is a view that carries no weight. The claim that the prohibition of fighting in the sacred months applied in that year only, and that this does not imply its prohibition in everything similar to it, but rather is silent on it, so it does not contradict the consensus, and its permissibility is known from another proof, is not a valid argument. This is because the apparent position is that whoever claims consensus claims it regarding permissibility in that year as well. In sum, there is no reliance on this interpretation.

This, as al-Jalal al-Suyuti said, is the verse of the sword, which abrogated the verses of pardon, forgiveness, aversion and reconciliation.

Al-Allamah Ibn Hajar said: The verse of the sword is ﴿And fight the polytheists all together﴾. It was also said that these two are meant together. The majority used its generality as evidence for fighting the Turks and the Abyssinians, as if it were said: "Kill the disbelievers absolutely," ﴿wherever you find them﴾ within the lawful area or the sacred precinct (*haram*). ﴿And seize them﴾. It was said: that is, take them captive. The *akhidh* is the captive. The seizing was explained as binding, not for enslavement, since the polytheists of the Arabs did not enslave.

It was also said: what is meant is to give them respite so as to offer them the choice between being killed and accepting Islam. It was said: it is an expression for harming them by every possible means. It has become common in usage to apply the term "seizing" to taking control of the enemy's property, so one says, "The sons of so-and-so seized the sons of so-and-so," meaning they took control of their property after overpowering them. ﴿And besiege them﴾. It was said: that is, confine them.

Al-Khazin related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that what is meant is to prevent them from leaving if they take refuge from you in a fortress.

Others related from him that the meaning is: prevent them from reaching the Sacred Mosque. ﴿And lie in wait for them at every place of ambush﴾, that is, every passage and route through which they pass on their journeys. Its accusative case, according to al-Zajjaj and those who followed him, is adverbial of place (*zarfiyya*). Abu Ali rejected this, stating that *marsad* is a specific place where the enemy is watched, so it is a particular place, and omitting *fi* from it and putting it in the accusative as an adverb is permitted only by transmission. Abu Hayyan countered him: there is no obstacle to its being in the accusative as an adverb, because His saying ﴿and lie in wait for them﴾ does not literally mean sitting, but rather watching and observing them. So the meaning is "watch them at every place where they may be watched." A temporal or locative adverb may, in general, take the accusative with the preposition dropped, when the verb is of its root or its meaning, as in "I sat and I sat in the assembly of the commander." What is restricted to transmission is what is not like this. *Kull* (every), although not itself an adverb, has the rule of what it is attached to, because it expresses that.

Ibn al-Munir allowed that *marsad* could be a noun of place in the form *mafal*, so it would be an absolute object (*maf'ul mutlaq*), with its governing verb being the verb having its meaning, as if it were said: "And watch them every watching." Its remoteness is not hidden. It is also related from al-Akhfash that it is in the accusative by dropping the preposition, the original being "at every place of ambush," and when the preposition was removed it became accusative. You know that the accusative by removing the preposition is not analogical, especially when the preposition is *'ala* (on), since removing it is rare, to the point that it was said it is specific to poetry.

﴿But if they repent﴾ from polytheism by believing, because of what befalls them from you, ﴿and establish prayer and give zakat﴾, confirming their repentance and faith. He mentioned only these two because they are the chief of the bodily and financial acts of worship. ﴿Then let them go their way﴾: that is, leave them and their affairs, and do not interfere with them in anything of what has been mentioned.

It was also said: what is meant is "let them go between them and the House," and do not prevent them from it. The first is preferable. The release of the way has come in Arabic speech as an expression for leaving alone, as in the verse:

"Leave the way for whoever builds the minaret upon it, and go forth at Barza wherever necessity compels you."

Then what is meant by it in every context is what suits that context.

It is related from al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, that he used this verse as evidence for killing one who abandons prayer and fighting one who withholds zakat, because Allah permitted the blood of the disbelievers in all ways and circumstances, then made it inviolable upon repentance from disbelief, establishing prayer, and giving zakat. So as long as this whole combination is not found, the permissibility of blood remains on its original basis.

Perhaps Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, used it as evidence for fighting those who withhold zakat. In the *Hawashi al-Shihabiyya*: al-Muzani, one of the eminent Shafi'i scholars, may Allah be pleased with them, raised a doubt against killing one who abandons prayer, which they were perplexed in answering, as al-Subki said in his *Tabaqat*. He said: it is inconceivable, for either it is for abandoning a prayer that has already passed, or for one that has not yet come. The first is invalid because a prayer that is to be made up (*maqdiyya*) is not killed for abandoning it; and the second is likewise, because as long as the time has not run out, he has the option of delay, so on what basis is he killed? They took various approaches to the answer.

The first: this doubt also applies to the view of those who hold for discretionary punishment (*ta'zir*), beating and imprisonment, as is the position of the Hanafis. So the answer—the answer—is a dialectical one, O Messenger of Allah.

The second: that it concerns a prayer already passed, because he abandoned it without excuse. It was rejected: making up a prayer is not obligatory immediately, and al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, explicitly stated that one is not killed for a prayer that is to be made up at all.

The third: that he is killed for a prayer that is performed at the end of its time. This entails that hastening to kill one who abandons prayer would be more appropriate than hastening to kill an apostate, since the apostate is asked to repent while this one is not asked to repent and is not given respite, for if he were given respite the prayer would become one to be made up, and this is a matter of debate. So there is no need for an answer from the side of Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, as it was said: the Shafi'i argument is based on the view of the implication of a condition (*mafhum al-shart*), which is not relied upon. Even if one granted it, "release" means absolute freedom from all that has been mentioned. In that case it may be said: one who abandons prayer is not released, and to prevent his release it is sufficient that he be imprisoned. Moreover, this is refuted by one who withholds zakat according to al-Shafi'i himself.

Also, it is possible that "establishing them" means committing to them. If he does not commit to them, he is a disbeliever. However, this is contrary to what is immediately understood, even though some exegetes said it.

[p. 52]

And you know that the position of the Shafi'is is that whoever abandons a single prayer out of laziness, on condition that he delays it beyond its time of necessity (by not praying, for example, the noon prayer until the sun sets), is to be killed as a penalty (hadd, a fixed punishment prescribed by divine law). Some of their eminent later scholars cited this verse and the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "I have been commanded to fight the people..." (the hadith in full). They reconciled the two by saying that the testimony of faith, the establishment of prayer, and the giving of zakat are the conditions for refraining from killing and fighting. However, the zakat can be taken by the imam even by force from those who refuse to pay it and fight against us, so it is meant literally in that case. This differs from prayer, since it cannot be performed by force, so the word is taken there in the sense of killing. Then he said: "It is therefore clear that there is a distinction between prayer and zakat. The same applies to fasting, for when it is known that the person will be detained the whole day, he intends it, so detention is effective in that case. This is not so with prayer, so killing is specified as its penalty."

It should not be overlooked that the apparent meaning of this is a view that combines the literal and the figurative meanings in the verse and the hadith. This is because prayer and zakat are both mentioned in each of them, while in the verse killing is meant, and its literal sense does not apply to one who withholds zakat. In the hadith fighting is meant, and its literal sense does not apply to one who abandons prayer. So it must be that killing is intended alongside fighting in the verse, and fighting alongside killing in the hadith, so that this ruling can apply to one who abandons prayer and one who withholds zakat. Combining the literal and figurative meaning is not permissible according to us. Moreover, interpreting the verse and the hadith in this way is something that hardly comes to mind, so the objection based on withholding zakat is very strong.

He pointed to what is reported from al-Muzani (d. 264 AH), together with his answer, by saying: "It may be said: there is no killing for one who neglects the present prayer, because he has not taken it out of its time, nor for one who neglects a missed prayer, because there is no killing for making up a prayer, even if it is obligatory immediately. We reply: rather, he is killed for the present prayer when he is ordered to perform it by the imam or his deputy, and by no one else, as it appears within its time when it is narrow, and he is warned about delaying it beyond that, yet he refuses until its time has passed. For at that point he is defiantly opposing the law, a defiance that calls for killing. So it is not only for the present prayer, nor only for a missed prayer, but for the combination of the two: the command and the delay together with determination."

Then they said: the one who abandons prayer is to be asked to repent immediately, as a recommendation (nadb, a non-obligatory but encouraged act). The difference from the obligation in the case of an apostate is that failing to ask him to repent makes him deserve eternal dwelling in Hell by consensus (ijma'), which is not the case here. Those who killed him before repentance are not held liable for compensation according to them in any case, but he commits a sin because he has usurped the authority of the imam (iftiyat). The full discussion of this is to be sought in its proper place.

Al-Jalal al-Suyuti said that those who hold that the one who abandons prayer and the one who withholds zakat are unbelievers also cited this verse as evidence. But this is not valid. The correct view is that both are believers who are disobedient, and whatever suggests disbelief is an expression of severe warning. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾: He forgives them what has passed from them and rewards them for their faith and obedience. This is a reason given for the command to let them go their way.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 6:**

﴿And if anyone among the polytheists seeks your protection﴾ This begins an explanation of the ruling concerning those who approach the beginnings of repentance by hearing the words of Allah the Exalted and standing before the rites of the religion, following the explanation of the ruling concerning those who repent of disbelief and those who persist in it. It also removes what might be suspected from His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Then when the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists﴾ [9:5],

[p. 53]

since the proof has been established against them, and what the Prophet (ﷺ) had mentioned earlier of the evidences and clear signs is sufficient to remove their excuse. Their seeking of evidence is not to be heeded after this. The particle *in* (إنْ) is conditional, and the noun (الاسم) is in the nominative by a hidden condition, which the apparent verb explains, not by the inceptive (الابتداء). Whoever claims this has erred, as al-Zajjaj said, because *in*, since it operates on a verb either verbally or in its position (لفظًا أو محلًّا), is specific to the verb, so its entry upon nouns is not valid. That is, "and if anyone among the polytheists seeks your protection" (﴿مِنَ المُشْرِكِينَ اسْتَجارَكَ﴾), meaning: asks you for safe conduct and requests to dwell with you after the appointed term has ended ﴿then grant him protection﴾, meaning: give him security ﴿until he hears the words of Allah﴾, and reflects upon them and comes to know the reality of what you call to. Limiting the mention to hearing is because there is no need for anything else in understanding, since they are people of eloquence and fluency. By "the words of Allah the Exalted" is meant the verses containing what indicates tawhid (divine oneness) and the negation of likeness and of the like. It is said: the surah of Bara'ah (al-Tawbah). It is said: the whole Qur'an, because the completeness of the proofs and clear signs is in it. The *hatta* (حتى) is for causation (للتعليل), connected to what is before it, and the verse is not an instance of *tanazu'* (the contention of two governors over one complement), as the excellent Ibn al-'Adil expressly stated, where he said: "This is not permitted according to the majority, for a verbal, technical reason: if we made it of that kind and made the first governor, namely *istajarak*, operative, it would necessitate affirming what they consider impossible, which is the governing of *hatta* over a pronoun. For they said: this is not resorted to except in necessity, as in the saying:

*Fa-la wallahi la yalqa unasun fataan hattaka ya ibna Abi Ziyad*
(By Allah, no people shall meet a youth like you, O son of Abi Ziyad.)

Because those who permit governing by the second [governor] also permit governing by the first, which requires what has been mentioned, especially according to the school of the Kufans, which is based on the preference for its governing." Whoever permits its governing over a pronoun holds that it is valid according to him, since there is no prohibition then. The apparent sense of the words of some learned scholars indicates the permissibility of connecting it to *istajarak*, where he said: "There is no reason for connecting it to *ajirhu* except the assumption that the estimate would have to be, on the basis of connecting it to the first: 'And if anyone among the polytheists seeks your protection until he hears the words of Allah, then grant him protection, *hattahu*', meaning: until the hearing." And does any intelligent person say that the completion of your statement "If Zayd seeks your protection for such-and-such a matter, then grant him protection" depends on saying "for that matter, all of it"? Let us grant the need and the necessity of the estimate. But what requires the estimate of *hattahu*, which is impossible outside of necessity? And why is it not permitted that there be estimated for it its first part, or *hatta yasma'ahu* (until he hears it), or something else of similar meaning? Another said: The necessity of the impossible pronoun on the supposition of governing by the first does not specify the governing of the second, so the construction does not leave the category of *tanazu'*; rather, one turns then to omission (الحذف). If that is also impracticable, it is mentioned explicitly, as is derived from the words of Najm al-A'immah and others of the verifying scholars.

It may be said that what prevents it from being of the category of *tanazu'* is that the intended purpose is not to give the reason for seeking protection by what was mentioned, just as the intended purpose is to give the reason for granting protection by it. Yes, Shaykh al-Islam said: The connection of granting protection to hearing the words of Allah the Exalted necessarily entails the connection of seeking protection to that as well, or to what is of similar meaning among the matters of religion. As for what is narrated from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, that a man from the polytheists came to him and said: "If one of us wishes to come to Muhammad (ﷺ) after the end of this term, to hear the words of Allah the Exalted, or for a need, will he be killed?" He said: "No, for Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And if anyone among the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection﴾," etc. So the need in it is the need connected with religion, not what includes it and other worldly needs, as his saying indicates: "to come to Muhammad (ﷺ)", for whoever comes to him, upon him be blessings and peace, comes only for matters connected with religion. End quotation. However, this is not a valid position, because the apparent sense of that questioner's words is generality, so the answer of the Commander of the Faithful, may Allah ennoble his face, supports what we have said. And his statement, may his secret be sanctified, that coming to him, upon him be blessings and peace, is only for matters connected with religion is a clear prohibition, so the building of the inference is not complete. Many have permitted that *hatta* is for the limit (للغاية), but the report mentioned and the solidity of the meaning both testify that it is for causation. Indeed, al-Mawla Siri al-Din al-Misri said:

[p. 54]

If one makes it for the limit, the saying of Allah the Exalted rejects it: ﴿Then convey him﴾ after his hearing, and the words of Allah, if he is not secured, ﴿to his place of safety﴾, meaning: his dwelling in which he feels safe, or the place of his safety, which is the abode of his people. Moreover, *ma'man* (مأمن, place of safety) is either a noun of place or a verbal noun with an estimated possessive; the first is preferable for its freedom from the burden of estimation. The conditional clause, according to what he explained in *al-Kashf*, is coordinated with the saying of Allah, glorified is He: ﴿Then kill the polytheists﴾. There is no proof in the verse for the Mu'tazilah to deny the inner speech (الكلام النفسي), because hearing may be attributed to it by way of the signifier of it, or it may be said that speech is understood by way of homonymy or by way of figurative and literal use, applying to inner speech and to verbal speech. The determination of one of them in the context of denying the establishment of the other in reality does not follow. What relates to this context has already been mentioned in the introductions concerning speech, so reflect on it. ﴿That﴾, meaning: the security or the command, ﴿is because they﴾, meaning: because of the fact that they ﴿are a people who do not know﴾, what Islam is and what is the reality of what you call them to; or, they are an ignorant people, so there must be given to them a guarantee of security until they understand that, and no excuse will remain for them at all. The verse, as al-Hasan said, is muhkam (not abrogated).

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Sa'id ibn Abi 'Arubah that it is abrogated by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And fight the polytheists all together as they fight you all together﴾ [9:36]. This was also narrated from al-Suddi and al-Dahhak. What al-Hasan said is better. There has been disagreement about the length of the period of respite. It was said: four months. Al-Naysaburi mentioned that this is the sound position of the school of al-Shafi'i. It was said: it is left to the judgment of the imam, and perhaps this is the more fitting.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 7:

﴿How can there be a covenant for the polytheists with Allah and with His Messenger?﴾ This is an explanation of the wisdom motivating what preceded regarding the disavowal (al-bara'a) and its related matters. What is meant by "from the polytheists" is those who broke their covenants, because the disavowal concerns only them. The interrogation is for the denial of occurrence. "Yakunu" (يَكُونُ) is complete (tammah), and "kayfa" (كَيْفَ) is in the accusative position by analogy with a circumstantial adverb (hal) or an adverb of time (zarf).

Others besides him said: it is incomplete (naqisah), and "kayfa" is its predicate, which must be placed first because the interrogative has the front position in the sentence. "Lilmushrikin" (لِلْمُشْرِكِينَ) is connected to "yakunu" according to those who permit the incomplete verbs to govern adverbials, or it is a description of "ahd" (covenant) that was moved forward, so it becomes a circumstantial qualifier (hal). "'Inda" (عِنْدَ) is either connected to "yakunu" as mentioned, or to "ahd" because it is a verbal noun, or to an omitted word that serves as a description of it. It is also permitted that the predicate be "lilmushrikin," with "'inda" in it having the aforementioned possibilities. It is also permitted that "'inda" be connected to the stability (al-istiqrar) that "lilmushrikin" is connected to, or that the predicate is "'inda Allah." As for "lilmushrikin," it is either an explanation, as in "suqya laka" (may it be watered for you), so it is connected to an implied element like "I say this denial for them," or it is connected to "yakunu," or it is a circumstantial qualifier of "ahd," or it is connected to the stability to which the predicate is connected. The advancing of a complement of the predicate is tolerated because it is a prepositional phrase. "Kayfa" in the last two cases is similar to an adverb of time or a circumstantial qualifier, as in the possibility that the verb is complete. This, according to what Shaykh al-Islam said, is the preferable view, because denying the existence of the covenant in itself carries an emphasis that denying its existence for the polytheists does not, since their having it in a relational sense is a branch of its having it in an essential sense; so the absence of the root necessitates the absence of the branch entirely.
