It has been objected that this is not correct, because it is established that the absence of the predicate's concept in external reality does not necessitate the absence of the external predication, since existents can be characterized by mental and negative attributes. So much so that they stated that "Zayd became blind" is an external proposition, although there is no essential existence of blindness. They also stated that the attribution of something to something, even if it does not require the existence of the attributed thing in the state of its attribution, does require its existence in itself, even in the place from which it is abstracted. The verification of this belongs in its proper place. Yes, in directing the denial to the manner in which the covenant exists there is an emphasis that is absent in directing it to its existence, because if all the states of a thing's existence are negated, and every existent must exist in some state, then its existence is negated by demonstrative method; that is, in no state does there exist for them a covenant worthy of consideration with Allah the Exalted and with His Messenger (ﷺ), one that deserves that its rights be observed and maintained until the end of its term, and that they not be confronted by killing or seizing according to it.

Page 55
The repetition of the word "'inda" (عِنْدَ) signals that the covenant is not regarded with Allah the Exalted and His Messenger, peace be upon him, each separately. ﴿Except those with whom you made a covenant﴾; they are the ones excepted in what passed. The disagreement is the same disagreement, and the relied-upon view is the relied-upon view. The mention that the covenant was ﴿at the Sacred Mosque﴾ is to add clarification about its parties and to indicate the reason for its strength. The exception is disjunctive (munqati'), meaning a corrective (istidrak) from the negation understood from the denying interrogative, which is clearly intended to include all the covenanters. The place of the relative pronoun is nominative as a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is omitted, or it is ﴿so as long as they are upright toward you, be upright toward them﴾. The fa' (فَ) is there because it includes the meaning of a condition, as previously explained. And "ma" (ما), as several others said, is either verbal (masdariyyah), in the accusative position as an adverb of time with an omitted noun in construction, meaning: be upright toward them for the duration of their uprightness toward you; or it is conditional (shartiyyah), in the accusative position as a temporal adverb, meaning: whatever time they are upright toward you, be upright toward them. The latter is more sound grammatically than the first possibility under the second interpretation. It is also possible that it is in the nominative position as a subject, and there is the well-known dispute about its predicate; "istaqimu" (اسْتَقِيمُوا) is the answer of the condition, and the fa' falls within the answer. On the verbal possibility, the fa' is additional for emphasis.

It is permitted that the exception be connected (muttasil), and the place of the relative pronoun is accusative or genitive, as a substitute (badal) for "al-mushrikin," because the interrogative carries the meaning of negation, and what is meant by them is the category, not specific known individuals. In either case, the ruling to be upright ends with the end of the covenant's term, so this returns to the command to complete mentioned earlier, except that here it has explicitly stated what was not explicitly stated there, though it is definitely a condition there as well, namely restricting the command to complete to their remaining in the faithfulness they had. The Exalted explained this with His saying, ﴿Indeed, Allah loves the righteous﴾, in the same pattern as what preceded, exactly matching.

How (﴿كَيْفَ﴾) is a repetition to express disapproval of what has been mentioned before: that the polytheists should have a covenant worthy of being upheld before Allah the Exalted and before His Messenger (ﷺ). It has also been said that it expresses improbability, that they would remain faithful to the covenant. The benefit of the repetition is emphasis and preparation for enumerating the reasons that necessitate what was mentioned, without the intervening material breaking the connection and closeness. The verb being disapproved of is omitted (ḥadhf), to indicate that the mind is already present with it, awaiting the arrival of what would necessitate this disapproval. The omission of the interrogated verb after "how" is common, and it is indicated by a circumstantial clause (jumla ḥāliyya) following it. Among this is the statement of Ka'b al-Ghanawī, lamenting his brother Abu al-Mighwār:

"You two told me that death is only in the villages,
so how (did he die), when here are a hill and a well?"

He means: "so how did he die, while the situation is what has been mentioned?" The intended meaning here is: how can they have a covenant that is considered valid before Allah and before His Messenger, peace be upon him, (and) their situation is that ﴿if they gain the upper hand over you﴾ (i.e., they prevail over you), ﴿they will not observe toward you any tie of kinship or covenant﴾ (i.e., they did not uphold that concerning you). The root of al-ruqūb is looking with the intent of protection and safeguarding, and from it comes al-raqīb (the watcher). Then it was used for protection in general. Al-murāqaba (vigilance) is stronger than it, like al-murā‘āt (observance). In negating ruqūb there is an exaggeration that is not in negating both. How subtle is the mention of ruqūb together with "prevailing"!

And al-Ill (الإلّ) with a kasra on the hamza, though it may be pronounced with a fatḥa, according to what has been narrated from Ibn ‘Abbās: it means kinship and blood relation. He recited the verse of Ḥassān:

"By your life, indeed your ill (kinship) with Quraysh
is like the ill of the young camel with the ostrich chicks."

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk went to this meaning. It is narrated from al-Suddī that it means alliance and covenant. It has been said: perhaps in this meaning it is derived from al-ill, which is protection, because when they made alliances they raised their voices. Then it was borrowed for kinship, because between two relatives there is a bond stronger than the bond of alliance. That it is stronger does not contradict it being a comparison, because the alliance is explicitly stated and pronounced, so it is stronger in one respect. The comparison is not inverted (al-maqlūb), as it has been imagined. It has also been said that it is derived from alla al-shay’ (to sharpen or define something) when he defined it, or from alla al-barq (the lightning) when it flashed and appeared. The suitability (munāsaba) is clear.

Page 56

Ibn al-Mundhir and Abū al-Shaykh narrated from ‘Ikrima and Mujāhid that al-Ill means Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. From this is what is narrated: that Abū Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, was read the speech of Musaylima, and he said: "This did not come out of an ill; so where are you taking you (people)?" It has been said: from it the word ill with the meaning of kinship was derived, just as al-raḥim (kinship) was derived from al-Raḥmān. The apparent view is that it is not Arabic, since al-ill is not heard in the speech of the Arabs except with the meaning of ilāh (god). From here some have said that it is Hebrew, and from it (comes) Jibrīl. He supported this by the fact that it was recited as īlan, and it means among them "Allah" or "God". That is: they do not fear Allah and do not observe Him concerning you.

Al-dhimma is the right that is blamed and censured for neglecting it, or the covenant, and it was so named because breaking it necessitates blame. In their saying "in my dhimma is such-and-such," it is the place of obligation. Some jurists said: it is a meaning by which a human being, specifically, becomes eligible for the rights that are obligatory upon him. It is also explained as security and guarantee, and these are close in meaning. Some claimed that both al-ill and al-dhimma here mean covenant, and the conjunction is for explanation (tafsīr). But repetition without an apparent (distinct) reason rejects this, so it is not like the verse of the poet:

"He found her word a lie and a falsehood."

The truth is that there is a difference between them. The purpose of the verse has been said to be: clarification that they are captives of an opportunity, so there is no covenant for them. It has also been said: guidance that the obligation to observe the rights of a covenant on each of the two contracting parties is conditional upon the other's observance of them. So when the polytheists do not observe them, how would you observe them? This is in the manner of his statement:

"Why do you accept ransom from them, when they
have accepted from us neither silver nor gold?"

I have not found for these people a likeness in this respect indicated by His statement, glorified is He: ﴿And if they gain the upper hand﴾, etc., except some people who dress in the garb of scholars and are not of them, not even a paring of a fingernail. For "they are with me, and Allah is sufficient for me." And enough of this pattern. So Allah the Exalted raised them in nothing but name, and lowered them, and did not lower from them any burden.

His statement, glorified is He: ﴿They please you with their mouths, but their hearts refuse﴾ is a new (independent) sentence, revealing the reality of their affairs, both open and hidden, and repelling what might be imagined from linking the non-observance of the covenant to their victory: that they would observe it when they are not victorious. It shows that in the state of their weakness as well they are not at all faithful, and that what they display, Allah has concealed it as flattery (mudāhana), not as conciliation (muhādana). The manner of their pleasing the believers is that they show them loyalty and friendship, promise them faith and obedience, and confirm that with false oaths. The believer is naive and generous: if he says something, he is truthful, and if it is said to him, he believes it. When the opposite becomes evident, they make excuses with false pretexts.

The restriction of pleasing to the mouths indicates that their speech is merely words they utter without having any reality in their hearts. He emphasized this with the content of the second sentence. Some claimed that the sentence is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of ﴿yarqubū﴾ (they observe), not an independent sentence. It was rejected on the grounds that a circumstantial clause requires simultaneity, while pleasing before the victory, which is before the non-observance that is the response (jazā’), where is the simultaneity? Also, there is clear incompatibility between the two states: pleasing with the mouths in a state of concealing disbelief and hatred is courtesy toward the believers, while the state of not observing and standing is a state of open hostility toward them. Since the two are incompatible, there is no sense in restricting one of them by the other.

﴿And most of them are defiant﴾: they are outside obedience, rebellious, having neither a creed to restrain them nor a sense of honor to turn them back. The specification of "most" is because some disbelievers keep away from excuse and avoid what would draw a bad reputation. Describing the disbelievers with defiance is in the extreme of censure.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 9:

﴿They have exchanged the signs of Allah﴾ That is, the signs containing the command to fulfil covenants and to be upright in every matter, or all of His signs, so that what has been mentioned enters therein as a primary inclusion. By "purchase" (ishtira') is meant "exchange" (istibdal). In the statement there is a metaphor (isti'arah) that is taba'iyyah (dependent upon a verb) and tasrihiyyah (explicit), and it is followed by a metonymy (kinayah), since the signs are likened to a commodity that is bought. There may also be a figurative relation of the metonymic type (majaz mursal) through the use of the restricted for the general: "purchase" (restricted) is used for the general sense, which is "exchange", in the manner of what they said about the nose (marsan), meaning they exchanged that for ﴿a small price﴾. That is, a worthless thing from the trifles of this world, namely their desires and lusts which they followed.

Page 57

The sentence, as al-Allamah al-Tibi said, is a resumptive (mustanaf'ah) clause, serving as a justification for His statement, exalted is He: ﴿and most of them are defiantly disobedient﴾. In it is the point that whoever commits transgression and rebellion, its cause is merely the following of lusts and the inclining toward pleasures. Some of them interpreted the "small price" as the food that Abu Sufyan spent and directed toward the Bedouins. ﴿So they averted﴾: that is, they deviated and turned away, taking it as intransitive from "sadda, sududan" (to turn away), or they diverted and prevented others, taking it as transitive from "sadda-hu 'an al-amr, sadda-n" (to turn him away from the matter). The fa' (so) indicates that their purchasing led them to aversion or to obstruction. ﴿from His way﴾: that is, the true religion that leads to Him, exalted is He, and the idafah (genitive construction) is for honour; or the way of His Sacred House, since they used to hinder pilgrims and visitors from it. So "the way" is either a metaphor or a literal meaning, and in that case either a noun is to be understood in the statement, or the idafah relation is taken as a figurative extension. ﴿Indeed, evil is what they used to do﴾: that is, wretched is what they used to do, or their continuous deed. The one singled out for blame is omitted.

It has also been permitted that the word sa'a (evil/was evil) be in its own usage of the conjugated type, intransitive in the sense of "qabuha" (was ugly), or transitive with an omitted object, meaning: "that which they do has displeased them" or "their deed displeased them." When it functions like ba'sa (wretched), it changes into the form with damm (bi'sa to sa'a with the vowel u, as a verb of praise and blame), and it is not conjugated, as established in its proper place.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They do not observe regarding a believer any tie of kinship or any covenant﴾ censures them for not observing the rights of the covenant with believers in general, unlike the first [phrase], because of the position of ( fikum ) in it, and ( ﴿fi mu'minin﴾ ) in this one, so there is no repetition, as in al-Madarik (Madarik al-Tanzil). It has been said that this is an explanation of "what they do" (ya'malun), and it implies that blame and evil are specific to this deed of theirs and not to anything else. It has also been said that the first [phrase] is general concerning those who break covenants, while this one is specific to those who "purchased" [the worldly price], namely the Jews and the Bedouins whom Abu Sufyan gathered and fed in order to seek their help in fighting the Prophet (ﷺ). Accordingly, "the verses" means what includes the Qur'an and the Torah. In this view there is a dislocation of pronouns and a departure from the apparent meaning.

Al-Jubba'i restricts this to the Jews, and there is what there is in that. ﴿And those﴾, i.e., those described by the evil qualities enumerated, ﴿they are the transgressors﴾, i.e., those who go beyond the furthest limit in wrongdoing and wickedness.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 11:

﴿But if they repent﴾ of what they are upon of disbelief and all the other grave matters, such as breaking the covenant and others. The fa' here indicates that their rebuke for the abominable deeds mentioned about them is a deterrent from them and a likely means to repentance. ﴿and establish the prayer and give the zakah﴾ in the manner commanded. ( ﴿then they are your brothers﴾ ) That is: they are your brothers ﴿in religion﴾, having what you have and owing what you owe. The prepositional phrase is connected to "your brothers", as Abu al-Baqa' said, because it carries the meaning of a verb. It has been said: the difference between the answer to this conditional and the answer to the preceding conditional, although the condition is the same in both, is that the first was placed directly after the command to kill and similar things, so its answer had to be a command, unlike this one. This one was placed after the ruling against them concerning transgression and similar things, so its answer must definitely be a judgment. This verse is more attractive to their hearts than that one, since there is a clear difference between letting them go on their way and establishing religious brotherhood for them. It was also used as evidence for the prohibition of shedding the blood of the people of the qiblah (ahl al-qiblah, those who face the Ka'bah in prayer). This was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. It is also reported in the narration of Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh from him that it prohibited fighting or the blood of the people of prayer, and the outcome is the same. Some used it as evidence for the disbelief of one who abandons the prayer, since its implication is the negation of religious brotherhood from him, and beyond the truth there is only error. It would also necessitate saying that one who withholds zakah is a disbeliever, by the very same reasoning. Some who do not hold them to be disbelievers have taken the view that establishing the prayer and giving zakah means committing to them and resolving to perform them. There is no doubt, by consensus, about the disbelief of one who does not commit to them.

Some of the eminent scholars have mentioned that Allah made the attainment of brotherhood in religion conditional on the combination of three matters: repentance, establishing the prayer, [p. 58] and giving zakah. Something conditioned by the word "if" (in) ceases to exist when that thing is absent. So it follows that whenever these three are not present, brotherhood in religion is not attained. This is problematic, because a Muslim who is legally responsible, if he is poor, or if he is rich but the year has not yet passed over him, is not obligated to give zakah. So if he does not give it, what brotherhood in religion depends upon has ceased to exist for him, and it would follow that he is not a believer. However, it may be said: the conditional with "if" only indicates that the conditioned thing entails what is conditioned upon it, and does not indicate that the conditioned thing ceases to exist when the condition is absent. That is derived from external evidence, because what is conditioned may be a more general consequence, so it may exist without the thing made its necessary consequence existing. Even if it is granted that the conditional itself indicates that the conditioned thing ceases to exist when the condition is absent, we do not grant that it follows from this that a poor Muslim is not a believer because he does not give zakah. That would follow only if the condition were giving it in all circumstances, and that is not the case. Rather, the condition is giving it when specific conditions, explained by legal evidence, are met. End of quotation.

You know the disagreement over the concept of implication of the condition (mafhum al-shart). The Hanafiyyah (Hanafi school) hold it, and it appears that this discussion applies to giving zakah just as it applies to establishing the prayer. Ibn Zayd used the pairing of the two as evidence that the prayer is not accepted without zakah.

From Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: "You were commanded to pray and to give zakah, so whoever does not [give zakah], there is no prayer for him."

﴿And We detail the verses﴾, that is, We make them clear. What is meant by "the verses" is either the verses already mentioned concerning the circumstances of the polytheists, including the covenant-breakers and others, and their rulings in the two states of disbelief and belief, or all the verses, in which case those verses are included initially. ﴿for a people who know﴾ what We have detailed, or "for people of knowledge", on the basis that the verb is transitive and its object is omitted, or that it is treated as intransitive. Knowledge, as has been said, is a metonymy for reflection and contemplation, or a figurative usage in that sense through the relation of causation. The clause is parenthetical, urging reflection upon the verses and pondering over them.

And the words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿But if they break their oaths﴾, are conjoined to His words, glorified is He, ﴿but if they repent﴾. That is: and if they do not do that, but rather break ﴿their oaths after their covenant﴾, the one confirmed by them, and they bring out into action the evil that is in their hearts, moving it from potential to actual. It is also permissible that the meaning is: and if they persist and continue in the breaking of oaths that they are upon. Some of them interpreted "breaking" (nakth) as apostasy (irtidad), by the indication of its being mentioned in contrast to ﴿but if they repent﴾. The first (interpretation) is more fitting to the context. ﴿And they revile your religion﴾: they disparage it by finding fault with it and denouncing its rulings openly.

Ibn al-Munir made the reviling of a dhimmi (a non-Muslim under protection) against our religion among the people of his own religion, when it reaches us, to be of this kind. Many, including the aforementioned virtuous scholar, count this as a breaking of the covenant. Thus the conjunction is the conjunction of the specific upon the general, and by this is resolved what is said: "The apparent wording would be 'or they revile' (aw ta'anu), because each of the reviling and what precedes it is sufficient for entitlement to killing and fighting." That the waw here means "or" is far-fetched. It has also been said that the conjunction is for explanation, as in your saying: "So-and-so belittled me and acted towards me in such-and-such a way," meaning: "if they break their oaths by their reviling of your religion." The first is more fitting. There is no difference between directing the reviling at the religion itself in general and directing it at some of its particulars, such as the prayer and the pilgrimage for example. Among this is reviling the Qur'an and mentioning the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, and far be it from him, with something bad. For this, the dhimmi is to be killed according to a group who take evidence from the verse, whether or not the breaking of the covenant is stipulated by it. Among those who said he should be killed if he openly insults (the Prophet) — and we seek refuge in Allah — are Malik and al-Shafi'i, and this is the view of al-Layth, and Ibn al-Humam issued a fatwa with it. As for the saying that the People of Protection are permitted to remain upon their original disbelief in exchange for the jizya, and that this (insulting the Prophet) is no greater than that, so they should be permitted to remain upon it too, it is not among the aforementioned reviling in any way, and it is not from fairness in any way. It also entails that they should not be disciplined either, just as they are not disciplined after the jizya for their original disbelief. In this, by my life, is the selling of the unique pearl of existence, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, for a paltry price, while the world in its entirety, and even the Hereafter in its totality, are, beside his lofty station, but the wing of a gnat or less.

[p. 59]

Some of them said: the verse does not indicate, by any one of the indications, what the group claimed, and it is explicit that the combination of breaking oaths and reviling brings about what it brings about. So how could it indicate killing merely on account of reviling? There is in this what there is. The excellence of the placement of reviling alongside fighting, which is implied by His words, the Exalted: ﴿so fight the leaders of disbelief﴾, is not hidden. That is: fight them. The apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun. They were called "leaders" (a'immah) because by this they became, in their own estimation, chiefs preceding others, so they are deserving of fighting and killing. This is reported from al-Hasan. It has also been said that what is meant by "their leaders" is their chiefs and notables, such as Abu Sufyan and al-Harith ibn Hisham. Their being singled out for mention is because killing them is more important, not because others are not killed. It has also been said: it is to prohibit being lenient toward them, since they are the object of such leniency, or to indicate their extermination, for killing them generally occurs after killing those below them. It is reported from Mujahid that they are Persia and Rome, but this is far-fetched.

Ibn Abi Shaybah and others reported from Hudhayfah, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "The people of this verse have not yet been fought against," and I do not know what he meant, and Allah the Exalted knows best what He means.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read ﴿a'immata﴾ with two hamzas, the second of which is "bayna bayna" (an intermediate sound between the hamza and the ya', that is, between the place of articulation of the hamza and that of the ya', with an alif between them). The Kufans and Ibn Dhakwan on the authority of Ibn 'Amir read it with both hamzas made clear, without inserting an alif. Hisham did likewise, except that he inserted an alif between them. This is the well-known reading of the Seven Readers. Abu Hayyan reported from Nafi' an extension (madd) between the two hamzas and the ya'.

As some of the scholars of verification said, a group of grammarians, such as al-Farisi, deemed weak the reading with both hamzas made clear and the bayna bayna. Some of them denied the facilitation of bayna bayna, and read with a light ya' with a slight kasra. As for the reading with ya', Abu 'Ali and a group approved of it, while al-Zamakhshari considered it a lahn (a solecism), and Abu Hayyan refuted him in that, because it is the reading of the head of the readers and grammarians, Abu 'Amr, and the reading of Ibn Kathir and Nafi', and it is authentic by transmission. The non-establishment of it by the path of taysir (the Seven-Readings handbook) necessitates restriction, and likewise by understanding, for he (al-Zamakhshari) himself mentioned in al-Mufassal, and the rest of the imams in their books, that when two hamzas come together in one word, the proper course is to convert the second into a soft vowel letter, as in Adam and a'immah. So what he offered as an excuse for it is not acceptable. The summary is that the readings here are: making both hamzas clear, and making the second bayna bayna without inserting an alif, and with it, and the fifth with a clear ya'. All of them are sound, and there is no basis for denying any of them.

The pattern (wazn) of a'immah is af'ilah, like himar and ahmirah (donkey and donkeys). Its original form was a'immmah; the vowel of the mim was moved onto the hamza and the two were assimilated. When the coming together of two hamzas was felt to be heavy, they fled from it and did what they did.

﴿Indeed they have no oaths﴾: that is, in reality, since they do not observe them, do not fulfil them, and do not regard breaking them as a defect, even if they pass them on their tongues. The negation was linked to the oaths, as the breaking was in what preceded, and not to the covenant confirmed by them, because they are the principal element in covenants. The clause is in the position of a justification, either for the content of the condition, as if it were said: "if they break their oaths and revile, as is expected of them, since they have no oaths in reality for them to break, so fight them," or for the continuation of the fighting commanded, which is derived from the context, so it is as if it were said: "fight them until they believe, for they have no oaths, until another contract is made with them." To take it as a justification for the command to fight does not fit with its being linked to breaking and reviling, because their state of having no oaths in reality after that is the same as their state before it. Taking it to mean that their oaths do not remain after breaking and reviling, besides the fact that there is no need to explain it, is contrary to the apparent meaning. It has also been said that it is a justification for what is understood from the speech of the ruling upon them that they are "leaders of disbelief," that is, they are the chiefs of the disbelievers and the worst of them in evil, since they added to their disbelief the lack of regard for oaths. This, as you see, is weak. The negation in the verse, according to Imam Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, is in its apparent sense, so the oath of a disbeliever is not an oath in his view, counted as valid in the Sharia. According to al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, it is an oath, because Allah the Exalted described it with breaking at the beginning of the verse, and breaking does not occur where there is no oath, as you know, and they have no oaths.

[p. 60]

It is answered that this is in terms of their belief that it is an oath. This is far-fetched, because the statement is from Allah the Exalted and the address is to the believers. Others said: deriving the proof from breaking to the existence of an oath is an allusion or an implication, while "they have no oaths" is an expression, so the expression takes precedence. The claim that they are to be interpreted, in order to combine the evidences, is problematic, because if there must be an interpretation in one of the two sides, then interpreting what is not explicit is preferable. Perhaps precedence and posteriority are not considered in this. The fruit of the disagreement is this: if a disbeliever swears an oath while disbelieving and then becomes Muslim and then breaks it, is he liable for the expiation (kaffarah)? According to Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, no. According to al-Shafi'i, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him, yes.

Ibn 'Amir read ﴿iman﴾ with a kasra on the hamza, as a verbal noun from "amanahu iman," meaning "he gave him security (aman)." It is also used in the sense of the result of the verbal noun, which is security. What is meant is that there is no way for you to give them security after that, ever. It has been said: this negation is based on the view that the verse concerns the polytheists of the Arabs, for they have no option but Islam or the sword. Some people claimed that what is meant is that there is no way for them to give you security after this. In this there is an implication that their covenant with us was on the basis that giving security would be from their side, and this is utterly false. Or it is based on the reading that "iman" means Islam, and the clause in this case is a justification for the content of the condition and nothing more, as Shaykh al-Islam explained: as if it were said: "if they break and revile, as is apparent from their state, since they have no Islam, so that they might refrain from breaking the very kind of their faith and from reviling your religion." Whoever clung to this verse in this reading, saying that the apostate's repentance is not accepted, on the basis that the breaker is the apostate and that He has negated faith from him, and that negation, even though it may occur from him, is a negation of its validity and its being counted, is also weak. This is not hidden, for what you know of the meaning of the verse. They have said: possibility removes the force of the proof. The Qadi, may Allah whiten the face of his states in explaining its weakness, said: it is possible that what is meant is the negation of faith from specific people, and the report that they were sealed upon their hearts, so no faith whatsoever proceeds from them. Or what is meant is that the polytheists have no faith, until they are kept under observation and granted respite for its sake. It is understood from this that he did not make the clause a justification for the content of the condition, as we mentioned. The apparent meaning is that he made it a justification for His words, glorified is He: ﴿so fight﴾. That is, the factor preventing their killing is one of two things: either the covenant, which they have broken, or faith, which they have forfeited. This may come back to making it a cause for what is understood from the speech, as if it were said: "if they break and revile, then fight them, and do not hesitate, for there is no barrier at all after that, since they have no faith to be a barrier." What is in this is not hidden.

If it is said that this removes what was said: that describing the leaders of disbelief as having no Islam is a superfluous repetition, and that making the clause a justification for what is understood from the speech about them, that they are the leaders of disbelief, that is, its chiefs, on the supposition that what is meant is the report about specific people with the sealing of hearts, is clearer than making it a justification for it on the previous reading. Yes, the report about sealing rejects His words, the Exalted: ﴿so that they may desist﴾, since with sealing, desisting is inconceivable. And this is connected to His words, glorified is He: ﴿so fight﴾, that is: fight them with the intention that they desist, meaning: let your purpose in fighting be their desisting from the disbelief and the other grave matters in which they are, not merely inflicting harm upon them, as is the habit of those who harm. From what has been established it is known that the hope (tarajji) is from the addressees, not from Allah, exalted is His majesty.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 9, verse 13:

﴿Will you not fight?﴾ This is an incitement (*tahrid*, urging) to fighting, because the interrogative (*istifham*) here is denunciatory (*inkar*, reproachful). A denunciatory interrogative has the sense of a negation, and it has been preceded by a negation. The negation of a negation is an affirmation. Since abandoning fighting was regarded as shameful and reprehensible, this conveys by a demonstrative method that bringing it about is something desired and sought after, and so it implies urging and inciting to it. It may also be said that the way this verse incites to fighting is that they are led to acknowledge its absence, as if it were a matter they could not admit willingly because of its extreme ugliness. Thus they are driven to it, unable to acknowledge it, and they choose fighting, so they fight ﴿a people who broke their oaths﴾ which they swore at the time of the treaty, ﴿to you﴾

[Page 61]

that they would not assist anyone against you. Yet they assisted their allies, the Banu Bakr, against the allies of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), the Khuza'a. By "them" is meant the Quraysh. ﴿And they plotted to expel the Messenger﴾ from Mecca, his birthplace (peace be upon him), when they consulted together in the House of Assembly (*Dar al-Nadwa*), as is mentioned in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And when those who disbelieved plotted against you﴾. Al-Jubba'i said: They are the Jews who broke the covenant and went out with the confederates (*al-Ahzab*), and they plotted to expel the Messenger (ﷺ) from Medina. It is not hidden that the context (*siyaq*) rejects this and there is no indicator (*qarina*) for it. The first view is the one related from Mujahid, al-Suddi, and others. It is objected: what occurred in the House of Assembly was the intention (*hamm*) to expel, imprison, or kill, and what they finally settled upon was killing, not expulsion; so what is the reason for specifying expulsion?

It is answered: the specification is because expulsion is what actually occurred in external reality, which resembles it among what resulted from their intention, even though it was not by their act but by God, exalted is He, for a wisdom. Whatever else is outside this is idle, so it was singled out for mention because it is what necessitates incitement, not anything else that did not manifest any effect.

It has also been said that He, glorified is He, mentioned the lesser matter so that others would be understood by a stronger inference (*tariq awla*). And it is not objected that expulsion is not less than imprisonment, as it is supposed, because his (ﷺ) remaining in the hands of his enemy, which necessitates harassment through threats and the like, is without doubt worse than that.

﴿And they were the first to attack you﴾ with fighting, ﴿the first time﴾. That was the day of Badr, when, after they received news of the safety of the caravan, they said: "We will not turn back until we uproot Muhammad (ﷺ) and those with him." Al-Zajjaj said: they began by fighting the Khuza'a, the allies of the Prophet (ﷺ), and most scholars went to this view. A group chose the first view because it is free from repetition.

He, glorified is He, has mentioned three matters, each of which would necessitate fighting them if taken alone, so how much more so when combined. In this is included the incitement to fighting that it contains. He then increased this with His words, glorified is He: ( ﴿Do you fear them?﴾ ) Here the cause and the reason have been placed in the position of the effect and the caused thing. The meaning is: Do you abandon fighting them out of fear that some harm from them will befall you? ﴿Yet God has more right that you should fear Him﴾ by opposing His command and abandoning the fighting of His enemy. The divine name (*al-ism al-jalil*) is the subject (*mubtada'*), and ( ﴿more right﴾ ) is its predicate (*khabar*), and ﴿that you should fear Him﴾ is an apposition (*badal*) to the divine name, a badal al-ishtimal (inclusive apposition), or with an implied preposition, meaning "in that you should fear Him," so its position is accusative or genitive after the deletion, according to the difference of opinion. It has also been said that ﴿that you should fear Him﴾ is a subject whose predicate is ( ﴿more right﴾ ), and the clause is the predicate of the divine name, meaning: fear of God, exalted is He, is more right, or God is more right to be feared than other than Him, or His being feared is more right. "And the best of matters, in my view, is the middle course." ﴿If you are believers﴾, for the requirement of the faith of a believer, who realizes that there is no one who harms or benefits except God, exalted is He, and no one has power to harm or benefit except by His will, is that he should fear none but God, exalted is He. Whoever fears God, exalted is He, is feared by everything. In this there is an intensification (*tashdid*) that is not hidden.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 14:**

﴿Fight them﴾ is an emphatic restatement (*tajrid*, a rhetorical device that strips a command to its core) of the order to fight, after its cause has been explained in the most complete way, together with a rebuke for abandoning it. It is also a promise of their victory, of God punishing their enemies and disgracing them, and an encouragement to them. ﴿God will punish them by your hands﴾ with killing, ( ﴿and disgrace them﴾ ) and humiliate them by taking them captive. It may also be said that He punishes them by killing and by capture, and humiliates them by this. ﴿And give you victory over them﴾, that is, He will make you all victorious over all of them. For this reason, as some of the *muhaqqiqun* (verifying scholars) said, this clause was placed after the punishment and the disgracing. ﴿And heal the breasts of a believing people﴾, who had suffered at their hands. By them are meant people from Khuza'a, the allies of the Prophet (peace be upon him), as Ikrimah and others said. And it is related from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that they were tribes from Yemen and Saba', who came to Makkah and embraced Islam, and then suffered much harm from its people. So they sent to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) complaining to him, and the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Rejoice, for relief is near."

Page 62

It is also related from him, may God be pleased with him, that the saying of the Most High, ﴿Will you not fight?﴾ etc. [9:13], is an encouragement to conquer Makkah. It was objected that this surah was revealed after the Conquest, so how can what was mentioned be possible? It is answered that its beginning was revealed after the Conquest, but this passage came before it. The benefit of presenting the disavowal of their covenant, although it is known from the fighting at the Conquest and what occurred in it, lies in indicating its generality to all polytheists and in preventing them from the House. So reflect and do not be heedless. It was said: It is not far-fetched to take "believers" in a general sense, because every believer is gladdened by the killing and humiliation of the disbelievers.

﴿And He will remove the rage of their hearts﴾ by what harm they suffered from them, which they were not able to repel. It has also been said that the meaning is that He will remove their rage at the violation of Allah's sacred prohibitions, at disbelief in Him, the Mighty and Majestic, and at the denial of His Messenger (ﷺ).

The apparent sense of the conjunction is that the removal of rage is other than the healing of hearts. It has been justified that the healing comes from killing the enemies and humiliating them, and the removal of rage comes from being given victory over them all. Because victory is the focus of the intent, its effect is the removal of rage from the heart, which is more specific than the breast. It has also been said that the removal of rage is like an emphasis on the healing of hearts, and its benefit is to intensify their joy at what Allah, exalted is He, bestows upon them of punishing their enemies, humiliating them, and His giving them victory over them. Perhaps the removal of rage from the heart is more eloquent than what it is conjoined to, so mentioning it is by way of progression (taraqqi), and this is not without beauty. It has also been said that the healing of hearts comes merely from the promise of conquest, while the removal of rage comes from the conquest actually occurring; but this is nothing. Allah, exalted is He, fulfilled all that He promised them in the most beautiful manner, so the verse is among the miracles, because it contains a report of the unseen and the occurrence of what was reported. It has been cited as evidence that the actions of servants are created by Allah, exalted is He. It has also been said that the attribution of the punishment to Him, glorified is He, is figurative (majaz), in view of the fact that He, exalted and high, enabled them to do it and empowered them over it.

In the Shihabi Glosses (al-Hawashi al-Shihabiyya) it is said: The words of Allah, glorified is He, ﴿by your hands﴾ are almost explicit that such acts, which are suitable for the Creator, are an action of His, the Exalted, while for the servant there is only acquisition (kasb) through the directing of powers and instruments. Interpreting it as figurative attribution (al-isnad al-majazi) is not satisfactory to one who knows the styles of speech, nor is the objection, by agreement, to the impermissibility of Allah writing by your hands, or of Allah, exalted is His affair, lying through the tongues of the disbelievers, a valid one. This is because the mere creation of an act does not validate its attribution to the Creator unless it is suitable as its locus. The impermissibility of what was mentioned is to avoid the ugliness of the expression, since one does not say "O Creator of filth," nor "the Decreer of fornication and the Enabler of it." Then he said: What is in it is not hidden, for He, exalted is He, is not a suitable locus for killing or for striking, or the like of what is intended for humiliation, but He is the Creator of it, and the act is not attributed literally to its creator, although He is the true agent, to distinguish between it and the linguistic agent. One does not say "Allah, exalted is He, wrote by the hand of Zayd," in the sense that it is literal without doubt, even though there is no ugliness in it, because of the words of Allah, glorified is He, ("Allah has decreed"). So what he mentioned is not accepted. End of quotation. I say: The question of the creation of acts has been settled by the verifying scholars, so there is no need to extend the discussion on it. They have spoken about the verse with what they spoke, but there remains in it something, namely the secret in attributing the punishment to Him, exalted is He, and the mention of hands, which they did not mention. Perhaps the purpose in the attribution is intensification, for it is the punishment of Allah, the Strong, the Mighty, even if it is by the hands of the servants. As for the mention of hands, it is either to specify that this is in this world and not in the Hereafter, or so that the glad tidings of punishment come in the most complete form, upon which the healing of hearts and the like depends in the most perfect way, for there is a difference between the enemy being punished by the hand of his enemy and his being punished not by his own hand. By my life, the first is sweeter and more effective in the soul, so understand.

There is no hiding the harmony in the verse, in that a complete line of poetry comes out of it. ﴿And Allah turns in forgiveness to whomever He wills﴾ is a beginning of a report that some of those who were commanded to fight them will repent of their disbelief, and Allah, exalted is He, will turn to them in forgiveness. This did happen, as some of them embraced Islam and their Islam was good. Al-A'raj, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Isa al-Thaqafi, and Amr ibn Ubayd read ("and He turns") with the accusative (naṣb), and it is narrated from Abu Amr and Ya'qub as well. Al-Zajjaj found this reading problematic, because Allah's turning in forgiveness to whomever He wills occurs whether they fight or not, while the accusative in the answer to the imperative is caused by it, so there is no basis for including the turning in forgiveness in its answer. Ibn Jinni said: This is like your saying, "If you visit me, I will do good to you, and give Zayd such-and-such," where what is caused by the visit is both matters together, not that each is caused independently. They have said something similar regarding the words of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, We have granted you a clear conquest﴾ ﴿that Allah may forgive you your earlier and later sins﴾, and so on; but this is forced.

Some have said: When He, exalted is He, commanded them to fight, it was hard for some of them, so when they fought, their fighting took the place of repentance from that aversion. The meaning becomes: If you fight them, Allah will punish them, and He will turn to you in forgiveness from your aversion to fighting them. There is no hiding that the apparent sense is that the turning in forgiveness is for the disbelievers. Some scrutinizers have mentioned that the inclusion of the turning in forgiveness among what the command was answered with is by way of meaning, because it is in the accusative after the particle (fa), so it is in the opposite of ﴿fa-aṣṣaddaqa wa-akun﴾, and this is what is called conjunction by apparent assumption (ʿaṭf al-tawahhum). Its basis is that fighting is a cause of breaking their strength and removing their arrogance, so it causes them to reflect and return from disbelief, as happened with Abu Sufyan, Ikrimah, and others. The restriction by the will is to indicate that the will is the original cause, and that the first is an ordinary cause; and to alert that fighting leading to repentance is not like its leading to the remaining matters. Some eminent scholars claimed that the reading of the nominative, in consideration of the meaning, since a present-tense verb in the nominative occurs after a jussive verb which is the answer to the imperative, so it is understood that the meaning is: "And Allah turns in forgiveness to whomever He wills," on the assumption of the reciprocal, in view of what they see of your steadfastness and their weakness. As for the reading with the accusative, it is consideration of the wording, since what is conjoined to the jussive is put in the accusative by estimating its accusative form; but this is nothing. The truth is that in the nominative it is a new sentence (mustaʾnaf), as we have already stated.

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing﴾, nothing is hidden from Him. ﴿Wise﴾, He does not act or command except what has wisdom and benefit in it, so obey His command, the Mighty and Majestic. The choice of stating the glorious Name explicitly rather than using a pronoun is to cultivate awe and to bring in dread.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 16:

﴿Or did you think﴾ is addressed to those among the believers or the hypocrites who found fighting burdensome. The particle (ام) here is munqati‘ah (disjunctive, "bal" in sense), brought in to shift from the command to fight to rebuke for them, or to shift from the preceding rebuke to another rebuke. The hamzah of interrogation, implied together with (بل), is for rebuke concerning the supposition mentioned, meaning: "Rather, did you suppose and think" ﴿that you would be left﴾ in the state you are in, and not be commanded to strive (jihad) nor be tested by that which would purify you. ﴿Yet Allah has not yet known those of you who strove﴾. The waw is circumstantial (ḥāliyyah), and (لما) is for negation with expectation (tawaqquʿ) and negation of knowledge. What is meant is the negation of what is known, namely the striving, in the most emphatic manner, since it is by way of proof: for if their striving occurred, Allah, exalted is He, would certainly know it, for the occurrence of what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, does not know is impossible, just as the non-occurrence of what He knows is likewise impossible; otherwise His knowledge would not correspond to the reality and would be ignorance, which is among the greatest impossibilities. So the statement is of the type of kinayah (metonymy). It has been said that knowledge (ʿilm) is a metaphor for manifestation (tabyīn), a metonymy (majāz mursal) by using it for its necessary meaning. In the Kashshaf there is an indication, first, that knowledge is a metaphor for what was mentioned, and second, an indication that it is of the type of kinayah. This has been answered by saying that he pointed by this to the fact that it is used to negate existence, as an intensification in negating manifestation. What he mentioned first, from his saying: "You will not be left in the state you are in until the sincere among you are distinguished, and they are those who strove in the way of Allah, exalted is His Majesty, purely for His sake," is the summary of the meaning. This is because it is an address to the believers to spur them on and urge them toward what He, exalted is He, urged them to by His saying: ﴿Fight them, and Allah will punish them﴾. So when they were rebuked for supposing that they would be left, and there was not found among them a sincere striver, this shows that if they do not fight they are not sincere, and that sincerity, if its effect is not manifested through striving in the way of Allah and opposing the disbelievers, is no sincerity at all. Had knowledge been interpreted as distinguishing, this intensification would not be conveyed, so reflect. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And have not taken﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon (جاهدوا) and falls within the scope of the relative clause, or it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from its subject, meaning: they strove while not taking ﴿besides Allah, and His Messenger, and the believers, any intimate (waliyjah)﴾, i.e., a confidant and one privy to secrets, as Ibn ʿAbbas said. It derives from (الولوج), which is entering, and everything you insert into something while it is not part of it is a waliyjah. It can apply to the singular and otherwise with one form, and it may be pluralized as walā'ij. The phrase ﴿besides﴾ (min dūn) is connected to the taking if it is kept in its own state, or is a second object of it if it is taken in the sense of making. ﴿And Allah is Aware of what you do﴾, i.e., of all your deeds, so He will recompense you for them: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil. It has been read in the third person (ghaybah). In this there is a removal of what might be suspected from the apparent sense of His saying: ﴿And Allah has not yet known﴾ etc., namely that He, exalted is He, does not know things before their occurrence, as Hisham held, citing this as evidence.

The manner of removal is that (﴿تعملون﴾) is in the future tense, which indicates the opposite of what he mentioned.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 17:

﴿It is not for the polytheists﴾ — that is, it is not proper for them, nor fitting, even if it happens — ﴿to maintain the mosques of Allah﴾. The apparent meaning is that what is intended is some of the mosques, since it is a plural construct (jam' mudaf) and therefore generalizes, and the Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram) enters into it by priority. Its upkeep is the basis of their pride. The negation of a plural indicates negation of each individual member, so its negation of a specific individual follows by way of implication (kinayah). It is reported from ʿIkrimah and others that what is meant is the Sacred Mosque, and some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqun) preferred this view. It is expressed in the plural because it is the qiblah of the mosques and their leader (imam), toward which their prayer niches (mihrabs) are directed, so its maintainer is like the maintainer of them all. Or, because each side of it in its various directions is a mosque in its own right, unlike the rest of the mosques. This is supported by the reading of Abu ʿAmr, Yaʿqub, Ibn Kathir and Kathir, "masjid" (in the singular), with the singular form. Some have taken "mā kāna" to mean the negation of existence and realization, and have supplied the qualifier "with right," since they maintained it without right. But there is no need for that according to what we have mentioned. ﴿Bearing witness against themselves to disbelief﴾ — by displaying what indicates it, even if they do not say, "We are disbelievers." It was said that it is by their saying, "Here I am, O Allah, You have no partner, except a partner who is Yours, You possess him and what he possesses." It was also said that it is by their saying, "We disbelieve in what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought." This phrase is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in ﴿maintain﴾. It was said: that is, it is not consistent for them to combine two contradictory matters, the maintenance of the House and disbelief in its Lord, glory be to Him. Some said: the meaning is that it is impossible for what they call the maintenance of the House of Allah, while they are engaged in what contradicts and nullifies it, the worship of other than Him, glory be to Him, to be maintenance at all. It has been objected to the statement "the meaning is that it is not consistent for them to combine two contradictories" that it does not express the true intent, for the inconsistency of combining two contradictories only requires the absence of one of them, unspecified, and not the absence of maintenance, which is the goal. Its apparent sense is that the negation in the sentence applies to the qualifier. In that case there is no barrier to what is meant by "mā kāna" being the negation of propriety, as we have stated, and the purpose is to nullify the polytheists' boasting in this, since it is attached to what contradicts it, which is polytheism. It is also permitted that the negation be directed at the qualifier, as is common, though this requires strained interpretation that is not free from scrutiny. Perhaps whoever said in explaining the meaning, "it is not consistent for them to combine..." made the focus of attention the concomitance that the circumstantial clause implies. Even so, it does not preclude that the intended meaning, given the context, is the negation of the validity of boasting about maintenance and providing water (siqayah). So reflect deeply.

Page 65

Among what indicates that the context is the negation of boasting is what Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Jarir reported from al-Dahhak: when al-Abbas was taken captive, the Muslims reproached him for polytheism and severing the ties of kinship, and ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face, spoke harshly to him. He said: "You mention our faults and conceal our virtues. Indeed, we maintain the Sacred Mosque, we serve the pilgrims, and we free the captive." Then this was revealed.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, something similar. ﴿Those﴾ — that is, the polytheists mentioned — ﴿their deeds have become void﴾, the deeds in which they take pride, because of the disbelief accompanying them, so they become as nothing. ﴿And in the Fire they will abide forever﴾ — because of the enormity of what they committed. The nominal form of the sentence is for emphasis on eternal abiding, and the adverbial phrase "in the Fire" is connected to the predicate, placed before it for emphasis on it and to observe the rhyme (fasilah).

This sentence was said to be coordinated (ʿatf) with the sentence ﴿their deeds have become void﴾, as another predicate for "those." It was said to be a new sentence, like the sentence ﴿those have become void﴾. Their benefit is to confirm the earlier negation: the first, in terms of negating the consequence of reward, and the second, in terms of negating the averting of punishment.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 18:

﴿Only he who maintains the mosques of Allah﴾ There is disagreement about what is meant by "the mosques" here, just as there is disagreement about it elsewhere. The difference is that whoever held there that the intended meaning is only the Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram) permitted here that it refers to all mosques. He said: "It does not contradict the requirements of the context, since affirmation is not like negation." He claimed that the purpose is to restrict the actual realization of maintenance to the believers, not to restrict its fitness and permissibility. I see that restricting fitness is appropriate without any restriction. It was also read in the singular (al-tawhid), meaning: it is only fitting that he maintain it ﴿who believes in Allah and the Last Day﴾ in the manner revealed by the Revelation ﴿and establishes the prayer and gives the zakat﴾ (obligatory alms), which the Messenger (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) brought. Thus belief in him (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) is necessarily included in this, since these matters are received only from him (may Allah bless him and grant him peace).

It is also permitted that the mention of belief in him (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) was entirely omitted under the mention of belief in Allah the Exalted, indicating that the two are like one thing: when one is mentioned, the other is understood. Moreover, by mentioning the origin and the return, it is pointed out what must be believed in entirely, and among its components is his (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) prophethood. It has also been said: the reason he (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) is not mentioned is that the intended "one who" (man) is the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) and his companions, that is, the one deserving of maintaining the mosques is whoever has this description, whoever he may be. The discussion is not about establishing his prophethood (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) and belief in him, but about the person himself, his maintenance of the mosque, and his entitlement to it. So the verse is in the manner of His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, I am the Messenger of Allah to you all﴾ up to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So believe in Allah and His Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, who believes in Allah and His words﴾. The second view is preferable.

By maintenance is meant what encompasses repairing what has fallen into disrepair, sweeping and cleaning it, and beautifying it by laying down carpets, provided this is not in a way that distracts the worshipper's heart from presence. Perhaps what is of the kind that grows from the earth, such as cotton and Samaniyya mats (a type of woven mat), is preferable to things like wool, since it has been said that praying on wool is disliked. Maintenance also includes illuminating mosques with lamps, even if there is no one there to benefit from the light, as stated by a group of scholars; continuing worship and remembrance in them; studying the religious sciences in them; and similar things; and protecting them from what they were not built for in the view of the Lawgiver, such as worldly talk. Among such things is singing from their minarets, as is customary among people today, especially with verses most of which are indecent speech.

It has been narrated from him (may Allah bless him and grant him peace): "Talking in the mosque devours good deeds as an animal devours grass." This hadith concerns permissible talk, so what do you think of forbidden talk absolutely, or raised above the minarets? Al-Tabarani narrated with a sound chain from Salman (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace), who said: "Whoever performs ablution in his house and then comes to the mosque, he is a visitor of Allah the Exalted, and it is a right upon the one visited to honor the visitor."

Sulaym al-Razi narrated in al-Targhib (Kitab al-Targhib wa-l-Tarhib) from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him), who said:
Page 66
The Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said: "Whoever lights a lamp in a mosque, the angels and the bearers of the Throne will continue to seek forgiveness for him for as long as its light remains in that mosque." Abu Bakr al-Shafi'i and others narrated from Abu Qirafa, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) say: 'Removing refuse from the mosque is the dowry of the dark-eyed maidens (al-hur al-'in).'" And I heard him (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) say: "Whoever builds a mosque for Allah the Exalted, Allah the Exalted will build a house for him in Paradise." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, and what about these mosques that are built on the roads?" He (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said: "And these mosques that are built on the roads."

Al-Tabarani narrated from Abu Umama, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said: 'Going to the mosque in the morning and in the evening is part of jihad in the way of Allah the Exalted.'" Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it sound (hasan), Ibn Majah, and al-Hakim, who graded it authentic (sahih), and a group narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said: 'When you see a man who regularly frequents the mosque, bear witness to his faith.'" Then the Messenger (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) recited: ﴿Only he who maintains﴾ the verse.

The mention of giving zakat in the verse has been questioned, since its relevance to maintenance is not apparent. It has been forced to explain this by saying that the poor attend mosques to receive zakat, so they populate them, and that whoever does not give money for obligatory zakat does not give it for maintaining mosques. But this, as you see, is far-fetched. The truth is that the purpose is to show that the one who maintains the mosques is the believer whose faith is manifest, and his faith becomes manifest only by performing his obligations. So the conjoining of establishing the prayer and giving zakat to faith is to point to this. ﴿And does not fear﴾ anyone ﴿except Allah﴾, so he acts according to the requirement of His command and prohibition, not taking in the cause of Allah the blame of any blamer, and no fear of a tyrant prevents him. This includes not fearing in battle, which is rebuked in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Do you fear them? Allah has more right that you should fear Him.﴾ As for natural fear of frightening things, it is not of this category, nor is it something that falls under obligation. The address and prohibition in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Take it and do not fear﴾ are not meant literally.

It has been said: they used to fear the idols and hope in them, so the intent is to negate that fear from them. ﴿It is hoped that those﴾ described with the most perfect of attributes ﴿may be among the guided﴾, that is, toward Paradise and what Allah the Exalted has prepared therein for His servants, as narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan. Presenting their guidance in this way, despite having these noble attributes, is in the form of expectation to cut off the desires of the disbelievers from reaching the positions of guidance. For these believers, who are as they are, if their matter is between "perhaps" and "it is hoped," then what is the state of the disbelievers, who are the house of disgrace and vile deeds? This also cuts off the believers' reliance on their deeds and their state, and guides them to prefer the side of fear over the side of hope. This is what is appropriate to the context, not desire or the way of kings, even though the intent is the obligatory. Since the disbelievers claim that they are right and that others are upon falsehood, the cutting off of their desires cannot be accomplished in this way, but they do not turn to it after the truth becomes manifest. This is beyond doubt.

It has also been said: although the mentioned attributes necessitate guidance, remaining steadfast upon them is something only Allah the Exalted knows, and something may occur that brings about the opposite, and what matters is the outcome. So the word of expectation may be for this. But what is wrong with this is not hidden, since considering the outcome here does not suit the context, which requires preferring the believers over them in the present state.

**[Page 67]**

﴿Do you consider the providing of water for the pilgrims and the maintenance of the Sacred Mosque as equal to one who believes in Allah and the Last Day and strives in the way of Allah?﴾

*al-siqayah* (providing water) and *al-'imarah* (maintenance) are verbal nouns of *asqa* and *'amara* in the light form. The intensive form *'ammara* is used of the lifespan of a person (*'umr*), not of the maintenance of a building, as the common people mistakenly think. The *ya'* in *siqayah* is sound because it is followed by the feminine *ta'* (*ha' al-ta'nith*).

The apparent sense of the verse is that an act is compared with an agent, and an attribute with a substance, and this is not appropriate here. Therefore an implied element must be supplied. It may be supplied on the side of the attribute, meaning: "Do you consider the people who provide water and maintain the mosque as equal to one who believes?" This is supported by the *qira'ah* (recitation) of Muhammad ibn 'Ali al-Baqir, may Allah be pleased with him, Ibn al-Zubayr, Abu Ja'far, and Abu Wajzah al-Sa'di, who was among the reciters although he was famous as a poet, who read *Aja'altum siqat al-hajj* (with a *damma* on the *sin*, as the plural of *saqin*) and *wa 'amarat al-masjid* (with two *fathahs*, as the plural of *'amir*). Likewise the recitation of al-Dahhak reads *siqayata* with a *damma* also, with the *ya'* and the *ta'*, and *'amarata* as in the previous recitation. The reading *siqayah* in this case may be understood as a plural formed on the pattern *fu'al* and then made feminine, as some plurals are made feminine, such as *hijarah*. In both recitations there is a comparison of substance with substance.

It may be supplied on the side of the substance, meaning: "Do you consider these two (the providing of water and the maintenance) as equal to the faith of one who believes and the struggle of one who strives?"

It was also said: there is no need for any supplied element in anything, and the verbal noun here has the meaning of the active participle. The meaning according to this is as in the first case. In any event, the address is either to the polytheists, by way of *iltifat* (a shift of address), which most of the verifying scholars preferred and which is the one that comes first to mind from the wording of the verse. The mention of faith is specified on the side of the thing compared to, and this is supported by what Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the polytheists said: "The maintenance of the House of Allah the Exalted and attending to the providing of water are better than faith and struggle." So Allah the Exalted mentioned the excellence of faith in Him, glorified be He, and the struggle along with His Prophet (ﷺ), over the polytheists' maintenance of the House and their attending to the providing of water.

And by what Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from al-Dahhak, who said: The Muslims turned to al-'Abbas and his companions who were taken captive on the day of Badr, reproaching them for polytheism. Al-'Abbas said: "By Allah, we used to maintain the Sacred Mosque, release the captives, cover the House, and provide water to the pilgrims." So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿Do you consider...﴾, the verse. This is clear in showing that the address is to them, and they are polytheists.

Or the address is to some believers who preferred the providing of water and the maintenance over emigration and struggle. This is supported by what Muslim, Abu Dawud, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and a group transmitted from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "I was by the pulpit of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with a group of his companions. One man among them said: 'I do not mind if I do no deed for Allah the Exalted after Islam except that I provide water to the pilgrims.' Another said: 'Rather, the maintenance of the Sacred Mosque.' Another said: 'Rather, struggle in the way of Allah the Exalted is better than what you have said.' So 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, rebuked them and said: 'Do not raise your voices by the pulpit of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and that was on Friday. But when you have prayed the Friday prayer, I shall enter upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and ask him for a ruling concerning what you have differed about.' So Allah the Exalted revealed the verse up to His saying, glorified be He: ﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾"

And by what was narrated through various chains that the verse was revealed concerning 'Ali, may Allah honour his face, and al-'Abbas. That is because the Commander of the Faithful, may Allah honour his face, said to him: "O 'Abbas, would it not be better if you emigrated to Medina?" He said to him: "Am I not in a position better than emigration? Do I not provide water to the pilgrims and maintain the House?" This is clear in showing that al-'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, was at that time a Muslim, contrary to what the other reports, some of which were mentioned earlier, require.

This view was supported by the claim that it is the more appropriate one, since the rebuttal of them is sufficient by clarifying that they are not equal in the sight of Allah to the second group, and by clarifying that the rank of the first group is higher in the sight of Allah, which apparently includes them in the rebuttal in a way that suggests they are not completely deprived. This is because of the presence of the comparative form (*af'al al-tafdil*). The inclusion of this is taken as a digression (*istitrad*) to prefer those who possess these attributes over other Muslims, which is contrary to the apparent meaning. Likewise the view that it was brought to prefer them over the disbelievers who provide water and maintain (the House). Although they have no rank in the sight of Allah the Exalted, they came according to their own claim and assertion. However, it has been said against this: it does not contain much benefit, for if it does not suggest non-deprivation, it does not suggest deprivation either. The speech according to the first (interpretation) is a rebuke of the polytheists, and its basis is the denial of comparing themselves, in terms of their being described by the two attributes mentioned, with the believers in terms of their being described by faith and struggle, setting aside what they were upon of polytheism. Or according to the second, the denial of comparing their two attributes mentioned in themselves, while overlooking their being accompanied by polytheism versus faith and struggle.

The view that considers accompaniment is one that the verifying scholars overlooked, because the context rejects it. How could it not, when the nullification of their deeds has been explained on that basis, and that they are as nothing? So rebuking them afterwards for comparing these deeds with faith and struggle, and then rejecting that with something that suggests they are not completely deprived of the basic virtue, is something the noble wording does not support. If that were intended, there would be no need to affirm the denial of comparison and to emphasize it with something else, since nothing is more obviously false than attributing the non-existent to the existent. It was also said: there is no obstacle to considering it, and one sets aside what preceded concerning the explanation of nullification, and the non-deprivation that is perceived is based on that. But in this there is what there is.

The meaning is: "Do you consider the people of the providing of water and the maintenance as equal in excellence and loftiness of rank to one who believes in Allah and the Last Day and strives in His way?" Or: "Do you consider these two in that respect as equal to faith and struggle? How far apart they are! For the providing of water and the maintenance, although in themselves they are among the acts of righteousness and goodness, yet even if they are free of defects, they are far from being such that their people should be compared with the people of faith and struggle, or that they themselves should be compared with the very essence of faith and struggle."

That is the statement of His, glorified be He: ﴿They are not equal in the sight of Allah﴾, meaning the first group is not equal to the second. By its apparent meaning the first interpretation is preferred. If the intended meaning is "they are not equal in their attributes," it returns to the negation of equality in attributes, which agrees with the denial in the second interpretation. The attributing of the non-equality to the two described parties is because the more important matter is to explain their difference. The directing of the negation and the denial here toward equality and comparison, whereas earlier it was directed toward the act of comparison, is for the sake of intensifying the rebuttal of them, although the claim of those who boast of the providing of water and the maintenance, whether from the polytheists or the believers, is only superiority, not equality and resemblance. For the negation of equality and resemblance is, by a stronger way, a negation of superiority. However, it should be known that the superiority claimed by the polytheists suggests the establishment of the basic virtue for the one they are preferred over, and they are far from believing this. How could it be imagined from them that there is virtue in their struggle and their killing, or that there is virtue in faith, which necessarily entails refuting their opinion about what they are upon? So that must be by way of accommodation to their claim. So do not overlook this.

The sentence is a resumption (*isti'naf*) to establish the aforementioned denial and to emphasize it. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the two objects of the verb of making (*ja'ala*), and the link is the plural pronoun, as if it were said: "You made them equal while they are differing in the sight of Allah." ﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾: by "the people" are meant the polytheists, and by "wrongdoing" is meant polytheism, or the placing of a thing in other than its proper place, whether it is polytheism or something else, so their wrongdoing in that act of making equal is included in it, and this is more forceful in censure. By "guidance" is meant the guidance that leads to the destination, not mere indication, because that would not suit the context. This is a judgment from Him, the Exalted, that He, glorified be He, does not grant success to these wrongdoers in knowing the truth and distinguishing the preponderant from the less preponderant. Perhaps it was brought to increase the affirmation of the non-equality.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 20:

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Those who believed and emigrated and strove in the way of Allah with their wealth and their selves are greater in rank with Allah﴾ is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) explaining the degrees of their excellence, as an increase in the refutation and a completion of it. The mention of emigration (hijrah) and the specification of the two kinds of struggle (jihad) serve to indicate that these are among the necessary requirements of jihad, not that something was taken into account by way of compensation which had not been taken into account previously. The apparent sense from the context is that the one being surpassed (al-mufaddal 'alayhi) is the people of the water-providing (al-siqayah) and the maintenance of the Sacred House ('imarah) among the polytheists. We have already pointed to what this involves and what is upon it, as mentioned by some of the scholars. I say: if by the elative form (af'al) is meant hyperbole in excellence and the height of rank and station, then the matter is easy. If it is meant in its literal sense, then there are two possibilities. The first: it is said that the one surpassed has been omitted to indicate generality, meaning that these who are characterized by these attributes are higher in rank and more honoured than whoever is not so characterized, whoever he may be, and the people of the water-providing and the maintenance are included within this. The existence of the root of the act in some of the individuals falling under the generality suffices for the realization of the reality of the elative form, as one says: "So-and-so is the most knowledgeable of creation," although among them are those who do not possess any knowledge at all, indeed it is impossible for them to possess it in any way. This is something that should not be doubted, except that it troubles us that the one intended as the one surpassed in the example is one who shares in the root of the act, and this is not the case in what we are dealing with. If this does no harm, then the matter is as such; otherwise it is as you see. The second: it is said that what the form conveys, namely that the water-providers and the maintainers among the polytheists have a degree, came according to the assumption of the polytheists, and the occurrence of the like in their speech with the believers made this acceptable, for they said, as indicated by some of the earlier reports: "The water-providing and the maintenance are better than faith and jihad."
