There is no doubt that what is implied, namely that there is good in the water-providing and maintenance, is better than saying that there is good in faith and jihad; this came according to the assumption of the believers. So what is in the verse is outside the form of correspondence (al-mushakalah) with what is in their speech, even though the wording differs. As for what has been said, that making the meaning of preference relative to the assumption of the unbelievers has little benefit, it is not without considerable harm, as is not hidden from one who has tasted the flavour of eloquence even at the tip of the tongue. The words of some of them imply that the preference is based on what was earlier mentioned of setting aside consideration and closing the eye, i.e., those characterized by these noble attributes are higher in rank than those devoid of them, even if the latter have gained all the other things that are perfections in themselves, such as the water-providing and the maintenance. The intended sense of "the way of Allah" here is sincerity or something similar, not jihad; so the meaning is: strive sincerely. ﴿And those﴾ who are described by what was mentioned ﴿are the triumphant﴾, i.e., those specially singled out for the great triumph, or for absolute triumph, as if the triumph of others is not a triumph in comparison with theirs.

As for the second possibility, the address is a rebuke to whoever prefers the water-providing and the maintenance of the believers over emigration and jihad. That is: do you make the people of these two among the believers equal in excellence and honour to one who believed in Allah and the Last Day and struggled in His way; or do you make these two like faith and jihad? They said: the mention of faith was not made on the side of the compared item (al-mushabbah) although it is necessarily considered in it with certainty, relying on the clarity of the matter, and to indicate that the focus of denying the comparison is the water-providing and the maintenance, not faith. Nor was its mention abandoned on the side of the item compared to (al-mushabbah bihi) also, to strengthen the denial and to remind of the causes of preponderance and the principles of superiority, and to indicate the complete mutual entailment between faith and what follows it.

The meaning of non-equality before Allah, the Exalted, and the greater rank of the second group according to this explanation, is evident.

By injustice (al-zulm) is meant injustice by placing each of the preponderant and the subordinate in the place of the other, not the more general sense of injustice. By non-guidance is meant that He, the Exalted, does not guide those who prefer such to the knowledge of that, not non-guidance absolutely. The restriction in His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Those are the triumphant﴾ is relative to the rank of the second group, or to absolute triumph, and is a claim, as has passed. End.

You know that the non-mention of faith on the side of the compared item is evident, because the believers did not dispute, as indicated by the earlier hadith of Muslim, except concerning what is most excellent after it: so some said the water-providing, some said the maintenance, and some said jihad. Yes, its mention on the side of the item compared to requires a particular point, and the rebuke in the verse on this assumption is more emphatic than on the first assumption, so reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 21:

﴿Their Lord gives them good tidings﴾, that is, in this world, through the tongue of His Messenger (ﷺ). Hamzah recited (yabshuruhum) with a fatha on the ya', a sukun on the ba', and a damma on the shin, and with the light form (al-takhfif), on the basis that it derives from the triliteral bashara. Abu al-Shaykh narrated it from Talhah ibn Musarrif. In mentioning the title of Lordship (al-Rububiyyah) together with its attribution to their pronoun, and in the fact that He, glory be to Him, is the one who gives the good tidings, there is a subtlety and gentleness that is not hidden. ﴿With mercy from Him﴾, vast; ﴿and approval﴾, great; ﴿and gardens﴾, lofty, whose fruits are near at hand; ﴿for them therein﴾, that is, in the gardens, and it has been said: in the mercy, ﴿is enduring bliss﴾, that does not move on or depart from them. And this is
page 70
a metaphor for what is lasting.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 22:**

﴿Abiding therein forever.﴾ That is, in the Gardens (*abadan*, "forever"), an emphasis on what *al-khulud* (eternal abiding) already indicates, and a removal of the possibility that it might mean a long stay. ﴿Indeed, with Allah is a great reward.﴾ It has no measure in comparison with the rewards of this world, or with the deeds that correspond to it. The sentence is a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*) that serves as a justification (*ta'lil*) for what preceded it.

Abu Hayyan mentioned that when Allah, exalted is He, described the believers with three attributes, namely faith, emigration (*hijrah*), and striving (*jihad*) with their selves and their wealth, He matched these with the good tidings of three things: mercy (*rahmah*), good pleasure (*ridwan*), and Paradise (*jannah*). Glorified is He, He began with mercy in correspondence to faith, because mercy depends upon it and because it is the most general and earliest of blessings, just as faith is the one that precedes. Then He mentioned good pleasure, which is the ultimate of beneficence, in correspondence to striving, in which there is the expenditure of souls and wealth. And mighty and majestic is He, He mentioned the Gardens (*jinan*) in correspondence to emigration and the abandonment of homelands, as an indication that, since they preferred leaving those (homelands), He replaced for them the abode of disbelief with the Gardens, the abode that is in His neighborhood.

In the authentic hadith, Allah, glorified is He, says: "O people of Paradise, are you pleased?" They say: "How could we not be pleased, when You have distanced us from Your Fire and admitted us into Your Garden?" Then He, glorified is He, says: "I have something better for you than that." They say: "And what is better than that?" He, whose majesty is exalted, says: "I make My good pleasure lawful for you, so I shall never be displeased with you after it, forever."

It is not hidden that describing the Gardens as having for them a lasting bliss (*na'im muqim*), in accordance with this distribution, is of the utmost subtlety, since in emigration there is the journey, which is a portion of punishment.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 23:

﴿O you who have believed, do not take your fathers and your brothers as allies﴾ is a prohibition addressed to each individual among those addressed, against allying with a single individual from among the polytheists, not against allying with a group of them. This is understood from the noble composition by implication (dalalah), not by direct expression (ibarah). The verse, according to what al-Tha'labi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, was revealed concerning the Emigrants (al-Muhajirun), for when they were commanded to emigrate, they said: "If we emigrate, we will have cut off our fathers, our sons, and our tribe, our trade will go, our wealth will perish, our homes will be ruined, and we will remain lost." So it was revealed: "Then emigrate." A man's son, father, brother, or some of his relatives would come to him, and he would pay them no attention, nor would he host them, nor would he spend on them. Then they were granted a concession in this matter. It is also narrated from Muqatil that it was revealed concerning the nine who apostatized and joined Makkah, as a prohibition against allying with them. It is narrated from Abu Ja'far and Abu 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with them both, that it was revealed concerning Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah when he wrote to the Quraysh informing them of the affair of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he resolved to conquer Makkah. This, and what resembles it, requires that this verse was revealed before the Conquest. Al-Imam al-Razi raised an objection to this, that the correct view is that this surah was revealed only after the Conquest of Makkah, so how can the cause of revelation be what has been mentioned? It is answered that its revelation before the Conquest does not contradict the revelation of the surah after it, because what is meant is most of it and its beginning. And on the view that it was revealed concerning Hatib, the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the cause, and Hatib clearly enters into the prohibition against taking them as allies.

﴿if﴾ i.e., they preferred ﴿disbelief over faith﴾ and persisted in it with a persistence after which there is no hope of their ever giving it up at all. And in order to include the meaning of what has been mentioned, "istahabba" is construed with "'ala" (i.e., it is made to carry the sense of preferring, hence the use of "over"). The linking of the prohibition on taking them as allies to this condition is because, before that, their contact with them may perhaps lead them to Islam through their awareness of the excellences of the religion. ﴿And whoever allies with them﴾ i.e., any one of them. The pronoun in the verb is for the sake of observing the wording of the relative pronoun, and to indicate that each one of them is independently characterized by the wrongdoing that follows, because what is meant is that a single individual among them takes an ally. And the "min" in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿from among you﴾ is for the genus, not for partition. ﴿Then those﴾ i.e., those who take them as allies ﴿are the wrongdoers﴾ by placing alliance in other than its proper place. So "wrongdoing" is in its linguistic sense. It may also be meant as transgression and exceeding what Allah has set as limits, if what is meant is "whoever allies with them" after the prohibition. The restriction is claimed (hasr idda'i), as if the wrongdoing of others were no wrongdoing in comparison with their wrongdoing.

Page 71
In this there is of the admonition against alliance what is in it.

**[Commentary of al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, on Surah 9, verse 24]**

﴿Say﴾: a shift in address and a command to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to strengthen the believers and encourage their resolve to abstain from what they were forbidden: taking as allies their fathers and brothers, and those who are like them. He is to make them averse to these people and to cut their attachment to the base adornments of this world, by way of rebuke and warning. That is, say, O Muhammad, to the believers: ﴿If your fathers, your sons, your brothers, your spouses﴾. The sons and spouses were not mentioned in what came before, and they are mentioned here because what preceded concerned allies (*awliya'*), who are people of judgment and counsel, whereas sons and spouses are followers and do not have that role. What is mentioned here concerns love, and these are the most beloved to every person. ﴿And your kinsfolk (*'ashiratukum*)﴾: that is, your blood relatives. It has been said that a man's *'ashira* are his nearest family. Whichever is the case, mentioning them is for generality and comprehensiveness. The word is derived from *'ishra*, meaning companionship, because it is the nature of closeness. It has also been said that it is derived from *'ashara*, the known number ten, and the clan is so called for their completeness, because ten, as you know, is a complete number; or because there is a bond of lineage among them like the counting of ten, which is a type of binding (*'aqd*). But this is a remote meaning.

Abu Bakr, transmitting from 'Asim, read *'ashiratukum* in the plural form *'ashiratukum*, and al-Hasan read *'asha'irukum*. Abu al-Hasan denied that the first plural form occurs in their speech, and said that only the second plural form occurs. ﴿And wealth that you have acquired (*iqtaraftumuha*)﴾: that is, that you have earned. The root meaning of *iqtiraf* is to detach something from its place and move it elsewhere, from *qarafta al-qarha* when you peel a scab. *Al-qarf* is peeling. The wealth is described in this way as an allusion to its value in their eyes, since it was obtained through the sweat of the hand and the sweat of the brow. ﴿And commerce﴾: that is, goods you purchased for trade and profit. ﴿Whose slump you fear﴾: through the loss of the time of their market, by your absence from Makkah the Honored during the seasons. ﴿And dwellings you are pleased with﴾: homes in which you find delight to reside. The mention of these described attributes indicates that blame for loving what was mentioned of the adornments of the worldly life does not contradict what there is of the beginnings of love and the causes of desire for them. Although they have many kinds of beauty, they are far from being what Allah, glorified is He, described in His saying: ﴿more beloved to you than Allah and His Messenger﴾, with the love of choice that entails its effect, which is constancy and preference of obedience, not the inclination of the nature, for that is an innate matter that cannot be abandoned, for which one is not held accountable, and a person is not charged with refraining from it. ﴿And jihad in His cause﴾: that is, the path to His reward and His good pleasure, glorified is He. It seems that what is meant here as well is sincerity and the like, not fighting, though it is also applied to fighting, as the path of Allah, exalted is He. He has placed the love of these in the same string as the love of Allah, exalted is His affair, and the love of His Messenger, upon whom be blessings and peace, to honor its status, to alert that it is among what must be loved, let alone hated, and to indicate that love of it returns to the love of Allah, mighty and majestic, and the love of His beloved, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Jihad is an expression of fighting their enemies for the sake of their enmity, so whoever loves both of them must love fighting those who do not love them. ﴿So wait﴾: that is, await ﴿until Allah brings His command﴾: that is, His punishment, glorified is He, upon you, sooner or later. This is according to what is related from al-Hasan and preferred by al-Jubba'i. It is also related from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and Muqatil that it is the conquest of Makkah.

﴿And Allah does not guide the defiant people﴾: that is, those who depart from obedience by allying with the polytheists and preferring love of those mentioned over love of Allah, mighty and majestic, and His Messenger ﷺ. Or it means the defiant people in general, and those mentioned enter it primarily. That is, He does not guide them to what is good for them. This verse is the most severe verse of warning against people from which none can free himself except one whom Allah, glorified is He, reaches with His gentleness. In a hadith from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: "None of you tastes the sweetness of faith until he loves for the sake of Allah, exalted is He, and hates for the sake of Allah, exalted is He, until he loves for the sake of Allah, glorified is He, the most distant of people, and hates for the sake of Allah, mighty and majestic, the nearest of people." And Allah, exalted is He, is the Granter of success for the best of deeds.
* * *

[p. 72]

Among the allusions (*ishara*): He, glorified is He, has indicated the firm establishment of His Messenger, upon whom be blessings and peace, and the arrival of his Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, at the station of the Essential Unity (*al-wahda al-dhatiyya*), after they had been veiled, at times by the actions and at other times by the attributes. Through this, the opposition between them and the polytheists was realized in the most complete manner. Thus the declaration of disavowal was revealed, and they were commanded to renounce the covenant, so that agreement between the inner and the outer might occur. The polytheists were commanded to travel through the earth for four months, corresponding to the number of their stations in this world and the Hereafter, as an alert to them. When they stood in this world with others through polytheism, they were veiled from religion, actions, attributes, and essence, in the isthmus of the human realm (*nasut*). Thus it was necessary for them to be made to stand in the Hereafter before Allah, mighty and majestic, then before the Realm of Sovereignty (*jabarut*), then before the Realm of Dominion (*malakut*), then before the Fire, in the hell of traces (*jahim al-athar*), where they will be punished with various kinds of punishment. Whoever applies the verses to what is within the souls mentions that this period is the period of the full perfection of the four attributes: the vegetative, the animal, the satanic, and the human. Then He, glorified is He, said to them: ﴿And know that you cannot escape Allah﴾, since you must be detained at those stations because of your standing with others in polytheism. ﴿And that Allah will disgrace the disbelievers﴾, who are veiled from the truth, by their exposure when the rank of what they worshipped besides Him becomes manifest, and their standing with it before the Fire. ﴿And an announcement from Allah and His Messenger to the people on the day of the greater pilgrimage﴾: that is, at the time of the manifestation of the essential collectivity (*al-jam' al-dhati*) in the form of detail. ﴿That Allah is free of obligation to the polytheists, and so is His Messenger﴾. What is meant by this is the utmost opposition and contrariety, and the cutting off of spiritual support. What is meant by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿except those among the polytheists with whom you made a covenant and who have not failed you in anything﴾ is those in whom remains a trace of readiness and an effect of the soundness of nature, and remnants of nobility. The believers were commanded to fulfill their covenant with them until its term, which is the term of the accumulation of religion and the realization of the veil, if they do not return and repent. Then, after mentioning what He mentioned, glorified is He said: ﴿Those who disbelieved﴾: that is, in knowledge; ﴿and emigrated﴾: that is, they abandoned the sensory desires and the carnal homelands; ﴿and strove in the cause of Allah with their wealth﴾, which is the wealth of their knowledge, their wills, and their capacities. Jihad with these is an allusion to the effacement of their attributes, and jihad with the souls is an allusion to their annihilation in Allah, exalted is He. ﴿They are greater in rank﴾ in unity (*tawhid*) ﴿with Allah﴾, exalted is He. ﴿Their Lord gives them good tidings of mercy from Him﴾, which is the reward of deeds; ﴿and good pleasure﴾, which is the reward of attributes; ﴿and gardens for them, wherein is lasting bliss﴾, which is the contemplation of the Beloved that does not cease, and that is the recompense of the souls. The order of this arrangement is clear. Allah, exalted is He, undertook to give them good tidings Himself, so that they would increase in love for Him, blessed and exalted is He, because hearts are naturally inclined to love the one who gives them good news. Then He, glorified is He, made clear that spiritual kinship, spiritual affinity, and true connection deserve more consideration than mere outward connection when spiritual connection is absent and the direction differs. He, glorified is He, censured attachment to sensory familiar things and preferring them over the true Beloved, the first determination of Him, and the strongest cause for reaching the Presence, and He threatened punishment for it with what He threatened. We ask Allah, exalted is He, for success in what brings us near to Him; indeed He is the Patron of that.

[p. 73]

﴿Indeed, Allah has given you victory on many occasions﴾: this is an address to the believers specifically, and a favour bestowed upon them with victory over the enemies, a victory for which the jealous one would give up the dearest of things to him. The word *mawātin* is the plural of *mawṭin*, which is the place where its occupant dwells, and it is intended here as the sites of battle, i.e. its stations and positions. From this is the saying of the poet:

"How many a place, but for me, you would have been flung down, as things fall from the top of a steep cliff, tumbling."

The non-application of tanwīn (*al-man' min al-ṣarf*, the diptote form) is due to the pattern of the plural of paucity/abundance (*ṣīghat muntahā al-jumū'*). The *lām* is a preparatory *lām* introducing an oath (*al-lām al-mūṭṭi'a lil-qasam*), meaning: "I swear by Allah, Allah has indeed given you victory in positions and encounters (﴿many﴾)." Among them is the Battle of Badr, through which the sun of Islam shone; the (Battle of) Qurayẓa, and (that of) al-Naḍīr, and al-Ḥudaybiyya. Some have raised their number to eighty. It is narrated that al-Mutawakkil fell seriously ill, and vowed to give charity in a large amount if Allah Most High cured him.

[p. 73]

When he recovered, he asked the scholars about the measure of "a large amount," and their opinions differed. He was directed to ask Abū al-Ḥasan ʿAlī ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Mūsā al-Kāẓim, may Allah Most High be pleased with them, who had been detained in his house. He ordered that a letter be written to him, and he (ʿAlī al-Hādī) replied, may Allah Most High be pleased with him: "Let him give eighty dirhams in charity." Then they asked him about the reason, and he recited this verse and said: "We counted those positions and they amounted to eighty."

﴿And on the Day of Ḥunayn﴾: this is a conjunction (*ʿaṭf*, coordination) with the grammatical position (*maḥall*) of *mawāṭin*, and the coordination of a temporal adverbial (*ẓarf al-zamān*) with a spatial one (*ẓarf al-makān*), or the reverse, is permissible according to what the words of Abū ʿAlī (al-Fārisī) and those who followed him require. However, the apparent statement of some scholars is prohibition, because each of the two adverbials is linked to the verb directly without an intervening conjunction, and the complements of a verb are only coordinated with one another when they are of one kind. Others said: there is no prohibition against coordinating a time with a place or vice versa, but the better practice is to omit the conjunction in such cases. Whoever prohibits the coordination, or regards its omission as preferable, says: it is coordinated by omitting a governed noun (*ḥadhf al-muḍāf*), i.e. "and (the place of) the Day of Ḥunayn." Perhaps the change (of construction) is to hint at the lack of steadfastness that occurred at the outset of the affair.

It may also be considered that the omission is on the side of the coordinated-to element, i.e. "in the days of positions," and the coordination then is of the specific upon the general. The distinction of this specific (day) which the coordination points to is that its matter was strange and what occurred in it was remarkable: victory after despair, relief after hardship, and so on. The intended meaning is not an abundance of reward or greatness of benefit, lest it be objected that the Day of Ḥunayn was not superior to the Day of Badr, in which they obtained the arrow of the highest lot (*al-qidḥ al-muʿallā*) and won the lofty ranks; thus the subtlety of the coordination would not apply. It has been said that *mawṭin* is a noun of time, like "the place of the killing of al-Ḥusayn," so the two coordinated elements are homogeneous; but this is far from comprehension. Al-Zamakhsharī made it obligatory that *yawm* be governed by an implied verb, and the coordination be of a clause upon a clause, i.e. "and He gave you victory on the Day of Ḥunayn." It is not valid that its governing verb be the verb *naṣarakum* mentioned, because His words, "when your great number made you vain," are a substitute (*badal*, apposition) for "the Day of Ḥunayn," and so it would follow that the time of being vain at the number becomes the time of the victory which occurred in the many positions, because the verb is one and because the coordinated element is restricted by what restricts the coordinated-to element, and vice versa.

The day is restricted by the vanity at the number, and the governing verb extends over the substitute and the substituted-for element together; it follows from this that the time of vanity would be an adverbial and a restriction on the victory occurring in the many positions, and this is invalid, since there was no vanity in those positions.

It is answered that the verb in the two coordinated elements need not be one in such a way that it has no plurality of instances, as in "I struck Zayd today and ʿAmr before him," and "I strike him when he stands and when he sits," and so on. Rather, in such a phrase as "Zayd and ʿAmr," the consideration of individual instances is necessary, otherwise it would follow that a single accident subsists in one substance in two different loci, and this is impossible by necessity. Therefore it does not follow that restricting it with respect to the coordinated element by the restriction applied to it with respect to the coordinated-to element is required. We do not concede that this is the original usage such that anything else would need proof. Some have said: this would only follow if the substituted-for element were in the status of a separate element together with the conjunction, so that it reverts to "Allah gave you victory in many positions when your great number made you vain." But that is not the case; rather it reverts to "Allah gave you victory in many positions and when your great number made you vain," and there is no objection to this. Yet the status of the substitute as a restriction of the substituted-for element is open to question.

Ḥunayn is a valley between Mecca and al-Ṭāʾif, three miles from Mecca, where the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the Muslims fought the Hawāzin, the Thaqīf, and the Ḥashm, among whom was Durayd ibn al-Ṣimma, whose opinion they sought for blessing, and some people of Banū Hilāl and others. They numbered four thousand. The Muslims, according to what al-Kalbī narrated, were ten thousand; according to what is narrated from ʿAṭāʾ, sixteen thousand; and it has been said eight thousand. It is sound that they were twelve thousand: the ten thousand who came from Mecca and two thousand who joined them from the Ṭulaqāʾ. When they met, Salama ibn Salāma, or Abū Bakr,

[p. 74]

may Allah Most High be pleased with them both, said: "We will not be defeated today through lack of numbers," out of vanity at their large number. It has also been said that the one who said that was the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but al-Imām (al-Rāzī) considered this unlikely, because he (ﷺ) was detached from everything other than Allah, Mighty and Majestic. What supports this is what al-Bayhaqī related in *al-Dalāʾil* from al-Rabīʿ: that a man said on the Day of Ḥunayn, "We will not be defeated through lack of numbers," and that this grieved the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The apparent meaning is that this statement, if no other matter is joined to it, does not contradict reliance upon Allah Most High, nor does it entail depending on means. It grieved the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) only because of the circumstantial indications that accompanied it, which pointed to vanity. Perhaps the speaker took it from his (ﷺ) saying: "The best of companions are four, the best of expeditions are four hundred, and the best of armies are four thousand, and twelve thousand will not be defeated through lack of numbers, their word being one." But there accompanied it what accompanied it of vanity. Then the people fought a fierce battle, and the Muslims were overtaken by their vanity, and a group may be held accountable for the act of some of them. So they turned their backs in flight. The first to flee were the Ṭulaqāʾ, by deceit on their part, and that was a cause of disorder and the rout of others. It has also been said that they first charged against the polytheists and routed them, then they turned to the spoils, and the enemy counterattacked them, and what happened, happened. The Prophet (ﷺ) was on his white mule, while the mountains moved and he did not move, with al-ʿAbbās, and his cousin Abū Sufyān ibn al-Ḥārith, and his son Jaʿfar, and ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may Allah ennoble his face, and Rabīʿa ibn al-Ḥārith, and al-Faḍl ibn al-ʿAbbās, and Usāma ibn Zayd, and Ayman ibn ʿUbayd, who was killed before him (ﷺ). These are from his household. Abū Bakr and ʿUmar stood firm with him, may Allah Most High be pleased with them both, so they were ten men. For this reason al-ʿAbbās, may Allah Most High be pleased with him, said:

"We aided the Messenger of Allah in the battle, nine of us, when those who fled had fled from them and dispersed.

And a tenth, who met death with his own soul, with what touched him for the sake of Allah, he did not complain."

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) there appeared in that encounter such bravery as dazzled minds, and for this reason his Companions, may Allah Most High be pleased with them, affirmed that he (ﷺ) was the bravest of people. He was saying at that time, unconcerned with the enemies of Allah Most High:

"I am the Prophet, no lie; I am the son of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib."

He chose to ride the mule to show his steadfastness, which none denies except the donkey; and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had never thought of abandoning the fight. "He said to al-ʿAbbās, and he was loud-voiced: 'Call out to the people,' so he called: 'O servants of Allah! O companions of the tree! O companions of Sūrat al-Baqara!' They turned back as one body, with a yearning cry, saying, 'Here we are, here we are!' The angels descended, and they met the polytheists. The Prophet (ﷺ) said, when the battle became fierce: 'Now the oven is heated.' Then he took a handful of dust and threw it at them, and said (ﷺ): 'They are routed, by the Lord of the Kaʿba!'" So they were routed. The full account is in the books of the biographies (*kutub al-siyar*). ﴿But it did not avail you at all﴾: that is, that multitude did not benefit you in any measure of benefit against the enemy, or it did not give you anything that would meet your need. ﴿And the earth grew strait for you, despite its vastness﴾: that is, with its breadth and expanse, on the basis that *mā* is a verbal-source particle (*maṣdariyya*) and the *bāʾ* is for accompaniment (*lil-mulābasa wa-l-muṣāḥaba*); meaning: it became strait for you together with its spaciousness. In this there is a subsequent metaphor (*istiʿāra tabaʿiyya*), either because they did not find a place where they could settle in tranquillity, or because they did not sit in a place, as one does not sit in a narrow place. ﴿Then you turned back﴾: that is, the disbelievers turned you (your) backs, on the basis that *walla* is transitive to two objects, as in His words, ﴿so do not turn their backs to them﴾; and al-Rāghib's words indicate this. Some claimed there is no need to supply two objects, because in *al-Qāmūs*, *walla tawliya* means "he turned his back." Yet this is not a sound position according to some, and it is not valid; relying on al-Rāghib's statement in such a matter is more preferable to the verifiers (*al-muḥaqqiqīn*), and indeed it is said that the statement of *al-Qāmūs* is not reliable in such a matter. His words, Exalted is He, ﴿retreating﴾ (*mudbirīn*) are a confirmatory circumstantial clause (*ḥāl mu'akkida*), and it derives from *al-idbār*, meaning going backward; and what is intended is "routed."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 26:

﴿Then Allah sent down His tranquility (sakinah) upon His Messenger﴾ (ﷺ), meaning His mercy by which hearts find rest and are fully reassured, which brings about near victory. As for tranquility in general, it was already present in him (ﷺ).

﴿and upon the believers﴾ is a conjunction with "His Messenger," and the repetition of the preposition indicates a difference between them. By "the believers" are meant those who fled. This indicates that a major sin does not negate faith.

From al-Hasan: they are those who remained steadfast with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It was also said: the meaning includes both groups, and this is not without merit. There is no harm in the basic tranquility being realized in those who had remained steadfast earlier. Some interpreters explained tranquility as security (amān). For the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) it was through witnessing the angels, peace be upon them, and for those with him through the appearance of signs of this. For those who fled it was through the removal of their anxiety and agitation by recalling that what Allah wills comes to pass and what He does not will does not come to pass, or something similar. The apparent meaning is that "then" (thumma) is in its proper place, indicating a time gap between the flight and the sending down of tranquility in this interpretation.

It was also said: if by "the believers" the fleeing ones are meant, then "then" remains in its proper place. If the steadfast ones are meant, the delay lies in the reporting, or in regard to the whole of this sending down and what is conjoined to it. Taking "then" to indicate a delay in rank is far-fetched.

﴿and He sent down hosts you did not see﴾ with your eyes, as some of you see others. They were the angels, peace be upon them, on piebald horses, with white markings. That the meaning is that you had not seen their like before that is contrary to the apparent sense, and we have not found in the reports anything that supports it. They differed regarding their number. It was said: eight thousand, based on His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When you said to the believers: "Is it not enough for you that your Lord reinforce you with three thousand angels sent down?"﴾ together with His saying after that: ﴿Your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand angels﴾. It was said: five thousand, the second verse and the third being included, and the first being included within these five. It was said: sixteen thousand, according to the number of the two armies: twelve thousand the army of the Muslims and four thousand the army of the polytheists. Likewise they differed as to whether they fought in this battle or not. The majority hold that the angels did not fight except on the day of Badr, and that they descended only to strengthen the hearts of the believers by casting good thoughts into them and supporting them thereby, and to cast terror into the hearts of the polytheists. Regarding this, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: a man who had been among the polytheists on the day of Hunayn told me: "When we routed the Muslims, we began driving them before us. When we reached the rider of the white mule, men with white faces met us and said: 'May the faces be defiled! Turn back!' So we turned back, and they mounted upon our shoulders."

Those who argued that they fought cited what is narrated: "A man from among the polytheists said to some of the believers after the fighting: 'Where are the piebald horses and the men wearing white garments? We did not see them among you except like the appearance of a mole, and our killing was only at their hands.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was informed of this, and he, peace be upon him, said: 'Those were the angels.'" But it has no chain of transmission on which one can rely.

﴿And He punished those who disbelieved﴾ by killing, capture and taking of captives. (﴿And that﴾) meaning what was done to them of what has been mentioned, ﴿is the recompense of the disbelievers﴾ for their disbelief in this world.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 27:

﴿Then Allah will turn in forgiveness after that [punishment]﴾ to whom He wills among them, if there is a wisdom that requires it; what is meant is that He grants them the guidance to Islam. ﴿And Allah is Ever-Forgiving﴾, who overlooks what has passed of their disbelief and sins, ﴿Most Merciful﴾ (﴿Rahim﴾), who bestows favour upon them and rewards them without any obligation upon Him, glory be to Him.

Al-Bukhari narrated from al-Miswar ibn Makhramah that "some men from them came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, pledged allegiance to him upon Islam, and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, you are the best of people and the most righteous of people. Our wives and children have been taken captive, and our property has been seized. On that day six thousand souls were taken captive, and camels and sheep were taken in uncountable numbers.' The Prophet ﷺ said: 'What you see is with me, and the truest speech is the most sincere. Choose either your offspring and your women, or your wealth.' They said: 'We do not value anything above our lineages.' The Prophet ﷺ then stood up and said: 'These people have come to us as Muslims, and we gave them the choice between their offspring and their wealth, and they did not value anything above their lineages. So whoever has something in his possession and is willing to return it, let him do so, and whoever does not, let him give us [something] and it will be a loan owed to us until we obtain something, and then we will give him its equivalent in return.' They said: 'We are content and have submitted.' The Prophet ﷺ said: 'We do not know; perhaps among you there are those who are not content. So instruct your ʿurafāʾ (chieftains/representatives) to bring this to us.' So the ʿurafāʾ reported to the Prophet ﷺ that they were content."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 28:

﴿O you who have believed, indeed the polytheists are unclean﴾. He described them by the verbal noun (maṣdar) for emphasis, as though they were the very essence of uncleanness (najāsah). Or the intended meaning is "possessors of uncleanness," because of the corruption of their inner selves and the corruption of their beliefs. Or because polytheism (al-shirk), which is with them, is in the position of uncleanness. Or because they do not purify themselves, do not perform ghusl, and do not avoid impurities, so impurity is attached to them. It is also permissible for ﴿unclean﴾ (najas) to be an adjective of the form ṣifah mushabbahah (the attributive adjective pattern), and al-Jawhari adopted this view. In that case, it is necessary to posit a singular noun modified by it, which is plural in meaning, so that the predication about the plural is valid. That is, "a kind of uncleanness" or something similar. Interpreting the verse in one of the senses of the masculine plural is what the speech of most jurists requires, since they held that the bodies of the polytheists are pure, and there is no difference between the worshippers of idols and other kinds of disbelievers in this ruling. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that their bodies are unclean like dogs and pigs. Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever shakes hands with a polytheist, let him perform wudu or let him wash his palms." Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Hisham ibn ʿUrwah, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) met Jibril, peace be upon him, and extended his hand to him, but he refused to take it. He said: 'O Jibril, what prevented you from taking my hand?' He said: 'You took the hand of a Jew, and I disliked that my hand should touch a hand that had been touched by a disbeliever.' So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called for water, performed wudu, and extended his hand, and he took it."

Al-Imam al-Razi inclined to what was reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, and this is what the apparent meaning of the verse requires, and one does not depart from it except by a separate proof. It has been said: according to this, it is not permissible to drink from their vessels, to eat with them, or to wear their clothing. However, the practice of the Prophet (ﷺ) and of the early generations (al-salaf) is contrary to this. The possibility that it was before the revelation of the verse is a remote abrogation (naskh, the cancellation of an earlier ruling by a later one). Caution is not hidden. The argument for their purity, that if their bodies were unclean, it would not be possible for their purity to be attained through faith, since it is not conceivable that faith purifies, is answered by: do you not see that if a pig said "There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah," it would not become pure? Physical uncleanness (najāsat al-ʿayn) is purified only by transformation (istihalah), according to the view of those who hold that. The body of the disbeliever has not been transformed by faith into another substance. This is nothing, though whoever is alarmed by the clatter thinks it is something. This is because purity and impurity are two matters that follow what is understood from the speech of the Lawgiver, upon him be prayer and peace, and they are not tied to transformation or its absence. So when it is understood from his speech that a thing is unclean at one time and pure at another time, or the reverse, as in the case of wine, it is followed, even if there is no transformation there. This is evident.

Ibn al-Sumayqaʿ read ﴿anjas﴾ in the plural form. Abu Haywah read ﴿nijs﴾ with a kasrah on the nun and a sukun on the jim, and it is a lightened form of najas, like kibd for kabad. In that case a modified noun is posited as we established just above, following what al-Jawhari said. The word most often occurs as a follower (tābiʿ) of rijs. The statement of al-Farra', which al-Hariri followed in his Durrah, that this is not permissible without the use of a follower, is refuted by this reading, since there is no following in it.

﴿So let them not approach al-Masjid al-Haram﴾: this is a consequence (tafriʿ) of their uncleanness. The intended meaning is prohibition of entering, except that they were forbidden from approaching for emphasis.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq and al-Nahhas narrated from

[p. 77]

ʿAta' that they were forbidden from entering the whole Haram. Then the prohibition of approaching the mosque itself is on its apparent meaning. Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him, adopted the apparent meaning, since he turned the prohibition of entering the Haram into a prohibition of Hajj and ʿUmrah. What supports this is His words, exalted is He: ﴿after this year of theirs﴾, for restricting the prohibition by this indicates that what is forbidden is specific to a time of the year. That is: they should not perform Hajj or ʿUmrah after the Hajj of this year of theirs, which was the year nine after the Hijrah, when Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, was appointed over the pilgrimage season. What indicates this is the proclamation of ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face, on the day he proclaimed the Declaration of Immunity (Bara'ah): "No polytheist shall perform Hajj after this year of ours." Likewise His words, glorified is He: ﴿and if you fear poverty﴾, that is, destitution, because of their being prevented, since they used to come during the season with merchandise. This only occurs if they were prevented from entering the Haram, as is not hidden.

The summary is that the great Imam (Abu Hanifah) says the prohibition is on Hajj and ʿUmrah, and the prohibition is understood as such; and they are not prevented from entering al-Masjid al-Haram and the rest of the mosques according to him. The school of al-Shafiʿi, Ahmad, and Malik, may Allah be pleased with them, as al-Khazin said, is that it is not permissible for a disbeliever, whether a dhimmi or a musta'min (one under safe conduct), to enter al-Masjid al-Haram under any circumstances. So if an envoy comes from the abode of disbelief while the Imam is there, he is not permitted to enter; rather the Imam goes out to him himself, or sends someone who hears his message outside it. Entering other mosques is permissible according to al-Shafiʿi, may Allah have mercy on him. According to Malik: all mosques are alike in prohibiting the disbeliever from entering them. Some claimed that the prohibition in the verse is only against taking charge of al-Masjid al-Haram and attending to its affairs, and this is very contrary to the apparent meaning. The apparent meaning is the prohibition, as you have known. That the cause of the prohibition is their uncleanness, even if we do not say that it is intrinsic, does not imply the permissibility of the act for one who has performed ghusl and wears pure clothing, because the specificity of the cause does not restrict the ruling, as in the case of istibra' (the waiting period). The discussion on the limit, "I shall not let you see it here," is a metaphor (kinayah) for forbidding the believers from enabling them to do what was mentioned. The evidence is that what precedes and what follows is addressed to the believers. Whoever takes it on its apparent meaning uses it as proof that disbelievers are addressed concerning the subsidiary rulings (al-furu'), since they were prohibited in it, and prohibition is among the rulings. That they do not desist from it does no harm after knowing the meaning of addressing them with it.

It is related that when the prohibition came, it was hard for the believers, and they said: "Who will bring us our food and goods?" So Allah, glorified is He, revealed: ﴿And if you fear poverty, Allah will enrich you from His bounty﴾, that is, from His gift, or His favouring in another way. ﴿Min﴾ (from) in the first interpretation is either the beginning of the limit (ibtidā'iyyah) or partitive (tab'īḍiyyah), and in the second it is causal (sababiyyah). Allah, exalted is He, indeed fulfilled His promise by sending the sky upon them in abundant rain, and He guided the people of Najd, Tubalah, and Jurash, so they embraced Islam and brought to them food and what they needed for their livelihood. Then He opened the lands and the spoils to them, and people came to them from every deep ravine. It is related from Ibn Jubayr that he interpreted "bounty" as the jizyah (poll tax). This is supported by the fact that the subsequent matter bears witness to it, but what we have mentioned is more preferable, and the matter of testimony is light. ﴿ʿAylah﴾ was read as well, either as a verbal noun like al-ʿāqibah and al-ʿāfiyah, or as an active participle adjective modifying a feminine noun posited as understood, that is, "a state of being destitute," i.e., "in need." The restriction of the enrichment by His words, glorified is He: ﴿if He wills﴾ is not for doubt, so as to be problematic since it does not suit the context and the occasion of revelation. Rather it is to clarify that this is by His will, and there is no cause for it other than His will, so that they turn to Him, glorified is He, and cut their gaze away from anything else. In it is an indication that He, glorified is He, bestows that enrichment as a favour, and nothing is obligatory upon Him, mighty and majestic is He, for if it were by obligation, it would not have been left to His will. It is also permissible that the restriction is because enrichment is not uniform according to individuals, states, and times. ﴿Indeed Allah is Knowing﴾ of your conditions and your interests, ﴿Wise﴾ in what He gives and withholds.

[Page 78]

This is a command to fight the People of the Book, following the command to fight the polytheists and preventing them from circling the Sacred Mosque. Within it is a hint to them about one of the ways of the promised enrichment. The expression of them by the relative pronoun is to indicate that the cause of the command to fight is what is in the clause of the relative (their lack of faith in God and the Last Day), and that they are, because of this, grouped with the polytheists, and that their belief, which they claim, is not as it should be; it is like no belief at all.

﴿And do not forbid what God and His Messenger have forbidden﴾, that is, what has been established as forbidden by revelation, recited and unrecited. By "the Messenger" is meant our Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace. It has been said that by "the Messenger" is meant their own messenger, whom they claim to follow, for they have altered his law and made lawful and unlawful things of their own accord, following their desires. So the meaning would be: they do not follow our law nor their own law. The combination of both matters is a cause for fighting them, even though alteration after abrogation (naskh) is not an independent cause.

﴿Nor do they follow the religion of truth﴾, that is, the established religion. The construction is then an idafah (genitive construction) of the attribute to the thing described, and by it is meant the religion of Islam, which is not abrogated by any religion, as every religion was abrogated by it. It is reported from Qatadah that by "the truth" is meant God Most High, and by His religion is meant Islam. It has also been said that it includes this and other things, that is, they do not follow any of the religions which God, glorified is He, revealed to His prophets and prescribed for His servants. On this view, the idafah is on its apparent meaning.

﴿From among those who were given the Book﴾, that is, its genus, which includes the Torah and the Gospel. The "min" (from) is explanatory (bayaniyyah), not partitive (tab'idiyyah), so that some of them would not be in contrast to what was described.

﴿Until they give﴾, that is, until they agree to give. (﴿the jizyah﴾), that is, what has been fixed upon them to give. It is derived from jaza dayna-hu, meaning he settled his debt, or from jaziytu-hu bi-ma fa'ala, meaning I requited him for what he did, because they are "requited" by it those who were pardoned from being killed. In the book al-Hidayah, it is said that it is the recompense for disbelief, and so it comes from requital (mujazah). It has also been said that its original root is hamz (the hamzah), from juz' (part) and tajzi'ah (division), because it is a portion of wealth that is given. Al-Khwarizmi said that it is arabized (mu'arrab), like zayt (oil) [i.e., of Persian origin], and it means the kharaj (land tax) in Persian. Its plural is juzya, like lihyah and lihan (beard, beards).

﴿Out of hand﴾ (ʿan yadin). It may be a circumstantial state (hal) of the pronoun in (yu'tu, "they give"), and it may be a circumstantial state of the jizyah. The "yad" (hand) may mean the giving hand, and may mean the receiving hand. The "ʿan" (from, out of) may indicate causation or other things. That is, they give the jizyah out of a hand that is compliant, meaning submissive, or accompanied by submission; or out of their own hand, meaning by themselves, or delivered by their own hands and not by the hands of others, such as an agent or a messenger, because the purpose in it is humiliation, and this contradicts that; and for this reason, delegation of it is forbidden by the law. Or it means "out of wealth," that is, they are wealthy, and for this reason it is not taken from a poor person who is unable to pay. Or "out of might and power," that is, they are humbled and powerless. Or it is accompanied by humiliation. Or "out of a favor bestowed upon them," for preserving their lives in exchange for what they have paid in jizyah is a great blessing; that is, they are favored, or it is one that comes from a favor bestowed upon them. Or it means "in cash," that is, delivered "hand to hand" (yadan bi-yad). The use of "yad" in the sense of submission is either literal or metaphorical. From this is the saying of ʿUthman, may God be pleased with him: "This is my hand for ʿAmmar," meaning: I am submissive and obedient to him. Its use in the sense of wealth is because it is a metaphor for power, which entails wealth. Its use in the sense of favor, and likewise the word "niʿmah" (blessing), is widespread and well known. As for the meaning of "in cash," it is due to the well-known expression "yadan bi-yad" in this regard. From this is the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri concerning usury (riba). What is in the verse can be interpreted in this way, as is not hidden from one who has mastery of the sciences of meaning and rhetoric (ma'ani and bayan).

The interpretation of "yad" here as "might and power" was transmitted by Ibn Abi Hatim from Qatadah. He also transmitted from Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah something indicating that he understood it in the way that most readily comes to mind from it, in the manner of what we mentioned in the second aspect. Other aspects were mentioned by many commentators.

The goal of fighting is not the giving itself, but its acceptance, as has been pointed out. Indeed, a group of jurists explicitly stated this, saying: "They are to be fought until they accept the jizyah." They expressed it with "giving" because it is the object sought from acceptance.

﴿And they are humbled﴾, that is, they are abased.

[Page 79]

This is done by having them give it while standing, while the one receiving it sits. This was said by Ikrimah. And it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that the jizyah is taken from the dhimmi (protected non-Muslim), and his neck is pushed (wajaʾ). In another narration, he is seized by the collar, shaken violently, and it is said to him: "Pay the jizyah, O dhimmi!" It has also been said that it means he is seized by the beard and struck on the jaw, and it is said: "Pay the right of God, O enemy of God!" It is related from al-Shafi'i that the humiliation (sighar) is the application of the rulings of the Muslims over them. All these opinions, we do not see any trace of them today, because the People of the Covenant (dhimmah) have already become distinguished over the Muslims, and the matter belongs to God, Mighty and Majestic, in many ways, to the extent that it is accepted from them that the jizyah be sent through a representative from among them. The most authentic reports, however, indicate that this is not accepted from them, but they are required to bring it themselves, on foot, not riding. All of this is due to the weakness of Islam; God, may He be exalted, deals with whoever was a cause of it according to His justice.

The jizyah is taken according to Abu Hanifah from the People of the Book absolutely, and from the polytheists of the non-Arabs (ʿajam) and the Magians, but not from the polytheists of the Arabs. This is because their disbelief has become more severe, since the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, grew up among them, and was sent to them, being, peace be upon him, from among themselves, and the Qur'an was revealed in their language. This is among the strongest incentives to their faith. Therefore, nothing is accepted from them except the sword or Islam, as an increase in punishment against them, along with the following of what is reported concerning this. It is not objected that the People of the Book have also had their disbelief made more severe, because they knew the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, with complete knowledge, and despite that, they rejected him and altered his name and description from the Book.

According to Abu Yusuf, it is not taken from an Arab, whether he is a People of the Book or a polytheist, and it is taken from a non-Arab, whether he is a People of the Book or a polytheist. Its taking from the Magians is established only by the Sunnah. It is authentically reported that ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, did not take it from them until ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf testified that "the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, took it from the Magians of Hajar."

Al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, said: It is taken from the People of the Book, whether they are Arab or non-Arab, and it is not taken from the People of Idols absolutely, because it is established for the People of the Book by the Book, and for the Magians by a report (khabar). So whoever is beyond them remains on the original ruling.

Our argument is that it is permissible to enslave them, and whoever it is permissible to enslave, it is permissible to impose the jizyah upon him, if he is from among the people of support (ahl al-nusrah), because each of the two involves the seizure of the self. As for enslavement, it is obvious, because the benefit of the slave returns to us entirely. As for the jizyah, it is because the unbeliever pays it from his earnings, while his maintenance is from his earnings. So the handing over of his earnings, which are the cause of his life, to the Muslims is, in meaning, equivalent to taking his self from him in judgment. Malik and al-Awza'i held that it is taken from all unbelievers. According to us, it is not taken from a woman, a child, a chronically ill person, or a blind person; likewise the paralyzed and the elderly. It is reported from Abu Yusuf that it is taken from the elderly if he has wealth, and not from a poor person who does not work, contrary to al-Shafi'i. Nor is it taken from a slave, a mukatab (a slave contracted for self-purchase), or a mudabbar (a slave whose master has freed him upon his death). It is not taken from the monks who do not mix with people, as some of our companions mentioned. Muhammad reported from Abu Hanifah that it is taken from them if they are able to work, and this is also the view of Abu Yusuf.

Then, it is of two kinds. One is the jizyah set by mutual consent and reconciliation, so it is determined according to what the agreement reaches, as the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, made a treaty with the people of Najran for two hundred garments; and because what makes it obligatory is mutual consent, it is not permissible to exceed what was agreed upon.

The second is the jizyah which the Imam begins to impose when he has overcome the unbelievers and left them in possession of their property. He imposes on the wealthy, the clearly wealthy, eight and forty dirhams each year, taken as four dirhams each month. On the middle-class, the moderately well-off, twenty-four dirhams each year, taken as two dirhams each month. On the poor who is able to work, that is, one who is able to work even if he has no skill, twelve dirhams each year, taken as one dirham each month. Apparently the reference for wealth and other categories is the custom (urf) of the locality. Abu Ja'far the jurist explicitly stated this. And to what we have followed concerning the differentiation of it by wealth, poverty, and moderate means, ʿUmar, ʿAli, and ʿUthman, may God be pleased with them, went. It is reported from al-Shafi'i that the Imam imposes on every adult male a dinar or its equivalent, and the rich and the poor are equal in this, based on what Ibn Abi Shaybah transmitted from Masruq, that the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, when he sent Mu'adh to Yemen, said to him: "Take from every adult male a dinar or its equivalent in ma'afir [a type of cloth]." He, peace be upon him, did not make distinctions. This has been answered by saying that it is to be understood as having been a reconciliation (sulh). This is supported by what is in some narrations: "from every adult male and female," because the jizyah is not obligatory upon women. According to us, the most correct view is that the obligation arises at the beginning of the year, because what is obligated as a substitute for something cannot be realized except in the future, so it is impossible to impose it after the year has passed; therefore we impose it at its beginning. It is reported from al-Shafi'i that it is obligatory at the end of the year, by analogy with zakat.

Al-Zayla'i objected to this, saying that zakat is not binding upon us, because it is due at the end of the year so that growth may be realized; it is due only on growing wealth, and the jizyah is not like that, so the analogy is invalid. And what al-Jassas stated in Ahkam al-Qur'an (The Rulings of the Qur'an) implies the obligation to kill those mentioned in the verse until the jizyah is taken from them in the manner of humiliation and abasement, since they have no protection (dhimmah) if they gain authority over the Muslims by holding office and enforcing commands and prohibitions. For God, glorified is He, granted them protection only through giving the jizyah and being humbled. Thus it is obligatory, on this basis, to kill whoever gains power over the Muslims through anger and through imposing unjust taxes, even if the sultan appointed him to that, and if he does so without his permission and command, then it is all the more obligatory. This indicates that these Jews and Christians who take charge of the sultan's affairs and his emirs, and in whom injustice, arrogance, and the imposition of taxes appear, have no protection, and their blood is lawful to shed. And if a Muslim attacks a Muslim to take his property, it is permitted to kill him in some cases; so what about these unbelieving infidels, enemies of the religion?

Our jurists have issued legal opinions prohibiting their holding of offices, since this is established by the explicit text. The rulers have been afflicted with this to the point that people have had to seek them out, indeed to kiss their hands, as we have witnessed many times. Not everything that is known is to be said. Indeed, we belong to God and to Him we return. This is it. The taking of the jizyah from these unbelievers has raised a difficulty: since their disbelief is among the greatest disbelief, how can they be left in it in exchange for a few counted dirhams?

Al-Qutb answered that the purpose of taking the jizya is not to confirm them in disbelief, but rather to give the disbeliever a period in which he may come to see the excellences of Islam and the strength of its proofs, and so embrace Islam.

Al-Itqani said: the jizya is not a substitute for permitting disbelief. Rather, it is a compensation for the killing and enslavement that were obligatory, and so it is permissible, like the waiving of retaliation (qisas) in exchange for a payment. Or it is a punishment for disbelief, like enslavement. The first alternative is more apparent, since the second would imply that the jizya may be imposed on women and the like. It may be answered that it is a substitute for support (nusra) for the fighters from among us. For this reason it varies (in amount), since everyone who is among the people of the Abode of Islam is obligated to support the Abode with his self and his wealth. And since the disbeliever is not fit for this, due to his inclination toward the Abode of War in belief, the jizya taken and spent on the warriors (ghuzat) is put in its place.

It is not objected that support is an act of obedience while this is a punishment, so how can a punishment be a substitute for obedience? This is because in the Nihaya it is stated that the substitute for support, with respect to the Muslims, is due to the increase in strength it brings them, and they are rewarded for that increase which results from their wealth. This is like the case of lending their animals to the warriors. From here you know that whoever says it is a substitute for acquiescence in disbelief has fallen into a grave delusion.

**[Commentary of al-Alusi, Ruh al-Ma'ani, on Surah 9, verse 30 (part 1 of 2)]**

﴿And the Jews said﴾ is a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*, a new sentence that picks up the discussion without grammatical dependence on what precedes it), brought in to confirm what came before about the People of the Two Scriptures not believing in God, Glorified is He, and their being grouped together with the polytheists in this. The one who said ﴿Uzayr is the son of God﴾ was among the leaders of the Jews. Attributing a repugnant statement made by some members of a group to the whole group is a common practice. The reason for this, as Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, is that 'Uzayr was among the People of the Book, and the Torah was with them, and they acted upon it as much as Allah willed them to act. Then they neglected it and acted contrary to the truth. The Ark (*al-tabut*) was with them. When Allah, Glorified and Exalted, saw that they had neglected the Torah and acted according to their desires, He lifted the Ark from them, made them forget the Torah, and removed it from their hearts. So 'Uzayr called upon his Lord, Mighty and Majestic,
[Page 81]
and implored Him to return to him what had been removed from his heart. While he was praying, imploring Allah, Mighty and Majestic, a light from Allah, Exalted is He, descended and entered his inner self, and what had gone from his inner self of the Torah returned. He then called out to his people and said: "O my people, Allah, Exalted is He, has given me the Torah and returned it to me." He then began to teach them, and they remained as long as Allah willed them to remain, while he taught them. Then the Ark descended upon them after its departure from them. They compared what was in it with what 'Uzayr had been teaching them, and found it to be the same. They said: "By Allah, 'Uzayr was given this only because he is the son of Allah, Glorified is He."

Al-Kalbi said regarding the reason for this: Bukhtansar (Nebuchadnezzar) invaded Jerusalem, prevailed over the Children of Israel, and killed those who recited the Torah. 'Uzayr was then a young boy, so he was not killed because of his youth. When the Children of Israel returned to Jerusalem and there was no one among them who could recite the Torah, Allah sent 'Uzayr to renew the Torah for them, and to be a sign for them after Allah had caused him to die for one hundred years. An angel came to him with a vessel containing water, and he drank from it, and the Torah took shape in his chest. When he came to them, he said: "I am 'Uzayr." They denied him and said: "If you are as you claim, then dictate the Torah to us." So he wrote it down for them from his chest. A man among them said: "My father told me on the authority of my grandfather that the Torah had been placed in a jar and buried in a vineyard." They set off with him until they took it out, and compared it with what 'Uzayr had written for them, and they found that he had not omitted a single letter. They said: "Allah, Exalted is He, would not have cast the Torah into the heart of 'Uzayr except because he is His son. Allah is exalted far above that, to a great degree." Other accounts have also been related, but all of the reports ultimately refer to the reason being his, peace be upon him, preservation of the Torah.

It has also been said that those who made this statement were a group of Jews of Medina, among them Sallam ibn Mishkam, Nu'man ibn Abi Awfa, Shas ibn Qays, and Malik ibn al-Sayf. Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they came to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, and said: "How can we follow you when you have abandoned our qibla, and you do not claim that 'Uzayr is the son of Allah?"

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Jurayj that the one who said this was Finhas ibn 'Azura, and he is, as some reports indicate, the one who said: ﴿Indeed Allah is poor and we are rich﴾.

In sum, this statement was widespread among them, and their denial of it carries no weight at all, nor does the claim of some of them that the actual statement was "Uzayr, Abana Allah," meaning "Uzayr, may Allah clarify His rulings," or something similar, after Allah had informed us of what He informed us of.

'Asim, al-Kisa'i, Ya'qub, and Sahl read ﴿'Uzayrun﴾ with tanwin (nunation), while the rest read it without tanwin. As for the tanwin, it is based on the view that it is an Arabic name, described as the subject of the predicate "son." Abu 'Ubayda said that it is a non-Arabic name (*a'jami*, of foreign origin), but it was given the diptote (non-declined) form (*sarf*) because of its lightness through the diminutive form, like Nuh and Lut. Al-Saghani also adopted this view.

It is a diminutive of 'Azar, formed by diminutive truncation (*tasghir al-tarkhim*, shortening a name and then making it diminutive). The claim that it is non-Arabic, which came in the form of a diminutive while not actually being one, is open to scrutiny.

As for the omission of the tanwin, it has been said that this is due to the meeting of two consonants (*iltiqa' al-sakinayn*). The nun of the tanwin is vowelless, and the ba' in "ibn" is also vowelless, so the two vowelless letters met, and the nun was deleted, just as weak letters (*huruf al-'illa*) are deleted for that reason. It is indeclinable on the basis of treating the nun as a letter of softness (*harf al-lin*); otherwise, the analogical expectation would have been to vocalize it. It is the subject (*mubtada'*), and "ibn" is also its predicate. This is why it is written with an alif in all the copies of the Qur'an. It has also been said that it is prohibited from the declension because of being a proper name and a foreign word. It has also been said that "ibn" is a descriptive term and the predicate is omitted, like "our worshipped one" (*ma'budana*). This has been criticized on the grounds that it is a far-fetched interpretation when there is a simpler option. Shaykh 'Abd al-Qahir (in *Dala'il al-I'jaz*) rejected it on the grounds that when a noun is described by an attribute and then a predicate is made about it, whoever denies that predicate directs his denial to the predicate, and that attribute becomes accepted. So if the intended object of denial were their statement "'Uzayr is the son of God, our worshipped one," the denial would be directed at his being worshipped by them, and it would imply accepting that he is the son of Allah, Glorified is He, and that is disbelief. Al-Imam (al-Razi) objected to this, saying: "The claim that the denial is directed at the predicate is accepted, but the claim that this would constitute acceptance of the attribute is not valid, because it does not follow from being one who denies that predicate that one confirms that attribute, unless it is said that this predicate indicates that nothing else denies it. This is based on *dalalat al-khitab* (implication by the form of speech), which is weak." Some have answered that the attribute is for causation (*'illiyya*), so denying the judgment entails denying its cause. This has the objection that denying the judgment may be due to the absence of an effect, not because the attribute, like the buildings for example, is absent.

In *al-Idah* it is stated that the statement carries the meaning of an attribute, and what is meant is that it requires supplying the predicate, just as when someone makes a statement, part of which one denies, and so one reports only the denied part. This, as in *al-Kashshaf*, is a good way to remove the far-fetched interpretation, but it goes against the apparent meaning, as the end of the verse indicates. Some researchers have said that ﴿'Uzayr is the son of God﴾ may be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "our companion 'Uzayr is the son of God, for example." When the predicate is described, the denial is directed at its description, as in "this intelligent man." This is consistent with rhetoric and conforms to Arabic grammar without artifice or difficulty. I do not see why it was left out when it is so evident. The apparent meaning is that the construction is a predicate, with no omission there.

There is disagreement about whether 'Uzayr was a prophet or not, and the majority hold the second view.

﴿And the Christians said: The Messiah is the son of God﴾. This is also the statement of some of them. Perhaps they said it because it is impossible for a child to be born without a father, or because of what they saw of his deeds. It is also possible, and this is what appears most likely to me, that they found the term "son" applied to him, peace be upon him, and likewise the term "father" applied to Allah, Exalted is He, in what they had of the Gospel, so they said what they said and erred in understanding what was meant by that. We have already discussed what is sufficient on this point.

Among the strange claims that barely hold up is what has been said: that the reason for their statement is that after the raising of Jesus, peace be upon him, eighty-one years passed during which they were upon the true religion, praying, fasting, and affirming the oneness of God, until a war broke out between them and the Jews. Among the Jews was a courageous man called Bulas, who killed a number of them. Then he said to the Jews: "If the truth is with Jesus, peace be upon him, then we have disbelieved, the Fire is our destination, and we are defrauded, for we will enter the Fire while they enter Paradise. I will scheme against them and lead them astray until they enter the Fire with us." Then he went to a horse he used to fight on, hamstrung it, showed regret and repentance, put dust on his head, and came to the Christians. They said to him: "Who are you?" He said: "Your enemy Bulas. I was called from heaven that there is no repentance for you unless you become a Christian. I have repented and have come to you." They admitted him into the church and supported him, and he entered a room in it and did not come out for a year until he had learned the Gospel. Then he came out and said: "I have been called that Allah, Exalted is He, has accepted your repentance." They believed him, loved him, and his status rose among them. Then he went to three men among them: Nestor, Ya'qub, and Malka. Nestor came to know that the God is three: Allah, Jesus, and Mary, Exalted is Allah above that. Ya'qub came to know that Jesus is not a human but the son of Allah, Glorified is He. Malka came to know that Jesus is Allah, Exalted, who has always been and always will be. When this had taken hold among them, he called each one of them in private and said to him: "You are my chosen one. Call the people to what I have taught you." He ordered him to go to a region of the lands. Then he said to them: "I have seen Jesus, peace be upon him, in a dream, and he is pleased with me, and I am sacrificing myself to draw near to him." Then he went to the altar and slaughtered himself. These three then separated. One of them went to Rome, one to Jerusalem, and the other to another region. Each one showed his doctrine and called the people to it. Those who followed him followed him, and there occurred what occurred of corruption and error.

﴿That﴾, i.e., what came from them of these two great falsehoods, ﴿is their statement with their mouths﴾, i.e., it is a statement not supported by any proof, similar to meaningless words that exist only in mouths without having any reality outside. It has also been said that this is an emphasis on the attribution of the aforementioned statement to them and a negation of any figurative sense in it, and this is the common usage in such cases. It has also been said that by "statement" is meant opinion and doctrine. The mention of the mouths is either to indicate that it has no effect in their hearts and that they only speak it out of ignorance and obstinacy, or to indicate that it is a choice for them, that they do not shy away from declaring it openly, since a person may indicate his doctrine in writing or by allusion, but when he declares it openly and states it with his tongue, that is the extreme of his choosing it. More than one scholar has claimed that treating it as emphasis, as in your saying "I saw him with my own eyes and heard him with my own ears," is incompatible with the context. But if the intent were emphasis together with expressing wonder at their declaring that false doctrine, the context would not oppose it, and there is no conflict among the rhetorical purposes.

﴿They imitate﴾, i.e., their statement resembles in disbelief and abomination ﴿the statement of those who disbelieved﴾. The object is omitted, and the object's complement is put in its place and given the nominative case. It may also be a figurative usage, as has been said regarding His statement: ﴿And that Allah does not guide the scheme of the treacherous﴾, meaning He does not guide them in their scheme. So the meaning is: they imitate in their statement the statement of those who disbelieved. ﴿Before﴾, i.e., before them. As related from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and Qatada, and as preferred by al-Farra', these are the polytheists who said: "The angels are the daughters of God," Glorified is He above what they say. It has also been said that what is meant is their predecessors. The one who imitates among them in the Prophet's time, peace be upon him, imitates their ancestors and forefathers, and the purpose is to inform of their long-standing rootedness in disbelief.

---

Al-Alusi, Ruh al-Ma'ani, commentary on surah 9, verse 30 (part 2 of 2):

You know that there is no multiplicity in the saying so that the comparison could be made, and that placing it between the statements of the two groups carries no added distinction. It has also been said that the intended people are the Jews, on the basis that the pronoun refers to the Christians. But it is not hidden that this goes against the apparent sense, even though Ibn al-Mundhir and others transmitted it from Qatadah, and given that their resemblance (to one another) is already known from the beginning of the verse. It also requires that the rebuttal and refutation be restricted to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is their saying with their mouths﴾, to the saying of the Christians.

Most readers recite (yuḍāhūna) with a dammah on the ha' followed by a waw. The verbs ḍāhaytu and ḍāha'tu have also come with the meaning of al-muḍāhāh, which is al-mushābahah (resemblance), and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, explained it this way. It is also reported from al-Hasan that it is explained as al-muwāfaqah (agreement). These are two dialectal forms. It has been said that the yā' is a derivative of the hamzah, as they say fariytu and tawaḍḍaytu. It has also been said that the hamzah is a substitute for the yā' because of its dammah, but this is refuted on the ground that the yā' does not remain in such a form to be changed; rather it is deleted, as in karāmūna from al-ramy.

It has been said that it is derived from their saying: imra'atun ḍahyā (with short vowel, meaning a woman without breasts, or one who does not menstruate, or one who does not bear children), because of her resemblance to men. It is said ḍahyā' (with a long vowel) like ḥamrā', and ḍahyā'ah (with long vowel and the feminine ta'). The combining of the two feminine markers in it is anomalous. This has been criticized as an error, because the two roots differ: the hamzah in ḍahyā', in its three dialects, is augmented, whereas in al-muḍāhāh it is original. They did not say that the hamzah of ḍahyā' is original and its yā' augmented, because the pattern fa'yal'ā' is not established in their morphological patterns. Nor did they say its measure is fa'lal like ja'far, because the augmentation of the hamzah in ḍahyā' with the long vowel is established, so it is determined in the other dialect as well. There is a detailed discussion of this matter in its proper place.

Among the people are those who permitted pausing at ﴿qawluhum﴾ and made ﴿bi-afwāhihim﴾ dependent on yuḍāhi'ūna. There is no doubt that this is not valid. Overall, there is condemnation of those who disbelieved in the most eloquent manner, even though the verse was not directed at their condemnation. ﴿Qātalahumu Allāh﴾ is a supplication against them for destruction, for whoever Allah fights, exalted is He, will be killed, and whoever opposes Him will be overcome.

Ibn Jarir and others transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that the meaning is "May Allah curse them," which is a metaphorical meaning of qātalahum.
