It is also possible that the intended meaning of this expression is amazement at the monstrousness of their saying, for it has become so common in that sense that it is used in praise, so one says: "Qātalahu Allah, how eloquent he is!"

It has also been said that it is for supplication and amazement, which is understood from the context, because it is a word said only in a context of amazement at the monstrousness of the act or saying of a people. The implications of this are not hidden, and restricting it to monstrousness is itself a monstrousness.

﴿Anná yu'fakūn﴾: that is, how are they turned away from the truth to falsehood after the clarity of the proof and the brightness of the evidence?

[Page 84]

﴿They took their rabbis﴾ is an added emphasis on what preceded of their disbelief in God, the Exalted. *Al-aḥbār* are the scholars of the Jews. Scholars differ regarding its singular. Al-Asma'i said: "I do not know whether it is *ḥibr* or *ḥabr*." Abu al-Haytham said: "It is only with a *fatḥah* (*ḥabr*)." Ibn al-Athir mentioned that it is both with a *fatḥah* and with a *kasrah* (*ḥibr*), and most lexicographers follow this. The correct usage is its application to a scholar, whether he is a *dhimmī* (a non-Muslim under Muslim protection) or a Muslim. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, was called *al-ḥabr*. As in *al-Qamus*, its plural is also *ḥubūr*. It appears to be derived from *taḥbīr al-ma'ānī* (embellishing meanings) through the beauty of expressing them.

﴿and their monks﴾: these are the scholars of the Christians, from the people of the monasteries (*ṣawāmi'*). It is the plural of *rāhib*, which may also be used for the singular, and its plurals are *rahābīn* and *rahābinah*. In *Majma' al-Bayan* it is stated that the *rāhib* is the one who fears, upon whom fear is visible, and its application became common for the ascetics of the Christians. It is derived from *al-rahbah*, meaning fear. Because of this, they withdrew from the affairs of this world, abandoned its pleasures, practised renunciation of it, isolated themselves from its people, and deliberately sought its hardships. Some of them would castrate themselves, place a chain around their necks, and other kinds of torment. From here the Prophet, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, said: "There is no monasticism (*rahbāniyyah*) in Islam." The meaning in the verse is that each of the two groups took its scholars (as lords), not that all of them did so entirely.

﴿as lords besides God﴾: by obeying them in forbidding what God, the Exalted, has permitted and permitting what He, glorified be He, has forbidden. This is the interpretation reported from the Messenger of God, may God's blessings and peace be upon him. Al-Tha'labi and others reported from 'Adi ibn Hatim, who said: "I came to the Messenger of God, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, while there was a golden cross around my neck. He said: 'O 'Adi, throw away this idol.' I heard him reciting in Surah Bara'ah: ﴿They took their rabbis and their monks as lords besides God,﴾ and I said to him: 'O Messenger of God, they did not worship them!' He, upon him be blessings and peace, said: 'Do they not forbid what God has permitted, so they forbid it, and permit what God has forbidden, so they treat it as permitted?' I said: 'Yes.' He said: 'That is their worship.'" Hudhayfah, may God be pleased with him, was asked about the verse and answered with the same as what the Messenger of God, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, had mentioned.

A parallel to this is the saying: "So-and-so worships so-and-so," when he exceeds the limits in obeying him. This is *isti'arah* (metaphor) by comparing obedience to worship, or a *majāz mursal* (a general metonymic usage) by applying the term "worship" (which is a specific kind of obedience) to its general sense. The first is more eloquent. It has also been said: taking them as lords means prostrating to them and the like, which is only fitting for the Lord, Mighty and Majestic. In that case there is no metaphor, but there is no argument for anyone after the authenticity of the report from the Messenger of God, may God's blessings and peace be upon him.

The verse also censures many of the misguided sects who abandoned the Book of God, the Exalted, and the Sunnah of His Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, in favour of the words of their scholars and leaders. The truth is more deserving of being followed. Therefore, when it becomes manifest, it becomes obligatory for the Muslim to follow it, even if the *ijtihād* (independent reasoning) of his *muqallid* (the one he follows by taqlid) has erred.

﴿and the Messiah, son of Mary﴾ is coordinated with (*rahbānahum*, their monks), in that they took him as a lord worshipped, or in that they made him a son of God, as the context of the verse requires according to what has been said. In this there is room for consideration.

The specification of taking (as lord) for him, peace be upon him, indicates that the Jews did not do this with 'Uzayr. Mentioning him later, although their taking him in this way is stronger than mere obedience in the matter of permitting and forbidding, is because it is specific to the Christians. Attributing him, peace be upon him, to his mother is to signal the complete feebleness of their opinion and the judgement against them with utmost ignorance and foolishness.

﴿Yet they were not commanded﴾, that is, while those disbelievers were not commanded in the divine books and through the tongues of the prophets, peace be upon them, ﴿except to worship one God﴾, of exalted rank, who is God, glorified be He, and to obey His command and not to obey the command of others in contradiction to it, for that contradicts His worship, exalted be His majesty. As for obeying the Messenger of God, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, and all others whom God has commanded to be obeyed, it is in reality obedience to God, Mighty and Majestic. Or: those whom the disbelievers took as lords, namely the Messiah, peace be upon him, the rabbis and the monks, were not commanded except to obey, or to make God, the Exalted, one. How then could they be lords, when they are themselves commanded and enslaved like them? It is not hidden that restricting worship to God, the Exalted, is not achieved except by restricting obedience also to Him, the Exalted. Whenever obedience is not restricted to Him, glorified be His majesty, worship is not restricted to Him, glorified be He.

﴿There is no god but He﴾ is a second attribute of *ilāhan* (one god), or a resumptive statement (*isti'nāf*). On both views it confirms the tawhid (oneness of God). It has also been said that it contains an additional benefit: what preceded could allow for something other than tawhid, namely that they were commanded to worship one god from among many gods. When the one commanded to be worshipped is described as being the sole one with divinity, the intended meaning is fixed. It was also permitted that it be an explanatory attribute for *wāḥidan* (one).

﴿Glorified be He above what they associate﴾: a declaration of His transcendence, that is, transcendence above associating anything with Him in worship and obedience.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 32:

﴿They wish to extinguish the light of Allah﴾. The extinguishing of fire, according to what is in al-Qamus (the Qamus, a classical Arabic lexicon), is the removal of its flame, which necessitates the removal of its light, not the removal of its light itself, as has been said. However, since the purpose of extinguishing a fire that is not meant for anything but its light, such as a lamp, is the removal of its light, the extinguishing of it was made a metaphor for that. Then this became common, until it was a metaphor for the removal of light in general, even if it is not of fire. By the light of Allah is meant His proof, the radiant and shining one, which indicates His oneness and His transcendence, glory be to Him, above partners and offspring; or the mighty Qur'an, which splits open and proclaims that. It has also been said: His prophethood, peace be upon him, which appeared after the darkness of disbelief had stretched on, as a bright dawn. Whatever the case, the light is an original, explicit metaphor for what has been mentioned, and its attribution to Allah, exalted is He, is a qarinah (indicator). By extinguishing is meant rejection and denial; that is, the People of the Two Books wish to reject what indicates the oneness and transcendence of Allah, the Exalted, from what they attribute to Him, glory be to Him. ( ﴿with their mouths﴾ ) That is, with their false sayings that have no referent to which they correspond nor any basis upon which they rest, but rather they were most like meaningless utterances. It has been said: it is also possible that there is a metaphorical image (isti'arah tamthiliyyah) in the speech, in that their state in attempting to nullify his prophethood, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, by denial, is likened to the state of one who wishes to blow upon a great light spread across the horizons. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah refuses except to perfect His light﴾ would be a tarshih (a development of the metaphor), because perfecting the light is an increase in its illumination and the spreading of its brightness; it is thus a branching upon the likened-to (al-mushabbah bihi). What follows in His saying, glory be to Him: ( ﴿He is the One who﴾ ) etc. is a tajrid (abstraction) upon the branch. In both the likened and the likened-to, the sense of excess and deficiency was observed, since he likened nullifying to extinguishing by the mouth, and attributed the light to Allah, the Exalted in majesty, and it is part of the nature of light attributed to Him, glory be to Him, that it be great; so how could it be extinguished by blowing of the mouth? He completed each of the tarshih and tajrid with what completes them, due to the suitability between disbelief, which is concealment and the removal of manifestness, and extinguishing, and the antithesis between the religion of truth, which is monotheism, and polytheism. End of quote.

And it is not devoid of beauty. The apparent meaning of "light" here is the first (the proof and the Qur'an), except that the apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun and was attributed to His pronoun, glory be to Him, to give greater importance to His matter and to indicate the reason for the ruling. The exception is an incomplete (mufarragh) exception, so the verbal noun is in the accusative as an object. What permits the incomplete exception, according to the majority, is that ﻳَﺄْﺑَﻰ (refuses) carries the sense of negation, and what is meant by it is either "does not desire," because it occurs in opposition to "they desire," as has been said, or "does not approve," as some of the verifiers have preferred, on the basis that what is meant by the desire of perfecting His light, glory be to Him, is a particular desire, namely desire in the manner of approval, as indicated by ﴿and though the disbelievers dislike it﴾, not the general desire that does not entail approval, as is the position of the People of Truth, in contrast to those who equate the two. Al-Zajjaj said: what permits the incomplete exception is the generality of the thing excepted from, which is omitted; and it does no harm that this generality is relative, since most generalities are like that; indeed, it has been said: there is no general statement but that some of it has been specified. That is, every thing connected to His light is disliked except its perfection, and the context is the indicator of the specification.

It is not permissible, in his view, to interpret the group (the majority position), since there is no affirmation that cannot be interpreted as a negation, so the incomplete exception would apply to everything, and that is, as you see, unacceptable. The truth is that there is no barrier to interpretation when the context calls for it, and the perfecting of the light is by elevating the word of monotheism and strengthening the religion of Islam. ﴿and though the disbelievers dislike it﴾: the answer to "though" (law) is omitted, due to what precedes it indicating it; that is, "He perfects His light."

The clause is conjoined to a clause before it that is implied, meaning: "even if the disbelievers do not dislike it, and even if they dislike it," and both are in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). What is meant is that He, glory be to Him, will perfect His light without fail.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 33:

﴿He it is Who sent His Messenger﴾ Muhammad (ﷺ), accompanied by ﴿the guidance﴾, i.e., the Qur'an, which is a guidance for the God-fearing, ﴿and the religion of truth﴾, i.e., the firm (established) one. It is also said: "His religion, Exalted is He," which is the religion of Islam, ﴿to make it prevail﴾, i.e., the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him), ﴿over all religion﴾, i.e., over the people of all religions, so that He humiliates them; or, to make the religion of truth prevail over all other religions by abrogating them (naskh, abrogation: the cancellation of a ruling by a later revelation) as wisdom requires. So the "al" (the definite article) in "ad-din" (the religion), whether the pronoun refers to the Messenger (ﷺ) or to the religion of truth, is for totality (istighraq, comprehensiveness).

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that the pronoun refers to the Messenger (peace be upon him), and the "al" is for specificity (al-'ahd, the known/previously referenced): that He may teach him all the laws of religion and make him prevail over them, so that no part of them remains hidden from him (peace be upon him). Most exegetes adopt the second possibility and said: this is at the time of the descent of 'Isa (peace be upon him), for then no religion will remain except the religion of Islam. The clause is an explanation and confirmation of the content of the preceding clause, since the outcome of completion (al-itmam) is manifestation (al-izhar). ﴿Even though the polytheists dislike it﴾, in the same pattern as what precedes it, except that describing them with polytheism after describing them with disbelief is said to indicate that they combined disbelief in the Messenger with associating partners with Allah, Exalted is He. The apparent meaning of this is that what is meant by "disbelief" earlier is disbelief in the Messenger (ﷺ) and denial of him, and what is meant by "polytheism" is disbelief in Allah, glory be to Him, by the indication of the contrast, and there is no obstacle to this.

You have already learned what relevance these two completing clauses have, which the sphere of eloquence should contain. So reflect upon it.

[Page 87]

﴿O you who have believed﴾ This begins an explanation of the state of the rabbis and monks in misleading their common people, following the explanation of the bad state of the followers in taking them as lords. In this there is a warning to the believers, so that they do not hover around that sanctuary. For this reason the address was directed to them: ﴿Indeed, many of the rabbis and the monks consume the wealth of people unjustly﴾, taking it through bribery in order to alter the rulings and laws and to make them lenient and easy. The expression "consuming" for "taking" is a *majaz mursal* (a figurative usage in which a general or related term is used for a specific one, here a metonymy), with the relation of causation and effect, or of necessity and what is necessitated, since eating necessarily involves taking, as has been said.

It is also permissible that the intended meaning of "wealth" is the foodstuffs by which people eat, as a *majaz mursal*, and from this is the verse:

*They eat a pack-saddle every night*

Here he means fodder bought with the price of a pack-saddle. Al-Allamah al-Tibi chose this, and it is one of the two views mentioned by al-Zamakhshari. The second is that eating is used as a *isti'arah* (metaphor) for taking. This is according to what al-Allamah established: that the state of their taking people's wealth, without distinguishing between truth and falsehood and without differentiating between the lawful and the unlawful, is compared to the state of one who is greedily hungry and does not distinguish between one food and another in consuming, in their eagerness to gather its debris. Then he claimed that there is no benefit under this metaphor, and that his citing the taking and consumption of food is absurd. It is answered that the citation of it is to show that there is a resemblance between taking and consuming. Otherwise, that would be the opposite of the intended meaning. The benefit of the metaphor is the emphasis that it was taken unjustly, because eating is the ultimate form of seizing something. On this view, the words of the Exalted, ﴿unjustly﴾, become an additional emphasis. This would not be the case if it were said "they take" ﴿and they bar﴾ people ...

[Page 87 continues]

﴿from the way of Allah﴾, that is, the religion of Islam, or from the path established in their books, toward what they have invented and distorted by taking bribes.

It is also permissible that "they bar" (*yasuddūna*) is from *sudūd* (turning away), meaning that they turn away from the way of Allah, so they distort and fabricate by their consuming the wealth of people unjustly. ﴿And those who hoard gold and silver﴾, that is, they gather them together. From this comes the expression "a camel with abundant meat" (*nāqa kinās al-lahm*), meaning one whose flesh is gathered together. Burial is not a condition of *kanz* (hoarding); rather, simply gathering and keeping suffices. The relative pronoun may refer either to the many rabbis and monks, since the discussion is about condemning them, and this would be an emphasis about them in that they are described as greedy after having been described with what preceded, namely taking bribes for falsehoods. Or it may refer to the Muslims, since they are also mentioned in the context, and this is more appropriate with the words of the Exalted, ﴿and do not spend it in the way of Allah﴾, because it indicates that they are among those who spend in His way, glorified is He, since that is what is understood from the negation according to custom. Thus their arrangement, in linking them with the bribe-takers among the People of the Book, is a severe rebuke and an indication that they are a model for them in deserving the announcement of punishment. Some of the verifiers chose to take it in a general sense, in which the rabbis and monks enter primarily. Many have interpreted spending in the way of Allah as zakat, based on what is related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that: "When this verse was revealed, it weighed heavily upon the Muslims. Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: 'I will relieve you of it.' He set off and said: 'O Prophet of Allah, this verse has weighed heavily on your companions.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed Allah, the Exalted, did not enjoin zakat except to purify what remains of your wealth.'"

Al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan, and others, related from Ibn Umar who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Whatever its zakat is paid, it is not hoarding.'" That is, it is not a hoarding for which a threat is made, since the threat is for withholding spending in what Allah, the Exalted, has commanded to be spent. The words of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), "Whoever leaves gold or silver, he will be branded with it," do not contradict this, because what is meant by that is the one who does not pay its due, as is indicated by what al-Shaykhan related from Abu Hurayrah: "There is no owner of gold or silver who does not pay its due from them, except that on the Day of Resurrection plates of fire will be fashioned for him, and his side and forehead will be branded with them." It has been said that this was before zakat was enjoined. On this is based what al-Tabarani related from Abu Umamah, who said: "A man from the People of the Suffah died, and in his loincloth a dinar was found. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'A brand.' Then another died, and in his loincloth two dinars were found. He (ﷺ) said: 'Two brands.'" It has been said: rather, this was for the two men displayed poverty and great need by being counted among the People of the Suffah, who are in that state, while they possessed what they possessed; so their recompense was the brand and two brands for that.

Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, took the apparent meaning of the verse and obligated the spending of all the wealth beyond need. A dispute occurred between him and Mu'awiyah, may Allah be pleased with him, in Syria over this, which he complained about to Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, in Medina. Uthman summoned him there and found him insisting on that, until Ka'b al-Ahbar, may Allah be pleased with him, said to him: "O Abu Dharr, indeed the upright religion (*al-millah al-hanifiyyah*) is the easiest and most just of religions. Since the obligation to spend all the wealth does not exist in the Jewish religion, which is the most restrictive and severe of religions, how could it be obligatory in it?" Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, became angry, and he had a sharpness of temper, which was what led him to reproach Bilal, may Allah be pleased with him, about his mother, and to complain about him to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and his saying to him: "You are a man in whom there is jahiliyyah." He raised his staff to strike him and said to him: "O Jew, this is not one of these matters!" Ka'b fled, and he pursued him until he sought refuge behind the back of Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, and he did not return until he struck him. In another narration, the blow landed on Uthman. Many objected to Abu Dharr in his claim, and people would recite to him the verse on inheritance and say: "If it were obligatory to spend all the wealth, the verse would have no meaning." They would gather around him, crowding wherever he alighted, astonished at this from him. So he chose seclusion, and he consulted Uthman about it, and Uthman advised him to go to al-Rabadhah, so he settled there, as he wished. This is what is relied upon in this story. The Shi'ah related it in a manner that they made into one of the criticisms of Dhu al-Nurayn, and their aim in that is to extinguish his light, but Allah refuses except to complete His light.

﴿Then give them good tidings of a painful punishment﴾. This is the predicate of the relative clause, and the *fa'* (then) is for what has passed more than once.

It is also permissible that the relative clause is in the accusative position, governed by a verb that is explained by *fabashshirhum* (give them good tidings). The expression "good tidings" is used for mockery.

The Quranic verse: "On the Day it will be heated in the fire of Hell" and so on.

*Allah's words, ﴿on the Day﴾ (yawma), are in the accusative (manṣūb) and are governed either by ﴿painful punishment﴾ (ʿadhābin alīm), or by an implied verb indicated by that phrase, meaning "they will be punished on the Day," or by "remember" (udhkur). It has also been said that the implied phrase is "the punishment of a Day." The implied word is then a substitute (badal) for the mentioned word. When the governing noun (muḍāf) was omitted, the genitive noun (muḍāf ilayhi) took its place.*

﴿It will be heated in it in the fire of Hell﴾, meaning the fire will be kindled, having intense heat and burning upon them. Its original form is "it will be heated by the fire," from your saying "I heated the branding iron" (ḥamaytu al-mīsam) and "I made it hot" (aḥmaytuhu). The heating is attributed to the fire for emphasis, because the fire in itself possesses heat. When it is described as being heated, this indicates the intensity of its kindling. Then the word "fire" was omitted and the verbal attribution was transferred to the prepositional phrase, to direct attention to the intended meaning in the most complete manner. The verb thus shifted from the feminine to the masculine form, as when you say, "I raised the matter to the emir," and when the matter is omitted and the verb is attributed to the prepositional phrase, you say, "It was raised to the emir."

It is related from Ibn ʿĀmir that he recited *tuḥmā* with a *tāʾ* at the beginning (tuḥmā), attributing it to the fire, as in its original form.

The phrase *ʿalayhā* ("upon them") is used although two things are mentioned. This is because the intended meaning is neither a specific quantity of them nor the genus that applies to both little and much. Rather, the intended meaning is the large amount of gold coins (dananīr) and silver coins (darāhim), because that is what becomes a hoard (kanz). He therefore used the plural pronoun to indicate abundance. Had he used the dual pronoun, it could have allowed for something else. The same applies to His words, ﴿nor do they spend it﴾.

It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the hoards of wealth which are understood from the context. In that case the ruling is general, and for this reason the pronoun was used in a way that departs from the apparent (ʿudila fīhi ʿan al-ẓāhir).

The specific mention of gold and silver is because they are the main and predominant foundations of wealth, not for the purpose of restriction. Or the mention is only of silver, and it was sufficient with it because it is more abundant and people are more in need of it. Also, gold is understood from it by a stronger inference, together with their closeness in wording.

﴿So their foreheads, their sides and their backs will be branded with them﴾. They were singled out for mention because the aim of the hoarders in hoarding and accumulating is to be people of standing and leadership among others through wealth, and to enjoy delicious foods and fine clothes. Thus, because of their standing, the branding is on their foreheads. Because their sides are filled with food, they are branded on the sides. Because of what they wore on their backs, the backs are branded. Or, when they see a poor beggar, they furrow the brow between their eyes, turn away, frown, bend their side, turn their backs to him, and face another direction. Or, because they are the most honorable of the visible limbs, since they contain the principal organs, which are the brain, the heart and the liver. It has also been said that they are the origins of the four directions, which are the front and back of the body, and its two sides. Thus what is mentioned is a metaphor (kināya) for the whole body. There remains the question of why only these four are mentioned out of the six directions. Some have strained to answer that the hoarder, at the time of hoarding, out of fear that someone might notice him, looks to the right, left, front and behind, and hardly looks up or imagines that anyone might observe him from below. Since those four directions were the objects of his gaze and the places of his caution, and not the other two, he was limited to them. Yet this rests on taking the burial of the hoard as a prohibited matter, as is not hidden.

It has also been said that these places were specified because their inner part is hollow, unlike the hand and foot. But this is objectionable, since the stomach is similarly hollow. Also, combining them with what is external carries a subtle point. It has also been said that the forehead is the place of branding because of its prominence, the side is the place of pain, and the back is the place of punishments (ḥudūd, prescribed penalties). This is because what drives the hoarder to hoard and not spend is fear of poverty, which is the "red death" (al-mawt al-aḥmar), since it causes toil, the sweat of the brow, agitation to the right and left, and the lack of stability of the side in seeking livelihood, together with the absence of anything to lean on and rely upon in important matters. Therefore, for the sake of safety from toil and the sweat of the brow, the forehead is branded. For the sake of safety from agitation, and the hope of stability for the side, the side is branded. And for the sake of the back leaning upon and relying on what he claims to be the strongest support and the firmest refuge, the back is branded. Other views have been stated, some of which resemble others. And Allah Most High knows best the reality of the matter.

Whatever the case, the meaning is not that a dinar is placed upon a dinar, or a dirham upon a dirham, so that he is branded with them. Nor is the meaning that he is branded with each one by lifting one and placing another in its place, until they have gone through them all. Rather, the skin of the hoarder is expanded so that each dinar and dirham is placed separately, as the reports have stated and the traditions have consistently affirmed.

﴿This is what you hoarded﴾, with an implied verb of speech, and the preceding adverbial phrase is connected to this in one view. That is, it will be said to him on the Day it is heated upon them: "This is what you hoarded."

﴿For yourselves﴾, that is, for their benefit. Thus it became the very cause of their harm and of their punishment. The *lām* is causal (lil-taʿlīl). You have a choice in the Qur'anic structure regarding the implied governing noun. The *lām* was not made to indicate ownership, because ownership is of no benefit here.

The *mā* in His words, ﴿So taste what you used to hoard﴾, may be a verbal noun (maṣdariyya), meaning "the consequence of your hoarding," or "the consequence of your being hoarders." The former is preferred, since the *kāna* in its deficient form (kāna al-nāqiṣa) has a verbal noun only with difficulty, and because the intended meaning is the report, whereas *kāna* was mentioned to bring to mind the past situation. It may also be a relative pronoun (mawṣūla), meaning "the consequence of what you used to hoard." In the statement there is a implicit metaphor (istiʿāra makniyya wa takhyīliyya) or a subordinate metaphor (tabaʿiyya).

It is also read *taknuzūna* with a *ḍamma* on the *nūn*, so the past tense is *kanaza*, like *ḍaraba* and *qaʿada*.

[Page 89]

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 36 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Indeed, the number of months﴾, i.e., the total count of the months of the year, ﴿with Allah﴾, i.e., in His judgment, ﴿is twelve months﴾, which are the lunar months known to all, since the sphere of the legal rulings (al-ahkam al-shar'iyyah) revolves around them. ﴿In the Book of Allah﴾, i.e., in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz).

It is also said: [it means] in what He has recorded and obligated His servants to follow. It is also said: [it means] the Qur'an, because it contains verses that indicate the reckoning (al-hisab) and the stations of the moon, but this is not correct. ﴿On the day He created the heavens and the earth﴾, i.e., at the beginning of the creation of this world. This adverbial phrase (zarf) is connected either to what is in "the Book of Allah" of the meaning of establishment (al-thubut), which is indicated by its explicit wording, or to its complement, or to "the Book" if it is a verbal noun (masdar) in the sense of writing. The meaning is that at the beginning of that time its count was what has been mentioned, and it is now as it was then. The phrase ﴿in the Book of Allah﴾ is a qualifier of ﴿twelve﴾, and it is the predicate of ﴿inna﴾ (indeed). ﴿'Inda﴾ (with) is the object of ﴿'iddah﴾ (number), because it is a verbal noun like "al-shirkah" (partnership). ﴿Shahran﴾ (months) is a specifying accusative (tamyiz) that is emphatic, as in your saying: "I have twenty dinars" (*'indi min al-dananir 'ishrun dinaran*). As for what is said, that it serves to remove ambiguity (raf' al-ibham), since if it were said: "The number of months with Allah is twelve years," it would be a sound sentence, yet it is not sound, as has been claimed. Its proponent defended this by saying that the intended meaning is that it is possible that those months were like that at the beginning of the world, as in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years﴾, and similar. There is no objection to this, for it is better than pure addition.

They did not permit ﴿fi kitab﴾ (in a book) to be connected to ﴿'iddah﴾, because when a verbal noun is given a predicate, it does not govern what comes after the predicate. Some people made it a substitute (badal) for ﴿'inda Allah﴾, but Abu al-Baqa' considered this weak, because it involves separating the substitute from what it substitutes by a predicate of the governing word of the substituted element. Some permitted making ﴿twelve﴾ the subject (mubtada') and ﴿'inda﴾ a fronted predicate, with the clause as the predicate of ﴿inna﴾; or [they permitted] that the adverbial phrase (zarf), by its reliance, governs the nominative case in ﴿twelve﴾. His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Of them four are sacred﴾ may be a qualifier of ﴿twelve﴾, or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in the adverbial phrase, or a new independent sentence. The pronoun in ﴿minha﴾ (of them) refers to ﴿twelve﴾ under every interpretation.

These four are Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, al-Muharram, and Rajab of Mudar. Their order has been disputed. It is said that the first of them is al-Muharram and the last is Dhu al-Hijjah, so they are months of one year. The apparent meaning of what Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas supports this.

It is also said that the first of them is Rajab, so they are [spread across] two years. This view is supported by what Ibn Jarir and others transmitted from Ibn 'Umar, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) addressed us during the Farewell Pilgrimage at Mina, in the middle of the days of Tashriq, and said: 'O people, indeed time has come full circle, and it is today as it was on the day Allah created the heavens and the earth. The number of months with Allah is twelve months, of which four are sacred: the first of them is Rajab of Mudar, which lies between Jumada and Sha'ban, and Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, and al-Muharram.'"

It is also said that the first of them is Dhu al-Qa'dah, and al-Nawawi authenticated this because they are consecutive. Al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) transmitted: "Indeed, time has come full circle as it was on the day Allah created the heavens and the earth. The year is twelve months, of which four are sacred: three consecutive ones, and Rajab of Mudar," and the hadith continues. Rajab was attributed to them because the Rabi'ah tribe used to sanctify Ramadan and call it Rajab. For this reason the hadith clarified what it clarified.

It is also said: what has been mentioned, that these are months of one year according to the first order and of two years according to the second order, holds only on the premise that the beginning of the year is al-Muharram. This [convention] came about in the time of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him. Before him they dated by the Year of the Elephant, and likewise by the death of Hisham ibn al-Mughirah. Then they dated from the early Islamic period by Rabi' al-Awwal, and according to this dating the matter is the reverse of what was mentioned. The one who said this did not clarify what the first month of the year was for the Arabs before the Elephant. What is understood from some of their statements is that al-Muharram was also the first month for them from earlier times, except that the people of Yemen and the Hijaz had many dating systems which they followed, inheriting them from predecessors. Perhaps these were based on events that occurred in past days. When the Prophet (ﷺ) migrated, the Muslims took his migration as the starting point of the calendar and disregarded what came before it. They named each year that came upon them after an event that occurred in it, such as the Year of Permission, the Year of Command, and the Year of Trial. This practice continued until the caliphate of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him. Some of the Companions asked him about this and said: "This is lengthy, and sometimes there is disagreement and error in some years." So he, may Allah be pleased with him, chose the year of the Hijrah as the starting point without naming the years after what happened in them. The Companions approved of his opinion in this.

In some commentaries on al-Bukhari it is mentioned that Abu Musa al-Ash'ari wrote to him: "Documents come to us from the Commander of the Believers, and we do not know which of them to act upon. We have read a deed whose due date is in Sha'ban, but we did not know which Sha'ban was meant, the past one or the coming one." It is also said that he, may Allah be pleased with him, was presented with a deed whose due date was Sha'ban, and he said: "Which Sha'ban is it?" Then he said: "Wealth has increased among us, and what we have distributed has not been dated. How can we manage its recording?" A king of al-Ahwaz, who had been captured and had accepted Islam at his hands, said to him: "The non-Arabs have a reckoning that they call *mahrouz*, which they attribute to whichever Chosroes prevailed." He then explained it to him and clarified its method. He, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Set up a dating system for the people by which they conduct their dealings and regulate their times." They mentioned to him the dating of the Jews, and he did not approve of it, and [the dating] of the Persians, and he did not approve of it either. Then they found the Hijrah a good date. End of quotation.

What was mentioned, that in the early Islamic period they dated by Rabi' al-Awwal, is vague. Its meaning becomes clear from what is in *al-Nibras*: that during the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) they dated by the year of arrival (*sanat al-qudum*) and by its first month, which is Rabi' al-Awwal according to the more correct view. This should be understood. The month, in their view, is divided into the legal (*shar'i*), the true (*haqiqi*), and the conventional (*istilahi*). The legal month is determined by the sighting of the crescent, under the conditions known in jurisprudence (fiqh). The first crescent of al-Muharram in the Hijri calendar was on the night of Thursday, as adopted by Yunus al-Hakimi al-Misri, who mentioned that this was according to calculation (*hisab*). As for determination by sighting, Ibn al-Shatir established that its crescent was seen in Makkah on the night of Friday. The true month is determined by the conjunction of the moon with the sun at the point of its return after separation. Emerging from beneath the sun's rays has no effect except on the possibility of sighting according to the common custom. It is said that the duration of this is twenty-nine days and one hundred and ninety-one parts out of three hundred and sixty parts of a day with its night. The lunar year is then three hundred and fifty-four days, a fifth of a day, a sixth of it, and a second. That equals eleven parts out of thirty parts of a day with its night. When these parts add up to more than half a day, they make a full day and add it to the days, and that year is then called *kabisah* (intercalary), its days being three hundred and fifty-five days. Since the earlier parts were more than half, they completed them with a full day. They agreed to make the months alternate between a full month and a deficient month. This is the conventional month (*shahr istilahi*). Thus al-Muharram in their convention is thirty days and Safar is twenty-nine days, and so on through the end of the lunar year. The odd-numbered months are thirty days, beginning with al-Muharram, and the even-numbered months are twenty-nine days, beginning with Safar, except Dhu al-Hijjah in an intercalary year, which is thirty days, because they agreed to place the days they added in an intercalary year in Dhu al-Hijjah, at the end of the year.

Since the basis of the legal month is sighting, the months varied: some were thirty days and some twenty-nine days, in different years. What al-Shaykhan and others transmitted from Abu Bakrah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Two months of festival do not diminish: Ramadan and Dhu al-Hijjah,'" is to be understood as meaning that their reward and the merit due to them do not diminish, even if their number is fewer. It is also said that it means they do not both diminish together in one year, usually. It is also said that it means the reward of Dhu al-Hijjah does not fall short of the reward of Ramadan. This was related by al-Khattabi, but it is weak. The first interpretation, as al-Nawawi said, is the correct and reliable one.

﴿That﴾, i.e., the sanctity of the four months, and what is implied by the distance in the demonstrative, is to exalt what is referred to. It is also said that it refers to the number being as described. Al-Imam (al-Razi) preferred this, because the number being four sacred months is accepted by the disbelievers, and the purpose is only to refute them concerning the intercalation (*nasi'*) and adding to the number. He preferred the first view, because the following consequence (*tafri'*) requires it. It is not far-fetched that the reference is to the whole of what the preceding speech indicates, and the consequence does not prevent this.

﴿The upright religion﴾, i.e., the straight religion of Ibrahim and Isma'il, peace be upon them both. The Arabs had held to it as an inheritance from them. They used to honor the sacred months so much that a man would meet the killer of his father or brother during them and not revile him. They called Rajab *al-Asamm* (the Deaf) and *Munsil al-Asinnah* (Remover of Spear-points), until they introduced intercalation and altered [the calendar]. It is also said that by "religion" is meant judgment and decree, and by "upright" is meant lasting, which does not cease. That is, that judgment which is not changed or altered. This is attributed to al-Kalbi. It is also said that "religion" here means reckoning, and from it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The intelligent one is he who holds himself accountable and works for what comes after death." That is, that reckoning is the straight one and the correct, balanced number, not what the Arabs did through intercalation. Al-Tabarsi chose this interpretation. According to it, the reference is to what al-Imam preferred.

﴿So do not wrong yourselves therein﴾, by violating their sanctity and committing what is forbidden in them. The pronoun refers to the sacred months. This is what was transmitted from Qatadah and was chosen by al-Farra' and most of the exegetes. It is also said that it refers to all the months, meaning: do not wrong yourselves in all the months of the year by committing sins and abandoning acts of obedience, or do not make what is lawful in them unlawful and what is unlawful lawful, as the polytheists did. This view is attributed to Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them. The shift from "fiha" (in them) to "fihinna" (in them, feminine plural), which would more naturally match "minha" (of them), supports what most scholars hold. The majority holds that the prohibition of fighting in them has been abrogated (*mansukh*), and that wrongdoing is interpreted as committing sins. Restricting the prohibition to committing that in them, although committing it is forbidden absolutely, is for the purpose of magnifying them. God, may He be exalted, may distinguish some times over others. So committing sin in them is graver in burden, like committing it in the Sacred Precinct (*al-haram*) or while in the state of ihram. It is reported from 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah that it is not lawful for people to launch raids in the Sacred Precinct or in the sacred months, except if they are attacked. He excepted this because it is for defense, and therefore it is not prohibited by consensus. Or [he excepted it] because violating the sanctity in that case is not on their part but on the part of the aggressor.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 36 (part 2 of 2):

What supports the view of abrogation (naskh) is that the Prophet (ﷺ) besieged Ta'if and fought Hawazin at Hunayn in Shawwal and Dhu al-Qa'dah of the eighth year (AH). ﴿And fight the polytheists all together as they fight you all together.﴾ Here kaffatan means "all together" (jami'an). It is well known that it must be indefinite (nakirah) and in the accusative (nasb) as a circumstantial qualifier (hal), and that the qualified element (dhu al-hal) must be rational. They faulted al-Zamakhshari for his statement in the introduction to al-Mufassal: "encompassing all (kaffat) the doors." But the one who faults him is himself in error, because when we know that a word has been established for a general meaning through transmission from the predecessors and examination of its occurrences in the speech of those whose usage is authoritative, and we see that they used it in a particular state of inflection, definiteness, indefiniteness and the like, it is permissible for us, according to what is apparent, to take it out of that state, because if we restricted words to what the Arabs—both the original Arabs (al-'arabah al-'aribah) and the Arabicized ones (al-musta'ribah)—used, we would be limiting what is broad and making speaking Arabic difficult for those who come after them. Since it has not thereby departed from what it was established for, it is a real (haqiqah) usage, and thus "kaffah" is valid. Even if the Arabs used it indefinite and accusative only with respect to people, it is permissible to use it definite and indefinite with the various grammatical cases, with respect to people and others, and in all of that it is a real usage, since it has not departed from the meaning for which they established it, which is the meaning of "all." What the establishment entails is that it is not bound by what has been mentioned, and none denies this except an ignorant or obstinate person. Moreover, it occurs in the speech of eloquent writers in accordance with what they claimed. In the letter of Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) to the family of Banu Kakilah: "I have granted the family of Banu Kakilah, from the entire (kaffat) treasury of the Muslims, two hundred mithqal of pure refined gold (dhahab ibriz) each year." This, as in Sharh al-Maqasid, is among what is authentic, and the document was extant with the family of Banu Kakilah until near this time in the lands of Iraq. When the caliphate came to the Commander of the Faithful Ali (may Allah ennoble his face), it was presented to him, and he executed what was in it for them and wrote upon it in his own hand: "To Allah belongs the command before and after, and on that day the believers will rejoice." I am the first who followed an affair of Islam and supported the religion and its rulings, Umar ibn al-Khattab. It was recorded for them the like of what was recorded for the family of Banu Kakilah: every year two hundred dinars of pure refined gold. I have followed his trace and made for them the like of what Umar decreed, since it is obligatory upon me and upon all Muslims to follow that. Written by Ali ibn Abi Talib. So observe how Umar ibn al-Khattab used it as a definite, non-accusative form for non-rational beings, and he is who he is in eloquence, and someone like Ali (may Allah ennoble his face) heard it and did not object, and he is the one who is unique among the unique. So what objection or disapproval could be accepted after this? Therefore his statement in al-Mughni, "kaffatan is specific to the rational," and al-Zamakhshari erred in interpreting the verse ﴿And We have not sent you except as a comprehensive messenger to mankind (kaffatan li-l-nas)﴾, since he took kaffatan as an attribute of an omitted verbal noun, meaning "a message encompassing (kaffatan)," because he considered its use for non-rational beings as removing it from what was required of it regarding the circumstantial state, like his error in the introduction to al-Mufassal, which is not worth attention. And if it is permissible to define it by an annexation (idafah), it is permissible to define it with al-alif wa-l-lam as well, and no account is taken of those who faulted it, such as the author of al-Qamus and Ibn al-Khashshab. According to al-Azhari, it is a verbal noun (masdar) on the pattern fa'ilah, like al-'afiyah and al-'aqibah, and it is not dualized or pluralized. It was also said that it is an active participle (ism fa'il) and its ta' is for intensification (mubalaghah), like the ta' in riwayah and 'allamah, and al-Raghib went to this. It is reported that the meaning here is: fight them restraining (kaffin) them just as they fight you restraining you. It was also said: its meaning is "a group," and it was said of a restraining group, just as they say "al-wazi'ah" for them because of their strength through gathering, and its ta' is like the ta' in jama'ah. The conclusion is that in transmission and in understanding they did not hit the mark in what they committed to regarding its indefiniteness, its accusative state, and its restriction to rational beings, and that they differed as to its origin, whether it is a verbal noun or an active participle from kaff, and whether its ta' is for intensification or for feminine marking. Then they handled it freely and used it for generalization in the sense of "all together," and most scholars interpreted the verse in this way. They said: it is a verbal noun of kaffa 'an al-shay', and its application to all is in view of it being restrained from excess, or in view of it restraining from confronting it or lagging behind it. It is a circumstantial qualifier either from the agent or from the object. So the meaning of "fight the polytheists all together" is that none of you should lag behind from fighting them, or that you should not leave off fighting any one of them. Likewise on the side of the comparison (al-mushabbah bihi). The verse is cited as evidence for the first possibility, that fighting is an individual obligation (fard 'ayn).
It was said: it was so in the early days of Islam and then abrogated. Ibn 'Atiyyah denied this. ﴿And know that Allah is with the God-fearing (al-muttaqin)﴾ means with support and aid, so fear Allah in order that you may gain His support and aid, glorified is He. This is guidance for them toward what benefits them in fighting after being commanded to it. It was also said: the meaning is that Allah is with you by way of aid and assistance in what you undertake of fighting. The apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun to praise them for piety and to urge those who fall short toward it, and to indicate that it is the basis of victory. It was also said: it is good news and a guarantee to them of victory because of their piety, as the conditioning with the derived noun suggests. What we have mentioned is not without merit, except that the command to piety in it is more general, encompassing both the occurrence of the act and its continuity, and similar usage is common in speech.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on Surah 9, verse 37:

﴿Indeed, the postponing (al-nasi')﴾ is a verbal noun (masdar) of *nasa'ahu*, meaning he postponed it. The forms *al-nasy*, *al-nasw* and *al-nisa'* also occur, on the pattern of *al-nahy*, *al-bad'* and *al-nida'*. All three are verbal nouns of *nasa'ahu*, like *al-nasi'*. It is also said that *al-nasi'* is an adjective, like *qatil* and *jarih*. The first view is preferred because, on it, no supposition (taqdir) is needed. If it is an adjective, one cannot predicate an increase of it except through the interpretation "one that is an increase" or "the postponing of the postponement is an increase." All of these readings have been recited.

Nafi' recited *al-nasiyy*, replacing the hamza with a *ya'* and assimilating it into the following *ya'*. The meaning is the postponement of the sanctity of one month to another. This was the practice of the Arabs: when a sacred month came while they were fighting, they would make it lawful and declare sacred another month in its place. So they would make the sacred month lawful and declare Safar sacred. If they still needed more, they would make that lawful and declare Rabi' al-Awwal sacred. They continued in this way until the sanctity had cycled through all the months of the year. In declaring months sacred, they considered only the number, not the specific months. Sometimes they would increase the number of months to thirteen or fourteen so that the time would accommodate them, and they would make four months of the year sacred as well. For this reason the specified number was stated explicitly in the Book and the Sunnah. Their time of pilgrimage would shift accordingly. In the ninth year after the Hijrah, the year in which Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) led the people in pilgrimage, it fell in Dhu al-Qa'dah. In the Farewell Pilgrimage it fell in Dhu al-Hijjah, which was the reckoning of the time of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) and the prophets before him (peace be upon them). Therefore the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Verily, time has come full circle," as the hadith continues in full. According to another report, they used to make the pilgrimage in each month for two years: they performed it in Dhu al-Hijjah for two years, then in Muharram for two years, and so on. The pilgrimage of al-Siddiq coincided with Dhu al-Qa'dah in their second year, while the pilgrimage of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took place at the time that was proper before that. Therefore he said what he said. That is, that postponement is ﴿an increase in disbelief﴾, which they practise, because it is the declaring unlawful of what Allah has made lawful. They regarded it as lawful and adopted it as a religious law (shari'ah), and that is disbelief, which they added to their disbelief.

It has also been said that it is a sin added to disbelief, and just as faith increases through obedience, disbelief increases through sin.

It was objected that sin is not part of disbelief, unlike obedience, which is part of faith according to one opinion. This was answered with a reply that is not free from turbidity.

﴿By it, those who disbelieve are led astray﴾: a leading astray upon their former straying. It is recited *yudill* (with the first letter vowelled), in the active form, with Allah the Exalted as the agent: that is, He creates straying in them when they engage in its beginnings and causes. This is also the meaning according to the first reading. It has also been said that the agent in both readings is Satan. It is permissible, on the second reading, for the relative pronoun to be the agent with the object omitted, meaning their followers. It has also been said that the agent is the leaders and the object is the relative pronoun. It has been recited *yadill* with a *fatha* on the *ya'* and the *dad*, from *dalla yadillu*, and *nadill* with the first-person plural "we" of majesty.

﴿They make it lawful﴾: that is, the postponed month. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to *al-nasi'* taken as a *fa'il* in the sense of a *maf'ul*.

﴿for a year﴾ of the years. ﴿And they declare sacred in its place another month﴾ which is not sacred.

﴿and they declare it sacred﴾: that is, they observe its sanctity as it was. The expression of this as declaring sacred is in view of their making it lawful in the previous year, or because they attribute it to their gods, as will come, if Allah the Exalted wills.

﴿for another year﴾, when the changing of it serves none of their purposes.

Al-Kalbi said: The first person to do this was a man of Kinanah called Nu'aym ibn Tha'labah. Whenever the people were about to depart from the season (of pilgrimage), he would stand and deliver a sermon, saying: "None can reverse what I have decided. I am the one who cannot be blamed or rejected." Then the polytheists would say to him: "At your service!" Then they would ask him to postpone for them a month in which they could raid. He would say: "Verily, Safar of this year is sacred." When he said that, they would untie their bowstrings and remove their spearheads and arrowheads. But if he said: "It is lawful," they would fasten their bowstrings, mount their mounts and make raids.

According to al-Dahhak, it was Junadah ibn 'Awf al-Kinani, who was obeyed in the pre-Islamic period. He would stand on a camel at the season and call out at the top of his voice: "Verily, your gods have made the sacred month lawful for you, so make it lawful." Then in the following year he would stand and say: "Verily, your gods have made the sacred month sacred for you, so declare it sacred."

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that he said: "The Nasa'ah was a clan of Banu Malik ibn Kinanah, and their last man was called al-Qalammas, who was the one who postponed the sacred month. He was a king among his people." Their poet recited:

"Among us is al-Qalammas, the postponer of the month."

Al-Kumayt said:

"We are the postponers among Ma'add; we make lawful the months of licence and make them sacred."

According to another report from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), the first to establish the postponement was 'Amr ibn Luhayy ibn Qam'ah ibn Khindif.

The two clauses are an explanation of the straying, so they have no place in grammatical analysis (i'rab). It has been permitted that they be in the accusative position, as a circumstantial clause (hal) of the relative pronoun, with the governing element being the governing element of the relative pronoun.

﴿That they may agree﴾: that is, that they may conform. Al-Zuhri recited *liyuwattiu* with the doubled letter.

﴿to the number of what Allah has made sacred﴾ of the four months. The *lam* is connected to *yuharrimunahu*, meaning they declare it sacred so as to conform to that number. Or it is connected to what the two verbs together indicate, meaning they did what they did in order to conform. Some have considered it to be a case of dispute (tanazu') between the two verbs.

﴿so that they make lawful what Allah has made sacred﴾, specifically, from the specified months. The summary is that what was obligatory for them was the number and the specification. Since they abandoned the specification, they have made lawful what Allah the Exalted has made sacred.

﴿Their evil deeds have been made attractive to them﴾. It is recited in the active form, with Allah the Exalted as the agent: that is, He made their deeds desirable to the natural disposition and beloved to the soul. It has also been said: He forsook them until they saw as good what is not good. It has also been said that the one who makes it attractive is Satan, by whispering and seducing with poetic premises.

﴿And Allah does not guide the disbelieving people﴾: a guidance that conveys to the desired end absolutely. He guides them only to what is reached when one follows its path, but they have turned away from it through their own wrong choice, so they wander in the wilderness of straying. By "the disbelievers" is meant either those already mentioned, in which case the apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun, or the wider category, which includes them as a first inclusion.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 38:**

﴿O you who have believed﴾ — this returns to encouraging the believers and urging them to fight, after mention of some of the disgraceful conduct of their enemies. (﴿What is [the matter] with you﴾) is an interrogative carrying the sense of disapproval and reproach. (﴿When you are told, "Go forth in the cause of Allah"﴾) means: set out for jihad. The root of *nafr* (going forth), it is said, is departing for a matter that necessitates it.
Page 95
(﴿You adhere heavily to the earth﴾) means: you were slow and did not hasten. Its original form is *tathaqaltum*, and al-A'mash read it so, whereupon the *ta'* was assimilated into the *tha'* and a *hamzat al-wasl* (connecting hamza) was introduced to enable pronunciation beginning with a sukun. A parallel is the poet's verse:

She gives her bedfellow, when he longs for her, a shy kiss, sweet in taste, when he follows up the kisses.

To this is attached (*idha*), and the clause is in the position of a circumstantial (*hal*): the verb is past in form but present in meaning, i.e., "What is [the matter] with you being sluggish at the time the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to you, 'Go forth'?" It is also permitted that the governing element of (*idha*) is the implied stability (*istiqrar*) within (*lakum*), or the meaning of the verb implied by that, i.e., "What is occurring to you, or what has occurred to you, or what are you doing when you are told, 'Go forth'?" It has also been read as *a-tha'aqaltum* with an opened hamza, as an interrogative of reproach and disapproval; the hamza of connection falls away in continuous speech. On this reading, *idha* cannot be attached to this verb, because the interrogative has priority of position, so its complement may not precede it. Perhaps whoever says that adverbs of time may be extended more than other elements would permit this.

His statement, glorified is He: (﴿to the earth﴾) is connected to *ithaqaltum*, with the verb taken as implying the sense of inclination and adherence; without this implication it would not take *ila* ("to"). That is, you adhered heavily, inclining toward the world and its perishable pleasures of a short time, and disliked the hardships of jihad and its toils, which entail everlasting rest and enduring life. Or [it means] "to dwelling in your land and your homes." The first is more eloquent in disapproval and reproach, and the second has been preferred on the ground that it is further from the suspicion of a trace of repetition in the verse.

This sluggishness occurred during the Expedition of Tabuk, which took place in Rajab of the ninth year, for after the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, returned from al-Ta'if he remained in Madinah briefly, then called the people to march in a time of hardship and severity, of intense heat and barren lands. The fruits of Madinah had ripened and its shade had become pleasant, combined with the great distance and the multitude of the enemy, so setting out was difficult for them.

Ibn Hisham mentioned: "The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, rarely went out on an expedition without alluding to it and informing [people] that he intended a direction other than the one he was facing, except for the Expedition of Tabuk, for he, upon him be blessings and peace, made it clear to the people so that they might prepare for it with its requisite preparation."

(﴿Are you content with the life of this world﴾) and its deceptions, (﴿rather than the Hereafter﴾): that is, in place of the Hereafter and its everlasting bliss. (﴿Then the enjoyment of the life of this world is but little compared with the Hereafter﴾): that is, what are its benefits and aims, or what is the enjoyment of it and its delights, in comparison with the Hereafter, (﴿except a little﴾), contemptible and of no account. The explicit noun in place of the pronoun is for added emphasis. This *fi* is called the *qiyasiyya* (comparative), because the thing measured is placed beside that against which it is measured. In describing the life of this world with what indicates its preciousness and calls for desire for it, while stripping the Hereafter of the like of that, there is an exaggeration in showing the lowliness and baseness of this world and the greatness and exaltation of the Hereafter.

Ahmad, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, and others transmitted from al-Miswar who said: "The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, 'By Allah, the world compared with the Hereafter is only like one of you dipping his finger in the sea, then lifting it out; let him look at what it returns with.'" Al-Hakim transmitted and authenticated from Sahl who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ passed by Dhu al-Hulayfa and saw a sheep lifting its leg. He said, 'Do you see this sheep as insignificant to its owner?' They said, 'Yes.' He, upon him be blessings and peace, said, 'By Him in whose hand is my soul, the world is more insignificant to Allah, Exalted, than this is to its owner; and if it were worth the wing of a mosquito to Allah, He would not have given a disbeliever a drink of water from it.'"

I see the use of evidence for the worthlessness of the world only as argument in a situation of necessity. Yes, it is an excellent abode for one who takes provision from it for his Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 39:

﴿Unless you go forth﴾ i.e., unless you go out to what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has called you to, to go forth with him. (﴿He will punish you﴾)
Page 96
i.e., Allah, Mighty and Majestic, (﴿with a painful punishment﴾) by destruction, through a dreadful cause such as drought and the appearance of thunder. Some restricted the punishment to the Hereafter, but this is not correct. Others generalized it and took destruction into account, so that the statement of Him, glorified is He, (﴿and will replace﴾) can be coordinated with it, i.e., and He will replace you, after your destruction, (﴿with another people﴾) whom He described as different from them, to emphasize the threat and intensify the warning by indicating a difference in attributes and essence that entails complete eradication. That is, a people who are obedient and who prefer the Hereafter over this world, who are not from your children or your relatives. They are the sons of Persia, as Sa'id ibn Jubayr said, or the people of Yemen, as narrated from Abu Rawq, or what encompasses both groups, as chosen by some of the verifiers. (﴿And they will not harm Him at all﴾) with anything, or any harm, and the pronoun refers to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. That is, your reluctance does not harm the support of His religion at all, for He, glorified is He, is free of need of everything and in every matter. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, promised him protection and victory, and His promise, glorified is He, is certainly to be fulfilled. The first is what is narrated from al-Hasan, and it was chosen by Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i and others. The second is brought closer by the return of the following pronoun to him, peace be upon him, by consensus. (﴿And Allah is over all things competent﴾) So He is able to destroy them and bring another people. It has also been said: over the replacement and the changing of causes and the support without aid, so the sentence serves as a completion of what precedes and a preparation for what follows.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 40 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Unless you support him, Allah has already supported him, when those who disbelieved drove him out﴾ from Makkah. Attributing the expulsion to them is attributing it to a remote cause, for Allah the Exalted had permitted him (ﷺ) to leave when they had done what they did, so he (ﷺ) went out by himself. ﴿The second of two﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to his pronoun (ﷺ), meaning one of two, without considering that he (ﷺ) was the second. The meaning of the expressions "the third of three," "the fourth of four," and the like is that one of these numbers is taken absolutely, not that the third or fourth in particular is meant. For this reason the majority of grammarians prohibited putting the following noun in the accusative, such as saying "thālith thalāthatan" or "rābiʿ arbaʿatan." So there is no need to strain to explain that he (ﷺ) was the second of the two, as some have done. It is also read as "thānī" with the yā' unvowelled, according to the dialect of those who treat a defective noun like a restricted noun in its grammatical inflection (iʿrāb). This is not a poetic necessity, contrary to those who claimed it and said it is one of the finest poetic licenses.

The conditional sentence raises a difficulty: its answer (jawāb) is in the past tense, whereas it must be in the future; if it is in the past, it is converted to the future. Here it was not converted. The answer is that the answer is omitted, and its cause has been put in its place, and that is future: meaning, "If you do not support him, then Allah, who has already supported him in a time of greater distress than this, will support him." This is what the words of Mujahid indicate. It is also allowed that the meaning is: "If you do not support him, then He has already made support for him obligatory when He supported him in a similar situation, so He will not forsake him at other times." There is a difference between the two interpretations, although both agree that the answer of the condition is omitted: the indicator of the answer in the first interpretation is the support restricted to a time of weakness and scarcity in the past, while in the second it is their knowledge that he (ﷺ) is among those who are supported. Al-Qutb said: "The two interpretations are close, except that the first is based on analogy (qiyās) and the second on continuity (istiṣḥāb), for the support was established in that situation and so it is established in the future, since the original state is the continuation of what was as it was." It was also said: on the first interpretation the answer is supposed, while on the second it is a continuous support, so it is correct to place it upon the future, because it encompasses it.

﴿When they were both in the cave﴾ is a substitute for ﴿when he drove him out﴾, a partial substitute (badal al-baʿḍ), since the time referred to is an extended period, so no difference that would prevent substitution is imagined. It was also said that it is an adverb of time (ẓarf) governing ﴿the second of two﴾. The cave (ghār) here is a hole at the top of Mount Thawr, a mountain on the right side of Makkah at a distance of one hour's journey. They remained in it, as has been related from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them, for three days. ʿĀmir ibn Fuhayrah used to go to them with food, and ʿAlī, may Allah ennoble his face, arranged their provisions. He bought three camels from the camels of Bahrain and hired a guide for them. When it was in some part of the night of the third night, ʿAlī, may Allah ennoble his face, came to them with the camels and the guide. They mounted and headed toward Madinah.

Because of the concealment of him (ﷺ) in the cave for three days, it is related that Imam Ahmad was concealed for the same length of time during the trial of the Qur'an, though not in a cave. This humble servant also was concealed during the conquest of Baghdad after the siege, in the year 1247 AH, out of fear of the common people and some of the elite, because of matters attributed to me and fabricated against me by some hypocrites. I was in a cellar at the home of some beloved ones for three days also for that reason. Then Allah brought me out from it with honour, by the Trustworthy One, and afterward Allah strengthened me with the blessed and auspicious ones.

﴿When he said﴾ is a second substitute. It was also said the first is ﴿to his companion﴾, who is Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him.

Al-Daraqutni, Ibn Shahin, Ibn Mardawayh and others have related from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him: 'You are my companion in the cave, and you will be with me at the Pool.'" Ibn ʿAsakir related a similar report from the narration of Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them, and Abu Hurayrah. He and Ibn ʿAdi related through the chain of al-Zuhri from Anas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Hassan: "Have you said anything about Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Say it, and I will listen." So Hassan, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

"The second of two in the lofty cave, when the enemy circled it, when he climbed the mountain.
He was the beloved of the Messenger of Allah, as they know, of all creation; he never equated any man with him."

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) laughed until his back teeth showed, then said: "You have spoken the truth, O Hassan; he is as you have said." No one has disagreed with this, as far as I know, not even the Shi'ah, but they say what you will come to know, and its refutation, if Allah wills.

﴿Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us﴾, with protection and help. This is a specific companionship, otherwise He, the Exalted, is with each one of His creatures. Al-Shaykhan and others related from Anas, who said: Abu Bakr told me, saying: "I was with the Prophet (ﷺ) in the cave, and I saw the traces of the polytheists. I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, if one of them were to lift his foot, he would see us beneath his foot.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'O Abu Bakr, what do you think of two whose third is Allah?'"

Al-Bayhaqi and others related that when they entered the cave, Allah commanded the spider, and it spun a web over the mouth of the cave, and He sent two wild doves, which laid eggs in it. The young men of Quraysh came from every clan, one man at a time, with their clubs and swords, until they were about forty cubits away. One of them hurried ahead and looked into the cave to see if anyone was there. He saw two doves, so he returned to his companions and said: "There is no one in the cave. If anyone had entered it, these two doves would not have remained." In one report, some of them said: "There was a spider over it before the birth of Muhammad (ﷺ)." So they turned back. The first person to enter the cave was Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Jundub ibn Sufyan, who said: "When Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, set out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) toward the cave, Abu Bakr said: 'Do not enter, O Messenger of Allah, until I have searched it.' He entered the cave, and something struck his hand, so he began wiping the blood from his finger, and he was saying:
'You are nothing but a finger that bled,
and in the way of Allah you have suffered what you have suffered.'"

[Page 98]

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il and Ibn ʿAsakir related: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set out as a emigrant, Abu Bakr followed him. He walked sometimes in front of him, sometimes behind him, sometimes on his right, and sometimes on his left. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: 'What is this, O Abu Bakr?' He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I remember the watchers, so I walk in front of you; and I remember the pursuers, so I walk behind you; and sometimes on your right, and sometimes on your left, for I am not secure for you.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) walked that night on the tips of his toes until his feet were worn. When Abu Bakr saw that, he carried him on his shoulders and began running with him until he reached the mouth of the cave. He set him down and said: 'By the One who sent you with the truth, do not enter until I have entered it. If there is anything in it, it will strike me before you.' He entered and saw nothing, so he carried him and brought him in. In the cave there was a hole in which there were snakes and vipers. Abu Bakr feared that something from them might come out and harm the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so he put his foot over it, and they began striking and stinging him, while his tears flowed, and he did not lift his foot out of love for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)."

In another report: "He sealed every hole in the cave with his garment, which he cut into pieces for this purpose, and one hole remained, which he sealed with his heel." May Allah be pleased with him.

﴿Then Allah sent down His tranquillity﴾, which is the calm in which hearts find rest, ﴿upon him﴾, that is, upon the Prophet (ﷺ). Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il and Ibn ʿAsakir in his History related from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that the pronoun refers to the companion. al-Khatib in his History related a similar report from Habib ibn Abi Thabit. It was also said, and this is the more apparent view, because the Prophet (ﷺ) was not disturbed so as to need calming. The fixing of the pronoun for ﴿and supported him with hosts you did not see﴾ as referring to him (ﷺ) does not contradict this, because it is coordinated with ﴿Allah supported him﴾, not with ﴿sent down﴾, so that the pronouns do not become disjointed. Moreover, if the coordination is with it, as has been said, the pronoun may also refer to the companion, as indicated by what Ibn Mardawayh related from Anas, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him: "O Abu Bakr, Allah the Exalted sent down His tranquillity upon you and supported you," and so on. And if you refuse this, what harm is there in the disjunction when the matter is clear?

Some have preferred the first view and claimed that it is the one suited to the context. The sending down of tranquillity does not necessarily have to be to remove agitation; it may also be for his elevation and support (ﷺ). The fāʾ (then) indicates sequence in mention, and this is weak. Some who interpreted it according to that possibility explained it in a way that does not come near any trace of fear at all. The "hosts" are the angels who descended on the day of Badr, the Confederates, and Hunayn. It was also said that they were angels sent by Allah, blessed and exalted, to guard him in the cave. This is supported by what Abu Nuʿaym related from Asmaʾ, daughter of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him: "Abu Bakr saw a man facing the cave and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, he has surely seen us.' He said: 'No, the angels are now covering him with their wings.' Then the man sat down and urinated facing them both. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'O Abu Bakr, if he had seen us, he would not have done this.'" The apparent meaning, on this view, is that they were in the cave in such a way that they could ordinarily be seen by someone outside the cave. This view has been objected to on the grounds that it is contradicted by the description of the hosts as unseen by the addressees. But it may be said that the purpose of this description is merely to magnify the matter of the hosts. Whoever makes the coordination with ﴿sent down﴾ must accept the view mentioned, because the fāʾ, in its apparent sense, requires that this sending down follow what came before it, which cannot be reconciled with the first view concerning the hosts.

﴿And made the word of those who disbelieved the lowest﴾, that is, their word upon which they agreed concerning the matter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the House of Assembly (Dar al-Nadwah), where his Lord, glory be to Him, saved him despite their noses being rubbed in the dust, and protected him from their scheming, although they left no means unused to bring harm to him. They set a blood-money for whoever would kill or capture him (ﷺ), and they went out in pursuit of him (ﷺ) on foot and on horseback, but they returned with empty hands and black faces. And some of those who were with him (ﷺ) became his... [text continues on the next page]

[Page 99]

...companions (ﷺ). Ibn Saʿd, Abu Nuʿaym and al-Bayhaqi (both in al-Dala'il) related from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) went out, and Abu Bakr was with him, Abu Bakr turned around and saw a horseman who had caught up with them. He said: 'O Prophet of Allah, this is a horseman who has caught up with us.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'O Allah, throw him down.' So he was thrown from his horse.
