He said: 'O Prophet of Allah, command me with whatever you wish.' He said: 'Stand where you are, and do not let anyone who comes after us pass.' So at the beginning of the day he was an enemy of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and at the end of the day he was a guard." This horseman was Suraqah. About this he says to Abu Jahl:

"O Abu al-Hakam, by Allah, had you been present
for the matter of my horse, when its legs sank,
you would have known, without doubt, that Muhammad
is a Messenger with proof; so who can oppose him?"

And it is authentically related in the hadith of the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and others that "the people sought the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and Abu Bakr. Abu Bakr said: 'None of them caught up with us except Suraqah, on his horse. I said: O Messenger of Allah, this pursuer has caught up with us.' He said: ﴿Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us.﴾ Then when he drew near, and there was between us and him the distance of a spear or two or three, I said: O Messenger of Allah, this pursuer has caught up with us.' And I wept. He said: 'Why do you weep?' I said: 'By Allah, I do not weep for myself, but I weep for you.' So he (peace be upon him) supplicated against him and said: 'O Allah, suffice us against him by whatever You will.' Then his horse sank into the ground up to its belly in hard earth, and he leapt off it and said: 'O Muhammad, this is your doing. Pray to Allah, the Exalted, that He deliver me from what I am in. By Allah, I will surely blind those behind me who pursue you. Here is my quiver; take from it an arrow, for you will pass by my camels and my sheep at such and such a place; take from them what you need.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'I have no need of them.' He prayed for him, and he departed and returned to his companions. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) continued on, and I was with him, until we arrived at Medina," the hadith.

It is permissible to interpret the word (kalimah, "word") as shirk (polytheism), and this is what Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. In that case it is majaz (figurative usage) for their belief, which is their habit to speak of. Some have interpreted it as the call to disbelief, so it carries the general meaning of speech. The Shaykh al-Islam claimed that the making (ja'l) mentioned is, on both interpretations, far from applying to the guarding angels, because it is not realized merely by deliverance but by killing, capturing, and the like. You know that there is no objection to the interpretation we have mentioned; and the fact that the deliverance is the starting point for the making, in both of its interpretations, is sufficient to remove the objection without any doubt.

﴿And the word of Allah is the highest.﴾ It may be meant as His promise, glorified is He, to His Prophet (ﷺ), alluded to by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when those who disbelieved plotted against you, to confine you, or kill you, or expel you; they plot, and Allah plots, and Allah is the best of plotters.﴾ Or it may be the word of Tawhid (monotheism), as Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said; or it may be the call of Islam, as it has been said. And there is no hiding the exaggeration in changing the style, because the nominal sentence indicates permanence and stability, together with the indication that the making did not reach that word, and that it is by itself exalted, unlike the exaltedness of other things, which is not essential but by making and artifice. So it is a passing accident and a non-stable matter. For this reason he placed the separating pronoun (damir al-fasl) in the middle.

Ya'qub recited (wa-kalimata Allah) with the accusative, in conjunction with (kalimata alladhina kafaru). This is less eloquent than the nominative, and the sentence with it is not like "Zayd freed Zayd's slave," as is not hidden.

﴿And Allah is Mighty﴾, not overcome in His command, ( ﴿Wise﴾ ), with no deficiency in His management.

This verse has been cited as evidence for the excellence of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him. By my life, this is one of the things that leaves the Rafidi (Rafidite) in a lizard's hole or in a desolate wilderness. For it came in the manner of rebuke addressed to the believers, excluding Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him. Ibn 'Asakir related from Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah who said: "Allah, glorified is He, rebuked all the Muslims regarding His Prophet (ﷺ) except Abu Bakr alone, for he was exempt from the rebuke, then He recited ﴿If you do not help him...﴾ the verse." Rather, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi related from al-Hasan who said: "Allah, exalted is He, rebuked all the people of the earth except Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, so He said: ﴿If you do not help him...﴾ etc."

And Ibn 'Asakir related from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, with the wording: "Indeed Allah, exalted is He, blamed all the people and praised Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, so He said: ﴿If you do not help him...﴾ etc." In it is the explicit statement of his companionship (suhbah) with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this has not been established for anyone else among the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) besides him. That the intended meaning of "companion" is this has been agreed upon (ijma'), just as the intended meaning of "servant" in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Glorified is He who took His servant by night﴾ is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). From here they said: denying his companionship is disbelief. Along with this, the verse includes the consolation of the Prophet (peace be upon him) for him with the words ﴿Do not grieve﴾, and the reason for this is the special companionship of Allah, glorified is He, indicated by the words ﴿indeed Allah is with us﴾. Nothing like this has been established for anyone else; rather, no Prophet has affirmed Allah's companionship for himself and for another of his companions. It seems that in this there is an allusion that there is none among them like Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him.

And in the sending down of tranquility (sakinah) upon him, based on the return of the pronoun to him, there is what indicates the tranquility is his, he himself, may Allah be pleased with him, and may Allah curse those who hate him. Likewise in its being sent down upon the Messenger (peace be upon him), although it is the companion who was disturbed; what guides the fair-minded person is that the two of them are like a single person. And more evident than that is the allusion that the grief was the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ), and what supports this is what has passed in the hadith of the two Shaykhs.

The Rafidah denied that the verse indicates any excellence for al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him. They said: "If the indicator of excellence is ﴿the second of two﴾, then there is in it no more than that Abu Bakr completed the number. If it is ﴿when they were both in the cave﴾, then it indicates no more than two persons being together in one place, and the righteous and the wicked often gather together. If it is ( ﴿his companion﴾ ), then companionship can exist between a believer and a disbeliever, as in His saying: ﴿His companion said to him while he was debating with him: Do you disbelieve in He who created you?﴾ and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Your companion is not mad﴾ and ﴿O companions of the prison﴾. Rather, it can exist between one who reasons and other than him, as in his saying:

*Indeed the donkey among donkeys is a mount,*
*and when you are alone with it, what a wretched companion it is.*

If it is ﴿Do not grieve﴾, then it is said: grief is either obedience or disobedience. It is not permissible that it be obedience, for otherwise he (ﷺ) would not have forbidden it. So it is necessarily disobedience, because of the prohibition, and that is established against your aim. Moreover, there is in it, as regards indication of cowardice, what there is. If it is ﴿indeed Allah is with us﴾, then it is possible that the meaning is affirming Allah's special companionship for him (ﷺ) alone, but He used 'we' to block the door of alienation. A parallel to this is the use of 'aw' (or) in His saying: ﴿And indeed we or you are upon guidance, or in manifest error.﴾ If it is ﴿so Allah sent down His tranquility upon him﴾, then the pronoun in it is for the Prophet (ﷺ), so that the pronouns do not get disconnected. In that case, specifying him (peace be upon him) with tranquility here, while there is no specification in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿so Allah sent down His tranquility upon His Messenger and upon the believers﴾, is an indication of the opposite of what you claim. And if what the verse indicates of his going out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at that time is so, then he (peace be upon him) did not bring him out with him except out of fear of their plot should he remain with the polytheists in Mecca. And in the fact that the one who equipped them by buying camels was 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, there is an indication of this. And if there is something beyond this, then explain it to us so that we may discuss it." End of their words.

By my life, it is most like the babbling of a feverish man or the raving of a drunk. Had Allah, glorified is He, not related in His glorious Book of their brothers the Jews and Christians something like this and rejected it, out of mercy to the weak among the believers, we would not have opened our mouths to refute it, nor have run our pens in the field of exposing its falseness. But for that, I say: it is not hidden that ﴿the second of two﴾ and likewise ﴿when they were both in the cave﴾ indicate, with the help of the context, the excellence of al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him; we do not claim that they indicate it absolutely. And the help of the context is clearer than fire on a mountain. Two rams do not butt heads over the fact that a man does not become a second to another by his own choice, nor is he with him in a place when fleeing from an enemy, unless he was relied upon and his sincerity was verified in his sight, especially since the other left for his sake a land where his midwives had settled and his amulets had been released, and parted from his beloved ones, and was estranged from his peers, and mounted the back of a wide desert where the sandgrouse lose their way and steps fall short.

Among what indicates the excellence of that two-ness is the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), calming the heart of Abu Bakr: "What do you think of two whose third is Allah, may He be exalted?" The linguistic companionship, although it does not by itself indicate the claim, does indicate it with the help of the context as well. So the annexing of "companion" to the pronoun is for definiteness, that is, his companion who was with him at a time when the intimate friend turns away from his intimate friend, his comrade who left his family and tribe for the sake of accompanying him. And "do not grieve" does not mean literally the prohibition of grief, for it is among the matters that do not fall under legal obligation; rather, what is meant by it is consolation for al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, or something similar. And what they mentioned of the dilemma runs in like manner in His saying, exalted is He, addressing Musa and Harun, peace be upon them both: ﴿Do not fear; indeed I am with you both.﴾ Likewise in His saying, glorified is He, to the Prophet (peace be upon him): ﴿Let not their saying grieve you; indeed all honour belongs to Allah.﴾ And so on. Do you think that Allah, glorified is He, forbade obedience to Himself? Or that any of those infallible ones, peace be upon them, committed a sin? Glory be to You, this is a tremendous slander.

And that grief is among the matters that do not fall under legal obligation, considered in itself, does not contradict that it may be the object of praise and blame, as grief over the loss of an act of obedience is praiseworthy, while grief over the loss of an act of disobedience is blameworthy, because that is by another consideration, as is not hidden. As for what was mentioned in the appended part, that there is in it, regarding indication of cowardice, what there is, there is in it of the commission of falsehood what there is. For we do not concede that fear indicates cowardice; otherwise the cowardice of Musa and his brother, peace be upon them both, would follow. So what do you think of grief? And the grief of al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, is not greater than hiding in the cave. And no Muslim thinks that it was out of cowardice, or that he was described by cowardice, when the bravest of creation absolutely, (ﷺ), is so described? And whoever is fair sees that his (peace be upon him) consolation of Abu Bakr with the words ﴿Do not grieve﴾ is like how his Lord, glorified is He, consoled him with His saying:

[Page 102]

(Let not their speech grieve you), pointing to al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, and his rank with the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, in the sight of his Lord, exalted is His majesty. He is the beloved of the Beloved of Allah. Moreover, even if one sets aside the occurrence of this consolation from Allah to His alert Prophet (ﷺ), the very address "do not grieve" would be sufficient to indicate that he, may Allah be pleased with him, is the beloved of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Otherwise, how could the converse of beloveds be explained? This is evident, except to enemies. As for what is mentioned, that the special companionship (al-ma'iyya al-khassa) was for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) alone, and that the use of "we" was to close the door of alienation, this is sheer obstinacy, as the report that passed just above indicates. Furthermore, if that grief was solely out of concern for the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, then what alienation is there in his saying, "Do not grieve, indeed Allah is with us"? And if it was concern for the Messenger (ﷺ) and for himself, may Allah be pleased with him, then the causal clause does not fall in its proper place, and the sentence is not directed to it. And if we grant that there is alienation in the first case and that the causal clause falls in its proper place in the second, then that grief would be a clear proof of the praise of al-Siddiq. And if it was only for himself, as the one with the wicked soul claims, then the causal clause would have no meaning at all. What sense is there in "Do not grieve for yourself, indeed Allah is with me, not with you"?

Moreover, it may be said to the Rafidi: Did al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, understand from the verse what you understood regarding the restriction, and that the expression with "we" was a closing of the door of alienation or not? If the former, then alienation necessarily occurs, and we have fallen into what we fled from. If the latter, then you have claimed for yourself a rank you could never reach, even if your soul departed. And if you claim equality in understanding the expressions and allusions of the sublime Qur'an with the eloquent Arabs who witnessed the revelation, that would not be granted to you, or you would die (in the attempt). So how can your claim of superiority over al-Siddiq be accepted, when he himself, from the Prophet's allusion in the hadith of the choice (hadith al-takhyir), understood what was hidden from the rest of the Companions, even from Ali, may Allah honour his face? That is why they were astonished at his weeping on that day. As for what is mentioned about the parallel (al-tanzir) in the verse, it points to the taqiyya (concealment of belief, dissimulation) which the Rafidah have adopted as a religion, and by which they have distorted words from their places. We have already set out for you the discussion of this in the fullest manner, so recall it. As for what is mentioned concerning the matter of tranquillity (al-sakina), its answer is known from what we have mentioned. And as for the claim that the restriction indicates the expulsion of al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, from the company of the believers, as the dog, the enemy of Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ), alluded to, then even if that were hidden from those witnesses of the revelation, among whom is the Amir, may Allah honour his face, how then did they enable him to hold the caliphate, which in the view of the Shi'a is the sister of prophethood? They are those who "fear not the blame of any blamer" in the cause of Allah. And as for the claim that the Companions had all agreed upon error in this matter, and that the Amir was oppressed among them or ordered to remain silent and sheathe the sword at that time, as the opponent claims, this has rolled up its carpet and been scattered to the winds. There is no need to tire the pen in blackening the face of the one who makes this claim.

As for what is mentioned, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not bring him out except out of fear of his plot, the answer is that the verse contains not the slightest indication of his expulsion at all, let alone that it was out of fear of a plot. Moreover, if there were fear in his companionship with him, peace and blessings be upon him, what opportunity could be like the opportunity that arose when the pursuers came to the door of the cave? Had there been (any such thing) with Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, and far be it from him, the least that would be said is: "Come here, for this is the target." It cannot be said that he feared for his own self as well, because he could have saved himself from them by means of various measures, and at least he could have said to them: "I have come out for this scheme." Also, if al-Siddiq were as the heretic claims, what prevented him from saying to his son Abd al-Rahman, or his daughter Asma, or his freedman Amir ibn Fuhayra, for they used to come and go to him in the cave, as Ibn Mardawayh reported from Aisha, so that one of them would inform the disbelievers of the place of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)? Moreover, on this claim the hadith of the (Quraysh's) authorization (of his safety) comes, and it is the strongest witness that he is who he is. Also, if the door of this nonsense is opened, it becomes possible for the Nasibi to say, and we seek refuge in Allah, concerning Ali, may Allah honour his face: "The Prophet (ﷺ) did not order him to sleep in his noble bed on the night of the hijra except that the polytheists might kill him, thinking him to be the Prophet (ﷺ), so that he would be rid of him." This claim is no more strange nor more false than the claim of the Shi'i: "The expulsion of al-Siddiq was only out of fear of the evil of (Abu Bakr)." Let him therefore fear Allah, glorified is He, from opening this shameful door in the sight of people of understanding. And he claims that the Amir, may Allah honour his face, preparing the camels for them by purchase is an allusion to that, which does not allude in any way. Moreover, that (report), though we mentioned it earlier, has come only in some narrations from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, and what is relied upon by the scholars of hadith is other than that. There is no harm in citing it to complete the benefit and to illuminate the virtue of al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him. So we say:

Abd al-Razzaq, Ahmad, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported, through al-Zuhri, from Urwa, from Aisha, who said: "I never knew my parents except that they were following the religion, and not a day passed over us but the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to us at both ends of the day, morning and evening. When the Muslims were tested, Abu Bakr set out as an emigrant toward the land of Abyssinia. When he reached Bark al-Ghimad, Ibn al-Daghina, who was the chief of the Qara, met him and said: 'Where are you going, O Abu Bakr?' Abu Bakr said: 'My people have driven me out, so I want to travel in the land and worship my Lord.' Ibn al-Daghina said: 'A man like you, O Abu Bakr, does not leave nor is he driven out. You earn what is lost, you maintain the ties of kinship, you bear the burdens of the weak, you host the guest, and you help in the calamities of truth. I am your protector, so return and worship your Lord in your land.' Ibn al-Daghina set off and returned with Abu Bakr. Ibn al-Daghina went around among the disbelieving Quraysh and said: 'Abu Bakr is not one who should leave, nor should he be driven out. Will you drive out a man who earns what is lost, maintains the ties of kinship, bears the burdens of the weak, hosts the guest, and helps in the calamities of truth?' So Quraysh accepted the protection of Ibn al-Daghina and gave Abu Bakr security, and they said to Ibn al-Daghina: 'Tell Abu Bakr to worship his Lord in his house, and let him pray there as he wishes and recite as he wishes, but let him not harm us, and let him not make his prayer and recitation public outside his house.' He did so. Then it occurred to Abu Bakr to build a mosque in the courtyard of his house, and he would pray and recite there, and the women and children of the polytheists would crowd around him, wondering at him and gazing at him. He was a man who wept much and could not control his tears when reciting the Qur'an. This frightened the nobles of Quraysh, so they sent for Ibn al-Daghina, who came to them. They said: 'We only granted Abu Bakr protection on condition that he worship his Lord in his house, but he has exceeded that, building a mosque in the courtyard of his house and making his prayer and recitation public. We fear that our women and children will be tempted. So if he wishes to be content with worshipping his Lord in his house, let him do so; but if he insists on making this public, ask him to return your protection to you, for we dislike breaking our pledge to you, and we do not accept Abu Bakr's public display.' Ibn al-Daghina came to Abu Bakr and said: 'O Abu Bakr, you know the agreement I made for you. Either be content with that, or return my protection to me, for I do not want the Arabs to hear that I broke the pledge of a man for whom I made a pledge.' Abu Bakr said: 'I return your protection to you, and I am content with the protection of Allah and His Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was in Mecca at that time. He said to the Muslims: 'I have been shown the land of your emigration. I was shown a salt flat with palm trees between two lava fields.' So those Muslims who emigrated, emigrated toward Medina, and some emigrated to the land of Abyssinia. Abu Bakr prepared to emigrate, but the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: 'Wait patiently, for I hope permission will be granted to me.' Abu Bakr said: 'Do you hope for that? May my father be your ransom!' He said: 'Yes.' So Abu Bakr restrained himself for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for the sake of companionship, and he fed two she-camels he had with him on the leaves of the samur tree for four months. Then, while we were sitting in our house at the height of noon, someone said to Abu Bakr: 'This is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) coming at an hour when he never came to us.' Abu Bakr said: 'May my father and mother be his ransom! If he has come at this hour, it must be for a matter.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came and asked permission to enter. He said: 'Who is with you?' Abu Bakr said: 'They are only your family, may my father be your ransom, O Messenger of Allah.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed, permission has been granted to me to depart.' Abu Bakr said: 'Then the companions, may my father be your ransom, O Messenger of Allah.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Yes.' Abu Bakr said: 'Then take, may my father be your ransom, O Messenger of Allah, one of these two mounts of mine.' The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said: 'For the price.' Aisha said: 'We prepared them with the utmost haste, and we made for them a provision bag in a leather pouch. Asma, daughter of Abu Bakr, cut from her waistband and tied the pouch with it, and for that reason she was called Dhat al-Nitaq (the one of the waistband).' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and Abu Bakr joined a cave on a mountain called Thawr, and they remained in it for three nights. Abd Allah ibn Abi Bakr stayed with them at night, and he was a young, intelligent, and quick-witted lad. He would leave them before dawn and be in the morning among Quraysh in Mecca as one who had spent the night there. He would not hear any plot against them without retaining it, until he brought them news of it when darkness fell. Amir ibn Fuhayra, a freedman of Abu Bakr, grazed a flock of sheep for them, and he would bring it to them when the night had gone a little, so that they would have milk. They would sleep in its milk until Amir called to the flock at dawn. He did this every night of those three nights. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) hired a man from the Dil, of the Banu Abd ibn Adi, an expert guide, who had sworn an oath of alliance with the family of al-As ibn Wa'il, and he was upon the religion of the disbelievers of Quraysh. They entrusted him, and they gave him their two mounts, and they arranged to meet him at the cave of Thawr after three nights. He brought them their two mounts on the morning of the third night. He took them by way of Adhakhir, which is the coastal road." The hadith in full, and in it is that which contains evidence of the virtue of al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him. It is explicit that their preparation was in the house of Abu Bakr, and that the two mounts were his. It is also mentioned that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not accept one of them except for a price, which refutes the Rafidi's claim of accusing the Truthful Woman (al-Siddiqa), and far be it from her in the hadith.

Furthermore, whoever has encompassed knowledge of the aspects of what we have said in this discussion knows that the claim "it was something other than that, so explain it to us that we may discuss it" arises from pure ignorance or obstinacy. "Whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide." In sum, the Shi'a have unified their word upon disbelief, by the evidence of the verse for the virtue of al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him. "But Allah refuses except that the word of those who disbelieved be the lowest, and the word of Allah is the highest."

**[Page 104]**

(﴿Go forth﴾) is a *tajrid* (a rhetorical device in which the speaker addresses a third party to reprimand a group). It is a command to go forth, following a rebuke for neglecting it and a denunciation of laxity regarding it. His words, glorified be He, ﴿light and heavy﴾, are two circumstantial clauses (*hal*) referring to the pronoun of the addressees. The meaning is: in every state, whether in ease or hardship, whether you are occupied by any cause, such as health or sickness, wealth or poverty, few or many dependents, old age or youth, fatness or thinness, or other circumstances that fall under the assistance or lack of means, after having the ability and capacity in general. Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Abu Yazid al-Madini, who said: Abu Ayyub al-Ansari and al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad used to say, "We were commanded to go forth in every state," and they interpreted the verse accordingly. Both of them also transmitted from Mujahid, who said: They said, "Among us are the heavy, the one with a need, the one with a craft, the one with an occupation, and the one whose affairs are scattered." So Allah, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿Go forth, light and heavy﴾, and He refused to excuse them unless they went forth, light and heavy, and in whatever state they were. What was reported in their explanation, such as "light" meaning with few weapons and "heavy" meaning with many, or "riders and pedestrians," or "young and old," or "healthy and sick," and so on, is not a restriction of the two opposing states to the exclusion of the rest. It is reported from Ibn Umm Maktum that he said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Is there an excuse for me not to go forth?" He said: "No," until there was revealed: ﴿There is no blame upon the blind﴾. Ibn Abi Hatim and others transmitted from al-Suddi, who said: When this verse was revealed, its matter weighed heavily upon the people, so Allah abrogated it (*naskh*, the replacement of a earlier ruling by a later one), saying: ﴿There is no blame upon the weak or upon the sick﴾, up to the end of the verse. It has been said that it is abrogated by His words, exalted is He: ﴿And it is not for the believers to go forth all together﴾, but this is contrary to the apparent meaning. Some of the reports imply that there is no abrogation. Ibn Jarir, al-Tabarani and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, transmitted from Abu Rashid, who said: I saw al-Miqdad, the rider of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), at Homs, wanting to go on a military expedition, so I said: "Allah has already excused you." He said: "The Surah of *al-Buhuth* (the Surah of Investigations), meaning this verse from it, has refused to leave us alone."

﴿And strive with your wealth and your selves in the way of Allah﴾, that is, with whatever is possible for you of both, or one of them. Striving with wealth is spending it on weapons, provisioning the fighters, and the like. (﴿That﴾), that is, what has been mentioned of going forth and striving, and what it contains of the sense of distance, as has passed many times, (﴿is better﴾), great in itself, (﴿for you﴾) in this world or in the Hereafter, or in both. It is also permissible that the meaning is: better for you than what is sought by abandoning it, such as ease, comfort, the abundance of life, and enjoying wealth and children.

﴿If you knew﴾, that is: if you know what is good, you will know that it is good; or: if you know that it is good, since there is no possibility of anything other than truth in the reports of Him, exalted is He, then hasten to it. The answer to "if" (*in*) is therefore omitted. The verb *alima* (to know) is either transitive to one object, meaning "to recognize," to reduce the estimation, or transitive to two objects in its original sense. This is the end.

* * *

**[Page 105]**

And from the category of allusory interpretation (*ishara*) in the verses: His words, glorified be He, ﴿Allah has already helped you in many battlefields, and on the day of Hunayn, when your great number pleased you﴾, etc., are an allusion that it is not fitting for the servant to veil himself with anything from witnessing Allah, exalted is He, and from reliance upon Him, and whoever veils himself with something is left to it. From here they said: seeking victory comes through humility, dependence and powerlessness. When He, glorified be He, saw the regret of the people for their self-admiration at their great number, He returned them to the courtyard of His generosity, clothed them with the lights of His nearness, and supported them with His armies. To this refers His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then Allah sent down His tranquility upon His Messenger and upon the believers﴾, up to the end of the verse. The tranquility of the Prophet (ﷺ), as some of the gnostics (*'arifin*) said, was from witnessing the Essence, and the tranquility of the believers was from beholding the Attributes. They have many expressions for defining tranquility, close in meaning. It has been said: it is the firmness of the heart when the judgment of the Lord takes effect, with the characteristic of serenity, with the fading of the traces of humanness entirely, and with contentment with what appears from the unseen without opposition or choice. It has been said: it is settling on the carpet of witnessing, with the signs of sobriety, and with courtesy, by establishing the purity of servitude without the arrival of hardship or the stirring of sweat through opposing a judgment. It has been said: it is remaining with Allah, exalted is He, with the annihilation of personal portions. The armies are the following traces of a strength that manifests the Truth, glorified be He. It is said: they are the arrivals of certainty and the surplus of insight.

The allusion in His words, exalted is He: ﴿The polytheists are only unclean﴾, etc., is that whoever is soiled by inclining toward other than Allah and commits shirk by worshipping desire is not fit for the divine presence. And is anything fit for the carpet of holiness except the sanctified? Abu Salih Hamdun mentioned that the polytheist in his deeds is one whose outward appearance is pleasing for meeting and mixing with people, who displays to creation the best of what he has, and who looks upon himself with the eye of approval, while his inward self becomes unclean with things such as ostentation, showing off, self-admiration, rancor, and the like. Thus the divine sanctuary is forbidden to such a person. Far, far away is it that he enters the kingdom, or that the camel passes through the eye of the needle. Some of the gnostics said: whoever has lost the purity of the secret through the water of tawhid (monotheism) and remains in the filth of suspicions and illusions, that is the polytheist, and he is prevented from approaching the mosques, which are the places of witnessing nearness. In the verse there is an allusion to the prohibition of mixing with the polytheists. The Sufis analogized the people of this world to them. From here al-Junayd said: "The Sufis are the people of the unseen, no one enters among them except those of their kind." Some of them said: whoever still has a glance at other than his Creator in his heart may not approach the sessions of the saints unless he seeks healing through them, for his companionship disturbs their thoughts and his own breath makes their breaths unclean. The companionship of one who denies the friends of Allah, exalted is He, produces a tear that the tailor finds difficult to mend, and produces a rent that the preacher cannot patch. Among the strange things related is that al-Junayd, may his secret be sanctified, sat one day with his select companions, having closed the door of the gathering out of fear of strangers, and they began to remember Allah, exalted is He. Their presence was not completed, and the door of manifestation that they were accustomed to find during remembrance was not opened for them. They were astonished by this. Al-Junayd said: "Is there with you a denier, because of whom we have been deprived?" They said: "No." Then they strove to know the impediment, and they found nothing except the sandal of a denier. Al-Junayd said: "From here we were struck." So consider, may Allah have mercy on you, if this is the condition of the denier's sandal, what then do you think of him when he comes in his own person with his beard?

Then, glorified be He, He censured the People of the Two Books for being veiled from seeing the Truth, glorified be He, when He, majestic is His glory, said: ﴿They took their rabbis and their monks as lords besides Allah﴾. In this there is an allusion to censuring blind imitation and censuring the miserly, through His words, glorified be He: ﴿And those who hoard gold and silver﴾, up to the end of the verse. By my life, they truly deserve censure. Some of them said: whoever is stingy with a little of his property has closed the door of his own salvation and opened upon himself the path of his destruction.

It is not hidden that gathering wealth, hoarding it, and not spending it, occurs only because the vice of avarice has become firmly established. Every vice is a brand by which its possessor is tormented in the Hereafter and disgraced in this world. Since the material of the firm establishment and entrenchment of that vice is that wealth, it is what will be heated in the fire of Hell, the nature and the abyss of desire, and its owner will be branded with it. These organs were singled out because avarice is fixed in the soul and overcomes the heart from these directions, not from the upper direction, which is the direction of the domination of the spirit and the source of realities and lights, nor from the lower direction, which is the direction of the corporeal nature, since nature cannot exert control over that. The remaining directions are left, so he is harmed and tormented from the four directions. This, as you see, is blamed in this world and disgraces him from these directions: he is confronted with reproach openly and is thus disgraced, or he is mocked to his face, or he is backbitten behind his back. This was said by some of the gnostics. As for His words, glorified be He: ﴿Indeed, the number of months with Allah is twelve months﴾, the gnostics have a distant interpretation, which should be sought in its proper place. His words, glorified be He: ﴿If you do not support him﴾, etc., are a rebuke to the slack, or to the people of the earth as a whole, and a guidance that He, upon Him be blessings and peace, is independent of the support of creatures through the support of Allah. In this there is an allusion to the rank of al-Siddiq (Abu Bakr), may Allah be pleased with him, for he was singled out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), in the same way that the Prophet (ﷺ) was singled out with his Lord, glorified be He, in the station of "two bow-lengths or nearer." The meaning of ﴿Indeed, Allah is with us﴾, according to what Ibn 'Ata' said, is that He is with us in pre-eternity, when He joined us with the bond of companionship. The effect of this togetherness has appeared in this world and the Hereafter, so He never left him, alive or dead. It has also been said: "with us" means through the manifestation of His care, His witnessing, and His nearness, which cannot be described in terms of how. By Allah, how excellent is the one who said:

*O seeker of Allah in the lofty throne, do not seek the throne in Him; glory belongs only to the cave.*

There is no hiding the clear difference, for those of taste, between the words of the Prophet (ﷺ), ﴿Indeed, Allah is with us﴾, and the words of Moses, peace be upon him: ﴿Indeed, my Lord is with me﴾. Our Prophet (ﷺ) placed the Name of Allah, exalted is He, first, while Moses, peace be upon him, reversed it. The Prophet (ﷺ) used the all-encompassing Name, while the Interlocutor used the Name "Lord." Our Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, used "us" in "with us," while Moses, peace be upon him, used the first-person pronoun "me," because our Prophet (ﷺ) had a disposition that Moses, peace be upon him, did not have.

As for the pronoun in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then Allah sent down His tranquility upon him﴾, if it refers to the companion, the matter is clear. If it refers to the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, then it is said that in this there is an allusion to the station of annihilation in the shaykh at that time.

Some of the great ones said: tranquility was sent down upon him, upon him be blessings and peace, to calm the heart of al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, and to remove sorrow from him by way of reflection and illumination. Had it been sent down upon al-Siddiq without an intermediary, he would have melted from it because of its greatness. So it is as if it were said: He sent down the tranquility of his companion upon him.

﴿Go forth, light and heavy﴾, that is: go forth to the obedience of your Master, light in spirits and heavy in hearts, or light in hearts and heavy in bodies, by obeying Him with the actions of the heart and the body. Or: light with the lights of love and heavy with the trusts of gnosis. Or: light in expansion and heavy in contraction. It has been said: light in obedience and heavy in turning away from disobedience. It has been said other than this. ﴿And strive with your wealth﴾, by spending it upon the poor, (﴿and your selves﴾), by being generous with them for the sake of Allah, exalted is He. ﴿That is better for you﴾ in both abodes, ﴿if you know﴾ this. And Allah, exalted is He, is the Granter of success to right guidance.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 42:

﴿Had it been﴾: i.e., had they been called to it, as what precedes indicates; ﴿a near gain﴾: i.e., easily obtained booty, close at hand; the root of ʿarad (gain) is whatever comes to you of the benefits and goods of this world, and in a hadith: "This world is a present gain (ʿaradun hadir), from which both the righteous and the wicked eat." ﴿and a moderate journey﴾: i.e., one midway between near and far, and it is of the pattern of tamir and laban (﴿Had it been a near gain and a moderate journey, they would have followed you﴾). I.e., they would have agreed to accompany you on the expedition, hoping to win the spoils. This is the beginning of enumerating the lapses that proceeded from them, in word and deed, and an explanation of the poverty of their resolve and what else they were upon. It was also said: it is an affirmation that they were sluggish and inclined to remain in their land. Linking following to both matters indicates that it would not be realised when the journey was of moderate length alone.

﴿But the distance seemed long to them﴾: i.e., the distance that is covered with hardship. ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar read (baʿidat) with a kasra on the ʿayn, and (ash-shuqqa) with a kasra on the shin. Baʿida yabʿadu, like ʿalima yaʿlamu, is a dialectal form, and it is specially used, for the most part, of the distance of death. And there came (la tubʿid) used in lamentation and grief over calamities, as the poet said:

May God not let our departed brothers be far away, whom the vicissitudes of time and eternity have consumed.

﴿And they will swear by God﴾: i.e., those who stayed behind from the campaign. ﴿By God﴾ is connected to (they will swear). It is permissible that it be part of their speech, and in both cases the saying must be understood: i.e., they will swear upon your return from the expedition of Tabuk, by God, saying ﴿If we had been able﴾; or, they will swear, saying by God, if we had been able, etc. It was also said: there is no need to supply the saying, because swearing is a kind of speech, which is one of the two well-known opinions. The meaning: had we had the capacity, either in terms of equipment or in terms of health, or in both together, according to what occurred to them of pretext and falsehood, ﴿we would have gone out with you﴾ in response to what you invited us to. This is the answer to the oath, and the answer to (if) is omitted according to the rule of the convergence of an oath and a condition when the oath precedes, and this is the choice of Ibn ʿUsfur. Ibn Malik chose that it is the answer to (law), and (law) with its answer is the answer to the oath. It was also said that it stood in place of both answers, the oath and the condition together. The oath according to the first possibility is clear; as for the second, ﴿If we had been able﴾ carries the force of "by God, if we had been able," because it is an explanation of ﴿they will swear by God﴾ and a confirmation of it, as has been said.

The last view has been objected to on the grounds that none of the grammarians of Arabic adopted it. It is answered that the intent of the one who said it is that, since the answer of (if) was omitted, it was indicated by the answer of the oath, and so it was treated as though it stood in place of both answers. Al-Hasan and al-Aʿmash read (lawu istaṭaʿna) with a damma on the waw, likening it to the waw of the plural, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so wish for death﴾ and ﴿they bought error﴾. It was also read with a fatha. ﴿They destroy themselves﴾: by casting themselves into punishment. It was said: this is a substitution for (they will swear). It was objected that destruction is not synonymous with swearing, nor is it a kind of it, and a verb may not be substituted for a verb unless it is synonymous with it or a kind of it.

It is answered that false swearing is a destruction of the self, and for this reason the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "A false oath leaves dwellings as wastelands." The essence of it is that the two are treated as synonymous by claim, so it is a substitution of the whole for the whole. It was also said that it is a substitution of inclusion, since swearing is a cause of destruction, and the caused is substituted for the cause because it encompasses it. It was also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from its subject, i.e., they will swear, destroying themselves; and that it be a circumstantial clause from the subject of (we would have gone out), brought in the manner of reporting about them, as if it were said: we would destroy ourselves, i.e., we would have gone out destroying ourselves, as in your saying: "He swore he would do it" in place of "I will surely do it." But there is remoteness in this. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be a new independent sentence.

﴿And God knows that they are surely liars﴾ regarding the content of the conditional, and regarding what they claimed implicitly, namely the non-realisation of the antecedent, since they were able to go out and did not go out.

The verse has been cited as evidence that capability precedes the act.

﴿May God pardon you. Why did you grant them permission?﴾ That is: for what reason did you grant permission to these liars, the ones who stayed behind, to stay behind, when they asked you for it, offering as their excuse their lack of ability? This is a gentle reproach from the Subtle, the All-Aware, glory be to Him, to His beloved (ﷺ) for leaving the better course (*tark al-awla*, leaving what is more preferable), which is refraining from granting permission until the matter becomes clear and the situation is uncovered, the situation indicated by His words, glory be to Him: ﴿until those who told the truth become clear to you﴾, that is, regarding what they reported when making their excuse of lack of ability, ﴿and you know the liars﴾, that is, regarding that. So it is correct, whether the *ila* (in ﴿until﴾) has the sense of the *lam*, or whether it is connected to what is implied by ﴿why did you grant them permission﴾, as if it were said: Why did you hasten to grant them permission and not wait until the matter became clear, as the resolve befitting your exalted station requires, O master of the steadfast messengers (*ulu al-azm*)?

It is not permissible to connect the phrase ﴿why did you grant them permission﴾ itself, without qualification, to the permission, because that would imply that his permission to them (peace be upon him) was caused by, or limited until, the clarification and knowledge, and that the interrogation would be directed at it from that angle. This is clearly corrupt. Both *lams* are connected to the permission, but they differ in meaning: the first is causal (*lil-ta'lil*), and the second is for conveying (*lil-tabligh*). The pronoun in ﴿them﴾ refers to all of those indicated.

The denunciation is directed at the permission in view of its covering all of them, not in view of its being connected to each individual separately, since the lack of ability was established for some of them, as is indicated by what falls within the scope of ﴿until﴾. The expression of the first group by the relative pronoun whose complement is a verb indicating occurrence (*huduth*) and of the second group by the active participle, which indicates continuity (*dawam*), serves to show that what appeared from the first group was a truthfulness that occurred in a particular matter, which does not make them fit to be counted among the truthful, and that what came from the others, even if it was a lie that occurred and was connected to a particular matter, was nonetheless proceeding according to their constant habit, arising from their being firmly rooted in lying. The expression of the appearance of truthfulness by *tabayyun* (clarification) and of what relates to lying by *ilm* (knowledge) is because it is well known that the meaning of a report is either truth or falsehood, and falsehood is a rational possibility. Attributing the knowledge to Him (ﷺ), and not to those known, by building the verb in the passive, while attributing the clarification to the first group, is because the intended meaning here is his (peace be upon him) knowledge of them and their being held accountable for what it entails, unlike the first group, for whom there is no accountability. Attributing the clarification to them, and connecting the knowledge to the others, is because the basis of attribution and connection, primarily and essentially, is the attribute of truth and falsehood, as has been indicated, since the aim is knowledge of both groups in terms of their being characterized by the two attributes mentioned and their being treated according to what they deserve, not knowledge of the two attributes in themselves or in terms of their subsisting in what they characterize. This is what Shaykh al-Islam said, and its excellence is not hidden.

In opening the address with what it opens with there is exaltation of the rank of the Prophet (ﷺ), honoring him, and magnifying his sanctity (peace be upon him). Often an address begins with something similar to what has been mentioned in order to exalt the one addressed, so it is said: "May God the Exalted pardon you, what did you do regarding my matter?" and "May God, glory be to Him, be pleased with you, what is your answer to my speech?" The purpose is exaltation. Among this is the verse of ʿAli ibn al-Jahm addressing al-Mutawakkil when he ordered his exile:

*May God pardon you, is there no sanctity
that would bestow its grace upon you, O son of the exalted?*

*Did you not see a servant who transgressed his bounds
and a master who pardoned, and guidance guided to right conduct?*

*Release me, may He who has never ceased release you,
who guards you and turns away from you destruction.*

Among what is strung in this line is what has been narrated of his saying (ﷺ): "I was amazed at Yusuf (peace be upon him), at his generosity and his patience, and God forgives him when he was asked about the lean cows and the fat ones. Had I been in his place, I would not have informed them until I stipulated that they bring me out."

Ibn al-Mundhir and others reported from ʿAwn ibn ʿAbd Allah, who said: "You have not heard of a reproach better than this. It begins with pardon before the reproach." Al-Sajawandi said: "In it is the teaching of exalting the Prophet, may the blessings and peace of God be upon him. Had the pardon not been placed at the beginning of the reproach, it would not have held the force of the address." And from Sufyan ibn ʿUyayna that he said: "Look at this gentleness: it begins with the pardon before mentioning what is pardoned." But he erred, behaved badly, and said an evil thing in what he said and wrote. The author of the *Kashshaf* (may God uncover his veil and not grant him permission to mention his excuse) claimed that the speech is a metaphor for the offense, and that its meaning is "I erred, and evil is what you did." In the *Intisaf* it is said: "He has no right to interpret this verse in this way. It is either that this is not what is meant, or that it is meant, but God, exalted be He, has exalted His noble Prophet above being addressed with that, and has been gentle with him through the use of metaphor. Will he not behave with the etiquette of God, especially regarding the Chosen One (ﷺ)?" So in either case, he is heedless of what is due to his right (peace be upon him).

Glory be to God! From where did he derive that God, dealing with him by His justice, expressed it with "evil is what you did"? Even if the pardon were established, it entails error, but it does not entail that the matter is of such ugliness and of such consequence as to validate this degree of verbal insult, and to permit expressing the disapproval with the phrase "evil is what," which indicates that the ugliness has reached a degree at which one is astonished. The author of the *Kashf* excused him, saying: "He meant that the original [wording] was that, and 'pardon' was substituted to exalt his rank (ﷺ) and to draw attention to the gentleness of his position. For this reason he placed the pardon before mentioning what necessitates the offense." His interpretation is not based on the premise that the shift to "God pardon" is not for exaltation, so that it would be deemed an error.

As for what is used purely for exaltation, it is when it is a supplication, not a report. Moreover, supplication may be used for implicit reproach regarding negligence, as in his saying (ﷺ): "May God the Exalted have mercy on my brother Lut, for he used to take refuge in a strong pillar." Its verification is that it is not free from a degree of belittlement of the one addressed or the one absent, according to the difference in form. As for exaltation or implicit reproach, it has been addressed and has ended. What is in it is not hidden, and his excuse is not acceptable to people of intellect. How many similar lapses are in the *Kashshaf*! For this reason some great scholars refrained from teaching it, such as Imam al-Subki (may mercy be upon him). Would that al-Baydawi had not followed him in any of that.

This is what I have. Whoever claims that the Prophet (ﷺ) committed a sin uses this verse as evidence, and that is from two aspects:

First: pardon presupposes a prior sin.

Second: the denunciatory interrogation in His words, glory be to Him, ﴿why did you grant them permission﴾ indicates that this permission was a disobedience. The scholars who verify matters hold that it came out in the mode of reproach, as you have learned, regarding leaving the better and the more complete course. They said: It is not hidden that it was not, as in their going out, a benefit for religion or a gain for the Muslims, but rather it contained corruption and mischief, as His words, exalted be He, express: ﴿Had they gone out with you, they would only have increased you in corruption﴾, etc. He, glorified and exalted, disliked it, as His words, majestic and exalted be He, make clear: ﴿But God disliked their being sent forth﴾, the verse. Yes, it would have been better to delay the permission until their lie became evident and they were disgraced before all eyes, and they could not enjoy life in security and ease, nor could they be pleased among themselves that they had deceived him (ﷺ) and satisfied him with falsehoods. Moreover, life was not pleasant for them, nor were their eyes comforted, since they were not in security and tranquility, but were in fear of their affair being exposed, and it was so.

Some people weakened the argument from the verse for what has been mentioned, saying: "Even if we grant that ﴿God pardon﴾ presupposes a prior sin, and the basis is what we have pointed out before, we still do not grant that His words, glory be to Him, ﴿why did you grant them permission﴾ is said as a denunciation directed at him (peace be upon him). For it is either that a sin proceeded from the Prophet (ﷺ) in this incident or it did not. In either case, it is impossible that what is mentioned be a denunciation. As for the first case, if no sin came from him, how could denunciation be directed at him? As for the second, the beginning of the verse indicates that pardon has been granted, and after that it is impossible for denunciation to be directed at him. So understand."

A group used it as evidence that he (ﷺ) had *ijtihad* (independent reasoning), and that he may receive from it one reward. The reasoning is evident. What he (ﷺ) did in this incident was one of two things that he did without being commanded to do them, as Ibn Jarir and others reported from ʿAmr ibn Maymun. The second is his (ﷺ) taking ransom from the captives, and this has been mentioned before. Some claimed that these two are exhaustive. This was objected to, as it is not correct: there is a third, which is what is mentioned in Surat al-Tahrim and other places, and like what is mentioned in Surat ʿAbasa. It was answered that it is possible to restrict the two to what relates to the matter of jihad. And God, the Exalted, is the Guide to right direction.

Page 110

﴿Those who believe in Allah and the Last Day do not ask your permission﴾. This is a reminder that the Prophet (ﷺ) should judge their state by their not asking permission, and should not grant it to them. That is, it is not the way or custom of believers to ask you for permission ﴿to strive with their wealth and their lives﴾,

for the sincere among them hasten to it without waiting for permission, let alone asking you for leave to stay behind from it. Muslim narrated from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The best of people's livelihood is a man holding the bridle of his horse in the cause of Allah, flying upon its back whenever he hears a call or an alarm, seeking death or killing where it is to be found." The negation of habit (nafy al-ʿada) is derived from the negation of the imperfect verb (al-fiʿl al-mustaqbal), which indicates continuity, as in "so-and-so hosts the guest and protects the sanctuary." Thus the statement is taken to negate continuity, not to be a continuous negation. If it were taken as a continuous negation, then ﴿there is no fear upon them, nor do they grieve﴾ would follow, and the meaning would be: their habit is not asking permission, which is not far off. A similar example is the words of al-Hamasi:

They do not ask their brother, when he calls them in calamities, for proof of what he has said.

It has been said: this courtesy must be observed absolutely. It is not fitting for a man to ask his brother for permission to do him a kindness, nor for a host to ask his guest for permission to offer him food, for asking permission in such situations is a sign of constraint and reluctance. The generosity and courtesy of the Friend (Khalil, Ibrahim), may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, toward his guests reached the point that he did not undertake any of the preparations for hospitality in their sight. Therefore Allah, the Exalted, praised him through the tongue of His Messenger (ﷺ) for this fine trait and noble courtesy, saying: ﴿So he turned quietly to his family and brought a fattened calf﴾, that is, he went away secretly from them so that they would not notice.

It is also permissible that the object of asking permission is omitted, and that ﴿that they strive﴾ is taken as ﴿the dislike that they strive﴾. The omitted element has been said to be "staying behind from it," and the meaning would be: the believers do not ask you for permission to stay behind out of dislike of striving. The negation then applies to both asking permission and dislike together. Some have said: the negation applies to the qualifier, and by it the believer is distinguished from the hypocrite. Although this is in itself a hidden matter that is not known at first, the general state of these people, since it reveals that, has been made into a manifest and established matter.

It has also been said: "striving" (al-jihad) means: the believers do not ask you for permission to strive out of dislike of striving. It has been objected that this is based on the premise that asking permission for striving is for a reason of dislike, and it is not hidden that asking permission for a thing because one dislikes it is something that does not occur, rather is not conceivable. And even if its occurrence were granted, asking permission for the reason of dislike is not distinguished, outwardly, from asking permission for the reason of desire. And even if granted, what is negated of the believers must be established for the hypocrites, and it is evident that they did not ask permission to strive out of dislike of it; rather they asked permission to stay behind. So reflect.

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of the God-fearing﴾. This is a testimony to them of piety, by placing the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun, or by intending the class of the God-fearing and their entering into it in the first instance, and it is a promise to them of abundant reward. For when we say, "You have done good to me, so I know the doer of good," he is promised the greatest reward; and "You have done evil to me, so I know the evildoer," he is promised the severest punishment. It has been said: in this there is a confirmation of the content of what preceded, as if it were said: "Allah knows that they are such," and an indication that what proceeded from them is caused by piety.

[p. 111]

﴿They only ask your permission﴾, that is, to stay behind, ﴿those who do not believe in God and the Last Day﴾. The restriction of faith to these two in both places indicates that what drives one to jihad and what prevents one from it is faith in them or the lack of faith in them. Whoever believes in them fights in the way of his religion and his monotheism, and killing in it becomes easy for him because of what he hopes for in the Last Day of lasting bliss. Whoever does not believe is far removed from that. Moreover, belief in them entails belief in everything else that must be believed. ﴿And their hearts are in doubt﴾ is a conjunction with the relative clause, and the use of the past tense form indicates that the doubt is established and fixed. ﴿So they are in their doubt﴾ and their constant suspicion in their hearts, ﴿wavering﴾ (﴿يَتَرَدَّدُونَ﴾), that is, they are bewildered. The basic meaning of taraddud is going and coming, and here it is meant as bewilderment, metaphorically or by implication, because the bewildered one does not stay in one place.

The verse was revealed, as is related from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with both of them, concerning the hypocrites when they asked permission to remain behind from jihad without an excuse. According to some reports they were thirty-nine men. Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and others narrated from him that the words of God Most High, ﴿They do not ask you﴾ and so on, were abrogated (naskh) by the verse in Surat al-Nur: ﴿The believers are only those who believe in God and His Messenger﴾ up to ﴿Indeed, God is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ Thus God left it to the Prophet (ﷺ) to choose, of the two views on this matter, whichever he wished: whoever went out to fight, went out for a virtuous cause, and whoever remained behind, remained without blame.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 46:

﴿And if they had intended to go out, they would have prepared for it some preparation.﴾ That is: provision (uhbah) of provisions and mounts and all else that the traveller needs for the journey he intends.

It has been recited as ( ʿuddahu ), with a ḍamma on the ʿayn, a shaddah on the dāl, and an idafah to the pronoun of "going out." Ibn Jinni said: Muhammad ibn ʿAbd al-Malik was heard reciting it thus. It is explained as the original being ʿuddatuhu, with the tā' dropped, as in iqām al-ṣalāh (the establishing of prayer), and this is a case known only through transmission (samaʿi). Al-Farra' adopted this view. The pronoun, as several scholars have stated explicitly, is a substitute (ʿiwaḍ) for the omitted tā'. It was said: the tā' is not dropped without a substitute, and yet they have done the like with ʿiddah in the lightened form meaning "promise," as in the verse of Zuhayr:

Indeed the companions have hastened to part, and they have departed, and they have broken with you the promise they made.

It has been recited as ( ʿidahu ), with a kasra on the ʿayn, both with and without an idafah.

﴿But God disliked their setting out﴾: that is, their going out, as narrated from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, or their rising up to go out, as several have said. ﴿So He held them back﴾: that is, He detained them and hindered them from that.

The istidrāk (the "but") has been said to be relative to what is understood from the antecedent of the conditional. The non-existence of the intention to go out entails the non-existence of their going out, and God's dislike of their setting out entails His holding them back from going out. It is as if it were said: "They did not go out, but they were held back from going out." This is the istidrāk of negating a thing by affirming its opposite, as the negation of kindness is corrected by affirming harm in your saying: "He was not kind to me, but he harmed me." Agreement in meaning does not prevent occurrence between the two sides of "but," after the difference in wording, positive and negative, has been established. Some scholars objected that "but" (lākin) occurs between opposites, contradictories, or differing things, according to one opinion, and here it occurs between things that agree under this formulation; so the apparent view is that it is for emphasis, as they affirmed its coming for that purpose. This is open to question. Some verifying scholars preferred that the istidrāk is from the antecedent itself, in the manner of the exceptive syllogisms, and the meaning is: "If they had intended to go out, they would have prepared for it some preparation. But they did not intend it, because God disliked their setting out, due to the corruptions, so He restrained them through cowardice and laziness, and they were held back from it and did not prepare for it."

﴿And it was said: Sit with those who sit.﴾ This is a figure for God Most High's creating in them the impulse to sit and His casting into their hearts, glorified is He, the dislike of going out, by the command to sit. Or it is a figure for the whispering of Satan with this. So there is not, in reality, any saying. A parallel to this is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿So God said to them: Die; then He revived them﴾, that is, He caused them to die. It may also be the report of some of them saying to others, or the permission of the Messenger, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, to them to sit, in which case "said" is on its literal sense. By "those who sit" are meant those whose nature is sitting and remaining in houses, such as women, children and the infirm, or men who have an excuse preventing them from going out. And there is in this, on some of the possibilities, a blame that is not hidden, so reflect.

﴿Had they gone out among you﴾ explains Allah's dislike of their setting out. That is, had they gone out mingling with you ﴿they would have added nothing to you﴾ of any kind ﴿except corruption﴾, meaning evil and mischief. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that it means weakness and cowardice, and from al-Dahhak that it means treachery and deceit. The root of khabal (corruption, disorder), as al-Khazin said, is agitation and a sickness that affects the intellect, like madness. In Majmaʿ al-Bayan it is said to be agitation in opinion. The exception is an incomplete (mufarragh) and connected (muttasil) exception, and the item excepted from is what you know.

[Page 112]

This does not imply that they have corruption, such that if they had gone out they would have increased it, because the increase is considered with respect to the most general category from which the exception is made. Some scholars, supposing that this implication necessarily follows, said: it is an incomplete and disconnected (munqatiʿ) exception, and the meaning is: they would have added to you no strength or good, but rather evil and corruption.

It has been objected that a disconnected exception cannot be incomplete. There is discussion on this, because it is not prevented when context indicates it, as when it is said: "What is your companion in the desert?" and you reply: "I have with me only the wild cattle (yaʿafir)", meaning: I have no companion there except that. You know that the existence of the context here is disputed.

Abu Hayyan said: during that expedition there were hypocrites who had corruption, so if these also went out and joined them, the corruption would increase. So there is no flaw in that implication if it is established. ﴿And they would have hurried about among you﴾. The ʾīḍāʿ is the pace of camels; it is said: "the she-camel awḍaʿat (quickened), and I awḍaʿtu her when I make her hasten." Khilal is the plural of khalal, which means a gap, and it is used as an adverb meaning "between." The object of īḍāʿ is omitted, meaning the tale-bearing (namāʾim), as indicated by the context. There is a implicit metaphor (istiʿarah makniyyah) here, in which tale-bearings are likened to riding-beasts in their running and movement, and īḍāʿ is attributed to them by way of imagination (takhyīl). The meaning is: they would have run between you with tale-bearing and the spreading of discord.

Al-ʿAllamah al-Tibi said: in it there is a subordinate metaphor (istiʿarah tabaʿiyyah), in which the speed of their spreading discord is likened to tale-bearing by the speed of a rider's pace; then īḍāʿ, which belongs to camels, was borrowed for it. The original would be: "they would have hurried their riding-beasts of tale-bearing among you", then the tale-bearings were omitted and the genitive attribute was put in its place, so it became "they would have hurried their riding-beasts", then the riding-beasts were omitted.

Al-Akhfash, in his book al-Ghayat, prohibited saying "the riding-beasts were quickened" and "the camel waḍaʿa" in the sense of hastened, saying that this is used only without a qualifier. Others permitted it and cited as evidence the verse:

"I did not see Suʿda after the day I met her,
at the morning when her camels were quickened, crying out."

It is read ﴿wa la-arqaṣū﴾ (they would have made [their mounts] dance), from raqasat al-naqatu (the she-camel danced/pranced) when she hastened, and arqaṣtuha (I made her dance) when I make her hasten. From this is his saying:

"O ʿĀm, if our spears could reach you,
and the dancing ones (the riding-beasts) toward Mina and al-Ghabghab..."

It is also read ﴿la-awfaḍū﴾ (they would have hastened), and the meaning is also "they would have hurried." It is said: awfaḍa and istawfaḍa, when he hurried and sped up, and al-wafḍ is haste.

The word ﴿la-awḍaʿū﴾ was written in the Imam (the standard codex) with two alifs, the second of which is the fatha of the hamza, and the fatha is written as an alif, as al-Dani mentioned. In al-Kashshaf it is said: the fatha used to be written as an alif before the Arabic script was invented, shortly before the revelation of the Qur'an, and a trace of that alif remained in the scribal habit, so they wrote the form of the hamza as an alif and its fatha as another alif. Similar to this is ﴿or I will surely slaughter him﴾ and ﴿they seek to cause you turmoil﴾, meaning they seek to tempt you by stirring up dissension among you, terrifying you about the enemy, and casting fear into your hearts. This is what is related from al-Dahhak. From al-Hasan it is related that fitnah here means shirk, that is, they wish you to be polytheists. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun of ﴿awḍaʿū﴾, meaning seeking for you the turmoil, and it may be a new sentence (istiʾnaf).

﴿And among you are listeners for them﴾, meaning tale-bearers who listen to your speech in order to convey it to them, as is related from Mujahid and Ibn Zayd; or among you are some weak Muslims who hear their words and obey them, as is related from Qatadah, Ibn Ishaq, and a group.

The lam is for causation according to the first interpretation, and for emphasis according to the second, as in His saying: ﴿Doer of what He wills﴾. The clause is a state from the object of ﴿yabghūnakumu﴾ or from its subject, since it contains a pronoun referring to both, or it is a new sentence.

Some scholars of verification said: perhaps these were not, in number and in the manner of their corruption, such that their presence would greatly disrupt the believers' affairs regarding jihad, and their corruption of going out was not equal to its benefit. For this reason wisdom did not require their not going out, so they went out with the believers. But since the joining of the hypocrites who stayed behind with them would have led to total disorder, Allah disliked their setting out, so their gathering did not come about, and their corruption was averted. End of quote. The need for this is more evident on the first interpretation than on the second, because the apparent meaning on the second is that these people were not hypocrites. The reason for the rebuke over the permission to stay behind, together with what Allah related about them, is that if they had stayed behind without his permission, peace and blessings be upon him, their hypocrisy would have become apparent among the Muslims from the start, and they would not have been able to mix with them and to work among them with rumors, nor would they have been able to enjoy life until their condition became evident through the thunderous verses that were revealed.

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾, with comprehensive knowledge of their outward and inward states, their past and future actions, so that He will recompense them for that. Placing the apparent noun in place of the pronoun serves to record their wrongdoing against them, to intensify the threat, and to signal that the punishment follows from wrongdoing. It is also possible that "the wrongdoers" refers to the category as a whole, so that those mentioned are included by primary inclusion. What is meant by them is either those who stayed behind, or those together with the listeners.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 48:

﴿Indeed, they had sought discord﴾ — the scattering of your unity and the dispersal of your companions — ﴿before﴾, that is, before this expedition (ghazwah). This is as was related from al-Hasan concerning the day of Uhud, when Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul (ibn Salul) withdrew with his hypocrite companions. They had also held back from this expedition, after having set out with the Prophet (ﷺ) as far as near Thaniyyat al-Wada'. It was also related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn Jurayj that the intended meaning of "discord" (fitnah) was the plot to assassinate the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the night of al-Aqabah. This was because twelve men of the hypocrites gathered and stood at the pass (thaniyyah) to assassinate him, peace and blessings be upon him, but Allah turned them back in disgrace. ﴿And they turned matters over for you﴾ — that is, the plots; their "turning" them over is a metaphor for planning them, or for the opinions, and the latter is a metaphor for examining them. That is: they devised schemes and stratagems against you, or they circulated opinions in order to nullify your affair. It has been read as (wa-qalabu) with light (tashdid-less) pronunciation. ﴿Until the truth came﴾ — that is, the victory and triumph which Allah, exalted is He, had promised. ﴿And the command of Allah prevailed﴾ — that is, His religion overcame and His law rose high, glory be to Him. ﴿While they were averse﴾ — that is, while they were in a state of disliking that, in spite of themselves. The coming (of the truth), as they said, is to console the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers regarding the holding back of those who held back, and to make clear what Allah, exalted is He, had hindered them for, and to expose their secrets and remove their excuses; it is a remedy for what might have been lost through the hastiness of granting permission, and an indication that what was lost by it is not something whose remedy is impossible, as a magnification of the matter.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 49:

﴿And among them is he who says, "Grant me leave and do not put me to trial."﴾ That is, to remain behind from the jihad. ﴿Do not put me to trial﴾ means: do not cause me to fall into the trial (fitnah) with the women of the Romans.

Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) intended to set out for the expedition of Tabuk, he said to Jadd ibn Qays: 'O Jadd ibn Qays, what do you say about fighting the Banu al-Asfar?' He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I am a man fond of women, and whenever I see the women of the Banu al-Asfar I am tempted. So grant me leave and do not put me to trial.' Then this was revealed." A similar report is narrated from 'A'ishah and Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with them both. The meaning is: do not cause me to fall into sin and wrongdoing by opposing your command to go out to jihad. This is also narrated from al-Hasan and Qatadah, and al-Jubba'i preferred it. The implication of this interpretation is that he would inevitably remain behind, whether or not the Prophet (ﷺ) granted him leave. Some have explained fitnah as harm, meaning: do not cause me to suffer that, for if I go out with you, my property and dependents will be ruined, since there is no one to attend to their affairs. Abu Muslim said: that is, do not punish me by imposing the obligation to go out in the intense heat. It has also been read ﴿wa la tuftinni﴾ from aftanahu, as a verbal noun (fitnah).

﴿Ala fi al-fitnah saqatu﴾ ("Indeed, in trial they have fallen"): that is, in the trial itself and its very essence and most complete instances. Attributing perfection to it (the noun of genus, ism al-jins, being specifically applied to it) makes this unnecessary. It is not in something other than it, let alone being a refuge and a means of escape from it. This is due to what they did: their resolve to stay behind, their audacity in seeking this leave and remaining with the permission upon which it was based, and their false excuses.

In the Mushaf of Ubayy it reads (saqatu) in the singular, in consideration of the wording of (man). The effect of opening the sentence with the particle of alertness (ala) in emphasis is not hidden. Expressing being fallen into trial by "falling" into it implies placing it in the position of a deadly pit, revealing their plunge into the depths of ruin, the lowest of the low. The fronting of the prepositional phrase has an evident purpose.

﴿And indeed, Hell is surrounding the disbelievers﴾: this is a warning to them for what they did. It is coordinated with the preceding sentence and falls under the alertness: that is, it will encompass them from every side without doubt, and that is on the Day of Resurrection. Thus the metaphor lies in the active participle, as it is used for the future on the basis that it is literally for the present. It is also possible that the meaning is that it already surrounds them now, with "Hell" meaning its causes, namely disbelief and the trial into which they fell, and similar things, figuratively.

It may also be said that the statement is an analogy: their condition of being encompassed by causes is likened to their condition when fire encompasses them, and that the deeds in which they are are the very fire itself, though they appear in the form of deeds in this world and will appear in fiery form in the next. A similar thing has been said regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly, they only consume fire into their bellies﴾, which is a Sufi interpretive approach.

By "the disbelievers" is meant either the hypocrites under discussion, and the choice of placing the apparent noun in place of the pronoun serves to brand them with disbelief and to indicate that it is the greatest of the causes of the aforementioned encompassing; or it means all disbelievers, and these (the hypocrites) enter into it primarily.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 50:
