﴿If good befalls you﴾ in some of your campaigns, ﴿it grieves them﴾ — that good, namely victory and booty, ﴿causes them harm and sorrow, due to their excessive envy, may Allah curse them, and their enmity.﴾ ( ﴿And if misfortune befalls you﴾ ) in some of them, ( ﴿such as the defeat of an army and hardship﴾ ), ( ﴿they say﴾ ), boasting of what they have done and praising their own opinions: ( ﴿We had already taken our precaution﴾ ), i.e., we had already attended to the matter that concerned us, meaning by it their staying behind and sitting out the war, their flattery of the disbelievers, and other matters of disbelief and hypocrisy, in word and deed, ( ﴿before﴾ ), i.e., before the misfortune struck, when precaution is still beneficial. By this they indicate that such actions as they performed are only made attractive to the disbelievers when they occur while Islam is strong, not after misfortune has struck. ( ﴿And they turn away﴾ ), i.e., they withdraw from their gathering for discussion and return to their families and close associates, or they disperse and turn away from you, O Messenger of Allah, ( ﴿while they are rejoicing﴾ ) at what they have done and at the evil that has befallen you. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) relating to the pronoun in (yaqūlū and yatawallaw), for the rejoicing accompanies both acts together. The choice of the nominal sentence serves to indicate the continuity of joy. The second conditional was not expressed in the same form as the first, namely "and if misfortune befalls you, it gladdens them," but rather something indicating that meaning was put in its place, for the sake of emphasis on the intensity of their joy, together with an indication that they are remote from perceiving the evil of their conduct, as the context requires. It may also be said: the attribution of harm to the good and of gladness to themselves indicates a difference in their state between the occurrence of harm and of gladness: in the first they are compelled, and in the second they are free to choose. Here good is contrasted with misfortune and is not contrasted with evil, as He, glorified is He, said in Surah Al ʿImran: ﴿If an evil befalls you, they rejoice in it﴾, because the address here is to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, while there it is to the believers. A distinction is made between the addressees, for hardship does not increase the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, except in reward, for he is the one protected in all his circumstances, upon him be prayer and peace. The restriction of the affliction to "some of the campaigns" is due to what the context indicates, and it is not meant to be a specific one, namely this expedition from which they sought permission to stay behind, which is evident. Yes, the occasion of revelation may suggest that, for Ibn Abi Hatim related from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, who said: The hypocrites who stayed behind in Medina began to report bad news about the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, saying: "Muhammad and his companions have been exhausted on their journey and have perished." Then news of the falsehood of their report and the well-being of the Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace, and his companions reached them, so Allah revealed the verse. So reflect.

﴿Say﴾ (as a rebuke to them), ﴿Nothing will befall us except what Allah has prescribed for us﴾, meaning: what Allah has specifically ordained and decreed for us of worldly or otherworldly benefit, such as victory or martyrdom that leads to lasting bliss. Here "prescribed" (al-katb) means "decreed" (al-taqdir, divine determination), and the lam indicates exclusivity (ikhtisas). It is also permissible that "prescribing" means "inscribing" in the Tablet (al-Lawh), and the lam then indicates cause and purpose (ta'lil wa-al-ajal), meaning: nothing will befall us except what Allah has inscribed for our sake in the Tablet, and this does not change by your agreement or your opposition. The verse thus indicates that all events are by the decree of Allah, the Exalted. This was narrated from al-Hasan. Some have claimed that this interpretation is not suitable to the context, and that His saying, ﴿He is our Protector﴾, that is, our Helper and the one who manages our affairs, determines the first meaning, because it shows that the lam means exclusivity, and it specifies the relative clause (al-mawsul) as referring to victory and martyrdom, meaning: nothing will befall us except that, and not humiliation or misery, as is the state of your condition, because we are believers, and Allah is the Protector of those who believe, and the disbelievers have no protector. It may also be said that it is a justification (ta'lil) for what is understood from the preceding statement of contentment, meaning: nothing will befall us except what He has decreed, whether good or evil, so what you are upon does not harm us, and we are content with what Allah, the Exalted, has done, because He, glory be to Him, is our Owner and we are His servants.

Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿Will there befall us﴾ (hal yuṣībunā), and Talhah read (hal yuṣayyibunā) with the yā' doubled, from ṣayyaba, whose pattern is fa'il-a (فَيْعَلَ) and not fa'-ala (فَعَّلَ) with gemination, because its analogical form would be ṣawwaba, since it derives from the waw-root, so there is no reason to change the waw into a yā'. This is unlike the case when it is ṣayyaba on the pattern fay'ala (فَيْعَلَ), because when the waw and the yā' come together and the first of them is quiescent, the waw is changed into a yā', and this is a regular, consistent rule. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that it be from the pattern tafʻīl (تَفْعِيل) according to the dialect of those who say ṣāba yuṣību, and from it is the saying of al-Kumayt:

"And he took captive the maiden, the noble one, when my arrows were the striking ones and the wounding ones."

﴿And upon Allah﴾ alone, ﴿let the believers rely﴾, by committing their affairs to Him, glory be to Him. This does not contradict taking the customary means (al-asbab al-adiyya), provided one does not rely upon them. The apparent meaning of the words of a group is that this sentence is part of the speech that was commanded to be said. The fronting of the complement (taqdim al-ma'mul) serves to express exclusivity, as we have indicated. The mention of the Glorious Name in the place of the pronoun serves to show blessing and delight in it.

The placement of "the believers" in the place of the first-person pronoun indicates that it is the characteristic of the believers that reliance be specifically upon Allah, the Exalted. The conditional fa' (al-fa' al-jaza'iyya) is used to indicate consequence, meaning: since nothing will befall us except what Allah has prescribed, that is, what Allah, glory be to Him, has specifically allotted to us of victory or martyrdom, and since He is the manager of our affairs, then let us do what is our right regarding His exclusivity, exalted is His majesty, in reliance upon Him. Al-Tibi said: It seems that the statement of the hypocrites was answered with this concluding phrase, and the meaning is that it is the habit of the believers not to rely upon their own resolve and the alertness of their souls, as it is the habit of the hypocrites to do so, but rather to rely upon Allah alone and commit their affairs to Him. It is not far-fetched that the speech branches off from His saying, glory be to Him, ﴿He is our Protector﴾, as is not hidden. It is also possible that this sentence is directed from Him, exalted be He, as a command to the believers to rely upon Him, following His command to His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, with what has been mentioned. In that case, the placement of the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun in both positions is clear, and likewise the repetition of the command in His saying, exalted be He:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 52:

﴿Say: "Do you await for us [anything] except one of the two best outcomes?"﴾ [The verb] "to await" (tarabbusa) here means: to wait for the termination of the first command by the second, even though it is an imperative addressed to an absent party. As for the reading of the plural speech, the repetition is to display full concern for the matter being commanded. Tarabbus means waiting and delaying. One of the two tā's is elided, and the bā' is for transitivity, i.e., "what do you wait for concerning us?" ﴿except one of the two best [outcomes]﴾, i.e., one of the two outcomes, each of which is better than all outcomes other than the other, or better than all the outcomes of the disbelievers, or each of them is better than the other in some respect. What is meant by them is victory and martyrdom. The summary is that what you await cannot be free of one of these two matters, and each of them has a good outcome, not as you claim, that what befalls us of killing in battle is an evil; for this reason you rejoice at it.

It is sound (ṣaḥīḥ) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Allah has guaranteed for whoever strives in His cause, and whom nothing brings out of his house except striving in His cause and belief in His word, that He will admit him to Paradise, or return him to the dwelling from which he went out, along with the reward and spoils he has gained."

﴿And we await for you﴾ one of the two evil outcomes: either that Allah will afflict you with a punishment from Him, destroying you as He did to the nations before you; and the adverbial phrase is an attribute of "punishment." That it is "from Him" is a metaphor for its being from Him, exalted is His majesty, without direct human involvement. This is shown by the contrast in His words, glorified is He: ﴿or by our hands﴾, i.e., or by a punishment brought about by our hands, such as killing for disbelief. The conjunction is to the attribute of "punishment," so it too is an attribute, not that there is an implied punishment. Restricting the killing to being for disbelief is because without it, it would be martyrdom. There is in this an indication that they will not be killed until they manifest disbelief and persist in it, since they are hypocrites, and a hypocrite is not killed initially.

﴿So wait﴾: the fa' is explanatory (faṣīḥah), i.e., if the matter is such, then wait for us to see what our end will be. ﴿Indeed, we are waiting with you﴾ for what your end will be. So when each of us meets what he awaits, we will see only what displeases you, and you will see only what gladdens us. What we have mentioned as the object of tarabbus is the apparent meaning, and perhaps what is reported from al-Hasan returns to it: i.e., "wait for the promises of Satan; indeed we are waiting for the promises of Allah, the Exalted, of raising His religion and uprooting those who oppose it." The purpose of the command is threat.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 53:

﴿Say: "Spend"﴾ your wealth on the needs of the fighters, "willingly or unwillingly," meaning as those who obey or as those who are unwilling. Both are verbal nouns (masdar) that stand in the position of the circumstantial accusative (hal). Although the form (﴿Spend﴾) is an imperative, what is meant by it is a report. The imperative is often used to mean a report, and vice versa. Among examples is the verse of Kuthayyir 'Azza:

"Be harsh with us or be kind, you will not be blamed by us,
nor will you be hated by us, even if you should change."

As al-Farra' said, this is in the sense of a conditional: "If you spend, in any state." (﴿It will not be accepted from you﴾). The statement is phrased as a command in order to emphasize that the two conditions are equal in non-acceptance, as if they were commanded to test it, so they spend in both states and then see whether it is accepted from them, and so they witness its non-acceptance. In it, as some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqin) said, there is an allegorical metaphor (isti'arah tamthiliyyah), which likens their state in spending and in its non-acceptance, in a certain respect, to the state of one who is commanded to do an act so that he may test it, and it becomes clear to him that it is useless. Thus it is not supposed that, if he is commanded to spend, how could it not be accepted.

The verse was revealed, as Ibn Jarir narrated, "from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, as a reply to what was said by al-Jadd ibn Qays when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: 'Would you like to fight the sons of al-Asfar? Indeed, when I see women I cannot be patient until I am tempted, but I will help you with my wealth.'" The negation of acceptance may mean that it is not taken from them, and it may mean that they are not rewarded for it. Each of the two meanings is used. So the people's acceptance of it is taking it, and Allah's acceptance of it is His reward for it. It is permissible to combine both. His saying, glorified is He: (﴿Indeed, you have always been a defiantly disobedient people﴾) is a justification for the rejection of their spending. The meaning of "defiant disobedience" (fisq) is rebellion and insolence. So it cannot be said: how did He give as the reason, together with disbelief, a matter (fisq) that is less than it? And how is that valid when His saying, may He be exalted, explicitly gives disbelief as its reason:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 54:

Page 117
﴿And nothing prevented their expenditures from being accepted from them except that they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger﴾. It may be meant by this what is complete, which is disbelief (kufr), and this from Him, exalted is He, would be an explanation and affirmation of that. The exception (istithna') is from the most general of things, meaning: nothing of all things prevented their expenditures from being accepted except their disbelief. The verb manaʿa (to prevent) is transitive to two objects directly, and it has been transitive to the second by a preposition, which is min or ʿan. When it is made transitive by a preposition, it is correct to say manaʿahu min haqqihi (he prevented him from his right) and manaʿa haqqahu minhu (he prevented his right from him), because it carries the meaning of interposing between the two and protecting. There is no inversion (qalb) in it as is supposed. In what we are dealing with, it is also permissible that it be transitive to the second directly and that a preposition be presumed; and omitting the preposition with an (that) and anna (that) is regular and common.

Abu al-Baqa' permitted that ﴿an tuqbala﴾ (that it be accepted) be a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for hum (them) in ﴿manaʿahum﴾ (prevented them), which goes against the apparent meaning. The subject of manaʿa is what falls within the scope of the exception. He also permitted that the pronoun refer to Allah, exalted is He, and ﴿wa annahum kafaru﴾ (because they disbelieved) be read as ﴿li-annahum kafaru﴾ (because they disbelieved).

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿yuqbala﴾ with the yaa' (third person masculine), because the feminine marking of nafaqat (expenditures) is not real, together with it being separated from the verb by the prepositional phrase. It is also read as ﴿nafaqatuhum﴾ in the singular.

al-Sulami read ﴿an yaqbala minhum nafaqatihim﴾ with yaqbala in the active voice and nafaqat in the accusative, and the subject is either the pronoun for Allah, exalted is He, or the pronoun for the Messenger, upon him be prayers and peace, based on the view that acceptance means taking.

﴿And they do not come to the prayer﴾ — the obligatory prayer — ﴿except while they are lazy﴾, meaning except while they are in a state of being sluggish. ﴿And they do not spend except while they are unwilling﴾ — the spending — because they do not hope for reward by these two, nor do they fear punishment for abandoning them. These two clauses fall within the scope of the causal explanation (ta'lil). It was raised as an objection that disbelief is an independent cause for non-acceptance, so what is the point of explaining by the combination of the three matters? And when the independent cause is present, nothing else retains an effect. Imam (al-Razi) answered that this applies only to the Mu'tazilah, who say that disbelief, by being disbelief, affects this ruling. As for the People of the Sunnah, it does not apply, because they say: these causes are indicators (mu'arrifat) that do not necessitate reward or punishment, and the gathering of many indicators upon one thing is permissible. The claim that the two were mentioned merely for the sake of blame, and are not within the scope of the causal explanation, although the objection is removed thereby according to the Mu'tazilah's view, contradicts the apparent meaning, as is not hidden. If it is said: unwillingness is the opposite of willing obedience, and these hypocrites were described earlier as obedient, and here they are described as not spending except while unwilling, and the apparent meaning of that is contradiction. It is answered that by their obedience is meant that they give without compulsion from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, not that they give out of desire, so there is no contradiction. Some of the scholars (muhaqqiqin) said regarding this: His saying, glorified is He, ﴿Spend willingly or unwillingly﴾ does not indicate that they spend willingly; rather its extent is only that He left their state between the two matters. That disjunction contradicts certainty is a matter for consideration, as when you say: "If you do good or do evil, I will not visit you," although it is certainly not good; and the disjunction is for widening the scope, and it is of wide scope.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 55:

﴿So do not let their wealth or their children impress you.﴾ That is, nothing of that should please you, for it is a gradual lure (istidraj) for them and a burden upon them, as indicated by the words of the Most High: ﴿Allah only intends to punish them through them in the life of this world.﴾ The address may be to the Prophet (ﷺ), or to anyone suitable for it, in the same way as what was said regarding the words of the Most High: ﴿Do not associate anything with Allah﴾. As for the object of the intention (iradah), it was said to be the punishment, and the lam is then extra (za'idah). It was also said to be omitted, and the lam is then causal (ta'liliyyah), meaning: He intends to give them [wealth and children] in order to punish them. Their punishment through wealth and children in this world is because they endure hardship in gathering and guarding them and suffer trials and calamities for them, and they do not have, in their belief in Allah's reward, anything that would make what they encounter easier for them. It was also said: their punishment in this world through wealth is by taking zakat from them and by spending in the way of Allah, ﴿Page 118﴾ with their not believing in a reward for that. And their punishment through children is that they may be killed in battle, so they grieve intensely over it, since they do not believe in their martyrdom, that they are alive with their Lord and provided for, and that reunion with them is near; the believers are not like this regarding what has been mentioned. It was also said: their punishment through wealth is that it becomes spoils for the Muslims, and through children that the children become a cause for them if they openly show disbelief and come under [the Muslims'] power.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Qatadah that there is an inversion in the verse, meaning: ﴿So do not let their wealth or their children impress you in the life of this world.﴾ ﴿Allah only intends to punish them through them in the Hereafter﴾ ﴿and that their souls depart﴾, that is, they die. The root of zuhuq is departure with difficulty. ﴿while they are disbelievers﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), that is, in the state of their being disbelievers. The verb is conjoined to what precedes it and is included with it in the scope of the intention. It has been used as evidence, from linking death to disbelief within His (may He be exalted) intention, that the disbelief of the disbeliever is by His intention, and in this is a refutation of the Mu'tazilah.

Al-Zamakhshari replied that what is meant is only that they are given respite and that blessings are continued for them until they die upon disbelief, occupied with what they are in and heedless of consideration of the outcome. Respite and the continuation of blessings just mentioned are things that may validly be intended by Him (may He be exalted). Al-Tibi objected that this does not help him at all, because the cause of a cause is in reality a cause, and its substance is that what leads to ugliness and is a cause of it has the same ruling as it regarding ugliness, and it falls within what is forbidden. Al-Jubba'i replied that the meaning of the verse is that Allah (may He be exalted) intended their souls to depart in the state of disbelief, and this does not require that He (glory be to Him) intends disbelief. For the patient wishes for treatment at the time of illness and does not wish for the illness, and the ruler tells his army: "Kill the rebels at the moment of their assault," and he does not wish their assault. The Imam rejected this, saying that the example mentioned has no meaning except the intention to remove the illness and the seeking of removal of the rebels' assault. And when the intended thing is the annihilation of something, it is impossible for its existence to be intended, unlike the intention of the departure of the disbeliever's soul, for that is not an expression of intending the removal of disbelief. So when Allah (may He be exalted) intended the departure of their souls while they were disbelievers, it must be that He intends their disbelief. How could it not be so, when departure in the state of disbelief can only occur in the state of disbelief, and the intention of a thing requires the intention of what is necessary to it, so it follows that He (may He be exalted) intends disbelief.

In reply: the apparent sense is that the intention of treatment is something other than the intention of removing the illness, and likewise the intention of killing is other than the intention of removing the assault. That is why one of the two intentions is explained by the other, so how could it be the same as it? As for the claim that the intention of what is necessary to a thing is one of the implications of intending it, this is not granted; for many things are necessary to something without coming to mind when it is intended, let alone what he claims. Therefore, the argument from the verse for what has been mentioned is not conclusive.

ويَحْلِفُونَ بِاللَّهِ إنَّهم لَمِنكُمْ — "And they swear by Allah that they are indeed of you" — i.e., in religion; the meaning is that they swear they are believers like you. ("وما هم مِنكُمْ") — "But they are not of you" in that, because of the disbelief in their hearts. ("ولَكِنَّهم قَوْمٌ يَفْرَقُونَ") — "But they are a people who are fearful," i.e., they fear from you that you will do to them what you do to the polytheists, so they show Islam out of dissimulation (taqiyyah) and reinforce it with false oaths. The root of farq (fear) is the agitation of the soul in anticipation of harm. It has been said: it is from departing from security to a state of fear.

**(Ruh al-Ma'ani)**, the commentary of al-Alusi, on surah 9, verse 57:

﴿Had they found a refuge﴾, i.e., a fortress to which they could flee, as Qatadah said. ﴿Or caves﴾, i.e., holes in which they could hide themselves. It is the plural of *maghara*, meaning *ghar* (cave). Some scholars distinguished between them, holding that the *ghar* is in a mountain and the *maghara* is in the ground. It is also read *maghrat* (with a *dammah* on the *mim*), from *aghara al-rajulu*, meaning "the man entered the lowland (*ghawr*)." It was said that it is the transitive form of *ghara al-shay'* and *aghartu-hu*, i.e., places where they could change their persons (their appearance). It may also be from *aghara al-tha'lab*, meaning "the fox fled quickly," in the sense of "places of escape."

Page 119

And *maghar* (plural of the same form). ﴿Or a hole﴾, i.e., a tunnel like the burrow of the jerboa, into which they could dive. It is *muftaʿal* from *al-dukhul* (entering), and after the *ta'* was changed to *dal* it was assimilated. Yaʿqub and Sahl read *madkhalan* (with a *fatḥah* on the *mim*), which is a noun of place from the basic verb *dakhala*, and this is the reading of Ibn Abi Ishaq and al-Hasan. Salamah ibn Muharib read *mudkhalan* (with a *dammah* on the *mim* and a *fatḥah* on the *kha'*), from the derived form *adkhala*, meaning a place into which they make themselves enter, or into which fear makes them enter. Ubayy ibn Ka'b read *mutadakhkhalan*, a noun of place from *tadakhkhala* (form V of *dakhala*). It is also read *mundakhalan*, from *indakhala*. It occurs in the poetry of al-Kumayt:

*"And my hand does not sink into the melted ghee."*

Abu Hatim denied this reading and said: "It is only with the *ta'*," on the basis of his denial of this dialect. But this is not so.

﴿They would have turned away﴾, i.e., they would have turned their faces and gone off. It is also read *la-wa'allu* (with a *hamzah*), i.e., they would have sought refuge. ﴿To it﴾, i.e., to one of the things mentioned. ﴿While they rushed headlong﴾, i.e., they would hasten to go to it, unable to be turned back by anything, like a bolting horse (*jamuh*), which is the kind of bolting that no bridle can restrain. Al-A'mash narrated from Anas ibn Malik that he read *yajmizun* with a *zay*, which has the same meaning as *yajmahun*, namely "they run hard." From it comes *al-jammazah*, meaning a she-camel that is very swift in running. Some scholars denied that what was mentioned is a reading and claimed that it is an explanation (*tafsir*), but this claim is rejected.

The conditional clause is a resumptive sentence (*istinaf*) that confirms the content of what preceded, namely that they are not among the Muslims, and that their resort to identifying themselves with them is only out of dissimulation (*taqiyyah*) under compulsion. The use of the future form in the condition, although the meaning is past, serves to express the continuation of their failure to find refuge, as the context requires. A parallel example is: "If you were to do good to me, I would thank you." Indeed, it is often the case that a negated present verb in the position of a past verb serves to express the non-continuation of the action, but that is not what is intended here.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 58:

﴿And among them are those who find fault with you concerning the charities﴾ i.e., they criticize you regarding them. Ya'qub read ﴿yalmuzuka﴾ with a dammah on the mim, which is the reading of al-Hasan and al-A'raj. Ibn Kathir read ﴿yulamizuka﴾, which is from al-mulamazah, meaning al-lamz. It is well known that it signifies blame in general, like al-hamz. Some scholars distinguished between the two, saying that al-lamz is to the face and al-hamz is in absence, and this is what is reported from al-Layth, though it has also been reversed. The original meaning of it is pushing. ﴿And if they are given from them﴾ is an explanation of the corruption of their blaming and that it has no source except their greed for the trifles of this world, i.e., if I give them from those charities the amount they desire, ﴿they are pleased﴾ with what took place in the distribution and approve of your action. ﴿And if they are not given from them﴾ that amount, ﴿behold, they become angry﴾, i.e., they are suddenly struck with anger. Idha (behold) takes the place of the response particle fa' (then), and a condition for it standing in for it is that the response be a nominal sentence. The reason it can stand in for it is that it indicates immediacy like fa'. Allah, glorified is He, varied between the two responses to indicate that their anger is firm and does not cease or perish, unlike their pleasure. Ibn Laqit read ﴿idha hum sakhituna﴾ [with the active participle]. The verse was revealed concerning "Dhu al-Khuwaysirah, whose name was Harqus ibn Zuhayr al-Tamimi, who came while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was distributing the spoils of Hawazin on the day of Hunayn and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, be just!' He (ﷺ) said: 'Who would be just if I am not just?' Umar ibn al-Khattab said: 'O Messenger of Allah, permit me to strike his neck.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Leave him, for he has companions among whom one of you would consider his prayer insignificant compared to their prayer, and his fasting compared to their fasting. They pass through the religion as an arrow passes through the game'" – the hadith. Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) distributed the spoils of Hunayn, I heard a man say: 'This distribution was not intended for the sake of Allah.' I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and mentioned that to him, and he said: 'May the mercy of Allah be upon Musa; he was harmed with more than this and was patient.'" Then the verse was revealed.

Page 120
Ibn Jarir and others narrated from Dawud ibn Abi 'Asim, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was brought a charity, and he distributed it here and there until it was gone, and behind him was a man from the Ansar who said: 'This is not justice,' and so the verse was revealed." And from al-Kalbi that it was revealed concerning Abu al-Jawwaz the hypocrite, who said: "Do you not see your companion? He distributes your charities among the shepherds of sheep, and he claims that he is just."

Wali al-Din al-'Iraqi critiqued this, saying that it is not found in any of the books of hadith. You know that the first narrations are the most authentic, except that the reason for revelation being his (ﷺ) distribution of charity in the manner he did is more fitting to the verse than it being his distribution of the spoils. So reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 59:

﴿And if only they had been content with what Allah and His Messenger gave them﴾ That is: what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave them of the charities (sadaqat), being content with it in their hearts, even if it was little. "Ma" (what) — although it is among the forms of generality (sigha al-'umum), the context before and after it is an indication of restriction (takhsis). Some scholars kept it on its generality, meaning: what He gave them from the charity or the spoils of war (ghanimah). It was said that this is the more fitting (al-ansab). The name of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is mentioned for glorification (ta'zim) and to draw attention to the fact that what the Messenger, peace be upon him, did was by His command, glorified is He. (﴿And said: "Allah is sufficient for us"﴾) That is: His bounty and what He has apportioned for us have sufficed us, as the meaning requires. (﴿"Allah will give us of His bounty, and so will His Messenger, after this; to Allah we are turning in hope"﴾) As we hope and aspire. (﴿Indeed, to Allah we are devoted﴾) That He grant us His bounty, exalted is His station. The whole verse falls within the scope of a conditional clause (shart), and its answer (jawab) is omitted because it is evident; that is: it would have been better for them and more beneficial to them. It was said that the answer of the conditional is (﴿they would have said﴾) and that the waw is superfluous, but this is not so.

Then, when He, glory be to Him, had mentioned the hypocrites, their slander and their discontent, He made clear that the action of His Messenger, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, was for the reform of the religion and its people, not for selfish aims like theirs. So He, majestic and exalted, said: ﴿Charity is only for the poor and the needy﴾, and so on. The meaning is that the wealth of Allah should be distributed only to those who possess one of these attributes and not to others, since the aim is reform, and the hypocrites have nothing in them but corruption, so they do not deserve it. In this there is a cutting off of their vain greed and a rejection of their false claim. By "charities" (sadaqat) is meant the obligatory zakat (zakah), so other voluntary charity is excluded.

The faqir (poor person), according to what is reported from Imam Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, is one who has some small thing, which is less than the nisab, or an amount equal to a nisab that is not growing (non-productive) and that is wholly absorbed by need. The miskin (needy person) is one who has nothing, so he must ask for food for his sustenance and for what covers his body, and this is permitted for him. This is unlike the first, for whom asking is not permitted, since it is not permitted for one who owns the food of his day after covering his body. According to some scholars, it is not permitted for one who earns a livelihood or owns fifty dirhams. Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i reported from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Whoever asks us while he has what suffices him will come on the Day of Resurrection with scratches, or scrapes, or gouges on his face." It was asked: "O Messenger of Allah, what suffices him?" He said: "Fifty dirhams, or its value in gold." This is the view of al-Thawri, Ibn al-Mubarak, Ahmad and Ishaq. It is also said: whoever owns forty dirhams, asking becomes forbidden for him, because of what Abu Dawud reported from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Whoever asks while he has the value of an uqiyya has indeed clung (to people)." At that time an uqiyya was forty dirhams.

It is permissible to give zakat to one who is not permitted to ask, provided he is poor. Owning many non-productive pieces of wealth that are wholly absorbed by need does not remove him from poverty. For this reason they said: it is permissible for a scholar to take zakat, even if he owns books worth many nisabs, if he needs them for teaching and the like, unlike the common person. The same applies to all the tools of craftsmen.

According to what is reported from the Imam, the miskin is in a worse state than the faqir. He cited the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿or a needy person in the dust﴾, meaning one who has pressed his skin into the dust in a pit in which he hid, in place of a garment, and pressed his belly to it due to extreme hunger; this indicates the utmost harm and hardship, and the faqir is not described in this way. Also, al-Asma'i, Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' and others among the lexicographers explained the miskin as one who has nothing, and the faqir as one who has a sufficiency of living. It is answered that the completion of the argument from the verse depends on the attribute being explanatory, which is contrary to the apparent meaning, and that the transmission from some lexicographers is contradicted by the transmission from others.

Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the faqir is one who has no wealth and no earnings that fall adequately within his need, and the miskin is one who has wealth or earnings that do not suffice him. Thus, for him, the faqir is in a worse state than the miskin. He cited in support the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿As for the boat, it belonged to needy people﴾, where He affirmed a boat for the miskin. He also cited what al-Tirmidhi reported from Anas, and Ibn Majah and al-Hakim from Abu Sa'id, both saying: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, said: "O Allah, give me life as a miskin, cause me to die as a miskin, and gather me among the company of the miskins." Also what Abu Dawud reported from Abu Bakra, that he, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, used to supplicate with: "O Allah, I seek refuge in You from disbelief and poverty." The report "Poverty is my pride" is a lie with no basis. He also argued that Allah, the Exalted, mentioned the faqir first in the verse, and had his need not been greater, He would not have begun with him. He also argued that faqir means maqsur, i.e., one whose spine is broken, that is, one with fragile bones, and so he is in a worse state.

As for the first argument, it is answered that the boat was not theirs as property; rather they were hired workers on it, or it was lent to them, or they were called miskins out of compassion, as in the hadith: "The miskins of the people of the Fire." As for the second, the poverty sought refuge from is nothing but poverty of the soul, because it is reported that he, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, used to ask for chastity and richness, and by richness is meant richness of the soul, not abundance of worldly goods. As for the third, precedence does not indicate anything, since placing one word before another has many considerations in their speech. As for the fourth, we do not accept that faqir is derived from fiqar (vertebrae), since it may be from faqartu lahu fiqratan min mali, when you cut off a portion of my wealth for him, so that he then has something. In any case, they are two categories.

Al-Jubba'i said: they are one category, and the conjunction is for difference in meaning. This is reported from Muhammad and Abu Yusuf. The effect of the disagreement appears in the case where one bequeaths, for example, a third of his wealth to a certain person and to the poor and the needy. Whoever says they are one category gives that person half, and whoever says they are two categories gives him a third of it.

﴿And those employed to collect them﴾: these are those whom the Imam sends to collect them. In al-Bahr it is stated that the employee includes the tax collector (ashir) and the collector (sa'i). The first is one whom the Imam appoints on the road to take charity from merchants passing with their goods. The second is one who goes among the tribes to collect the charity of livestock in their places, and gives the employee and his assistants, in a moderate manner, what suffices them during their going and returning, as long as the property remains. However, if the amount of their sufficiency exhausts the zakat, then nothing more than half is given, because division is itself equity.

It is reported from al-Shafi'i that he is given an eighth, because division requires it, but this is open to examination. It is restricted to moderation because it is not permitted for him to follow his desire in food, drink and clothing, as that would be pure extravagance. The Imam must send one who is content with moderation, without extravagance or stinginess. It is also restricted to the preservation of the property, because if he took the charity and it was lost from his hand, his wage would be void; and he may not give himself anything from among the property, since what he takes is charity. From here they said: the wage is not permitted for a Hashimi, because of his nobility. It is permitted for a rich man despite the prohibition of charity for him, because he has devoted himself to this work and so needs sufficiency, and wealth does not prevent him from taking it when needed, like the wayfarer. So says al-Bada'i'. The verification is that in this there is a resemblance to a wage and a resemblance to charity. By the first consideration it is permitted for the rich man, and therefore it is not given if the owner of the property pays it directly to the Imam; by the second consideration it is not permitted for the Hashimi. In al-Nihaya: a man from the Banu Hashim was employed over the charity, and provision was assigned to him from it; he should not take from that, but if he worked on it and was provided for from other sources, there is no harm in it. This indicates the validity of his appointment, and that taking from it is disliked, not forbidden. In al-Ghaya it is explicitly stated that a Hashimi, a slave, or a disbeliever cannot validly be the employee. From this it is known that appointing Jews to some functions is forbidden, and a portion of discussion on this has already passed.

﴿And those whose hearts are to be reconciled﴾: they were of three kinds. One kind the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, would win over so that they would embrace Islam. Another kind had embraced Islam but with weakness, such as Uyayna ibn Hisn, al-Aqra' ibn Habis, and al-Abbas ibn Mirdas al-Sulami; so he, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, would give them in order to strengthen their intention in Islam. A third kind were given to avert their evil from the believers. Also counted among them is one whose heart is won over by giving him some of the charities in return for fighting the disbelievers and those who withhold zakat. In al-Hidaya it is stated that this category among the eight has fallen away, and the consensus of the Companions was established on this in the caliphate of al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him. It is narrated that Uyayna and al-Aqra' came seeking land from Abu Bakr, so he wrote a document to that effect, but Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, tore it up and said: "This is something the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, gave you to win you over. But today Allah, the Mighty, has strengthened Islam and made you independent of it. If you remain upon Islam, well and good; otherwise, between us and you is the sword." They returned to Abu Bakr and said: "Are you the caliph or is Umar?" You gave us the document and Umar tore it up. Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "He has the right if he wishes," and he agreed with him, and none of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, objected to it, despite the possibility that it might involve harm, such as the apostasy of some of them and the stirring up of unrest.

The scholars differed concerning how this category fell away after the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, having been established by the Book up to his death, my father and mother be his ransom, peace be upon him. Some of them permitted the abrogation of what was established by the Book through consensus, on the basis that consensus is a definitive proof like the Book; but this is not correct according to the school. Others said: it is from the category of a ruling ending when its cause ends, like the permissibility of fasting ending when its time ends, which is the day. This was refuted: a ruling in its continuation does not need a cause, as in the ramal and idtiba' in the tawaf; so the ending of its cause does not entail the ending of the ruling itself. There is discussion on this. 'Ala' al-Din 'Abd al-'Aziz said: the better view is to say that this is a confirmation of what existed in the time of the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, in meaning. The purpose of giving to them was to strengthen Islam, which was weak at that time due to the dominance of the people of disbelief, and strengthening was through giving. When the situation changed with the dominance of the people of Islam, strengthening became through withholding. Giving in that time and withholding in this time served as means to strengthen the religion, and strengthening is the aim, which remains in its state; so this was not abrogation, like the one who performs tayammum, who is obliged to use dust for purification because it is a determined means for achieving purification when water is absent. When his condition changes and he finds water, the first ceases and the use of water becomes obligatory, because it has become determined for achieving the aim; this is not abrogation of the first, and so is this. It is like the imposition of blood money upon the 'aqila: it was obligatory upon the clan in the time of the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, and after him upon the people of the register (diwan), because the obligation upon the 'aqila was due to support and seeking aid, which in his time was through the clan, and after him through the people of the register. Its imposition upon them was therefore not abrogation, but a confirmation of the meaning for which the blood money was obligatory, namely seeking aid. End of quotation. In al-Nihaya he approved this.

Ibn al-Humam objected that this does not negate abrogation, since the permissibility of giving to them is a legal ruling that was established and has now been lifted. Some verifiers said: this is indeed abrogation. And it is not said that the Book was abrogated by consensus, which is not permitted according to the correct view, since the abrogator is the evidence of consensus, not consensus itself, on the basis that there is no consensus except on a basis; if the basis appears, well and good, and if not, it must be ruled that the ruling remains established. Furthermore, the verse to which Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, pointed, namely the words of Allah, glory be to Him: ﴿And say: The truth is from your Lord; so whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾, is suitable for this; but there is room for examination, since this holds only if the revelation of this verse is established as coming after that one, and it is not established.

Some people said: the share of this category has not fallen away. This is the view of al-Zuhri and Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn 'Ali, Abu Thawr, and it is reported from al-Hasan. Ahmad said: they are given if the Muslims need that.

Some said: the "those whose hearts are to be reconciled" (al-Mu'allafa qulubuhum) are of two kinds, Muslims and disbelievers, and only the share of the disbelievers is dropped. It has been affirmed (ṣuḥḥiḥa) that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to give them from the one-fifth of the one-fifth (khums al-khums) that was his own personal property (ṣallā Allāhu ta'ālā 'alayhi wa-sallam).

﴿And for the slaves﴾: that is, for spending on the freeing of slaves, by helping those under a contract of manumission (mukatabūn) with some of it toward paying their installments (nujūm). It was also said: by using it to buy slaves so that they are freed. And it was said: by ransoming captives. The first view was taken by al-Nakha'ī, al-Layth, al-Zuhrī, and al-Shāfi'ī. It is also what is transmitted from Sa'īd ibn Jubayr, and most jurists (fuqahā') follow it. The second view was taken by Mālik, Aḥmad, and Isḥāq, and al-Ṭībī attributed it to al-Ḥasan. In the tafsir of al-Ṭabarī, the first view is the one reported from him.

﴿And the debtors﴾: that is, those who have debts upon them. Giving to them, as stated in al-Ẓahīriyya, is better than giving to the poor. The jurists restricted the debt to one not incurred in sin, such as debts for wine or extravagance in what does not concern a person. However, al-Nawawī said in al-Minhāj: "I say: the more correct view is that whoever borrows for a sinful purpose is given (from zakat) if he repents, and he affirmed this in al-Rawḍa." Those who prevent it absolutely said: he may show repentance merely to take the money. He also stipulated that they should not have something with which they could pay their debt beyond their needs and the needs of those they support. Otherwise, mere capacity to repay does not prevent entitlement. This is one of two views among the Shāfi'īs, and it is the more apparent (al-azhar).

It was also said: it is not stipulated, for the generality of the verse. Al-Qudūrī and the author of al-Kanz among our (Ḥanafī) companions stated it without restriction in the section on expenditure, while the author of al-Kāfī restricted it to one who does not own a niṣāb beyond his debt. It is mentioned in al-Baḥr that this is what is meant by the debtor in the verse, since linguistically it refers to one upon whom there is debt and who cannot find repayment, as al-'Utbī stated. The lack of restriction was defended by saying that poverty is a condition in all the categories except the collector (al-'āmil) and the wayfarer (ibn al-sabīl), who, if he has wealth in his homeland, is in the position of one who is poor. Whether the debt must be due (ḥulūl al-dayn) first is a question with two views among the Shāfi'īs. According to them, the one who borrows to reconcile people (iṣlāḥ dhāt al-bayn) is given, such as when one fears strife between two tribes that dispute over a slain man whose killer has not been identified, or was identified and then the blood-money (diya) is given to quell the strife. He is given even if he is rich, absolutely. It was also said: if he is rich in cash, he is not given.

﴿And in the way of Allah﴾: according to Abū Yūsuf, this means those cut off from raiders (munqaṭi'ū al-ghuzāt). According to Muḥammad, it means those cut off from pilgrims (munqaṭi'ū al-ḥajīj). It was said: it refers to students of knowledge, and al-Ẓahīriyya restricted itself to this. In al-Badā'i', it is explained as all acts of devotion, so that everyone who strives in obedience to Allah ta'ālā and the paths of good is included. Al-Baḥr says: "It is not hidden that the condition of poverty is necessary in all these views, so its effect does not appear in zakat, but only in bequests (waṣāyā) and endowments (awqāf)." End of quote. In al-Nihāya: If it is said that His saying ﴿and in the way of Allah﴾ is repeated, whether one means those cut off from raiders or others, because he either has wealth in his homeland or does not. If he has, he is the wayfarer; if not, he is poor. So from where does the count become seven, according to what the companions (aṣḥāb) say, or eight, according to what others say? It is answered: he is poor, but something else has been added to him besides poverty, which is being cut off in the worship of Allah ta'ālā, through jihad or pilgrimage. Therefore he differs from the absolute poor, for the restricted differs from the absolute without doubt. The effect of this difference also appears in another ruling, namely the increase in encouragement and incentive to care for his side. If that is so, the categories are not fewer than seven. There is something to consider in this." End of quote. Its point is not hidden.

Some have said that the verification (al-taḥqīq) is what al-Jaṣṣāṣ mentioned in al-Aḥkām: whoever is rich in his town, with his house, servants, and horse, and has a surplus of dirhams, such that charity is not lawful for him, when he resolves on a journey of jihad and needs equipment and weapons which he did not need while residing, then he may be given from the charity even though he is rich in his city. This is the meaning of the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Charity is lawful for the rich raider." So understand this, and do not be negligent.

[Page 124]

﴿And the wayfarer﴾: he is the traveler cut off from his wealth. Borrowing for him is better than accepting charity, according to al-Ẓahīriyya. In Fatḥ al-Qadīr, it is stated that it is not lawful for him to take more than his need. Anyone who is absent from his wealth is included with him, even if he is in his own town. In al-Muḥīṭ: even if he is a merchant who has debts owed by people which he cannot collect, and he finds nothing that makes taking zakat lawful for him, then he is poor in hand, like the wayfarer. In al-Khāniyya there is a detailed distinction in this matter. It says: one who has a deferred debt (dayn mu'ajjal) owed by a person, if he needs expenses, it is lawful for him to take from zakat an amount sufficient for his needs until the term falls due. If the debt is not deferred, and the debtor is insolvent, it is lawful for him to take zakat according to the most correct views, since he is in the position of the wayfarer. If the debtor is wealthy and acknowledges it, it is not lawful for him to take zakat. Likewise, if he denies it and he has a just witness against him. If the witness is not just, it is also not lawful for him to take, until he brings the matter before the judge, who makes the debtor swear. When he swears, it becomes lawful for him to take after that." End of quote. What is meant by the debt is that which reaches the niṣāb, as is not hidden.

In Fatḥ al-Qadīr: "If one gives to a poor woman who has a dowry debt upon her husband which reaches the niṣāb, and he is wealthy such that if she asked he would give her, it is not lawful. If he is in a state where he would not give her if she asked, it is lawful." End of quote. This is restricted by the generality of what is in al-Khāniyya. What is meant by the dowry is that which is customarily paid promptly, because what is customarily deferred is a deferred debt, which does not prevent taking zakat. In the first case, his not giving is equivalent to his insolvency. The distinction between it and other debts is that the husband's being taken to the judge is something not befitting for a woman, unlike other cases. However, in al-Bazzāziyya: giving zakat to his sister who is under a husband, if her prompt dowry is less than the niṣāb or more. But if the husband is insolvent, he may give her zakat even if he is wealthy. If the prompt amount is the niṣāb, it is not lawful according to the two (Abū Yūsuf and Muḥammad), and by this it is issued as a fatwa out of caution. According to Imam (Abū Ḥanīfa), it is lawful absolutely. This is the case.

The change from the preposition li- (for) to fī (in) in the last four categories, as al-Zamakhsharī said, is to signify that they are more firmly entitled to charity than those previously mentioned. This is because fī denotes containment, indicating that they surround it and are its place and center. On this basis, the lām is merely for the sense of specification (ikhtiṣāṣ). In al-Intiṣāf, it is stated that there is another secret which is more apparent and closer: the first categories are owners of what may be given to them, and they take it as ownership, so the lām fits them. As for the last four, they do not own what is spent toward them, nor is it spent into their hands. Rather, it is spent on interests connected with them. So the wealth spent on slaves is taken by their masters, the contracting parties or sellers, and their share is not delivered into their hands, so as to be expressed by the lām which indicates ownership of what is delivered to them. Rather, they are the locus for this expenditure and its related interests. Likewise, the debtors: their share is spent on the creditors of their debts, to free their obligations, not for them. As for "in the way of Allah," it is clear in this regard. As for the wayfarer, he seems to have been included under "in the way of Allah," and he was singled out for mention to draw attention to his particularity, although he is free of both particles (lām and fī)."

Its coordination (ʿaṭf) with what is governed by the lām is possible, but coordinating it with the nearer one is closer. What he pointed to, that the mukātab does not own but the mukātib owns, is what some of our companions pointed out. In al-Muḥīṭ they said: it is not permitted to give zakat to a Hāshimite mukātab, because ownership falls to the master in one respect, and doubt is attached to reality in their case. In al-Badā'i' there is something apparent indicating that ownership falls to the mukātab. In that case, the remaining four are a fortiori (bil-ṭarīq al-ūlā).

It is well known that the lām is for ownership according to the Shāfi'īs, and this is what their school requires, since they said: it is necessary to distribute zakat among all the categories when they exist, and it is not to be given to one category alone, nor to fewer than three from each category, but to three or more when these are available. According to us, the owner may give zakat to each one of them, and he may limit himself to one category, because the purpose of the verse is to state the categories to whom giving is permitted, not to specify the giving to them. What supports this is His saying, ta'ālā: ﴿If you disclose your acts of charity, it is good; but if you conceal them and give them to the poor, it is better for you﴾, and that the Prophet (ﷺ) received money from charity and placed it in one category, namely those whose hearts are to be reconciled. Then another sum came to him and he placed it among the debtors. This indicates that it is permissible to restrict to one category. The proof that it is permissible to restrict to one individual is that the plural defined by the article (al-) is used to mean the genus. So if someone swears he will not marry women or buy slaves, he breaches the oath by one. The meaning in the verse is that the genus of charity is for the genus of poor, so giving to one is permitted, because total inclusiveness (istighrāq) is not correct, for it would mean that every charity is for every poor person, which is manifestly corrupt. There is no known referent (ma'hūd) to justify the reading of a specific reference. And one should not object with "divorce me for what is in my hand of dirhams" when she has nothing in her hand, for three (divorces) fall on her. And if he swears he will not speak to him "for days" or "for months," it falls upon ten according to Abū Ḥanīfa, and upon a week or a year according to the two companions, because the reference is possible, so it is not carried to the genus. The conclusion is that reading the plural as genus is a metaphor, while reading it as a specific reference or as totality is literal. Recourse to the metaphor is not permitted except when the literal is impossible. On this basis, a bequest to Zayd and the poor is divided in halves, like a bequest to Zayd and a poor man.

What we have adopted is what is narrated from Umar and Ibn 'Abbās, may Allah be pleased with them. Sa'īd ibn Jubayr, 'Aṭā', Sufyān al-Thawrī, Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, and Mālik, may Allah's mercy be upon them, also held this. Ibn al-Munīr mentioned that his grandfather Abū al-'Abbās Aḥmad ibn Fāris used to derive from the difference between the two particles a proof that the purpose is to specify the expenditure, and the lām is for that. He would say: the object of the prepositional phrase that falls as predicate of "the charities" is omitted. Either the estimate is "the charities are spent upon the poor," as Mālik and those with him say, or "the charities are owned by the poor," as al-Shāfi'ī says. But the first is determined, because it is an estimate which suffices for both particles together, and the lām and fī may both be attached to it. So one may say: "this thing is spent on such and for such." By contrast, estimating "owned" fits only with lām, and when one reaches fī, one needs to estimate "spent" in order to fit. So his estimate from the first is of general attachment, inclusive of correctness, and is determined. In sum, the strength of the approach of the three imams in taking this view is not hidden.

For this reason, some Shāfi'īs chose what the three imams held. The father of the scholar al-Bayḍāwī, 'Umar ibn Muḥammad, who was the Shāfi'ī mufti of his era, used to issue fatwas accordingly.

﴿An obligation from Allah﴾: this is an infinitive (maṣdar) emphasizing an implied verb derived from the sense of the speech, meaning: charities are obligated for them as an obligation. It is transmitted from Sībawayh that it is in the accusative governed by an implied verb of its own, meaning: Allah ta'ālā has made that an obligation. Abū al-Baqā' chose that it is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) of the pronoun implied in His saying ta'ālā: ﴿for the poor﴾, meaning: charities are for them in the state of being an obligation, that is, obligated. It is said that the feminine ending (tā') entered it to attach it to nouns, as in naṭīḥa.

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing﴾ of the conditions of people and the degrees of their entitlement, ﴿All-Wise﴾, who does only what wisdom requires of good matters, among which is delivering rights to their rightful recipients.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 61:

﴿And among them are those who harm the Prophet and say, "He is an ear."﴾ Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi that it was revealed concerning a group of hypocrites, among them al-Hulas ibn Suwayd ibn Samit, Rifa'ah ibn Abd al-Mundhir, Wadi'ah ibn Thabit, and others, who said what was not fitting regarding his rights, peace and blessings be upon him. A man among them said, "Do not do this, for we fear that what you say will reach Muhammad (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) and that it will fall upon us." Al-Hulas said, "Rather, we will say whatever we wish, then we will come to him and he will believe us in what we say, for Muhammad (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) is an ear." In another narration: "an ear that hears." And from Muhammad ibn Ishaq: it was revealed concerning a man among the hypocrites called Nabtal ibn al-Harith, who was dark-skinned, red-eyed, with dark marks on his cheeks, deformed in appearance, and who used to carry the Prophet's (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) words to the hypocrites. It was said to him, "Do not do this," and he said, "Muhammad (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) is only an ear: whoever tells him something, he believes it. We say something, then we come to him and swear to him, and he believes us." He is the one about whom the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said: "Whoever wishes to look at the devil, let him look at Nabtal ibn al-Harith." They intended, may Allah blacken their faces, deafen them and blind their sight, by their saying "he is an ear," that he, peace be upon him, hears what is said to him and believes it; so the description "ear" (udhun) in their speech, with what conveys this meaning, is a disclosure of it. The word is originally a name for the organ, and its application to a person in the sense mentioned, as some narrations support, is metaphor by way of metonymy (al-majaz al-mursal), according to what is in al-Miftah, like the application of "eye" to a people's lookout, where the eye is what is intended by it. Many have stated that this is application of the part to the whole for emphasis, like his saying:

When Layla appears, I am all eyes,
and when she speaks to me, I am all ears.

It has been said that it is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), like "a just man" ('adl), but this is open to question. The emphasis here, as has been said, lies in his hearing every saying in the sense that he believes it, not in mere hearing. As for what has been said, that their meaning in describing him, peace be upon him, as an ear is that he believes everything that is heard without distinguishing between what deserves acceptance because signs of truth support it and what does not, this is not of the kind of applying "eye" to the lookout; for this reason some have made it a comparison to the ear, in that there is nothing in it beyond hearing, no distinguishing of truth from falsehood. This is not worth considering. It has also been said that it is on the supposition of an omitted modifier, i.e., "possessor of an ear"; and it is not hidden that this view is weak in its elegance. It is also permitted that "udhun" be an adjective (sifah mushabbahah) from adhina, yaʾdhanu, idhnan, when one listens. Al-Jawhari recited for Qa'nab:

If they hear a doubt, they fly with it in joy from me,
and what they hear of good they bury.
Deaf when they hear good spoken of me,
but if I am mentioned with evil among them, they give ear.

On this view it is an adjective meaning "hearing" (sami'), and no metaphor is involved. As for what the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) was harmed by, it may be that what they said concerning him, peace be upon him, was among the other false sayings, so that the words of the Most High, "and they say" etc., refer to something other than that by which he was harmed; or it may be that the very saying "he is an ear" is what harmed him, and the clause is then an explanatory apposition (ʿatf tafsir). "Yu'dhun" is the present tense of adhahu; its well-known verbal nouns are adha, adhah, and adhiyyah, and "idhha'" (idha'') has also come, as Al-Raghib affirmed; the statement of the author of al-Qamus, "do not say idha'," is an error on his part.

﴿Say: an ear of good for you﴾: this is of the type of "a man of truth" (rajul sidq); it is an idafah of the qualified noun to its qualifiers for emphasis on goodness and righteousness, as if it were said: "Yes, he is an ear, but what a good ear!" It is also permissible that the idafah be in the sense of "in," i.e., he is an ear in good and truth and in what must be heard and accepted, and not an ear in anything else. This is supported by the reading of Hamzah, "wa-rahmatun" with the genitive in the following verse, as coordinated with "khayr," for it is not fitting to describe an ear as "mercy," whereas it is fitting to say: "an ear in good and mercy." Ibn al-Munir said this is the most eloquent style in refuting them, because it holds out to them hope of agreement with their claim, then turns back on them, cutting off their hope and ending their wish; it is like the "qawl al-mujib" (the conceding statement).

Nafi' read "udhun" with light pronunciation in both places, and [another reader] read "udhunun" with tanwin, so "khayrun" is an adjective of it, meaning "khayyir" (intensive), or an elative (af'al tafdil), or a verbal noun described by it for emphasis, or by the well-known interpretation. His saying, "He believes in Allah," is an explanation of his, peace be upon him, being an ear of good for them: that is, he confirms Allah the Most High because of the proofs and signs that have been established before him which necessitate that. That this is a description of "good" for the addressees, just as it is good for all the worlds, is not hidden. "And he believes the believers" means he confirms them because of what he knows of their sincerity. The apparent sense is that this falls within the scope of the explanation, but most exegetes did not clarify its aspect as a description of "good" for the addressees. Indeed, Mawlana al-Shihab said: the meaning is "an ear of good that hears the signs and proofs of Allah and confirms them, and hears the believers' speech and accepts it from them and confirms them in it"; and this is an allusion that the hypocrites are an ear of evil, who hear the signs of Allah and do not benefit from them, and hear the believers' speech and do not accept it; and that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, does not listen to their speech except out of compassion for them, not because he accepts it, for lack of discernment on his part, as they claimed; and by this the reading of the explanation is sound, so consider it. It is not hidden that to intend this meaning from this portion of the verse is a stretch. It may perhaps be said that the intended meaning is that he, peace be upon him, hears the speech of the sincere believers and confirms them, and does not confirm the hypocrites, though he hears their speech; and that this being a description of "good" for the addressees is either because it may lead them to sincerity, since it implies a lowering of their rank below that of the sincere, or because his, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, confirming the sincere believers in what they say of the truth is among the completions of his confirmation of Allah's signs; and there is no doubt in the goodness of that for the addressees, and indeed for others as well, so let this be understood.

The faith in His saying, "He believes in Allah," means acknowledgment and affirmation, as we have pointed out; this is why it is transitive with "bi" (in). As for His saying, "and he believes the believers," it means he gave them safety from being called liars, so the "li" in it is extra for emphasis, since in that sense it is transitive by itself; this is what has been said. But it is objected that the addition for strengthening a verb preceding its object is rare. Al-Zamakhshari said: he intended by faith in the first clause the affirmation of Allah the Most High, which is the opposite of disbelief, so it was made transitive with "bi," with which disbelief is transitive, treating the opposite as with its opposite; and he intended by faith in the second clause hearing from the believers and letting them have what they say, and confirming them because they are truthful in his sight, so it was made transitive with "li." Do you not see His saying, "And you would not believe us even if we were truthful" (12:17)? There the faith is transitive with "li," because it means submitting to them. The apparent sense is that "li" here is not extra for strengthening as in the first case, though some of the scholars' statements seem to indicate its being extra. His saying, "And mercy," is coordinated with "an ear of good," meaning "and he is mercy," and in it is the reporting of a verbal noun as a predicate, a matter well known. "For those among you who believe": that is, for those who show faith, as he accepts it from them, but not confirming them in that, rather out of gentleness toward them and compassion for them, and not disclosing their secrets nor exposing their concealed matters.

The apparent sense of al-Khazin's words is that what is meant by "of those who believe" is the sincere ones, and "among you" was mentioned on account of the hypocrites who claimed that they were believers; the truth is that this is carried to the hypocrites. Attributing faith to them with a verbal form after ascribing it to the sincere believers with an active participle, which signals firmness and continuity, indicates that their faith is a recent matter that has no permanence; and perhaps the shift from "mercy for you" to what was mentioned is to point to this. Ibn Abi Abla read "rahmatan" in the accusative, as an object of a implied verb indicated by "an ear of good," meaning "he gives you permission and hears out of mercy"; and it is permitted that it be coordinated with an implied final element, meaning "confirming them and mercy to you."

﴿And those who harm the Messenger of Allah﴾: that is, with whatever kind of harm it may be. The use of the future tense, which indicates that the threat is consequent upon continuing in their state, is an indication of the acceptance of their repentance. ﴿For them is a painful punishment﴾: that is, because of that, as is shown by the construction of the judgment upon the relative pronoun. The relative clause and its predicate are a discourse from the Mighty and Majestic on the path of threat, not included within the address. In repeating the attribution by affirming the painful punishment for them, and then making the clause a predicate, there is the emphasis that is not hidden. Mentioning him, peace be upon him, with the title of messengership together with the attribution to the Glorious Name is for the utmost honour, and to draw attention to the fact that harming him, peace be upon him, returns to the presence of the Mighty and Majestic and necessitates complete wrath and anger from Him, glorified be He.

Some have mentioned that harming does not apply only during his life, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, but also after his death, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. They counted among it speaking ill of his parents, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and likewise harming the people of his household, may Allah be pleased with them, as Yazid's harming them, beyond what they deserve. And this is not far-fetched.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 62:

﴿They swear by Allah to you, to please you.﴾ The address is to the believers. The hypocrites used to say things that were not fitting, then they would come to them and make excuses to them, and they would confirm their excuses with oaths, so that they would excuse them and be pleased with them. Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah, who said: "It was mentioned to us that a man from among the hypocrites said: 'By Allah, these people are our best and our nobles. And if what Muhammad (ﷺ) says is true, they are worse than donkeys.' A man from among the Muslims heard it and said: 'By Allah, what Muhammad (ﷺ) says is indeed true, and you are worse than the donkey.' The man went and reported it to the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) and informed him. He sent for the man and summoned him, and said: 'What led you to say what you said?' So he began to swear and take oaths by Allah that he had not said that. The Muslim man began to say: 'O Allah, make the truthful one truthful and the liar a liar.' Then Allah, glorified is He, revealed concerning that: (They swear...) etc." That is, they swear to you that they did not say what was reported about them, which would cause harm to the Prophet (ﷺ), in order to please you by that.

It is also reported from Muqatil and al-Kalbi that it was revealed concerning a group of hypocrites who stayed behind from the expedition of Tabuk. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned from it, they came to the believers making excuses to them for their staying behind, offering pretexts, and swearing oaths.

Some scholars denied this, limiting the verse to the first explanation, and perhaps they regarded that as more suitable to the context. The reason their pleasing the believers is mentioned separately, although the main aim of their efforts is to please the Messenger (ﷺ), is to indicate that this (pleasing the believers) is far from being a means of pleasing him (peace be upon him). The Prophet (ﷺ) only refrained from denying them out of kindness toward them and to conceal their faults, not out of approval of what they did or inward acceptance of what they said.

﴿And Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him.﴾ That is, they have more right to be pleased than anyone else. This is achieved only through obedience, compliance with His command, and fulfilling the rights due to him (peace be upon him) in matters of honour and veneration, whether he is present or absent. As for belief, one is pleased by it only if the path of his knowledge is limited to reports, until the truth comes and falsehood vanishes.

The sentence is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the subject of ﴿they swear﴾, and the intended meaning is to censure them for occupying themselves with what does not concern them and turning away from what is important and beneficial to them.

The pronoun in ﴿that they should please Him﴾ is singular, although after the conjunction "and" one would expect the dual. This is because the Messenger's being pleased is inseparable from Allah's being pleased, and ﴿whoever obeys the Messenger has indeed obeyed Allah﴾. Because the two are linked, they are treated as one thing, and so the singular pronoun refers to them both. Alternatively, the pronoun is used in place of the demonstrative, which refers to one or many according to the thing mentioned. The dual was not used out of courtesy, so that Allah would not be joined with another in a dual pronoun, which has been forbidden, with some discussion on that point. Or the pronoun refers to His Messenger, and the sentence consists of two clauses, with the predicate (khabar) of the first omitted because the predicate of the second indicates it, as in the verse of poetry:

"We are content with what we have, and you are content with what you have, though opinions differ."

Or the pronoun refers to Allah, the Exalted, and the predicate mentioned is the predicate of the first clause, while the predicate of the second clause is omitted. Sibawayh preferred the first of these possibilities in such constructions, because the thing made the predicate of the first clause is close to it, and the sentence avoids separating the subject (mubtada') from its predicate. Al-Mubarrad preferred the second, for priority of mention. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the Messenger (peace be upon him) alone, and the predicate belongs to him alone, with nothing omitted in the sentence. This is because the discussion concerns harming and pleasing the Messenger (peace be upon him), so mentioning Allah, the Exalted, serves to honour him (peace be upon him) and to prepare the ground. For this reason the predicate was not stated for Allah, and it was specified for the Messenger (ﷺ). A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿And when they are called to Allah and His Messenger, that he may judge between them﴾. It is not hidden that considering the predication to concern the conjoined noun, while not treating the conjoined subject as having any predicate of its own, is extremely strange, though the difference between the two verses is as clear as the sun.

[Page 129]

﴿If they are believers﴾: the answer to the conditional (jawab al-shart) is omitted, indicated by what precedes it. That is: if they are believers with sincere faith, outwardly and inwardly, then let them please Allah, the Exalted, and His Messenger (peace be upon him) by what has been mentioned, for they are more deserving of being pleased.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 63:

﴿Did they not know﴾ i.e., those hypocrites. The interrogative is for rebuke over the grave deed they undertook, while they knew, from what they heard from the Messenger (ﷺ), its dire consequence. It is also read as "ta'lamu" (you know) with the ta' (taa'), by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), to increase the reproach and rebuke, if the address is to the hypocrites and not to the believers, as has been said. In another reading, "Did you not know" (alam ta'lam), and the address is either to the Prophet (ﷺ) or to everyone who comes upon it. The verb "knew" may be transitive to two objects, or transitive to one. "That" (annahu), i.e., the matter: ﴿whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger﴾, i.e., contravenes the command of Allah and the command of His Messenger, peace be upon him. The root of muhaddah (opposition) is a form of mufa'alah from hadd, meaning side or direction, like mushaqqah (opposition) from shaqq (split), and mu'adah (enmity) from 'udwah, with the same meaning. So if one of the agents of each of the mentioned actions is in a hadd, shaqq or 'udwah other than where his companion is, [this is the sense]. It may also be from hadd in the sense of prohibition. "Whoever" (man) is conditional, and its response is the words of the Most Glorified: ﴿then for him is the fire of Hell﴾, on the basis that its predicate is omitted, i.e., "then it is certain that for him is the fire of Hell." This was estimated because the response of a conditional can only be a clause, and "anna" with an open hamzah together with what follows it is, by interpretation, a single noun. It was estimated as preceding because it does not occur at the beginning of speech as the kasrah form does. It is also permitted that the omitted element be a predicate, i.e., "the matter is that for him..." etc. It was also said that the meaning is "then for him is the fire of Hell," and that the repetition of "anna" in the words of the Most Glorified, "annahu," is for emphasis. It was said: there is a problem with this, because if the intended meaning were "then for him," and "anna" were for emphasis, then "fire of Hell" would be in the nominative and "anna" would not govern it, and the emphasizing and emphasized would be separated by the conditional clause, and a foreign element would stand between the particle of response and what it governs. It is answered that this is not a case of verbal emphasis but of repetition due to the distance of the antecedent, and it belongs to the category of tatriyah (renewal of mention), and such does not prevent government or the entry of the fa'.
