A parallel is the words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed your Lord, for those who do evil in ignorance and then repent after that and make amends, indeed your Lord after it is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. And the poet's words:

"The tribe of the Yamanis surely knows that I, when I say 'amma ba'du,' am its orator."

And "kam wa kam." The placing of the verse in this category was transmitted by Sibawayh in al-Kitab from al-Khalil, and he himself [said it]. "Zaʿama" (it is claimed) in his speech is not a weakening of it, because that is his custom in everything he transmits, as his commentators have explained. It is also permitted that it be coordinated with "annahu," and the response of the conditional is omitted, i.e., "Did they not know that whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger will perish, then indeed for him..." etc. Its sum: "Did they not know this, and this after it?" Its remoteness is not hidden. Moreover, Abu Hayyan said: this is not valid, because they have stated that the omission of the response occurs only when the conditional verb is past or a present verb jussed by lam, and what is here is not so.

Some have objected that what he mentioned is not agreed upon, for Ibn Hisham explicitly stated otherwise, so it appears to be a condition for the majority. As for the claim that the correct coordination in what was mentioned is with waw, al-Shihab said regarding it: "It is nothing, except that his deserving of the fire is due to opposition without any doubt." It was also read "fa-inna" with a kasrah, which needs no explanation because it is clear. The words of the Most Glorified, ﴿abiding therein﴾, are a hal muqaddarah (anticipated circumstantial clause) from the pronoun in the prepositional phrase, if the beginning and occurrence of settlement is considered in the adverbial, and if the absolute settlement is considered, then the matter is clear. ﴿That﴾, i.e., what was mentioned of the punishment, is ﴿the great disgrace﴾, i.e., humiliation and abasement accompanied by exposure. The excess in this expression is not hidden, and the sentence is a concluding summary of what preceded.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 64:**

﴿The hypocrites fear that a surah will be sent down﴾ That is, "from [the fear] that it be sent down." It is also possible that يَحْذَرُ (yahdharu, "fears") is transitive by itself (mu'addi binafsihi), as is shown by what Sibawayh recited of the verse:

*"Wary of matters that do not harm him, and secure in what does not save him from decrees."*

Al-Mubarrad denied that it is transitive, because حَذَر (hadhar, "fear/wariness") is one of the states of the soul (hay'at al-nafs), like فَزَع (faza', "alarm"). It has been said that the verse is fabricated (masnu'). The reply to al-Mubarrad is that some states are transitive, such as خافَ (khafa, "feared") and خَشِيَ (khashiya, "dreaded"), so what he mentioned is not a necessary rule.

(عَلَيْهِمْ) ("against them"), that is, concerning them, for what is sent down concerning them is sent down upon them. This is only needed if the prepositional phrase and its object are connected to تُنَزَّلُ (tunazzalu, "is sent down"). If, however, it is connected to an implied element (muqaddar) that serves as an attribute (sifah) of the word سُورَةٌ (surah, "a surah") in the words of the Exalted, as has been said, then the meaning is: "a surah sent down that is against them," from the expression هَذا لَكَ وهَذا عَلَيْكَ ("this is for you and this is against you"). So there is no need for it, as is not hidden. However, this is extremely contrary to the apparent meaning, and the apparent meaning is that the prepositional phrase is connected to what precedes it.

(تُنَبِّئُهم) ("informs them") is an attribute of سُورَةٌ, [and it means] the hypocrites ﴿of what is in their hearts﴾ of hidden secrets, let alone what they used to display among themselves in particular, of statements of disbelief and hypocrisy. The meaning is that it [the surah] will broadcast what they used to conceal of their secrets, so it spreads among the people, and they hear it from men's mouths as something publicized, as if it [the surah] were informing them of it. Otherwise, what is in their hearts is known to them, and what they fear is the believers' awareness of it.

It has been said that the meaning is: it informs them of what is in their hearts in such a way that the purpose of it is the necessary result of the benefit of the news, which is the Messenger's ﷺ knowledge of it. It has also been said that the meaning of the informing (al-tanbi'ah) is exaggeration in the surah's containing their secrets, as if it knew from their inward states what they do not know, so it informs them of these and condemns their ugly deeds.

It is permitted that the first two pronouns refer to the believers and the third to the hypocrites. Dividing the pronouns (tafkik al-damair, "separating pronouns' references") is not absolutely prohibited; rather, it is permissible when the contextual indicator (qarinah) is strong and the indication is clear, as here. That is: "the hypocrites fear that a surah will be sent down upon the believers that informs them of what is in the hearts of the hypocrites, exposes their concealments, and reveals their secrets." In reporting about them that they fear this, there is an indication that they were not certain about the matter of the Messenger ﷺ.

Abu Muslim said: the display of fear was by way of mockery, for whenever they heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ mention everything and say that it was by way of revelation, they would deny him and mock him, based on the words of the Exalted: ﴿Say: Mock!﴾ This indicates that they did mock this statement. The imperative here is for threat.

Those who held the previous view said: the meaning is that they were hypocritical, because the hypocrite is a mocker. Just as their saying "We believe" while they are not believers was made deceit in al-Baqarah, here it was made mockery.

It has also been said that يَحْذَرُ is a khabar (informative statement) with the meaning of an imperative, i.e., "let him beware." This was objected to on the grounds that the words of the Exalted ﴿Indeed Allah will bring out what you fear﴾ reject this to some degree, unless what is meant is what they fear according to the requirement of this command, which is contrary to the apparent meaning. The apparent wording would have been: "Indeed Allah sends down a surah like that," or "sends down what you fear," but it turned from that to what is in the noble wording, for exaggeration, since its meaning is "brings forth what you fear of the sending down of the surah." Or, because it is more general, since the meaning is "brings forth every ugly thing whose appearance you fear." Attributing the bringing forth to Allah the Exalted is to indicate that He, glory be to Him, brings it forth in a manner beyond which there is nothing more. The emphasis (al-ta'kid) is to remove doubt or to reject denial.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 65:

﴿And if you ask them﴾ about what they said, ﴿they will surely say, "We were only conversing and playing."﴾ Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, who said: "While the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was on his expedition to Tabuk, he saw some hypocrites ahead of him saying, 'Does this man expect to conquer the palaces and fortresses of Syria? Far-fetched, far-fetched!' Allah informed His Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) of this, and he said, 'Hold back these riders.' He came to them and said, (ﷺ) 'Did you say such-and-such?' They said, 'O Prophet of Allah, we were only conversing and playing,' and this was revealed."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Mardawayh and others narrated from Abdullah ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "A man said during the expedition to Tabuk, 'We have never seen anyone like these reciters of ours: they have the greatest appetites, the most lying tongues, and the greatest cowardice when facing the enemy.' A man said, 'You lie, but you are a hypocrite; I will certainly inform the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).' This reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the Qur'an was revealed." Abdullah said: "I saw the man clinging to the strap of the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) camel, with the stones striking him, while he was saying, 'O Messenger of Allah, we were only conversing and playing.' And the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) was saying what Allah the Exalted had commanded him to say in His words: ﴿Say: Was it Allah and His verses and His Messenger that you were mocking?﴾"

In some narrations it is reported that this man clinging to the camel was Abdullah ibn Ubayy, the chief of the hypocrites. Whether they denied what they had said and offered this false excuse, or did not deny it and simply said what they said, is a matter of disagreement. The Imam (al-Alusi's preferred view) holds the second position, and it is more in keeping with the apparent sense of this majestic wording.

The root meaning of al-Khawd (immersion, plunging into a fluid such as water or mud) is entering into a liquid. Its usage later became widespread until it became a term for any entering into something that involves defilement and harm. They meant: "We were only conversing and passing the time, so that the distance of the journey would be shortened by talk, and joking, as travelling companions do to pass the road; this was not from us in earnest." The interrogative is for rebuke. The mention of the object of mockery first (﴿Allah and His verses and His Messenger﴾) indicates that the mockery was certainly taking place, but the address is directed at the one being mocked. That is, say to them, without paying attention to their excuse, condemning their crimes: "You have mocked One with whom mockery is not fitting, and you have erred in the place of your shameful act, which you have committed often." Whoever reflects will know that their earlier statement concerning the occasion of revelation includes the aforementioned mockery.

[p. 131]

**"Do not make excuses"**: that is, do not occupy yourselves with making excuses and persist in them. The prohibition is not against the act itself, since it has already occurred. Rather, they were forbidden because what they claim is known to be false and its invalidity is clear. As for *i'tidhar* (excuse-making), it has been said that it is an expression for erasing the trace of a sin, from the saying "*i'tadhara al-manazil*" (the abodes became effaced) when they were obliterated, because the one making an excuse tries to remove the trace of his sin and its obliteration.

It has also been said that it means *cutting off*. From this comes the term *'udhrah* for the foreskin, because it is cut off (*tu'adhar*, i.e., cut), and *'udhrah* for virginity, because it is cut by deflowering. It is also said: "*i'tadhharat al-miyah*" (the waters ceased) when they stopped flowing. Thus, since the excuse (*'udhr*) was a cause for cutting off blame, it was called *'udhr*. Both views are transmitted from the lexicographers, and according to al-Wahidi they are close in meaning.

**"You have disbelieved"**: that is, you have manifested disbelief by harming the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and by slandering him. **"After your faith"**: that is, after your manifestation of faith. This and what precedes it is because these people are hypocrites, so the root of disbelief is within them, and in reality there is no faith for them at all.

Some scholars have used this verse to argue that jesting and seriousness are equal in uttering a word of disbelief, and there is no disagreement among the imams on this.

**"If We pardon a group among you"**: for their repentance and sincerity. It is according to the view that the address is to all the hypocrites, or for their refraining from harming and mocking, according to the view that the address is to those among them who were harming and mocking. The pardon in this is from the worldly punishment that comes swiftly. **"We will punish a group because they were criminals"**: that is, persisting in hypocrisy, and they are those who did not repent, or those who were engaged in it and did not refrain from it.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ka'b ibn Malik, who said, in a report that is lengthy: The one who was pardoned was Makhshi ibn Himyar al-Ashja'i. He named himself Abd al-Rahman, and asked Allah, exalted is He, that he be killed as a martyr whose death is not known. He was killed on the day of Yamama, and his death was not known, nor was his killer, and no trace or sign of him was seen.

In some narrations, when this verse was revealed, he repented of his hypocrisy and said: "O Allah, I still hear a verse that makes the skins shiver and the hearts tremble. O Allah, make my death a killing in Your path, such that no one can say, 'I washed him, I shrouded him, I buried him.'" He was then struck down on the day of Yamama, and his supplication was answered. May Allah be pleased with him.

From here, Mujahid said: the word *ta'ifah* (group) is applied to one person, except for a thousand. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: *ta'ifah* is one person and a small group.

It was recited as *"yu'fa"* and *"yu'adhdhib"* with the *ya'* and the active form in both, the agent being Allah, exalted is He. It was also recited as *"in ta'fu"* and *"yu'adhdhab"* with the *ta'* and the passive form. This recitation (*qira'ah*) raises a difficulty, because the first verb is attributed in it to a prepositional phrase (*al-jar wa al-majrur*), and such a verb must be masculine, not feminine when the object of the preposition is feminine. One says *"sir 'ala al-dabbah"* (travel upon the beast) but not *"sayyartu 'alayha"*. It is answered that this is by inclining toward the meaning and taking it into account, so it was made feminine because the prepositional object is feminine, since the meaning of *"ta'fu 'an ta'ifah"* is "a group is shown mercy." This is one of the rare features of Arabic. It has also been said that if it were said with harmonization (*mushakalah*) it would not be far-fetched. And it has been said that the deputy subject (*na'ib al-fa'il*) is a pronoun referring to the sins, the sense being: "If the sins are pardoned," i.e., the sins.

Among people there are those who have raised a difficulty concerning the conditional statement itself, in that it is not valid for "*We will punish a group*" to be the response (*jawab*) to the preceding condition and to the condition of the condition (*shart al-shart*), since the response requires a connection either by way of causation or by necessity in the sentence, and both are absent from the sentence. Al-Izz ibn Abd al-Salam mentioned this in his *Amali*, and the scholar Ibn Hajar transmitted it from him in *Dhayl al-Fatawi*. He mentioned that he had not seen anyone draw attention to an answer to it, but that it can be known from the occasion of revelation. After he related the report, he spoke in a manner that is not free from obscurity. I had raised this question in the prime of my youth, together with his answer to the aforementioned scholar, before a scholar who had weathered the ages, and I asked him to resolve it. He turned away from restating the answer given in the *Dhayl*, and I think that was because he was ignorant of it. He then rolled up his sleeves and uncovered a shin for an answer of his own, saying: "The conditional (*shartiyyah*) is conjunctive (*ittifaqiyyah*), like your saying: 'If man is speaking, then the donkey is braying.'" He began to establish this with things at which the bereaved mother would laugh. There is no power nor might except with Allah, the Most High, the Mighty.

Mawlana Sari al-Din answered: the response is an omitted clause (*mahdhuf*) caused by what has been mentioned, meaning: "so they should not slacken," or "so they should not slacken; therefore a group must be punished." Then he said: If it is said that this estimation does not indicate that the content of the condition is the cause of the content of the response, I say: it is taken to mean that it is a cause for informing of the content of the response, or its causation for commanding non-deception, analogous to informing. The scholar al-Taftazani has investigated this matter thoroughly at his saying, exalted is He: "*Say: Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel, for indeed he has brought it down upon your heart*" in Surat al-Baqarah, in the margin of the *Kashshaf*.

*Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 67:*

﴿The hypocrite men and the hypocrite women are of one another.﴾ That is, they resemble one another in hypocrisy, like the parts of one thing that resemble each other. What is meant is unity in reality and in form, like water and earth. The verse is connected to all the vile deeds mentioned of them. It has also been said that it is connected to His words, exalted is He: ﴿And they swear by Allah that they are surely of you﴾. What is meant by it is the refutation and nullification of their stated claim and the affirmation of His words, glorified is He: ﴿And they are not of you﴾. What follows of the difference between their attributes and the attributes of the believers serves as evidence for this. The particle *min* (from/of), under both interpretations, is *ittisaliyyah* (connective, indicating attachment), as in his words, upon him be prayer and peace: "You are to me in the position of Harun to Musa." The mention of the conditions of the females serves to announce their complete deep-rootedness in disbelief and hypocrisy. ﴿They enjoin what is evil﴾, i.e., denial of the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him. ﴿And they forbid what is good﴾, i.e., the testimony that there is no god but Allah and the acknowledgment of what Allah, exalted is He, has sent down, as Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.

It is also related from Abu al-Aliyah that he said: "Every evil mentioned in the Qur'an is meant to refer to the worship of idols and of Satan." It is not far-fetched that *al-munkar* (the evil) and *al-ma'ruf* (the good) are meant in a general sense, encompassing what has been mentioned and other things, and that what has been mentioned enters into it in a primary way. The clause is a resumptive clause (*istinaf*) affirming the content of what preceded, revealing the opposition of their condition to the condition of the believers; or it is a second predicate (*khabar thani*). ﴿And they withhold their hands﴾, i.e., from spending in obedience to Allah and seeking His pleasure, as reported from Qatadah and al-Hasan. The withholding of the hand is a *kinayah* (metonymy) for stinginess and miserliness, just as extending the hand is a *kinayah* for generosity, because one who gives extends his hand, unlike one who withholds. It is reported from al-Jubba'i that what is meant is that they hold back their hands from jihad in the way of Allah, but this is contrary to the common usage of this expression. ﴿They forgot Allah﴾. The forgetting is a *majaz* (figurative usage) for abandoning, and it is a *kinayah* for abandoning obedience; so what is meant is that they did not obey Him, glorified is He. ﴿So He forgot them﴾, i.e., He withheld His gentleness and bounty from them. The expression "forgetting" is used for *al-mushakalah* (congruity of expression, i.e., naming a thing by the term used for its counterpart).

﴿Indeed, the hypocrites, they are the defiantly disobedient﴾, i.e., those who are complete in rebellion and defiant disobedience, which is departing from obedience and stripping oneself of everything, to the extent that they are as if they constituted the entire category. From here the restriction derived from the separating pronoun and the definiteness of the predicate is valid; otherwise, how many defiantly disobedient people there are besides them!

The use of the explicit noun in place of the pronoun is for the increase of affirmation. Perhaps he did not mention the female hypocrites, relying on the recency of the reference. Similar to this, in terms of the purpose of the explicit noun, is His words, glorified is He: ﴿Allah has promised the hypocrite men and the hypocrite women and the disbelievers﴾, i.e., the openly defiant ones. Thus it is a conjunction of the different (*'atf al-mughayir*); it may also be a conjunction of the general upon the particular (*'atf al-'amm 'ala al-khass*). ﴿The fire of Hell, abiding therein﴾ is a *hal muqaddarah* (anticipated circumstantial clause) from the object of the verb.

[p. 133]

﴿Wa'ada﴾ (He promised): that is, [they are] estimating the eternity [of their stay]. It has been said that what is meant is their entry into and punishment by the Fire of Hell in that state, since what appears to them makes them estimate eternity within themselves. So there is no need for what some have said, that the phrase means "those whose eternity is estimated," in the passive form.

The addition of "eternity" (al-khulud) is because they did not estimate it; rather, God Most High estimated it for them. It has also been said that if the meaning is that God, glorified is He, punishes them with the Fire of Hell, abiding in it, then no estimation is needed. The expression "promised" is used sarcastically, like His saying, glorified is He: ﴿so give them the good news of a painful punishment﴾ [9:34], and ﴿it is enough for them﴾ [as punishment and recompense], meaning that in it is what suffices of that. This also indicates the greatness of its punishment and torment, for when it is said to the one being punished, "This is enough," it shows that he has reached the utmost of affliction. ﴿And God has cursed them﴾, meaning He has removed them far from His mercy and goodness and has humiliated them. In the explicit mention of the Glorious Name there is an indication of intense wrath that is not hidden. ﴿And for them is a lasting punishment﴾, meaning a kind of punishment other than the punishment of the Fire, which is everlasting and never ends. So there is no repetition with what came before, and this does not contradict ﴿it is enough for them﴾, because that refers to their punishment by the Fire. It has also been said, to avoid repetition, that what came before is a threat, while this is an explanation of the occurrence of what they were promised, and there is no obstacle to emphasis. It has also been said that the first refers to the punishment of the Hereafter, and this refers to the punishment they suffer in this world, such as fatigue, fear, disgrace, killing, and the like. The word "lasting" (iqamah) has been interpreted as "not ceasing," because it is a attribute of rational beings, so punishment is not described by it; thus it is a figurative usage (majaz) for what has been mentioned.

It is also permissible that describing the punishment with it is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿a life well-pleasing﴾ [69:21]; in that case the figurative usage is an attributive metaphor (majaz 'aqli).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 69:

﴿Like those before you﴾ is a shift from the third person to the second person for emphasis. The kaf (ك) is either in the nominative position as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "You are like those before you of the destroyed nations," or in the accusative position governed by an omitted verb, meaning "You did like those before you." A similar example is the verse of al-Namir describing a wild bull and dogs:

ḥattā idhā al-kilābu qāla lahā kal-yawmi maṭlūban wa-lā ṭāliban
(Until, when the dogs said to them, "Like today, one pursued and no pursuer.")

Its underlying form is: "I have not seen one pursued like a pursued one I saw today, nor a pursuit like a pursuit I saw today." The speech was abridged and it became: "I have not seen one pursued like the pursued of today," because of its association with it. Then the modified noun was omitted for breadth, and there is no harm. It is also said that "kal-yawm" (like today) was placed before the described noun, so it became a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) for emphasis and intensification, and the verb was omitted due to the situational indication. The point of resemblance is the state of being the object of an omitted verb. His statement, glorified is He: ﴿They were stronger than you in power and more abundant in wealth and children﴾ and so on, is an explanation of the comparison and a clarification of the point of resemblance between the addressees and those before them, so it has no place in i'rab. In it is an indication that the addressees are more deserving and more entitled to suffer what those before them suffered. ﴿So they enjoyed their share﴾ means they enjoyed their portion of the worldly pleasures. In the form istif'āl there is a meaning not found in tafa''ul, namely the seeking of benefit and the continuation of enjoyment. The derivation of khalāq (share) is from khalq (creation) in the sense of measuring, which is the root of its meaning linguistically. ﴿So you enjoyed your share as those before you enjoyed their share﴾: He censures the earlier ones for enjoying their base portions of transient desires and being absorbed in them, distracted from reflecting on the outcome and striving to attain true delights, as a preparation for censuring the addressees by their resemblance to them and their following in their footsteps. For this reason, elaboration was chosen by the repetition of ﴿So they enjoyed their share﴾. This is like when you want to alert some oppressor to the ugliness of his act, so you say: "You are like Pharaoh, who used to kill without a crime, torture, and oppress, and you do the same." The position of the kaf is accusative, as it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning "you enjoyed an enjoyment like the enjoyment of those..." ( ﴿And you engaged﴾ ) means you entered into falsehood. ﴿Like those who engaged﴾ means "like those who," and its nūn was dropped for lightness, as in the saying:

inna alladhīna ḥānat bi-falj dimāʾuhum ∗∗∗ hum al-qawmu kullu al-qawmi yā umma khālid
(Indeed those whose blood was spilled at Falaj, they are the people, all the people, O mother of Khalid.)

It is also permissible that alladhī be an adjective of a singular-form word with a plural meaning, like "fawj" (group) and "farīq" (party), so the adjective takes account of the wording while the pronoun takes account of the meaning. Or it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning "like the engaging in which they engaged," and this is preferred because it involves no strain. Al-Farra' said that alladhī may be a verbal particle (maṣdariyya), and this was derived as meaning "like their engaging," and it is, as Abu al-Baqa' said, rare. This clause is conjoined to what precedes it, and in that case either something is supposed in it that makes it of its pattern, for its conjunction to it, or nothing is supposed, as an indication of attention to the first. ﴿Those﴾ refers to those characterized by the enumerated attributes, both the compared and those compared to. Its being a reference to the latter requires that the judgment of the compared be understood implicitly, and it leads to the loss of benefit from the shift in address, since the apparent form would then be "those of you." The address is to the master of the addressees, upon him be prayers and peace, or to everyone suitable for it, meaning: those characterized by what has been mentioned of vices. ﴿Their deeds have become void﴾ means the deeds by which they would have deserved good rewards had they accompanied faith. Ḥabṭ means falling, nullification, and dissolution; the meaning is that they did not deserve reward and honor for them. ﴿In this world and the Hereafter﴾: as for the Hereafter, it is clear; as for this world, what they obtained of health, abundance, and the like was only by way of gradual leading on (istidrāj), as the verses have declared, not as honor. ﴿And those﴾ described as having their deeds voided in both abodes ﴿they are the losers﴾, meaning those who are complete in loss, comprising all its origins and causes entirely.

The use of the demonstrative noun in both places is to indicate that the described attributes are the cause of the voiding and the loss.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 9, verse 70:

﴿Has there not come to them﴾, i.e., to the hypocrites, ﴿the news of those before them﴾, i.e., their report, which is of great significance. The interrogative here serves *taqrir* (affirmation, bringing to acknowledgement) and *tahdhir* (warning). ﴿The people of Noah﴾ were drowned by the flood. ( ﴿And ʿAd﴾ ) were destroyed by the wind. ( ﴿And Thamud﴾ ) were destroyed by the earthquake. The style was varied with regard to the two peoples because they were not known for their prophet. It was also said that this was because many of them believed. ﴿And the people of Ibrahim﴾: their leader Nimrod was destroyed by a gnat, and they were annihilated after him, but not by a heavenly cause like the others. ﴿And the companions of Madyan﴾, i.e., its inhabitants, who were the people of Shuʿayb, peace be upon him, were destroyed
Page 135
by fire on the day of the canopy, or by the Cry and the earthquake, or by fire and the earthquake, according to the differing reports. ( ﴿And the overturned cities﴾ ) is the plural of *mu’tafikah*, from *i’tifak*, which is overturning, by making the top of a thing its bottom, through subsidence into the earth. What is meant by them is either the towns of the people of Lut, peace be upon him, so *i’tifak* is in its literal sense, for they were overturned with their inhabitants and their upper parts became their lower parts, and He rained upon those within them stones of baked clay. Or what is meant is the towns of the rebellious deniers in general, so *i’tifak* is a figurative use for the reversal of their condition from good to evil, by way of *isti’arah* (metaphor), like the saying of Ibn al-Rumi:

"And subsidence is not that the lowest parts of a town become its highest, but that the base-born come to rule."

Because not all of them underwent the literal overturning. ﴿Their messengers came to them with clear proofs﴾: this is a *istithnaf* (resumptive sentence) explaining their news, and the plural pronoun refers to all of them, not only to the overturned cities. ﴿So Allah would not have wronged them﴾: i.e., they denied their messengers, so Allah the Exalted destroyed them, and so He would not have... etc. The *fa* (so) is for conjunction with that implied clause which the sentence presupposes and which the structure calls for. That is, it was not among His customary practice, glorified is He, to do anything resembling the wronging of people, such as punishing without crime. It may also be taken to indicate the continuation of negation, i.e., such a thing never proceeds from Him, glorified is He, at all, rather this is more emphatic, as is not hidden. As for al-Zamakhshari's saying: "i.e., it was not valid for Him to wrong them, and He is Wise, and what is ugly is not permissible for Him," it is based on Mu'tazilism.

﴿But they were wronging themselves﴾: in that they exposed themselves, by the requirement of their readiness, to punishment through disbelief and denial. The combination of the past and the present forms indicates continuity. The fronting of the object, which some scholars have settled upon merely for the sake of emphasis while observing the *fasilah* (verse-ending rhyme), without intending to restrict the wronging to them, according to the view of those who do not regard fronting as implying restriction, such as Ibn al-Athir, as has been said.

[Page 135]

﴿And the believing men and the believing women﴾ is an exposition of the good condition of the believing men and women, in their state and their outcome, after the exposition of the condition of their opposites in this world and the next. His saying, glorified is He: ﴿some of them are allies of others﴾ corresponds to His saying, exalted is He, earlier: ﴿some of them are from others﴾. The change of expression indicates their mutual support and solidarity, unlike those others. His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿they enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong﴾ is clearly the counterpart of ﴿they enjoin what is wrong﴾, and so on. The discussion of "what is wrong" and "what is right" is well known. His saying, may His majesty be exalted: ﴿and they establish prayer﴾ is in counterpart to ﴿they forgot Allah﴾. His saying, exalted is His majesty: ﴿and they give zakat﴾ is in counterpart to ﴿and they withhold their hands﴾. His saying, blessed and exalted is He: ﴿and they obey Allah and His Messenger﴾, meaning in all matters, is in counterpart to the description of the hypocrites with complete corruption and departure from obedience. It has also been said that it is in counterpart to ﴿they forgot Allah﴾. His saying, glorified is He: ﴿they establish prayer﴾ is an additional praise. His saying, exalted is His state: ﴿Those, Allah will surely have mercy upon them﴾ is in counterpart to (﴿so He caused them to forget themselves﴾), which is explained as the withholding of His kindness and mercy, glorified is He. It has also been said that it is in counterpart to ﴿indeed, the hypocrites are the defiantly disobedient﴾, because it means the God-fearing who are shown mercy. The demonstrative pointing to the believing men and believing women is in view of their being characterized by the noble attributes that preceded, and the use of a form indicating distance is due to what has passed more than once.

The sin (السين) [in ﴿sa-yarhamuhumu﴾], according to what al-Zamakhshari said and which many others followed, is for emphasizing the promise. Just as it conveys that, it also conveys the emphasis of the threat. Sahib al-Taqrib (al-Taqrib) examined this and explained it by saying that the sin in affirmation corresponds to lan in negation, so it is, in this respect, an emphasis of what it precedes, and there is no difference in that between being a promise, a threat, or other than these. The scholar Ibn Hajar said: what al-Zamakhshari claimed, that the sin conveys the certainty of what follows it, is rejected, because certainty is understood from the context and not from the lexical form, and this is a preparation for his corrupt doctrine of the necessity of retribution (tahtim al-jaza', i.e., that reward and punishment are necessarily binding). Whoever was unaware of this subtle point directed it [toward a sound reading], and Ibn Qasim, the eminent scholar, criticized him, saying that this has no basis, because it is a transmitted matter that is not refuted by what was mentioned, and attributing heedlessness to the imams arises only from love of objection. In that case, the meaning is: those described by the noble attributes that have been detailed, Allah will certainly have mercy upon them. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Mighty﴾, strong and capable over everything, nothing He wills is beyond His power, (﴿Wise﴾) who places things in their proper places, and among that is blessing and retribution. The clause is a justification for the promise.

﴿Allah has promised the believing men and the believing women gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein﴾. This is in contrast to the preceding threat against the hypocrites, which was expressed as a "promise" in mockery, as has already passed. It is understood from the words of some scholars that His saying, glorified is He, ( ﴿He will have mercy upon them﴾ ) explains the bestowal of the worldly effects of His mercy, namely support and victory, and that this is a detailing of the effects of His mercy in the Hereafter. The use of the apparent noun in place of the pronoun serves greater confirmation and indicates that faith is the cause of what the promise is attached to. He did not join to it the rest of the attributes, to signal that it is among its necessary consequences and concomitants. The discussion of "abiding" (khalidin) here is like the discussion regarding what has passed. ﴿And pleasant dwellings﴾, meaning dwellings that souls find pleasant, or in which life is pleasant. The attribution (the grammatical ascription of the predicate) is therefore either literal or metaphorical.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh reported from al-Hasan, who said: "I asked Imran ibn Husayn and Abu Hurayrah about the interpretation of ﴿and pleasant dwellings﴾. They said: 'You have fallen upon one who knows. We asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about it, and he said: "A palace of pearl in Paradise. In that palace are seventy houses of red ruby, and in each house are seventy chambers of green emerald, and in each chamber are seventy couches, and on each couch are seventy couches of every color, and on each couch is a wife from the dark-eyed houris, and in each chamber are seventy tables, and on each table are seventy kinds of every food, and in each chamber are seventy male and female servants. The believer is given strength each morning sufficient for all of that."'"

﴿In gardens of Eden﴾. It has been said that "Eden" (ʿAdn, meaning settled and permanent residence) is a proper name for a specific place, as is indicated by His saying: ﴿gardens of Eden which the Most Merciful has promised﴾, where it is described with definiteness. Also, al-Bazzar and al-Daraqutni in al-Mukhtalif wa'l-Mu'talif (a work on identical-spelling names of people and places), and Ibn Mardawayh, reported from the hadith of Abu al-Darda', who said that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Eden is the abode of Allah, which no eye has seen and which has not occurred to the heart of any human. Only three will dwell in it: the prophets, the truthful ones (al-siddiqun), and the martyrs. Allah, glorified is He, says: 'Blessed is whoever enters you.'" It is also related from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs that in Paradise there is a palace called Eden, around which are towers and meadows. It has five thousand doors, and none enters it except a prophet, a truthful one, or a martyr. And from Ibn Mas'ud that it is the innermost part and the navel of Paradise. ʿAta' ibn al-Sa'ib said: "Eden is a river in Paradise, its gardens on its banks." It has also been said that ʿAdn, originally, means settlement and firmness, and one says "ʿadana bi'l-makan" when he stays in a place. The meaning here is residence in the manner of perpetuity, since that is the complete singular form appropriate to the context of praise, i.e., in gardens of residence and perpetuity. On this view, all the gardens are gardens of Eden, from which they do not seek any transfer.

The difference between the dwellings and the gardens, which the conjunction indicates, is either essential, on the basis that by "gardens" is meant other than Eden, and these are for the general body of believers, while Eden is for the prophets, peace be upon them, the truthful ones, and the martyrs. Or the gardens themselves are meant, which are other than the dwellings, as is apparent. In that case the promise explicitly includes two things, the gardens and the dwellings, so each person has a garden and a dwelling. Or the difference is descriptive, in which case each of them is general, but the first is in terms of its containing rivers and gardens, while the second is not in this respect. It is as if He first described what they were promised as being of the kind of the most noble of the known places among them, gardens with flowing rivers, so that their natures would incline toward it at the first striking of their ears. Then He described it as surrounded by pleasant living, free from the impurities of troubles which the places of this world and its people rarely lack, and in it is what the souls desire and the eyes delight in. Then it was described as an abode of residence without departure, and firmness without cessation. This is not a repetition of His saying, ﴿abiding therein﴾, as is not hidden. Then He promised them, may His majesty be great, as the context indicates, something greater and higher than all of that, by His saying, blessed and exalted is He: ﴿and approval from Allah﴾, meaning and a small portion of His approval, glorified is He, is greater. For the purpose of conveying this, He turned away from the shorter expression "the approval of Allah" to what is in this sublime arrangement. It has been said that the purpose of the deviation is that what was mentioned is more evident in directing the approval toward them. Perhaps the reason He did not express it with "ridā" (contentment) is to magnify the status of Allah Himself, because "ridwan" (approval) contains an intensity that is not hidden. For this reason it is not used in the Qur'an except for the approval of Allah, glorified is He. That this is greater is because it is the source of settling in the abode of residence and the arrival of every happiness and honor, and it is the ultimate aim of the desire of lovers and the final goal of the hope of those who seek.

Al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and others reported from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Allah, exalted is He, says to the people of Paradise: "O people of Paradise!" They say: "Here we are, our Lord, at Your service, and the good is in Your hands." He says: "Are you content?" They say: "Our Lord, why would we not be content, when You have given us what You have not given to any of Your creation?" He says: "Shall I not give you something better than that?" They say: "And what is better than that, our Lord?" He says: "I shall make My approval descend upon you, so I shall never be angry with you after it, ever."'"

Perhaps the reason this approval was not arranged in the thread of the promise in the manner of what came before, despite its great worth in itself, is that it is realized within every existing thing, and that it is continuous in both abodes. ﴿That﴾, i.e., all that has been mentioned, ﴿is the great triumph﴾, beyond what people consider success in the enjoyments of this world. For the worldly pleasures, even apart from their passing away, their changing, and their being spoiled by pains, are, in comparison with the least of the blessings of the Hereafter, only like the wing of a gnat. In a hadith: "If the world were worth the wing of a gnat in the sight of Allah, He would not give a disbeliever a single sip of water from it." And how excellent is the one who said:

By Allah, if the whole world remained for us, with all its abundant provision,
it would not be right for a free person to humble himself for it; how much less when it is a enjoyment that vanishes by tomorrow.

It is also permissible that the reference (ذَلِكَ) be to the approval, so it is a great triumph in whose presence the blessings of this world and its portions are also held in contempt, or to the world and its blessings and Paradise and what is in it. On both possibilities, His saying, glorified is He, ﴿Allah has prepared for them gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein; that is the great triumph﴾ does not contradict it, for in it "the great" is explained as that in whose presence the blessings of this world are held in contempt. So reflect.

[Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 73]

﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾. Its apparent meaning requires fighting the hypocrites, although they do not openly display disbelief. We do not judge by what is hidden, but we judge by outward appearance, as in the report. For this reason Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi and Mujahid explained the striving against the first group (the disbelievers) as being with the sword, and against the latter (the hypocrites) as being with the tongue, that is, through admonition and establishing the proof against them. This is based on the view that jihad is exerting effort to repel what is not pleasing (to Allah), and it is more general than fighting or other things. If it is taken literally, then it is clear; otherwise it is understood in the general sense of metaphor. It is also narrated from al-Hasan and Qatadah that the striving against the hypocrites is by enforcing the hudud (prescribed punishments) upon them. This raises a difficulty, since enforcing them is obligatory upon others as well, so this would not be specific to them. In al-Ahkam he pointed to resolving this by saying that the causes for the hadd (prescribed punishment) at the time of the Prophet ﷺ mostly came from them. As for the claim that "the hypocrite" means "the sinner" according to al-Hasan, it is not a sound view. It is also narrated, though responsibility for it rests with the narrator, that the reading of the Ahl al-Bayt, may Allah be pleased with them, was "strive against the disbelievers with the hypocrites." Apparently this reading was never established, and none transmitted it except the Shi'a, who are the "house of lies." ﴿And be harsh against them﴾, that is, against both groups in the striving in its two kinds, and do not be gentle with them. It is narrated from Ata that this verse abrogated every form of pardon and forgiveness. ﴿And their refuge is Hell﴾. This is a resumed statement explaining their final outcome after explaining their immediate one. Abu al-Baqa mentioned that in these three words there are several possibilities. First, the waw is a waw of circumstance (hal), and the meaning is: do this while they deserve Hell, and that circumstance is the state of their disbelief and hypocrisy. Second, it was brought as a signal that a deleted verb is intended, that is: know that their refuge is Hell. Third, the statement is understood according to its meaning, namely that for them there has been combined the punishment of this world through jihad and harshness, and the punishment of the Hereafter by making Hell their refuge. ﴿And evil is the destination﴾. This is a concluding statement to what precedes it, and the object of the blame is omitted, that is, "their destination."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 74 (part 1 of 2):

﴿They swear by Allah that they did not say [it]﴾ is a resumptive clause explaining the crimes that proceeded from them, which necessitated what has passed.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah, who said: "It was mentioned to us that two men fought, one of them from Juhayna and the other from Ghifar. Juhayna were allies of the Ansar. The Ghifari prevailed over the Juhayni, so Abdullah ibn Ubayy said to the Aws: 'Help your brother! By Allah, our example and the example of Muhammad ﷺ—and far be it from him what this hypocrite says—is only as the saying goes: Fatten your dog and it will devour you. By Allah, if we return to Medina, the mightier will surely expel the meaner from it.' A man among the Muslims reported this to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, so he sent for him, and he began to swear by Allah, the Exalted, that he had not said it. So it was revealed."

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ka'b ibn Malik, who said: "When the Qur'an was revealed mentioning the hypocrites, al-Jullas ibn Suwayd said: 'By Allah, if this man is truthful, then we are worse than donkeys.' Umayr ibn Sa'd heard them both and said: 'By Allah, O Jullas, you are the most beloved of people to me and the best of them in my regard, and you have said a statement which, if I mention it, will expose you, and if I keep silent about it, it will destroy me; and one of the two is harder upon me than the other.' So he went to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and related to him what al-Jullas had said. He swore by Allah, the Exalted, that he had not said it, and [said]: 'Umayr has lied against me.' So it was revealed."

Abd al-Razzaq related from Ibn Sirin that when it was revealed, "the Prophet ﷺ took hold of Umayr's ear and said: 'May your ear be fulfilled, O boy, and your Lord has confirmed you.' He used to supplicate when al-Jullas swore: 'O Allah, send down upon Your servant and Prophet the confirmation of the truthful and the refutation of the liar.'" He also related from Urwa that al-Jullas repented after its revelation and his repentance was accepted.

Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was sitting in the shade of a tree and said: 'A person will come to you who looks at you with the eyes of a devil. When he comes, do not speak to him.' Not long after, a man with blue eyes appeared, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called him and said: 'Why do you and your companions revile me?' He left and brought his companions, and they swore by Allah, the Exalted, that they had not said it, until he overlooked them, and Allah the Exalted revealed the verse."

The attribution of the swearing to a plural pronoun according to this narration is evident. As for the first two narrations, it has been said: because they were pleased with it and agreed upon it, so it is the attribution of the act to its cause; or because he made the speech as if it were theirs due to their approval of it. There is no need for a general metaphor, for combining the literal and the metaphorical is permissible in the rational metaphor and is not a matter of dispute. The choice of the present tense form in ﴿yahlifun﴾ over the other narrations is either to evoke the scene or to indicate the repetition of the act, and it stands in place of the oath. The answer to ﴿ma qalu﴾ is ﴿wa-laqad qalu kalimat al-kufr﴾ [And they have certainly uttered the word of disbelief].
Page 139
This is what has been related of their words: "By Allah, our example, etc.," or "By Allah, if this man is truthful, etc.," or the reviling for which he, peace be upon him, rebuked them. The sentence together with what is conjoined to it is a parenthetical clause. ﴿And they disbelieved after their Islam﴾: they manifested what was in their hearts of disbelief after manifesting Islam; otherwise their inner disbelief was already established before, and true Islam has no existence for them. ﴿And they planned what they could not attain﴾: the plotting to assassinate the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when he returned from the Battle of Tabuk.

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il related from Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman, who said: "I was holding the halter of the she-camel of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, leading it, while Ammar was driving, or I was driving and Ammar was leading, until when we were at the ascent, behold, there were twelve riders who had blocked the way. I alerted the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he shouted at them, and they turned back in flight. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to us: 'Did you recognize the people?' We said: 'No, O Messenger of Allah, they were masked, but we did recognize the mounts.' He said: 'These are the hypocrites until the Day of Resurrection. Do you know what they intended?' We said: 'No.' He said: 'They intended to cause the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to slip at the ascent so that they would throw him down from it.' We said: 'O Messenger of Allah, should you not send to their clans so that every people send you the head of their companion?' He said: 'I dislike that the Arabs should speak of us that Muhammad, peace be upon him, fought with a people until, when Allah gave him victory over them, he turned upon them to kill them.' Then he said: 'O Allah, strike them with the Dubayla.' We said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what is the Dubayla?' He said: 'A flame of fire that falls upon the sinew of the heart of one of them, and he perishes.'" All of them were, as Ibn Sa'd related from Nafi' ibn Jubayr, from the Ansar or their allies, with no Qurayshi among them. Al-Tabarsi related from al-Baqir, may Allah be pleased with him, that eight of them were from Quraysh and four from the Arabs, but this is not relied upon.

Al-Bayhaqi mentioned from the narration of Ibn Ishaq their names, and he counted al-Jullas ibn Suwayd among them. The report that he repented and his repentance was good is problematic in light of the statement of the Prophet, peace be upon him, in the report: "These are the hypocrites until the Day of Resurrection," unless it is said that this is according to what is predominant. It has also been said: the intent of the relative clause is the expulsion of the believers from Medina, according to what the report from Qatadah above implies. Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi, and Abu al-Shaykh from him and from Abu Salih, that they intended to crown Abdullah ibn Ubayy with a crown and make him a judge and chief among them, even if the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not agree. It has also been said: they intended to kill Umayr for his reply to al-Jullas, as has passed.

﴿And they did not resent﴾, i.e., they did not dislike and find fault with anything, ﴿except that Allah and His Messenger enriched them from His bounty﴾. The exception is a detached (mufarragh) exception from the most general of the objects, i.e., "they did not resent faith for any reason except the enrichment of them by Allah, the Exalted." Thus the exception is detached from the most general of the causes, and this is like the saying: "I have no fault with you except that I did you good," and the saying of the poet:

The people resented nothing of Umayya except that they are forbearing when angered.

It is a connected exception on the claim that it is included, based on the view that a detached exception cannot be discontinuous. In it there is mockery and the affirmation of a thing by its opposite, like the poet's saying:

"And there is no fault in them, except that their swords..." [the verse].

The root of resentment (niqmah), as al-Raghib said, is denunciation by the tongue and punishment. The matter according to the first is clear; but according to the second it requires resorting to a metaphor, namely that what produces and calls for resentment is found. The pronoun in ﴿aghnahum﴾ refers to the hypocrites, as is the apparent meaning, and their enrichment was by the receiving of blood money. It is related that al-Jullas had a client who was killed, and his blood money was owed, so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered twelve thousand to be given for it, and he took it and became rich. From Qatadah: the blood money was for Abdullah ibn Ubayy, and the addition of two thousand was according to their custom of adding to the blood money out of generosity, and they called it shanaq, as in al-Sihah. Ibn Abi Hatim related "from Urwa, who said: Jullas had taken on a debt or had a debt upon him, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ paid it on his behalf, and that is His statement, glory be to Him: ﴿And they did not resent﴾, the verse." It is not hidden that the enrichment is more evident on the first view. It has been said: their enrichment was by what Allah bestowed through the spoils; for they were, as al-Kalbi said, before the arrival of the Prophet ﷺ at Medina, needy and in hardship of life, and when he, peace be upon him, came to them, they became prosperous through them. The pronoun on this view may refer to the believers, so the statement would include a censure of the hypocrites for envy, just as on the first view it includes their censure for disbelief and failure to give thanks. The singularity of the pronoun in ﴿fadlihi﴾ is of evident wisdom. ﴿So if they repent﴾ from their present vices, ﴿it will be good (yakun)﴾ — i.e., the repentance; and it has been said: i.e., the repentance (al-tawbah). Such a shift is excused in verbal nouns (masadir).

It may be said that the masculine form is according to the predicate, namely His statement, glory be to Him: ﴿good for them (khayran lahum)﴾, i.e., in both abodes. This verse, according to some narrations, was a cause of his repentance and the goodness of his Islam, by Allah's kindness toward him and generosity. ﴿And if they turn away﴾, i.e., they persist in what they were upon of turning away and withdrawing from sincere faith, or they turn away from repentance.

﴿Allah will punish them with a painful punishment in this world﴾ by the hardships of hypocrisy, bad reputation and the like. It has been said: what is meant by the punishment of this world is the punishment of the grave, or what they witness at death. It has also been said: what is meant is killing and the like, in the sense that they will be killed if they manifest disbelief, based on the view that turning away is the likely occasion of manifestation; this does not contradict what passed, that they are not to be killed, and that fighting against them is not what is most evident.

﴿And the Hereafter﴾, and their punishment therein by the Fire and other forms of retribution. ﴿And they will have no guardian nor helper in the earth﴾, i.e., in this world; the expression is used for generality, i.e., they will have no one in all its regions and all its lands ﴿to save them from the punishment by intercession or defense﴾. The limitation to this world is because they certainly have no guardian nor helper in the Hereafter, so there is no need to negate it there.

* * *

Furthermore, among the allusive (ishari) interpretations in the verses: ﴿Allah pardon you; why did you grant them permission?﴾ etc. In it is an allusion to the exaltedness of his station, peace be upon him, and the elevation of his rank above all beloved ones, in that He granted him pardon before reproach. Had He said to him, "Why did you grant them permission? Allah pardon you," he would have melted. The Exalted expressed it in the past tense, indicating the precedence of selection, so that the waiting would not distress him, peace be upon him, and his noble heart would not be occupied with seeking pardon from the cloud of that abundant promise. And consider how great the difference is between His, glory be to Him, reproach to His beloved, peace be upon him, for granting permission to those hypocrites, and His, exalted be He, response to Noah, peace be upon him, when he said: ﴿Indeed, my son is of my family﴾, with His statement, glory be to Him: ﴿He said, "O Noah, indeed he is not of your family"﴾ up to His statement, blessed and exalted be He: ﴿"I admonish you lest you be among the ignorant."﴾ From this the difference is known, and by my life it is not hidden, between the station of the Beloved and the rank of the chosen one. It has been said: the lover makes excuses for his beloved, and the words of his critic do not diminish him in his sight. And it was recited:

The slanderers have not lowered you from a rank, never; nor has the backbiter harmed you.
As if they praised, while not knowing
what I know of you in what they found fault with.

And another said:

In his face is an intercessor who erases his offense
from hearts, and brings excuses.

And he said:

And when the beloved commits a single sin,
his good qualities come with a thousand intercessors.
Page 141

His statement, glory be to Him: ﴿Those who believe in Allah and the Last Day do not ask your permission﴾ contains an allusion that the believer, when he hears of a good report, flies to it and comes to it, even if walking on his head and hands, and does not open his mouth with a request for permission. Would a thirsty man ask permission to drink water? Al-Wasiti said: the perfect believer is permitted in all his states; if he stands, he stands by permission, and if he sits, he sits by permission. Allah, glory be to Him, has servants by Whom they stand and by Whom they sit, and it is among the qualities of love to comply with the command of the Beloved, however it may be:

If he said, in arrogance, "Stand upon the embers of the ghada tree,"
I would stand complying and not hesitate.

﴿Only those ask your permission who do not believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾, etc., i.e., only the hypocrites ask your permission, hoping that you will not permit them to go out, so that they may rest from the toil of jihad. ﴿And if they had intended to go out, they would have prepared for it some preparation.﴾ It has been said:

If desire from you were sound, you would be guided to stratagems.

(ﷺ) [Original text] ( ﴿But Allah disliked their being sent forth, so He held them back﴾ ) an indication of their abandonment (khidhlan) due to the badness of their preparedness (isti'dad). ﴿Indeed, Hell is surrounding the disbelievers﴾, because bad characteristics and ugly deeds surround them, and these are the very Fire itself. The only difference is that they appear in this created existence in the form of characteristics and deeds, and they will appear in the other existence in another form. His saying, exalted is He: ( ﴿And they do not come to prayer except while they are lazy﴾ ) contains an indication of their deprivation of the delight of the taste of servitude (ubudiyyah), their being veiled from witnessing the beauty of their Worshipped One, and that they did not know that the one who prays is intimately conversing with his Lord, and that prayer is the ascent (mi'raj) of the servant to his Master. For this reason the Prophet, may Allah exalt him and his family and grant them peace, said: "The coolness of my eye has been placed in prayer." Muhammad ibn al-Fadl said: Whoever does not know the Commander stands to the command with the limit of laziness, and whoever knows the Commander stands to the command with the limit of delight and relief. For this reason, "the peace and blessings of Allah be upon him used to say to Bilal: 'Give us rest, O Bilal.'" His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So let not their wealth nor their children impress you﴾ contains a warning to the believers not to find pleasing what is with the people of this world of wealth and adornment, so that they would be veiled by that from the works of the Hereafter and from seeing them. They have mentioned that the one who looks at this world with the eye of approval, through desire, self and passion, falls in that very moment from witnessing the secrets of the Kingdom (malakut) and the lights of the Sovereignty (jabarut). His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And if only they had been content with what Allah and His Messenger gave them﴾ etc. contains guidance to the etiquette of the sincere, the gnostics (arifin) and the seekers (muridin). The sign of the content one is eagerness for what he receives from Allah, exalted is He, and taking delight in trial. So everything the Beloved does is beloved.

A blind, one-handed, paralyzed man was cast on the ground, praising Allah, exalted is He, and thanking Him. He was asked about that, and he said: "By His might and majesty, if He were to cut me into pieces, I would only increase in love for Him." And how excellent is what the one who said it said:

I am content with what you are pleased with,
For you is the favor, whether in pardon or in retribution.

Then He, glorified is He, divided the gifts of His bounty among eight categories of His servants, so He said, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, the charities are only for the poor﴾ etc. The poor (fuqara), according to one opinion, are those who have stripped themselves, in heart and body, from the two worlds. ( ﴿And the needy (masakin)﴾ ) are those who have found tranquility in the beauty of intimacy and the light of holiness, present in servitude with their selves, absent in the lights of lordship with their hearts. Whoever sees them thinks they have no hearts, and he does not know that their hearts are wandering in the gardens of the beauty of the Beloved. And he recited:

The needy among the lovers of passion have lost their hearts,
So they are souls that live without hearts.

( ﴿And the workers (amilin)﴾ ) are the people of firm establishment (tamkin) among the gnostics and the people of steadfastness (istiqamah) among the monotheists, who have entered into the light of permanence, which bequeathed to them expansion and openness. They take from Him, glorified is He, and they give to Him. They are the treasurers of the treasuries of His generosity, spending on His friends. Their hearts are attached to Allah, glorified is He, and not to anything else, from the Throne to the earth. ( ﴿And those whose hearts are to be reconciled (al-mu'allafah qulubuhum)﴾ ) are the aspirants (muridun) traveling the path of His love, exalted is He, with the tenderness of their hearts and the purity of their intentions. They have spent their souls in the market of His longing. In the presence of the strong, they are weak in states. ﴿And for freeing slaves (fi al-riqab)﴾ [p. 142] are those whose hearts have been pledged to the delight of the love of Allah, exalted is He, while their souls remain striving on His path, glorified is He. They have not reached witnessing completely. Sometimes you see them in the depths of the sea of will, and at other times on the shores of the sea of nearness; at times they are targets of the arrows of subjugation, and at other times the place of rising of the lights of kindness. They do not reach the reality as long as some remnant of striving remains upon them. The mukatib (slave under a contract of manumission) is a slave as long as a dirham remains owed on him, and the free are what lies beyond that. But they are few:

I wish of time the impossible:
That my two eyes would see the sight of a free man.

( ﴿And the debtors (al-gharimin)﴾ ) are those who have not fulfilled the rights of their knowledge in servitude and have not attained, in their certainty, the realities of lordship. Gnosis (ma'rifah) is a creditor who never settles its debt. ( ﴿And in the cause of Allah﴾ ) are those who wage war against their own selves through spiritual striving (mujahadat) and who stand guard with their hearts in witnessing the Unseen, to unveil the witnessed things. ( ﴿And the wayfarer (ibn al-sabil)﴾ ) are those who travel with their hearts in the valleys of eternity, with their spirits in the deserts of perpetuity, with their intellects on the paths of the signs, and with their selves in seeking the people of sainthood (awliya'). ﴿An obligation from Allah﴾ upon the people of faith to give these categories from the wealth of Allah, glorified is He, to remove their natural need. ( ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing﴾ ) of the states of these people and their absence from the world. ( ﴿All-Wise﴾ ) in that He made obligatory for them what He made obligatory. Among the people are those who have interpreted these categories otherwise than what has been mentioned, and I do not see that the interpretations in their entirety are capable of encompassing both the collecting and the prevention.

﴿And among them are those who harm the Prophet and say, "He is an ear."﴾ They found fault with him, peace be upon him, and he is far removed from fault, through the soundness of his heart, the swiftness of his acceptance, and his affirmation of what he hears. So Allah, majestic is His glory, confirmed them and responded to them with His saying, glorified is He: ( Say ) he is ﴿an ear of good for you﴾, meaning he is so, but in relation to good. This is from the utmost praise, for the holy, good soul is affected by what suits it. That is, peace be upon him, he hears what benefits you and what contains your welfare, and not otherwise. Then He clarified that with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He believes in Allah﴾ etc. Allah, may He exalt Him, has confused them until they said what they said, and the generosity of the Prophet, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace, deceived them, in that he did not confront them with rejecting what they said, out of mercy toward them. He, peace be upon him, is the vast mercy. It is reported of one of them that he was asked about the intelligent person, and he said: "The clever one who feigns heedlessness." And he recited:

When the generous one you come to with deception,
And you see him hastening toward what you seek,
Know that you did not deceive an ignorant one;
Indeed the generous, in his bounty, is himself deceiving.

﴿The hypocrite men and the hypocrite women are of one another﴾, meaning they are alike in ugliness, baseness and bad preparedness. ﴿They enjoin what is wrong and forbid what is right, and they close their hands﴾, meaning they are stingy, or they hate the believers. This is an indication of the meaning of His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And when they are alone, they bite their fingertips at you out of rage﴾. Or they do not help the believers, or they do not humble themselves before their Lord and raise their hands in supplications. ﴿They forgot Allah﴾ by being veiled through what they are in, so ( He forgot them ) from His mercy and His bounty. ﴿And for them is a lasting punishment﴾, which is the punishment of being veiled by the Lesser. ( ﴿Allah has promised the believing men and believing women gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾ ) These are the gardens of the souls. ﴿And pleasant dwellings﴾ are the stations of the people of trust (tawakkul) in the gardens of actions. ﴿And approval from Allah is greater﴾ is an indication of the gardens of attributes. ( That ) meaning the approval ﴿is the great achievement﴾, because of the honor of its people with Allah, exalted is He, and the intensity of their nearness. There is no harm in keeping the speech on its apparent meaning, and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And pleasant dwellings﴾ may be an indication of the vision (ru'yah), for the lover's abode is not pleasant to him without seeing his beloved:

O our neighbors, how desolate the abode is after you,
When you are absent from it while we are present.

Since approval is the pivot of every good and happiness, and the cause of every honor and lordship, it was greater than [p. 143] those gardens and dwellings.

If you are pleased with me, O wish of my heart,
I see everyone in existence smiling at me.

We ask Allah, exalted is He, for His approval, and that He settle us in His gardens.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 75:

﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah: "If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity and we will surely be among the righteous."﴾ This is an exposition of the foul deeds of another group of the hypocrites (munafiqun). The verse was revealed concerning Tha'labah ibn Hatib, who is also called Ibn Abi Hatib, and he was from the Banu Umayyah ibn Zayd. He was not the Badri (the veteran of Badr), because that one was martyred at Uhud, may Allah be pleased with him.

al-Tabarani, al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il, Ibn al-Mundhir, and others narrated from Abu Umamah al-Bahili, who said: "Tha'labah ibn Hatib came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, pray to Allah that He grant me wealth.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Woe to you, O Tha'labah! Do you not love to be like me? By Him in whose hand my soul is, if I wished that Allah make the mountains of this land run with gold alongside me, they would run.' He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, pray to Allah that He grant me wealth. By the One who sent you with the truth, if Allah, glorified is He, grants me wealth, I will surely give to every person with a right his due.' He said: 'Woe to you, O Tha'labah! A little that you can thank for is better than a lot that you cannot bear.' He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, pray to Allah.' So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'O Allah, grant him wealth.' He acquired sheep, and they were blessed and multiplied as worms multiply, until Medina became too small for him, so he moved away with them. He would attend the prayer by day with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) but not by night. Then they multiplied as worms multiply, and his place became too small for him, so he moved away with them, and he would attend the prayer by day with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) but not by night. Then they multiplied as worms multiply, so he moved away, and he would not attend the prayer, neither by night nor by day, except from Friday to Friday with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Then they multiplied as worms multiply, and his place became too small for him, so he moved away with them, and he would not attend a Friday prayer or a funeral with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He began to meet the riders and ask them for news. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) missed him and asked about him, and they informed him that he had bought sheep and that Medina had become too small for him. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Woe to Tha'labah ibn Hatib! Woe to Tha'labah ibn Hatib!' Then Allah commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to take the charities, and He revealed: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them﴾, the verse. So he sent two men, a man from Juhaynah and a man from Banu Salamah, to collect the charities, and he wrote for them the ages of the camels and sheep and how they should collect them. He commanded them to pass by Tha'labah and a man from Banu Sulaym. They set out and passed by Tha'labah, and they asked him for the charity. He said: 'Show me your letter.' He looked into it and said: 'This is nothing but a jizyah (poll tax). Go on until you are free, then pass by me again.' They went on, and the Sulami heard of them, so he met them with the best of his camels. They said: 'It is only required of you, not this.' He said: 'I would not draw near to Allah except with the best of my wealth.' They accepted it. When they had finished, they passed by Tha'labah, and he said: 'Show me your letter.' He looked into it and said: 'This is nothing but a jizyah. Go on until I consider my opinion.' They went on until they reached Medina. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw them, before he spoke to them, he said: 'Woe to Tha'labah ibn Hatib!' and he prayed for blessing for the Sulami. Then Allah revealed: ﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah﴾, the three verses. Some of his relatives heard of this and came to him and said: 'Woe to you, O Tha'labah! Such and such has been revealed concerning you.' So he came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, this is the charity of my wealth.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed Allah has forbidden me to accept from you.' He began to weep and throw dust upon his head. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'This is your deed by yourself; I commanded you but you did not obey me.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not accept it from him until he passed away. Then he came to Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) and said: 'O Abu Bakr, accept my charity from me, for you know my standing among the Ansar.' Abu Bakr said: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not accept it, and shall I accept it?' So Abu Bakr did not accept it. Then 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) took office, and he came to him and said: 'O Abu Hafs, O Commander of the Faithful, accept my charity.' He said: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not accept it, nor did Abu Bakr; shall I accept it?' He refused to accept it. Then 'Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him) took office, and he did not accept it from him, and he perished during his caliphate."

In some narrations: "This Tha'labah had previously been constantly at the mosque of the Prophet (ﷺ), until he was nicknamed 'the dove of the mosque.' Then the Prophet (ﷺ) saw him hastening out of it after the prayer, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'What is wrong with you that you act like the hypocrites?' He said: 'I have become poor, and my wife and I have only one garment. I come with it for the prayer, then I go and take it off so that she may wear it and pray in it. So pray to Allah that He widen my provision.'" The report continues to its end. Apparently, Allah's prohibiting His Messenger (ﷺ) from accepting from him was by a revelation from Him that he was a hypocrite, and charity is not taken from hypocrites even if they are not killed, due to the absence of outward profession. His throwing of dust was not for repentance from his hypocrisy but out of shame at the non-acceptance of his zakat alongside the Muslims.

The meaning of ﴿this is the recompense of your deed﴾ is: this is the consequence of your deed and of what you said. It is also said that the intended meaning of his "deed" is his request for increased provision, and "this" refers to the withholding, i.e., it is the outcome of your action. It is also said that the intended meaning of "deed" is his not giving to those who give charity. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that Tha'labah came to a gathering of the Ansar and made them witness: "If Allah grants me of His bounty, I will give charity from it and give every person with a right his right." Then his paternal cousin died and he inherited wealth from him, but he did not fulfill what he had covenanted with Allah, so Allah revealed these verses concerning him. Al-Hasan said: they were revealed concerning Tha'labah and Mu'attib ibn Qushayr, who went out to a seated assembly and swore by Allah: "If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity." When He gave them, they became miserly.

al-Sa'ib said: Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah had wealth in Syria, but it was delayed to him, so he was greatly distressed by that and swore by Allah: "If Allah gives us of His bounty, meaning that wealth, we will surely give charity and surely maintain ties of kinship." When that came to him, he did not fulfill what he had covenanted with Allah. This is related from al-Kalbi. The first is more well-known and is the sound account regarding the occasion of revelation. As for "charity," it is said to mean giving obligatory zakat, and what follows it indicates performing the rest of the acts of righteousness such as maintaining ties of kinship and the like. It is also said that "charity" means giving zakat and other charities, and what follows it points to the Hajj, according to what is related from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), or to what encompasses it and spending in jihad, as has been said. It is also recited as (لَنَصَّدَّقَنْ وَلَنَكُونَنْ) with the light nun in both.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 76:

﴿So when He gave them of His bounty, they were stingy with it﴾, i.e., they withheld the right of Allah, exalted is He, from it. ﴿And they turned away﴾, i.e., they turned aside from obedience to Allah, glorified is He, ﴿while they were averse﴾. I.e., they were a people whose habit was to turn away from acts of obedience, so this is not to be denied of them. The clause is either resumed (mustaʾnafah) or circumstantial (ḥāliyyah), and the continuity (istimrar) implied by the past tense (al-tafaddum) does not contradict this. The intended meaning, as has been said, is: they turned away through their wrongdoing (bi-ijramihim), while they were averse in their hearts.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 77:

﴿So He caused them to follow up﴾ i.e., God, exalted is He, made the consequence of their act that (﴿hypocrisy﴾), i.e., bad belief and concealed disbelief, ﴿in their hearts until the Day they meet Him﴾, i.e., God, exalted is He. The intended "Day" is the time of death. Thus the hidden pronoun in a'qaba refers to God, exalted is He, and likewise the object pronoun in (﴿yalqawnahu﴾) refers to Him. The statement contains an elided genitive (muḍāf maḥdhūf), and "hypocrisy" is taken in part of its meaning, whose full sense is showing Islam while concealing disbelief. This is not what is intended, as we have indicated, all of it. Al-Zamakhshari reported from al-Hasan and Qatada that the first pronoun refers to stinginess (bukhl), which is contrary to the apparent meaning. Indeed some verifying scholars said: it is rejected by the words of God, exalted is He: ﴿because they broke to God what they had promised Him and because they used to lie﴾, since saying "stinginess made them follow up with hypocrisy because of their breaking of promise" etc. has no great meaning. And it cannot be conceived, according to what has been said, that hypocrisy be caused by stinginess first and then be caused by two other things without a conjunction.
