Do you not see that if you said: "his knowledge of Zayd moved me to honour him because he is brave and generous," it would be defective, until you say: "his knowledge of Zayd, his bravery and his generosity moved me to honour him."

Al-Imam said: Also, the utmost of stinginess is leaving some obligations, and this does not necessitate the occurrence of hypocrisy, which is disbelief and ignorance in the heart, which is perfected in the case of many sinners. That this particular stinginess causes hypocrisy and disbelief is because of what it contains of not obeying God, exalted is He, and His Messenger, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, and breaking his promise. As it has been said, this does not entail preference but validity, and perhaps it is not denied. Al-Zamakhshari's choice was due to a Mu'tazili inclination, namely that God, exalted is He, does not decree hypocrisy nor create it, on the basis of the principle of good and evil (al-taḥsin wa-l-taqbih). It is also permitted that the object pronoun refers to stinginess too, and the intended "Day" is the Day of Resurrection, and there is an elided genitive, i.e., they meet its recompense, and (﴿ma﴾) is verbal-nominal (maṣdariyya).

The combination of the past and present forms is to indicate continuity, i.e., because of their breaking what they promised God, exalted is He, of charity and righteousness, and because of their being continuously persistent in lying in all their statements, of which their aforementioned promise is one. It has been said: the intended meaning is their lying in what the breaking of promise implies, for a promise, although it is an performative utterance (inshā'), contains a report (khabar), so when it is not fulfilled it is ugly from two aspects: breaking and implicit lying. In this there is consideration, because restricting lying to that makes the combination of the two forms devoid of distinction. The verse includes two of the traits of hypocrites. Al-Shaykhan and others reported from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, that he said: "The sign of the hypocrite is three: when he speaks he lies, when he promises he breaks it, and when he is entrusted he betrays." And from the sound reports another sign of his is derived: "when he disputes he acts wickedly." This was challenged on the ground that these traits may be found in a Muslim about whom there is no doubt and no suspicion touches him; indeed many of our scholars today are characterized by most of them or by all of them. It is answered that the meaning is that these traits are traits of hypocrisy, and their possessor resembles the hypocrites in adopting them. What is meant by the words of the Prophet, prayers and peace be upon him, according to some sound narrations: "Whoever has four in him is a pure hypocrite," is that he was very similar to the hypocrites, not that he was truly a hypocrite.

It has been said: the reports narrated on this topic concern only one in whom those traits predominate, not concerned about them nor regretful for committing them, and such a person may not be far from being a true hypocrite. It has also been said: they concern the hypocrites who lived in his time, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, for they spoke in their oaths and lied, were entrusted with their religion and betrayed, were promised support for the truth and broke it, and disputed and acted wickedly. This is related from Ibn Abbas and Ibn Umar, and it is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, and al-Hasan returned to it after having held the opposite view. Qadi 'Iyad said: most of our imams inclined to it. It has also been said that it concerned a specific man, and it is in the manner of the Prophet's saying, may God's blessings and peace be upon him: "What is the matter with people who do such-and-such," addressed to particular people, whose nobility prevented him, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, from confronting them with explicit speech. Al-Khattabi related from some that the purpose of the reports is to warn the Muslim against habituating himself to these traits, and perhaps this returns to what was answered first. In sum, it is obligatory upon the believer to avoid these traits, for they are in extreme ugliness in the eyes of people of perfection:

Vices which, if distributed among the beautiful women, they would not be dowered except with divorce.

And it was read (﴿yukadhdhibun﴾) with a doubled dhal.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 78:

﴿Did they not know﴾ — i.e., the hypocrites, or those who made a covenant with Allah, the Exalted. It is related from ʿAlī, may Allah ennoble his face, that he read it with the letter tāʾ (ta'lamū, "do you not know"), taking it as an address to the believers. It has also been said that it is addressed to the first group, by way of iltifāt (shift of address), but his words, may He be exalted, ﴿that Allah knows their secret and their private talk﴾ contradict this. Making it a different iltifāt is far-fetched.

The meaning of "secret" (sirr), on the assumption that the pronoun refers to the hypocrites, is what they concealed within themselves of hypocrisy, and "private talk" (najwā) is what they confide to one another of disparagement. On the other assumption, the meaning of the first is the resolve to break the covenant, and of the second, calling zakāh "jizya" (tribute). The mention of "secret" before "private talk" is because knowledge of it is greater, in what is witnessed, than knowledge of the latter; and also because of what its mention first and attaching knowledge to it entails, namely hastening the arousal of awe or joy, according to the difference between the two readings. What will benefit you here as well will come, Allah willing. ﴿And that Allah is the Knower of the unseen⁠﴾ — so nothing among things is hidden from Him, glorified is He. The interrogative hamzah is either for denunciation, reproach and threat, i.e., "Did they not know this, so that they dared to commit the great offences they committed?", or for affirmation and alerting that Allah, glorified is He, will call them to account and recompense them for what He knows of their deeds. The explicit mention of the Majestic Name serves to instil awe and cultivate reverence, or to magnify the matter of accountability and recompense. In the presentation of knowledge concerning their secret and private talk, which are occurrences arising gradually, in the verbal form that denotes occurrence and renewal, and of knowledge concerning the many unseen things, in the nominal form that denotes permanence and intensity, there is a grandeur and majesty that is not hidden.

[Page 147]

﴿Those who find fault﴾ is in the nominative case as the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada', subject): "they are those who." It was also said: "some of them are those who." It was also said: it is a subject whose predicate is (﴿they mock﴾). It is in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "they are those who." It was also said: "some of them are those who." It was also said: it is a subject whose predicate is (﴿they mock﴾), and the fa' (فَ, "so") is there because the relative clause (mawsul) resembles a conditional clause (shart). Or the predicate is ﴿God has mocked them﴾. Or it is in the accusative governed by an omitted verb, meaning "I mean" or "I condemn." Or it is in the genitive by apposition (badaliyya) to the pronoun in (﴿their secret﴾), on the understanding that it refers to the hypocrites in general. It was also read with a ḍammah on the mīm (سِرُّهُمْ, "their secret") and this is lexically as you know, meaning they criticize (﴿the volunteers﴾), that is, those who give voluntarily (al-mutaṭawwi'īn), and what is meant by them is whoever gives voluntarily. ﴿from among the believers﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun. His saying, glorified is He: ﴿in the charities﴾ is related to (they find fault). It is not permissible, as Abu al-Baqa' said, for it to be related to (the volunteers) because of the separation (fasl) it would create. Al-Baghawi in his Mu'jam, and Abu al-Shaykh, reported from al-Ḥasan who said: "The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, stood before the people and said: 'O people, give charity. I will bear witness for you with it on the Day of Resurrection. Does not one of you hope that when he spends the night his young camel is full and his son beside him is hungry? Does not one of you hope that his wealth increases while his neighbour is a poor man who cannot afford anything? Is there not a man who gives a she-camel from his herd, who goes out in the morning with a provision and comes back in the evening with a provision, providing the morning milk for his household and the evening milk for them? Surely its reward is great.' A man stood up and said: 'O Messenger of God, I have camels, I have four head.' Another man stood up, short in stature and ugly in appearance, leading a beautiful, hornless she-camel of his. A man from among the hypocrites said to him a hidden word, thinking that the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, would not hear it: 'Your she-camel is better than him.' The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, heard it and said: 'You lie. He is better than you and better than it.' Then 'Abd al-Raḥmān ibn 'Awf stood up and said: 'O Messenger of God, I have eight thousand. I left four thousand of it for my dependants and I have brought four thousand which I offer to God, exalted is He.' The hypocrites multiplied (their criticism of) what he had brought. Then 'Āṣim ibn 'Adī al-Anṣārī stood up and said: 'O Messenger of God, I have seventy wasq of dates.' The hypocrites multiplied (their criticism of) what he had brought, and they said: 'This one has brought four thousand, and this one has brought seventy wasq, out of showing off and seeking reputation. Why did they not conceal it? Why did they not distribute it?' Then a man of the Anṣār named al-Ḥabḥāb, whose kunya was Abu 'Aqīl, stood up and said: 'O Messenger of God, I have no wealth except that I hired myself out last night to the Banu so-and-so, dragging a yoke on my neck for two ṣā' of dates. I left one ṣā' for my dependants and have brought one ṣā' which I offer to God, exalted is He.' The hypocrites mocked him and said: 'The owners of camels have brought camels, the owners of silver have brought silver, and this one has brought a few dates which he carries.' So God, exalted is He, revealed the verse.'" He did not specify the thousands that 'Abd al-Raḥmān mentioned in this narration. According to what Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Mujāhid, they were dinars, and in another report they were dirhams. Ibn Abi Ḥātim reported from al-Rabī' ibn Anas that "'Abd al-Raḥmān brought four hundred ūqiyya of gold, which was half of what he had, and the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: 'O God, bless him in what he gave and bless him in what he kept.'" It is reported in the narration of al-Ṭabarānī that God blessed him so that one of his two wives was reconciled, in exchange for half of the price, for eighty thousand dirhams. In al-Kashshāf, and al-Ṭībī attributed it to al-Istī'āb, it is said that his wife Tumāḍir was reconciled for a quarter of the price, for eighty thousand. According to the first report he would have two wives, and according to the second he would have four wives. The totals of the two sums differ greatly according to the two reports. In the narration of Ibn Abi Ḥātim from Ibn Zayd, 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may God be pleased with him, was among the volunteers, and he brought a large amount of wealth carrying it, and a man from among the hypocrites said to him: "Do you show off, O 'Umar?" He said: "Yes, I show off to God and His Messenger, may God bless him" and as for others, no.

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and those who find nothing but their effort﴾ is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to (﴿the volunteers﴾), and this is a conjunction of the specific to the general ('aṭf al-khāṣṣ 'alā al-'āmm). It was also said that it is conjoined to (﴿the believers﴾). Al-Ajhūrī objected to this, saying that it gives the impression that the conjoined group is not among the believers.

Abu al-Baqa' said: it is conjoined to (﴿those who find fault﴾). I consider this utter error. The juhd (جُهْدُ, effort), with a ḍammah, means capacity, that is, and they find fault with those who find nothing but their capacity and what their strength reaches, and they are the poor, such as Abu 'Aqīl, whose name was mentioned just before. It is reported from Ibn Isḥāq that his name was Sahl ibn Rāfi'. It is reported from Mujāhid that he explained the relative pronoun as referring to Rifā'a ibn Sa'd. Perhaps the plural is then for honour, and it is possible that it is meant literally, and the mentioned incident is the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzūl). Ibn Hurmuz read (جَهْدَهُمْ, juhdahum) with a fatḥah, and this is one of the two dialectal forms for juhd. The meaning of the ḍammah and the fatḥah is therefore one. It was also said that the fatḥah means hardship and the ḍammah means capacity, as al-Qutaybī said. It was also said that the ḍammah refers to a small amount by which one sustains life, and the fatḥah refers to work.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so they mock them﴾ is conjoined to (﴿they find fault﴾), or it is a predicate, as you know. That is, they ridicule them. What is meant by them, as it has been said, is the last group. ﴿God has mocked them﴾, that is, He requites them for their mockery. The sentence is therefore declarative, and the expression is used by way of correspondence (mushākala). It is not performative (inshā'iyya) as a supplication against them that they become a laughing-stock, because His saying, glorified is His majesty: ﴿and for them is a painful punishment﴾ is a declarative sentence conjoined to it. If it were a supplication, it would follow that a declarative sentence was conjoined to a performative one, and there is discussion about that. They differ in being verbal and nominal only because the mockery is in this world and is continuous and renewed, while the punishment is in the Hereafter and is lasting and fixed. The tanwīn (تَنْوِينُ, nunation) in (عَذَابٌ, punishment) is for magnification (tahwīl) and exaltation (tafkhīm).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 80 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Ask forgiveness for them, or do not ask forgiveness for them﴾. The apparent meaning is that what is intended by this and similar expressions is takhyir (choice). What confirms that it is intended here is that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ understood it so, as you will learn, God willing. It is as if He, glory be to Him, said to him, peace and blessings be upon him: "If you wish, ask forgiveness for them, and if you wish, do not." The words of al-Nasafi are blown away (tanfusuhu) by the soundness of the reports, a complete blowing away. Others have chosen that what is meant is taswiyah (equalization) between the two matters, as in the words of God Most High: ﴿Spend, willingly or unwillingly﴾, and the verse that has passed: "Treat me harshly or treat me kindly, etc." The purpose is to inform that there is no benefit in that, and there is in it what there is of exaggeration. Some of the muhaqqiqun (verifiers), after choosing taswiyah in such cases, said: it does not contradict takhyir; if it is established, then it is by way of iqtida' (implication), since it falls between two opposites neither of which is permissible to leave or to do, so one of the two must be. The situation varies: sometimes affirmation is the case, as in the words of God Most High: ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe﴾, and at other times negation, as here and in His words, glory be to Him: ﴿It is the same for them whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them﴾, and ﴿Even if you ask forgiveness for them seventy times, Allah will never forgive them﴾, which is an explanation of the absence of forgiveness, even if he asks forgiveness for them, as is intended after the takhyir, or an explanation of the impossibility of forgiveness after exaggeration in seeking forgiveness, following the explanation of equality between asking forgiveness and not asking.
Page 148
As for the occasion of revelation, according to what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them: when the words of God, glory be to Him, ﴿Allah has mocked them﴾ were revealed, etc., those who mocked asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to ask forgiveness for them, so he resolved to do so, and then it was revealed, so he did not do it. It was said: it was revealed after he had done it. Al-Imam (al-Razi) chose that it did not happen, and said: it is not permissible to ask forgiveness for an unbeliever, so how could it proceed from him, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace? It was refuted that it is permissible for their living ones, in the sense of seeking the cause of forgiveness. And the claim that asking forgiveness for one who persists is of no benefit does not hold, because there is no certainty that it is of no benefit unless it is revealed to him, peace and blessings be upon him, that he will not believe, like Abu Lahab. And the claim that asking forgiveness for a hypocrite is an incitement to him to hypocrisy does not hold, since he has no hypocrisy at all; otherwise asking forgiveness for sinful believers would be forbidden, and no one holds that. Some said: on the assumption that asking forgiveness did occur from him, peace and blessings be upon him, and the claim that the prohibition indicated by the words of God Most High ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists﴾ was advanced has no problem, since the prohibition is not for prohibition but to explain the absence of benefit. This is a feeble statement, because the most that the verse indicates is a prohibition on asking forgiveness for unbelievers, and this does not require a prohibition on asking forgiveness for one whose apparent state is Islam. And the claim that since he was not answered it would be a deficiency in the station of prophethood is disputed, because, peace and blessings be upon him, his supplication may not be answered for a wisdom, just as the supplication of some of his brother prophets, peace be upon them, was not answered, and this is not counted as a deficiency, as is not hidden. The connection of the verse with what precedes it according to this narration is most clear. However, it has been said: the sound report relied upon in this matter is that 'Abd Allah, whose name was al-Hubab and who was among the sincere, the son of 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ during his father's illness to ask forgiveness for him, and he did so, and then it was revealed, and he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "I will surely add to the seventy," and then it was revealed: ﴿It is the same for them whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them﴾, etc. In this is also a refutation of al-Imam in his choice of not asking forgiveness, and likewise in his denial that the concept of number is a proof, as al-Asnawi related from him in al-Tamhid, differing in this from al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, for he holds it to be a proof, as al-Ghazali related from him in al-Mankhul, and his teacher Imam al-Haramayn in al-Burhan, and he stated that this is the view of the majority.
In al-Matlab of Ibn al-Rif'ah: the concept of number is the principal basis for us in not reducing the stones in istinja' to three, and in not extending the period of khiyar beyond three days. What is related from al-Nawawi, that the concept of number is invalid according to the usulis, is to be understood as meaning invalid according to a group of usulis, as his statement in his Sharh Muslim in the "Chapter on Funerals" indicates; otherwise it would be strange of him.
The words of al-'Allamah al-Baydawi are inconsistent. In al-Minhaj, specification by a number does not indicate the excess or deficiency, i.e., it is a text in its meaning that does not admit increase or decrease. In his commentary, at this verse, after citing the report of the occasion of revelation, he said that the Messenger ﷺ understood from "seventy" the specific number, because it is the origin, so it is permissible that this be a limit whose judgment differs from what lies beyond it; so he, peace and blessings be upon him, made clear that what is intended by it is multiplication, not limitation. It was also mentioned in the commentary of Surah al-Baqarah, at the words of God, glory be to Him: ﴿Then He completed them as seven heavens﴾, that the verse does not negate more, and that the intention of multiplicity by seventy is common in their speech, and likewise by seven and seven hundred. In Sharh al-Masabih, this is explained by the fact that seven includes all the kinds of number: it is divided into odd and even, and each of these into first and composite. The first odd is three, the composite odd is five, the first even is two, and the composite even is four. It is also divided into mantiq (rational/ having a proper fraction) such as four, and asamm (irrational/ without one) such as six; seven includes all these kinds. Then, if exaggeration is intended, its units are made tens and its tens hundreds, and by the first odd is meant that which is not preceded by another numerical odd, like three, since one is not a number according to the view that it is what equals half the sum of its two correct margins; and by the composite odd is meant that which is preceded by another odd, as five is preceded by three; and by the first even is meant that not preceded by another even, like two; and by the composite is meant that which is preceded by it, like four preceded by two. The number may also be divided at the outset into first and composite, where the first is what only one divides, like three, five and seven, and the composite is what a number other than one divides, like four, which two divides, and nine, which three divides. The term mantiq has two usages: it is used to mean what has a proper fraction among the nine fractions, and its opposite asamm is what does not have this, like eleven; and it is used to mean the squared (majdhur), which is what results from multiplying a number by itself, like four resulting from two multiplied by itself, and nine resulting from three multiplied by itself, and its opposite asamm is what is not so, like two and three. This is the intention of the commentator of al-Masabih, in that he illustrated asamm by six, although six has a proper fraction, indeed two fractions, half and a sixth, but it does not result from multiplying a number by itself. The meaning of seven's inclusion of these kinds is that when the first odd is added to the composite even, or the composite odd to the first even, the sum is seven; and likewise when the mantiq, like four, is added to the asamm, like three, the sum is seven. This property does not occur in any number before seven. Thus whoever thinks that the more fitting, by consideration of this inclusion, is six and not seven, because six is the one that includes what has been mentioned, has not grasped the meaning of inclusion, or has not known these technical terms, since they belong to the science of arithmetic.
What we have mentioned about the meaning of inclusion also dispels what may be imagined, namely that the verified view is that every composite number is composed of units, not of the numbers beneath it, since the intended sense of inclusion is not composition. In this verified view there is a discussion mentioned in its proper place.
Ibn 'Isa al-Rab'i said: seven is the most perfect of numbers, because six is the first perfect number, and with one it makes seven, so it was perfect, since after perfection there is only completeness; for this reason the lion was called sab' (seven) for the completeness of its strength. He defined a perfect number as that which equals the sum of its fractions. That six is such is evident: its fractions are a sixth, which is one, a third, which is two, and a half, which is three, and their sum is six. But it was deemed unlikely that the one most eloquent of men and most knowledgeable of the tongue, Allah bless him and grant him peace, would not understand the intention of multiplicity from "seventy" here. For this reason some said: the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was not unaware of that, but he made the statement as an imagining, to display the utmost of his compassion and mercy toward those sent to him, like the words of Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿Whoever disobeys me, then You are Forgiving, Merciful﴾. That is, he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, created in the hearer's imagination that he understood the specific number and not multiplicity, so he permitted an answer with an increase, intending to display kindness and mercy, just as Abraham, peace be upon him, made the recompense for whoever disobeyed him, that is, did not comply with the command to abandon idol worship, the words "then You are Forgiving, Merciful" rather than, for example, "You are severe in punishment." Thus it was imagined that He, glory be to Him, would show mercy to them and forgive them, out of compassion for them and to urge them to follow. It was objected that mentioning this as an embellishment and imagining, after he, peace and blessings be upon him, had understood multiplicity from it, is not fitting for his lofty station; and understanding the real meaning of a word whose figurative sense has become famous does not contradict eloquence and knowledge of the tongue, for there is no error in it and no remoteness, since it is the origin. Preferred over this, in his view, peace and blessings be upon him, was his eagerness for their guidance, his compassion for them, and his wish to win over others; and perhaps this is better than saying there is embellishment without embellishment. Imam al-Haramayn denied the soundness of what indicates that he, peace and blessings be upon him, understood that the judgment beyond seventy is contrary to it, and this is strange from him, for this has come through the narrations of al-Bukhari, Muslim, Ibn Majah and al-Nasa'i, and these suffice. The statement of al-Tabarsi, that the report "I will surely add" etc. is a single report on which one cannot rely, is not to be relied upon; he held to this by what is like the sun's halo, and it is, for those who hold the concept of number, like the mountains of the moon. Those who deny it replied by denying that this is understood, because the mention of seventy is for exaggeration, and what exceeds it is similar to it in the judgment, which is the immediate absence of forgiveness; so how is contrariety understood from it? Perhaps he, peace and blessings be upon him, knew that it was not intended specifically here. Granting that, we do not grant that it is understood from it; and perhaps he remained upon the original permissibility, for if he had not addressed it with negation or affirmation, and the origin is the permissibility of asking forgiveness for the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and its being a likely occasion for answer, it would be understood from the standpoint that it is the origin, not from the specification by mention. The sum of the first is that it is understood from it absolutely; rather it is understood only from external evidence. The sum of the second is conceding that it is understood from it in a general way, but not by way of the concept, rather from the standpoint of the origin.

You know that the apparent sense of the report, according to those who hold the doctrine of mafhum (the implied meaning drawn from the converse of a statement), is this: Allah, glorified is He, informed His Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace, through the verse about the hypocrites, that the number here is meant as a multiplicity and not as a fixed limit. Thus the ruling for what exceeds the number is contrary to the ruling for what is mentioned. Accordingly, the meaning of the two verses with Allah, exalted is He, is one thing, namely that forgiveness is denied to them absolutely. However, there is a difficulty in the claim that the verse about the hypocrites was revealed after this verse. As for the view that Bara'a (Surat al-Tawbah) was the last thing revealed, the matter is clear. But as for the view that most of it, or its beginning, was revealed in that order, then there is no obstacle to some of its verses being revealed after some verses of other surahs. Yet the beginning of what is in Surat al-Munafiqun requires that it was revealed concerning an incident other than the one that has just preceded. The apparent sense of the reports, as you will learn, God willing, indicates that it was revealed concerning Ibn Ubayy when he was not ill. What has preceded regarding the occasion of revelation of what is here is explicit that it was revealed while he was ill. The claim that the former was revealed twice requires transmission and cannot be supported by opinion alone, and how could it be? Moreover, on that assumption, the saying of the Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace, "I will increase beyond seventy," becomes problematic, given that the verse clarifying its intended meaning was revealed earlier. The claim of inattention I consider to arise only from inattention to the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿We shall make you recite, so you will not forget﴾. Rather, it arises from ignorance of his lofty station, upon him be prayer and peace, and of his great care for the words of his Lord, glorified is He. I have not seen anyone address the resolution of this difficulty, and there is no way to resolve it except by denying that what is in Surat al-Munafiqun was revealed concerning another incident, and by denying that its beginning indicates that. Yes, they mentioned that the beginning was revealed concerning Ibn Ubayy when he was not ill at that time. However, we have not found an explicit report that the latter part was revealed concerning him in the same way. Apparently, it was revealed after His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And do not pray over any of them﴾ etc. What supports this will come, God willing, when interpreting the verse, so understand.

( ﴿That﴾ ) i.e., the denial of forgiveness for them, even after that seeking of forgiveness. ( ﴿Because they﴾ ) i.e., because they ﴿disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger﴾. Meaning: the refusal is not due to disregarding your seeking forgiveness, but due to their lack of readiness, because they disbelieved with a disbelief that exceeds all bounds, as indicated by describing them with fisq (defiance) in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And Allah does not guide the defiant people﴾. Fisq in everything is an expression for rebellion and transgressing its limits. The guidance meant is guidance that leads to the destination, not mere indication of the path, since that was indeed given, but they did not accept it because of their poor choice. The sentence is a concluding affirmation of the ruling preceding it, for the forgiveness of disbelievers comes through giving up disbelief and turning to the truth, while one who is immersed in it and sealed upon it is far from that. This contains an indication of the excuse of the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, in seeking forgiveness for them, namely that he had not despaired of their faith, since at that time he did not know that they were sealed in error, that treatment would not benefit them and guidance would not profit them. What is prohibited is seeking forgiveness after knowing that they died as disbelievers, as His saying, glorified is He, testifies: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to seek forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they were of near kin, after it has become clear to them that they are companions of the Blazing Fire﴾. Perhaps the revelation of His saying, glorified is He, ( ﴿Because they﴾ ) etc. was delayed relative to the revelation of His saying, ﴿Seek forgiveness for them﴾ etc., as has been said; otherwise he, upon him be prayer and peace, would have had no excuse for seeking forgiveness after the revelation.

The view that this excuse is valid only if the seeking of forgiveness was for a living person, as was mentioned earlier from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, is open to scrutiny.

[Page 151]

﴿Those who were left behind rejoiced﴾, i.e., those whom the Prophet ﷺ left behind and whom he permitted to stay back, or whom Allah the Exalted left behind by discouraging them for a wisdom known to Him, or whom Satan left behind by his incitement, or whom indolence and hypocrisy left behind. (﴿Over their sitting [behind]﴾) is connected to "rejoiced." It is a verbal noun of the mīmī type (maṣdar mīmī, a verbal noun beginning with the letter mīm) meaning "sitting." It was also said to be a noun of place, and the intended meaning would then be Madinah. Most scholars hold the first view, i.e., they rejoiced at their sitting back from the raid. ﴿Contrary to the Messenger of Allah﴾, i.e., behind him, peace be upon him, after his departure, since he went out and they did not. It is in the accusative as an adverb (ẓarf) meaning "after" and "behind," and the Arabs have used it in this way. The governing element is, as Abu al-Baqa' said, "sitting" (maqʿad). It was also permitted that the governing element be "rejoiced." It was also said that it means opposition, so it is a verbal noun of "to oppose," like "fighting." In that case, it may be a circumstantial qualifier, meaning "opposing the Messenger of Allah ﷺ," or an object of purpose (mafʿūl lahu). The governing element is either "rejoiced," i.e., they rejoiced because of their opposition to him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, by sitting back; or "over their sitting [behind]," i.e., they rejoiced at their sitting back because of opposition. The opposition is taken as the cause, on the basis that their intention in this was their hypocrisy. There is no need to say that their intention was rest; rather, when their situation came to that, it was made a cause, as they said regarding the lam of consequence (lām al-ʿāqibah). It was also permitted that it be in the accusative as a verbal noun governed by a verb indicated by the context.

﴿And they disliked striving with their wealth and their lives in the way of Allah﴾, preferring ease and luxury with food and drink, together with what was in their hearts of disbelief and hypocrisy. Between "rejoiced" and "disliked" there is a semantic antithesis, because one rejoices at what is loved.

The choice of this wording over saying "and they disliked going out with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ" is an indication that striving in the way of Allah the Exalted, although it is among the most noble desirable things that competitors should compete for, is something they disliked, just as they rejoiced at the worst of ugly deeds, namely sitting back contrary to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The statement contains an allusion to the believers who preferred that and loved it, seeking the pleasure of Allah the Exalted and His Messenger.

﴿And they said﴾, i.e., to their brethren, to make them firm in sitting back and to counsel one another toward corruption; or to the believers, to discourage them from striving, to forbid them what is good, and to show some of the pretexts that prompted them to what they rejoiced at. The speakers were men of the hypocrites, as was narrated from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, and this is what the apparent meaning requires.

Ibn Jarir reported from Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi that the speaker was a man from Banu Salima. The reference of the plural pronoun according to this view is understood from what has passed more than once. ﴿Do not march out﴾, i.e., do not go out to the raid, ﴿in the heat﴾, for its intensity cannot be endured. (Say) O Muhammad, in reply to them and to show their ignorance: ﴿The Fire of Hell﴾, which is your destination because of what you have done, ﴿is hotter﴾ than this heat which you see as preventing marching out. So what is wrong with you that you do not beware of it, and expose yourselves to it by preferring sitting back and opposing Allah the Exalted and His Messenger, peace be upon him? ﴿If only they understood﴾. This is a concluding remark from Him, the Exalted, not part of the statement commanded to be spoken; it confirms its content. The answer to "if only" (law) is omitted, and so is the object of ﴿understand﴾, i.e., if only they knew that it is so, or its conditions and terrors, or that their return is to it, when they preferred the ease of a short time over the punishment of eternity. The most ignorant of people is one who protects himself from a small trifle while exposing himself to a great calamity. Al-Zamakhshari quoted the following for the son of his maternal aunt:

A pleasure lasting for ages, after which I met
A day of grief showing its bitterness like aloes.

So how then will you meet the pleasure of an hour
Whose aftermath is the grief of ages?

Some scholars estimated the answer to be: "they would have been affected by this rebuke," but this is contrary to the apparent meaning. It was also permitted that "if only" be merely expressive of wishing, indicating the impossibility of what follows it, and that the transitive verb be treated as intransitive, so there is no answer and no object. The meaning then reverts to the sense that they were not among the people of discernment and understanding. The statement would then be similar to His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Say: Look at what is in the heavens and the earth; but signs and warnings do not avail a people who do not believe﴾. This too is contrary to the apparent meaning.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 82:**

﴿So let them laugh little and let them weep much.﴾ This is a report of their immediate and eventual state: little laughter in this world and much weeping in the Hereafter. It is expressed in the form of a command to show that what is reported is certain to occur. This is because the imperative form is, in its primary and most common use, for obligation, so it is used to signify the necessary consequence of its meaning. Alternatively, it is because the imperative does not admit of truth and falsehood the way a report does. This is how al-Shihab (al-Khafaji) settled it. He then said: If you say, "Obligation does not entail existence, and they have said that a command is expressed as a report for emphasis, since a report implies the realisation of what is commanded. So the report is more emphatic, and a similar case has already passed. Why then is it reversed?" I say: there is no contradiction between them, as has been said, because every situation has its own mode of speech, and the subtle points do not clash. When the command is expressed as a report, it conveys that the one commanded, due to the intensity of his compliance, has as it were already done it and realised it before the command, and this is more eloquent. When the report is expressed as a command, it conveys its necessity and obligation, as if it were something commanded, and this conveys emphasis from another angle. It has also been said that the command here is a creative command (takwini), as in His saying: ﴿When He intends a thing, He only says to it, "Be," and it is.﴾ But what is wrong with this is not hidden.

The fa' (so) indicates that what precedes is the cause of the report about the laughing and weeping that is mentioned. It is not that the laughing and weeping are themselves the cause, since the first (laughing) cannot be conceived of at all in that way. To make that the cause of the combination of the two matters is far-fetched. Qalilan (little) and kathiran (much) are in the accusative, either as a verbal noun (maf'ul mutlaq, object of the cognate type) or as an adverb of time (zarf). The meaning is: laughter that is little, or a little time; and weeping that is much, or a long time. The purpose of the first (little) in its expression, according to what has been said, is the attribute of paucity alone, while the purpose of the second (much) is the attribute of abundance together with what it qualifies. It is related that the hypocrites will weep in the Fire throughout the lifetime of the world, their tears never drying up, and they will not enjoy sleep.

It is also permissible that laughing is a metonymy (kinayah) for joy and weeping is a metonymy for grief. The first is in this world and the second is in the Hereafter as well. The "little" is in its ordinary sense, and there is no need to take it to mean non-existence, just as "much" was taken to mean perpetuity. Indeed, if each of the two matters is considered in the Hereafter, we would need this interpretation, since there is no joy at all for them there. It is understood from the words of Ibn 'Atiyyah that weeping and laughing are in this world, as in the hadith related by the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and others: "If you knew what I know, you would laugh little and weep much." That is, they have reached such a state of evil and such danger with Allah, the Exalted, that their laughter should be little and their weeping on account of it should be much.

﴿As recompense for what they used to earn.﴾ That is: for the various kinds of sins. The combination of the two forms, the past and the future, is to indicate continuous renewal. "Jaza'an" (as recompense) is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu) for the second verb. You may also make it an object of purpose for both verbs, or a verbal noun from the passive construction with its governing verb omitted, meaning: they will be recompensed with what has been mentioned of much weeping, or with it and with little laughter, as a recompense for what they persisted in of sins.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 83:**

﴿So if Allah returns you﴾: that is, from your journey. The fa' (the "so") introduces the command that follows, based on what has been explained about their situation. "Raja'a" (returned) here is transitive (muta'addi, taking an object), meaning "radda" (sent back), and its verbal noun is al-ratj'. It can also be intransitive (lazim, not taking an object), with the verbal noun al-ruju'. The transitive form was preferred, although the intransitive is more common in usage, to indicate that this journey, because of the danger it involved, needed a return from it by divine support. For this reason the word "in" (if) was used rather than "idha" (when). That is, "if Allah, glorified is He, sends you back" ﴿to a group of them﴾: that is, to the hypocrites among those who stayed behind, on the basis that some of them were not hypocrites; or to those of the hypocrites who remained behind, some of whom had gone away, either by death, by being absent from the town, or because some of them had not asked your permission. It has been said that the intended group is those of the hypocrites who remained upon their hypocrisy and did not repent, but this is not the right view.

Ibn al-Mundhir and others related from Qatadah that he said regarding the verse: "It was mentioned to us that they were twelve men from among the hypocrites, and about them was said what was said."

﴿Then they will ask your permission to go out﴾ with you to another military campaign after this campaign of yours, from which Allah returned you with His support. ﴿Then say﴾ to them, as a complete form of humiliation: ﴿"You will never go out with me, ever"﴾, for as long as I and you remain (as we are). ﴿And you will never fight with me against any enemy﴾ from among the enemies. This is an informative statement carrying the meaning of a prohibition, for the sake of emphasis.

Mention of fighting, as some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqin) said, is because it is the purpose of going out. Had he mentioned only one of the two, it would have sufficed in excluding them from the status of companionship and the status of holy struggle (jihad), or from the registers of the warriors and the register of the mujahidin, and in showing dislike for their company and that the army has no need of them. Or the second was mentioned for emphasis, because it is clearer in meaning, while the first was mentioned to correspond to the question. A parallel to this is the verse of poetry:

"I say to him: depart, do not let yourself remain with us,
for the second is more indicative of dislike."

﴿Indeed, you were pleased with sitting﴾ (staying behind) away from going out with me, and you rejoiced in it ﴿the first time﴾, that is, of going out. So the superlative (af'al) in the construct phrase was put in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar). It has been said that it is in the accusative as a temporal adverb (zarf zamani), but Abu Hayyan considered this unlikely. The apparent view is that this difference is due to a difference over the word "marrah" (time/occasion). It is transmitted from Abu al-Baqa' that it was originally a verbal noun from "marra yamurru," and then it came to be used as an adverb. Al-Qadi al-Baydawi, may God illuminate the brightness of his circumstances, preferred the accusative as a verbal noun, and he pointed to the feminine gender of the qualified noun when he said: "And the first time is the going out to the campaign of Tabuk." He mentioned the superlative (af'al) because masculine forms are more common in such usage. In al-Kashshaf it is stated that "marrah" is indefinite, placed in the position of the plural "marrat" for the purpose of the superlative, and the superlative mentioned with it indicates one of the occasions, because the most common of the two forms is: "Hind is the greatest of women," and she is their greatest. And it is said: "She is the greatest woman, the first occasion and the last occasion." In al-Kashf the failure to find a parallel of the type "she is the greatest woman" is explained by the fact that the superlative in it is joined to a non-superlative standard of comparison, but rather to a countable plurality in which it is contained, as an explanation of it, so it is as if it were said: "She is a woman greater than each one of the women." In a construction like this the superlative does not vary. So the verification is that it is not similar to what contains the definite article (al-), but rather the agreement is between the described noun and what is annexed to it, and there is no place for its agreement in form and meaning. So reflect upon this.

The clause is in the position of a causal explanation of what preceded it, so it is a resumed clause of explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani), that is, "because you were pleased." ﴿So sit with those who stay behind﴾, that is, those who are left behind because of their unfitness, like women, children, and the men who are incapable. The masculine plural form was used by way of predominance (taghlib). Ibn Abbas limited it to the last category. Interpreting "khalif" as "mutakhallif" (one who stays behind) is what is transmitted from most of the early exegetes. It has been said that it derives from "khalafa" meaning "fasada" (to spoil or decay), and from it comes "khuluf al-fam" of the fasting person, due to the change of its smell.

The adverbial phrase ("with") is connected either to what precedes it, or to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the plural pronoun. The fa' (the "so") introduces the command to sit as a consequence, by way of punishment, for what came from them of being pleased with sitting. That is: if you were pleased with sitting the first time, then sit from now on.

Ikrimah read "al-khalifin" with the pattern of "hadhirin." Perhaps it is an adjective of the form al-sifa al-mushabbaha (the resembling adjective) like it. It has been said that it is a shortened form of "al-khalifin," since its use in that way is not established, apart from being a resembling adjective.

﴿And do not pray over any of them who has died, ever﴾: an indication of their humiliation after death.

Al-Bukhari reported from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, who said: "When Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul died, his son Abdullah ibn Abdullah came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and asked him to give him his shirt so that he could shroud his father in it. He gave it to him. Then he asked him to pray over him. [p. 154] The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood up to pray over him, but Umar stood up, took hold of the garment of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, will you pray over him when your Lord has forbidden you to pray over him?!' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Allah only gave me a choice when He said: ﴿Ask forgiveness for them, or do not ask forgiveness for them. Even if you ask forgiveness for them seventy times﴾, and I will add to the seventy.' He said: 'He is a hypocrite.' So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed over him, and then Allah, glorified is He, revealed: ﴿And do not pray over any of them﴾ to the end of the verse."

In another narration of his, from Ibn Abbas, from Umar ibn al-Khattab: "When Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul died, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was called to pray over him. When he stood up and went towards him, I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, will you pray over Ibn Ubayy when he said on such-and-such a day such-and-such things?' I listed his words. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) smiled and said: 'Step back from me, O Umar.' When I persisted, he said: 'Step back from me. Had I known that if I added to the seventy he would be forgiven, I would have added to them.' He then prayed over him and departed. He did not remain long before the two verses from Bara'ah were revealed: ﴿And do not pray over any of them﴾ up to His saying: ﴿and they are defiant﴾. So I was amazed at my boldness towards the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)."

The apparent meaning of these two reports is that the verse ﴿Ask forgiveness for them, or do not ask forgiveness for them﴾ and His saying: ﴿And do not pray over any of them﴾ were not revealed in between, since nothing in these reports benefits Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, otherwise it would have been mentioned. The apparent meaning is that by the prohibition in the first report he meant what he understood from the first verse, not what is understood from His saying: ﴿The Prophet and those who believe are not to ask forgiveness for the polytheists﴾, as has been said, because the answer would not then correspond, as is not hidden.

Abu Ya'la and others reported from Anas that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wished to pray over Ibn Ubayy, but Jibril (peace be upon him) took hold of his garment and said: ﴿And do not pray﴾, the verse." Most of the reports say that he (ﷺ) did pray over him, and that Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, preferred that he not pray over him, and this is counted as one of his agreements with revelation. The Messenger (ﷺ) did not forbid the shrouding in his shirt, but he forbade praying over him, because being stingy with a shirt would be a likely cause of falling short in generosity. Moreover, it was a repayment for the shirt that he had put on al-Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, when he was taken captive at Badr, for he was brought in without any garment on, and he was tall and large, so there was no garment of a size fitting his height except the garment of Ibn Ubayy, and so he clothed him in it.

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Qatadah that "they mentioned the shirt after the revelation of the verse, and the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'What good is my shirt to him? By Allah, I hope that more than a thousand of the Banu al-Khazraj will become Muslim through it.'" Allah has fulfilled the hope of His Prophet, as is found in some reports and narrations. As for what happened between the Prophet (peace be upon him) and Ibn Ubayy regarding praying over him and other matters, the reports are not free of contradiction. Scholars of hadith have reconciled them as far as possible, and there is a summary of this in Lubab al-Ta'wil, so let it be consulted.

The praying that is forbidden is the well-known funeral prayer over the dead, which includes supplication, asking forgiveness, and seeking intercession on his behalf. It has been said that the prohibition on it is because of his (peace be upon him) prohibition from supplicating for the hypocrites, which is understood from the preceding verse, or from His saying, glorified is He: ﴿The Prophet is not...﴾, and so on. It has been said that here "praying" means supplication, but this is not the right view. The word "ever" (abadan) is an adverbial of time related to the prohibition. It has been said that it is related to "died", and that the eternal death is a metaphor for dying in disbelief, because the Muslim is raised and lives a good life, while the disbeliever, though he is raised, is raised for punishment, so it is as if he has not lived. Some people claimed that if it were related to the prohibition it would follow that prayer would not be permitted over those among them who repent and die in faith; but there is no need for the prohibition on praying over them to be restricted by the qualifier of eternity. It is not hidden that he erred and was unaware that "of them" (minhum) is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the pronoun in "died", meaning: he died while being of them, that is, characterised by their attribute, which is hypocrisy, like their saying: "You are of me", meaning: on my path and my attribute, as they have stated explicitly. Moreover, if the prepositional phrase were made a qualifier of "anyone", what he mentioned would hardly be imagined; and how could it be imagined, given His later saying: ﴿Indeed they disbelieved﴾, and so on? And his saying: "there is no need for the prohibition..." and so on, is because what is in it is evident, so there is no need to mention it. "Died" is in the past tense in view of the occasion of revelation and the time of the prohibition, and this does not conflict with its generality and inclusion of those who will die. It has been said that it is in the sense of the future, and it was expressed in this form to indicate its certainty; and the clause is in the position of a qualifier of "anyone".

﴿And do not stand over his grave﴾: that is, do not stand over it, and do not take charge of his burial. This is from their saying: "So-and-so stood over so-and-so's affair" when he took care of it for him and acted on his behalf in it. It is understood from the words of some of them that "over" (ʿala) means "at" (ʿinda), and the meaning is: do not stand at his grave for burial or for visiting. The grave, in the commonly accepted usage, is the burial place of the dead, and it may also mean the burial itself, and they permitted that meaning here too.

In the fatawa of Jalal al-Suyuti: "Is standing here to be interpreted as visiting graves? And can it be used as evidence that the wisdom in the Prophet's (ﷺ) visiting the grave of his mother was her revival so that she might believe in him, given that the date of the visit was after the prohibition?"

The answer: By standing over the grave is meant standing over it at the time of burial and for an hour after it. It is possible that it also includes visiting, on the basis of the general wording. The date of the visit was before the prohibition, not after it, for what is established in the hadiths is that he (ﷺ) visited her in the year of al-Hudaybiyah, while the verse was revealed after the Battle of Tabuk. Then, the pronoun in "of them" is specific to the hypocrites, although the rest of the polytheists are analogically included with them. It is established in the hadith of the visit that he asked his Lord for permission to do so, and He granted it to him. In my opinion, this permission is used as evidence that she was among the monotheists, not among the polytheists, as is my own view. The basis for this evidence is that he forbade him to stand over the graves of the disbelievers and permitted him to stand over the grave of his mother, which indicates that she was not among them; otherwise he would not have permitted him to do so. The possibility of specification is contrary to the apparent meaning and requires clear evidence. Perhaps the Prophet (peace be upon him) had some hesitation about the validity of the monotheism of those who lived in the pre-Islamic period, until he was informed by revelation (ﷺ) of the validity of that. So it cannot be objected that his asking permission indicates otherwise, for otherwise he would have visited her without asking permission. End quote.

As for whether the meaning of standing over the grave is standing over it at the time of burial and for an hour after it, there is some obscurity, since what is understood from "standing over a grave" is something more general than that. Indeed, standing after burial for the length of time it takes to slaughter a camel was recommended, and perhaps because this was widespread at that time, it came to be understood by the phrase "standing over the grave".

There is a difference of opinion regarding the permissibility of visiting the graves of disbelievers. Many of those who hold that it is impermissible understood "standing" to mean something that includes visiting. Those who permit it cite the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "I had forbidden you to visit graves, so visit them, for they remind you of the Hereafter." He (ﷺ) gave the reason for visiting as reminding of the Hereafter, and there is no difference in this between visiting the graves of Muslims and those of others. The full discussion is in its proper place. My own caution is not to visit the graves of disbelievers.

﴿Indeed they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger﴾: this is a new sentence, brought to give the reason for the prohibition, meaning that praying over the dead and honouring him is only for his sanctity, and they are far from that, because they persisted in disbelief in Allah, the Exalted, and His Messenger (ﷺ) throughout their lives. ﴿And they died while they were defiant﴾: that is, rebellious in disbelief, going beyond its limits.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 85:

﴿Let not their wealth nor their children impress you. Allah only intends to punish them with them in this world, and that their souls depart while they are disbelievers.﴾ This is an emphasis on what preceded its counterpart, and the matter truly calls for this because of the widespread trial of loving what has been mentioned and being impressed by it. Al-Farisi said: what preceded concerns one group and this concerns others, so there is no emphasis. The conjunction "wa" (and) is used here to match the coordination of a prohibition with a prohibition before it, namely His, glory be to Him, saying: ﴿And do not pray﴾ etc., while "fa" (so) is used there to match the sense of consequence to His, exalted is He, saying before it: ﴿And they do not spend except while they are averse﴾. Its meaning is: they do not spend except while they are averse to giving, so they are impressed by the abundance of wealth and children, and He forbade the impression that follows from it.

Page 156

It has also been said: here it is "﴿wa-awladuhum﴾" without "la" (no), because He forbade being impressed by them together; and there it is with the addition of "la" because He forbade each one individually. The two verses together thus indicate the prohibition of being impressed by them both together and separately. Here it is "﴿an yu'adhdhibahum﴾" and there "﴿li-yu'adhdhibahum﴾", to indicate that the will of something for something returns to the will of that thing, on the basis that the object of the will there is the giving, and the "lam" is for causation, meaning: He only wills to give them so that they may be punished. As for if we say that the "lam" in what preceded is superfluous, the difference may be because the emphasis there is for the prior mention of what could serve as a cause of punishment, namely wealth, which is more fitting than here, since that was not previously mentioned. There it is ﴿in the life of this world﴾ and here ﴿in the world﴾, as an alert that their life is as no life in it, and this here indicates that they are as the dead.

Ibn al-Khazin explained the secret of the difference between the two noble structures in a manner whose shortcomings are not hidden. And the mention of wealth before children, although children are dearer than it, is because the need for it touches everyone more generally than children. It has also been said: because wealth is older in existence than them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 86:

﴿And when a surah is sent down﴾ from the Qur'an. What is meant by it, as has been said, is a particular surah, namely Bara'ah (al-Tawbah). It has also been said that what is meant is every surah in which faith and jihad are mentioned, and this is preferable and more fruitful, because their seeking permission at the revelation of the verses of Bara'ah is known from what has passed. The particle "idha" (when) indicates repetition by the context of the situation, even though it does not indicate it by its lexical form, as some verifying scholars have stated explicitly. It is also permissible that "surah" means part of a surah, metaphorically, by the usage of naming the part for the whole. The words of al-Kashshaf seem to imply that applying "surah" to a part of it is by way of homonymy (ishtirak), like applying "Qur'an" to a part of it, but this is not so. The tanwin (indefinite ending) is for magnification, meaning a surah of great rank. ﴿That believe﴾, i.e., "bi-an aminu" (that you believe). Here "an" is a verbal-source particle (masdariyyah) from which the preposition has been omitted. It is also permissible that it be explanatory (mufassirah), since the sending down precedes it, and it carries the meaning of speech without its letters. The address is to the hypocrites, and what is meant is: make your faith sincere. ﴿In God and strive alongside His Messenger﴾ for the strengthening of His religion and the elevation of His word. As for generalizing it, or intending the believers in the sense of "persist in faith in God," etc., as al-Tabarsi and others held, this does not suit the context, and linking the condition and the consequence would require straining over what is not needed, such as considering what belongs to the state of the sincere believers within this sublime composition. ﴿They sought your permission﴾, i.e., they requested permission from you, and there is an iltifat (shift of grammatical person) in it. ﴿The men of wealth among them﴾, i.e., the people of bounty and ample means from among the hypocrites, those who have financial capacity. From this one knows that bodily capacity is included by analogy. They were singled out for mention because they are the ones who were blamed. ﴿And said: Leave us﴾, i.e., let us be, ﴿that we may be with those who sit back﴾, i.e., those who did not strive for a valid excuse, from among men and women, so this is an instance of taghlib (the masculine being given precedence). The conjunction of "qalu" with "istaadhanaka" serves as an explanation, which dispenses with mentioning what they sought permission for, namely remaining behind.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 87:

﴿They were content to be with those who stay behind﴾ That is, with the women, as related from Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah. It is the plural of khalifah (one who stays behind), and it was applied to women because of their staying behind from the works of men, such as jihad and other things. The intent is to censure them and to equate them with women in staying behind from jihad. The term khalifah is also applied to one in whom there is no good, and the taʾ (ta marbutah) in it is for transferring the word to the status of a noun (ismiyyah). Some have interpreted the verse according to this meaning, so the intended sense is then one who has no benefit for jihad. Its plural being formed as fawaʾil is clear according to the first meaning, but according to the second meaning it is due to the feminine form of its wording, because fa'il is not pluralized as fawaʾil for male rational beings except in an anomalous manner. ﴿And a seal was set upon their hearts, so they﴾ because of that ﴿do not understand﴾ what benefits them and what harms them in both abodes.

﴿But the Messenger and those who believed with him strove with their wealth and their lives﴾ is an *istidrak* (a corrective exception that qualifies what has been understood from the preceding statement). The meaning is: if these people stayed behind and did not strive, there is no harm, because one who is better than them has risen to the fullest degree. He is in the manner of His saying, exalted is He:

[p. 157]

﴿If these disbelieve in it, then We have entrusted it to a people who are not disbelievers in it﴾. In the verse there is an allusion that these people have no share of faith in God, the Exalted, even though they did not openly turn away from it, as shown by their turning away from jihad through their seeking permission to remain behind. (﴿And those﴾) that is, those described with the sublime qualities, (﴿for them﴾) by means of that, (﴿are the good things﴾), that is, the benefits in which the soul finds rest and comfort. The apparent sense of the word here is its generality, encompassing the benefits of both abodes, such as victory and spoils in this world and the Garden and its bliss in the next. It has been said that what is meant by them is the maidens of paradise, because of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Therein are good, beautiful [women]﴾, since the word there carries the meaning of the maidens, so it is interpreted accordingly here too. Al-Mubarrad stated that *al-khayrat* is applied to excellent female slaves. It is the plural of *khayrah*, with the *ya'* sukun, a lightened form of *khayyirah* (with shaddah), the feminine of *khayyir*, which means the excellent of everything, the most desirable of it. (﴿And those, they are the successful﴾), that is, the ones who attain their goals, unlike one who gains a portion that will perish after a little while. He repeated the demonstrative noun to honor their status.

﴿Allah has prepared for them﴾ is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) explaining why they are successful (muflihun). It was also said: it may be an explanation of the otherworldly benefits they have, and what precedes it is restricted to worldly benefits by the cue of contrast. The i'dad (preparation) means al-tahy'a (readying), i.e., He readied for them ﴿gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever﴾. The phrase "abiding therein" is a circumstantial clause (hal) that is determined in advance (muqaddarah) from the pronoun in "for them," and the governing element is "a'adda" (He prepared). ﴿That﴾ is a demonstrative referring to what is understood from the discourse, namely attaining the great honor. ( ﴿The triumph﴾ ) i.e., the attainment (al-zafar), ( ﴿the great﴾ ) which has no triumph beyond it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 90:

﴿And those who make excuses among the Bedouins came, seeking permission﴾. This begins an explanation of the states of the hypocrites among the Bedouins, following the explanation of the states of the hypocrites of the people of Madinah. Al-Mu'adhdhirun (المُعَذِّرُونَ) derives from "adhara fi al-amr" (عَذَرَ في الأمْرِ), meaning he fell short in the matter and was lax and did not succeed. Its real meaning is that he gives the impression that he has an excuse for what he does while he has no excuse. It may also be from "i'tadhara" (اعْتَذَرَ), and the original form is al-mu'tadhirun (المُعْتَذِرُونَ), in which the ta' was assimilated into the dhal (idgham, the merging of one consonant into the next) after its vowel was transferred to the 'ayn. It is permissible to vocalize the ta' with kasra because of the meeting of two sukun-bearing letters, and with damma to match the mim, but these readings were not recited. Ya'qub read (المُعْذِرُونَ) with a single letter (i.e., without tashdid, from the form a'dhara), and this is related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them. Thus it is from "a'dhara" (أعْذَرَ), meaning he had an excuse. It is also reported from Maslamah that he read (المُعَذِّرُونَ) with shaddah on the 'ayn and the dhal, from "ta'adhdhara" (تَعَذَّرَ), meaning "i'tadhara" (اعْتَذَرَ).

Abu Hayyan critiqued this, saying: "This reading is either an error on the part of the reader or it is attributed to him falsely, because the ta' may not be assimilated into the 'ayn, given their opposition (in articulation and nature). As for treating opposition as if it were affinity, no grammarian or reciter has said this, so occupying oneself with such a thing is a fault. Furthermore, these who came are liars according to the first possibility of the first reading, and they may be liars or truthful according to the second of the two, and likewise according to the last reading, and truthful according to the second reading."

The scholars differed about who is meant by them. Al-Dahhak reported that "they were the company of Amir ibn al-Tufayl. They came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Prophet of Allah, if we join you in the expedition, Tayy will raid our families and our livestock.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Allah has informed me of your news, and Allah, glorified is He, will suffice you without you.'"

It was also said: they were Asad and Ghatafan, who sought permission to stay behind, making excuses of hardship and the large number of dependents. Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn Ishaq that he said: "It was mentioned to me that they were a group from Banu Ghifar." Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that they were "the people of excuse," without specifying who they were.

From what we have mentioned, it is known that there is disagreement over whether these who came were truthful in their excuse or not. According to the view that they were truthful, the referent of the relative pronoun in His words, glorified is He: ﴿And those who lied to Allah and His Messenger sat back﴾, is other than them, namely some people from the Bedouins who were also hypocrites, while the first group had no hypocrisy among them. According to the view that they were liars, the referent is the first group. The shift from the pronoun to the explicit noun is to expose their blame by means of the relative clause. The lying, according to the first view, is by claiming faith, and according to the second, by making excuses. Perhaps the sitting back (القُعُودَ) also differs.

Ubayy read (كَذَّبُوا) with shaddah. ﴿Those among them who disbelieved will be afflicted﴾, meaning: among the Bedouins in general, and their hypocrites, or among those who made excuses. The partitive sense (تَبْعِيض, indicating only some of them) is that some of them made excuses out of laziness, not out of disbelief. That is, the ones who made excuses because of their disbelief will be afflicted. ﴿a painful punishment﴾, which is the punishment of the Fire in the Hereafter, and this does not contradict the deserving of those who stayed behind out of laziness. This is according to us, because we do not hold the doctrine of mafhum (the implicit meaning by contrary inference). Whoever holds it interprets the painful punishment as the combination of killing and the Fire. The first (killing) does not apply to the believer who stayed behind out of laziness, so the combination is negated as well.

It was also said: the referent of the relative pronoun is those who persist in disbelief.

[Page 158]

﴿There is no blame upon the weak﴾, such as the elderly and those with an innate frailty that prevents them from going out [to fight] with it. It is the plural of ḍaʿīf (weak). It is said ḍuʿūf and ḍiʿfān. The plural also came as ḍiʿāf, ḍaʿafah, ḍaʿfā and ḍiʿāfā. ﴿Nor upon the sick﴾, the plural of marīḍ (sick). It is also pluralized as mirāḍ and murāḍā. It refers to one afflicted by illness and disturbance of constitution, whether it is of that which quickly passes, like many illnesses, or of that which is chronic, like zamānah (chronic disability). They counted among it what does not pass away, such as innate blindness and innate lameness. So the blind and the lame are included among the sick. And if you refuse this, it is not far-fetched that they are included among the weak. What indicates the inclusion of the blind in one of the two coordinated categories (mutaʿāṭifayn) is what Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Daraqutni in al-Afrad narrated, "From Zayd ibn Thabit, who said: I was writing for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and Surat Bara'ah was revealed. I was placing the pen behind my ear when he (ﷺ) commanded us to fight. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) began looking at what was being revealed to him when a blind man came to him and said: 'What about me, O Messenger of Allah, while I am blind?' So it was revealed: ﴿There is no blame upon the weak nor upon the sick﴾."

﴿Nor is there any blame upon those who find nothing to spend﴾, i.e., the poor who are unable to obtain the provisions for travel and for jihad. It was said that they were Muzaynah, Juhaynah, and Banu Udhrah. (﴿ḥaraj﴾) means sin in staying behind. Its root meaning is constriction, and the discussion of it has already passed. (﴿idha naṣaḥū lillāhi wa-rasūlihi﴾) means by faith and obedience, outwardly and inwardly, as the sincere well-wisher (al-muwālī al-nāṣiḥ) acts. So nuṣḥ (sincere counsel) is used here figuratively for this. It may also be intended that their sincere counsel, mentioned above, is the exerting of their effort for the benefit of Islam and the Muslims, by attending to their affairs and their families and conveying their news to them, and not being like the hypocrites who spread rumors when they stayed behind. The root meaning of nuṣḥ in the language is sincerity. It is said: naṣaḥtuhu and naṣaḥtu lahu. In al-Nihayah it is said that nasīḥah is used to express a whole notion, which is the desire of good for the one advised, and that this meaning cannot be expressed by a single word that encompasses it. The governing element of the adverbial phrase, according to Abu al-Baqa', is the meaning of the sentence, i.e., they do not go out at that time.

﴿There is no blame upon the doers of good﴾, i.e., there is no blame upon them. Here ihsan is sincere counsel to Allah the Exalted and to His Messenger (ﷺ). Placing the explicit noun in place of their pronoun is to give attention to their status and to describe them with this noble title. (min) is added for emphasis. The sentence is a resumptive clause confirming the content of what came before, in the most eloquent manner and most refined composition, and it is of eloquent speech, because its meaning is: there is no path for any blamer against them, i.e., the blamer does not pass by them or enter their land. How far, then, is blame from them! It operates as a proverb. It may also be that it is a causal explanation for the negation of blame from them, and (the doers of good) is general, i.e., there is no blame upon them, because there is no path against the category of doers of good, and they are among them. Ibn al-Faras said: From the verse it is derived that one who kills a beast that attacks does not owe compensation for it. (﴿wa-Allāhu ghafūrun raḥīm﴾) is a concluding remark confirming the content of what was mentioned, and in it is an indication that everyone is incapable and in need of forgiveness and mercy, since a human being is never free of some shortcoming. So it is not said: He first negated sin from them, so what is the need for forgiveness that requires a sin? If what is meant is their past sins, then by this consideration they are included among the offenders.

﴿Nor upon those who, when they come to you to be given mounts﴾, is a conjunction upon (the doers of good), as indicated by
page 159
the words of the Exalted that come later, in shā' Allāh, (﴿innamā al-sabīl﴾) and so on. It is a conjunction of the particular upon the general, giving attention to their status and making them, because of their distinction, as if they were another category. It was also said that it is a conjunction upon (the weak), and they, as Ibn Ishaq and others said, are the weepers. They were seven men from the Ansar and others from Banu 'Amr ibn 'Awf: Salim ibn 'Umayr, 'Ulayyah ibn Zayd, brother of Banu Harithah, Abu Layla 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Ka'b, brother of Banu Mazin ibn al-Najjar, 'Amr ibn al-Humam ibn al-Jamuh, brother of Banu Salamah, 'Abd Allah ibn Ma'qil al-Muzani, Haramiy ibn 'Abd Allah, brother of Banu Waqif, and 'Irbad ibn Sariyah al-Fazari. They came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and asked him for mounts, and they were people in need. He said to them, peace and blessings be upon him, what Allah the Exalted related in His saying: ﴿You said: I do not find anything to mount you on﴾. So they turned away while weeping, as He, glorified is He, informed. The apparent meaning is that none of them went out for the expedition with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). But Ibn Ishaq said: It reached me that Ibn Yamin ibn 'Umayr ibn Ka'b al-Nadri met Abu Layla and Ibn Ma'qil while they were weeping, and he said: What makes you weep? They said: We came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) so that he might mount us, but we did not find with him anything to mount us on, and we have nothing with which to strengthen ourselves for going out with him. So he gave them a camel of his, and they mounted, and he provided them with some dates, and they went out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). In some reports it is said that the rest were helped to go out, and they went out. From Mujahid it is related that they were the sons of Muqrin: Ma'qil, Suwayd, and al-Nu'man. It was also said: they were Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and his companions from the people of Yemen. It was also said, and it was said. The apparent meaning of the verse requires that they sought what they could ride of the animals, and this is what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them. Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from 'Ali ibn Salih, who said: "Some elders from Juhaynah told me, saying: We met those who asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for mounts, and they said: We asked him only for mounts on sandals." Similar to this is what Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibrahim ibn Adham, from one who narrated to him, who said: They asked him for nothing but sandals. In some reports it is related that they said: Mount us on patched leather socks and stitched sandals, and we will fight with you. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said what he said. And whoever inclines to the apparent meaning, supported by what was related from al-Hibr, said: With patched leather socks and stitched sandals one may substitute for the one with a hoof or a sock, so it is as if they said: Mount us on whatever is available, or the meaning is: mount us even on our sandals and socks, in exaggeration of contentment and out of love for going with him, peace and blessings be upon him.

You know that the apparent meaning of the two preceding reports makes that distant, and that it is in itself contrary to the apparent meaning.
