Yes, reports that contradict the apparent meaning of the verse have their problems, as known to one who has knowledge of the terminology of hadith (muṣṭalaḥ al-ḥadīth), and the difference of this category, based on what the apparent meaning requires, is that they are able to provide for what other than the mount, for those who do not find the expenditure, if what is meant by them is the poor who lack provisions, mount, and other things, is evident. Between the two there is general and specific relation, if what is meant by one who does not find the expenditure is one who lacks something that makes him unable to travel because of its absence. The first view was adopted by al-Imam (al-Razi), and many of the verifiers (muhaqqiqun) chose it. There was disagreement regarding the response of (idha). Some verifiers chose that it is (﴿qulta﴾) and so on, so that His saying, glorified is He: (﴿tawallaw﴾) and so on, is a new sentence, a clarifying new sentence (istinaf bayani). It was also said: The response is it, and (qulta) is a new sentence, or by omitting the conjunctive particle, i.e., and you said, or so you said, and it is conjoined to (﴿atawka﴾), or it is in the position of a circumstantial clause from the kaf in (﴿atawka﴾), with qad understood, as in ﴿they came to you, their breasts constricted﴾. The time of coming is considered broad, like its day and its month, so it is with the turning away in one time, and it suffices that his coming is a cause for it, even if their times differ, as al-Radi mentioned in your saying: If you come to me today, I will honor you tomorrow, i.e., your coming was a cause for my honoring you tomorrow. In choosing (﴿lā ajidu﴾) over (laysa 'indī) there is some refinement of speech and comforting of the hearts of the askers, which is not hidden,
page 160
as if he, peace and blessings be upon him, sought what they asked of him continually and did not find it, and that is fitting for one who is, toward the believers, compassionate and merciful (ﷺ). His saying, glorified is He: (﴿wa-a'yunuhum tafīḍu min al-dam'﴾) is in the position of a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of (﴿tawallaw﴾). Fayḍ is outpouring from fullness, and here it is a metaphor for fullness through the relation of causality. Dam' is that specific water. It is permissible to keep fayḍ in its literal sense, and its attribution to the eye would then be a metaphor, like "the river flowed." Dam' is the verbal noun of damaʿat al-ʿayn damʿan. (min) indicates cause and reason. It was also said that it is for explanation (bayān), and it together with the genitive is in the position of an accusative of specification (tamyīz), which has been transferred from the agent. Abu Hayyan objected that a tamyīz whose origin is an agent may not be prefixed with min, and also that only the Kufans permit making the tamyīz definite. It is answered regarding the first that it is refuted by such phrases as "great is one who says," and regarding the second that the permission of the Kufans suffices. Al-Qutb mentioned that the original structure is "their eyes overflow its tears," then "their eyes overflow with tears," and this is more eloquent because it attributes the verb to a non-agent and makes it a tamyīz, following the path of clarification after ambiguity, and because the eye is treated as if it were overflowing tears, and then ("their eyes overflow with tears") is more eloquent than what precedes it, through the abstracting min, since he made their eyes overflowing, then abstracted the overflowing eyes from the tears by considering the overflowing. It was objected that min here is for explanation of what has been made ambiguous, which may be clarified by the mere tamyīz, because the meaning of "the eye overflows" is that some of the eye's things overflow, just as the meaning of your saying "Zayd is good" is that some of Zayd's qualities are good, and the tamyīz removes the ambiguity of that thing; so likewise "from the tears." So it is in the position of an accusative of tamyīz. The notion of abstraction should not come from one who has knowledge of the methods of speech. Some of the discussion on this sentence has passed in al-Ma'idah, so remember it.

His saying, glorified is He: (﴿ḥazanan﴾) is in the accusative of causation, and grief is attributed to the eye just as outpouring is, so it is not said: How is that, since the agent of outpouring differs from the agent of grief, and with a difference of agent there is no accusative? It was said: That is permitted by considering the meaning, since its essence is: they turned away while weeping out of grief. It is also permitted to make it accusative as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of (﴿tafīḍu﴾), i.e., grieving, and as a verbal noun of a verb indicated by what precedes it, i.e., do not grieve with grief; and the clause is also a circumstantial clause from the indicated pronoun. Its connection may be to (tawallaw) on several possibilities: i.e., they turned away out of grief, or while grieving, or they grieve with grief. (﴿allā yajidū﴾) with the lām omitted, and omitting the preposition in such a construction is regular. It is connected to (ḥazanan) in any case. It was said: It is not permissible for it to be connected to it when it is accusative as a verbal noun, because an emphatic verbal noun does not govern. Perhaps whoever holds the first view would prevent that and say: One may extend the latitude for the adverbial element more than for other elements. It was permitted to connect it to (tafīḍu). It was said: This is when (ḥazanan) is not the cause of it; otherwise it is not permitted, because one verb cannot have two objects of cause. The substitution (ibdāl) is contrary to the apparent meaning. That is: so that they do not find (﴿mā yunfiqūna﴾) to spend in buying what they need for going out with you, if they do not find it with you. This, according to the apparent meaning, supports that this category is included under His saying, glorified is He: (﴿Nor upon those who find nothing to spend﴾).

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿The blame is only upon those who ask you for permission while they are rich.﴾ That is, [the blame is] by reproach and punishment. ﴿Those who ask you for permission﴾ to stay behind ﴿while they are rich﴾, having the means (al-uhbah, "equipment for the journey") and being able to go out with you. ﴿They are content﴾ is an explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani, a clause that answers an implied question), as if it were said: "Why did they ask permission, or why did they deserve what they deserved?" So it is answered: they are content ﴿to be with the ones left behind (al-khawalif)﴾, whose meaning has already been explained. ﴿And God sealed their hearts﴾, that is, He forsook them, so they became heedless of the evil outcome. ﴿So they﴾, because of that, ﴿do not know﴾ 93, ever, the ill consequence (wakhamah) of what they were content with and what it entails in this world, just as they did not know the foulness of its matter in the next world.

﴿They will make excuses to you﴾ explains what they will be doing upon your return to them. The address is said to be to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the plural is for honor. It is preferable that it be addressed to him, peace be upon him, and to his companions, because they used to make excuses on behalf of everyone; that is, they would make excuses to you for staying behind. ﴿When you return﴾ from the expedition, having arrived ﴿to them﴾. God, glorified is He, did not say "to Medina" to indicate that the basis of the excuse-making is the return to them, not the return to Medina. Perhaps some of them hurried to make excuses before returning to it. ﴿Say﴾ is an address to him, may God bless him and grant him peace (ﷺ), and it was singled out for this because responding is his duty, peace be upon him. ﴿Do not make excuses﴾, that is, do not make the excuse, or do not make excuses with what you have of excuses. ﴿We will not believe you﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining the reason for the prohibition. And His saying: ﴿God has already informed us of your news﴾ is a resumptive clause explaining the reason for the negation, as if it were said: "Why have you forbidden us from making excuses?" It is answered: "Because we would not believe your excuse, so it would be pointless." Then it is said: "Why will you not believe us?" It is answered: "Because God, the Exalted, has already informed us through revelation of what is in your hearts of evil and corruption."

According to a group, "informed" (nabba'a) is transitive to two objects: the first is the pronoun, and the second is ﴿of your news﴾. This is either because it is a description (ṣifah) of the second object, the sense being "a piece of your news," or because it means "some of your news." The "min" is not superfluous according to the view of al-Akhfash (al-Akhfash, Abu al-Hasan), regarding its being superfluous in affirmative speech.

Some of them said: it is transitive to three objects, and ﴿of your news﴾ takes the place of two objects, because it means "that you are such and such," or the third object is omitted, meaning "occurring, for example." This is criticized on the grounds that the said substitution is far-fetched, and that omitting the third object when the second object is mentioned in this construction is an error or weak. The meaning of "informed us" according to the first view is "made us know," as has been said, and according to the second it is "made us aware." It was also said: its meaning is "reported to us," and "min" means "about," but this is not correct.

The plural of the first-person pronoun in both places is for emphasis in cutting off the hopes of the hypocrites who make excuses, altogether, by clarifying that their excuses are not accepted by any of the believers at all. For the acceptance of some of them for their excuses may lead them to hope that the Messenger, peace be upon him, will also accept them. It is also to announce their disgrace among all the believers. The transitivity of ﴿we believe﴾ with the preposition "lam" has already been explained.

﴿And God will see your deed﴾, that is, He, glorified is He, will know it with a knowledge that is connected to the recompense. So the "seeing" is cognitive, and the second object is omitted, meaning: "Will you repent of the hypocrisy you are in, or will you persist in it?" It seems that, because of the sīn, which indicates futurity and postponement, this is an invitation to repentance and a grace of respite for repentance. The placing of the object of seeing before the subject, in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and His Messenger﴾,

is to announce the difference between the two kinds of seeing and their distinction, and to indicate that the basis of the threat is His knowledge, exalted and majestic is He, of their deeds. ﴿Then you will be returned﴾ on the Day of Resurrection to ﴿the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾ for recompense for what appeared from you of deeds. He placed the attribute in the position of the pronoun to intensify the threat, for His knowledge, glorified is He, of all their deeds, apparent and hidden, and His encompassing of their conditions, manifest and concealed, requires great restraint. The placing of "the unseen" before "the witnessed" has been said to be to establish that the relation of His all-encompassing knowledge to all things, secret and public, is one, in the most eloquent and emphatic manner. How could it not be, since His knowledge, exalted is He, of His known things is exalted above being through the way of the acquisition of an image; rather, the existence of each thing and its realization in itself is knowledge with respect to Him, exalted is He. In this meaning, the situation does not differ between manifest and hidden matters. The end of the quotation.

It should not be hidden from you that this is a statement that His knowledge, glorified is He, of things is presential (ḥuḍūrī, knowledge by the presence of the thing itself) and not acquired (ḥuṣūlī, knowledge by the acquisition of a representation). They have objected to it on the grounds that His knowledge, exalted and high is He, includes impossibilities and non-existent possibles, while presential knowledge is restricted to existent concrete things, because it is the presence of the known object in its concrete form before the knower. So how does the situation not differ in it between manifest and hidden matters, given that the hidden includes non-existent possibles and impossibles, and it is not conceivable that they be realized in themselves so as to be knowledge for Him, exalted is He? So it has been said, but there is room for examination. The investigation of the knowledge of the Necessary Being, glorified is He, of things is among the problematic inquiries and perplexing questions in which understandings have been bewildered and the feet of the great scholars have slipped. Perhaps the occasion, if God, exalted is He, wills, will lead to an investigation of this.

﴿Then He will inform you﴾ upon your return to Him, glorified is He, and your standing before Him, ﴿of what you used to do﴾, that is, of what you were doing continuously in the world of the evil deeds, the earlier and later ones, according to whether ﴿what﴾ is a relative pronoun, or of your continuous deed, according to whether ﴿what﴾ is a verbal (maṣdariyyah) particle. What is meant by informing about it is recompense for it, and the choice of this word over the other is to observe what preceded in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿God has already informed us﴾, etc., and to announce that they were not aware in the world of the reality of their deeds, and that they only come to know them on that day.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 95:

﴿They will swear to you by Allah﴾ to emphasize their false excuses and to make them appear acceptable. The sin (al-sin) here is for emphasis, as has been explained earlier. The thing sworn to is what is understood from the speech, namely the false excuses they offered. The clause is either a substitute (badal) for "they make excuses" or an explanation (bayan) of it. ﴿When you return﴾ from your journey ﴿to them﴾. Al-inqilab (returning) is going back and turning away, with the added meaning of arriving and taking hold. The benefit of restricting their oath, as some of the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun) have said, is an indication that it is not meant to cancel what the Prophet ﷺ addressed them with, namely the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Do not make excuses﴾, and so on. Rather, it is a fresh command: ﴿so that you may turn away from them﴾, meaning do not rebuke them, and overlook what has passed from them with the overlooking of contentment, as His saying the Exalted indicates: ﴿so that you may be pleased with them﴾, ﴿so turn away from them﴾. However, it is not a turning away of contentment as they wished, but a turning away of avoidance and abhorrence, as the reasoning in His words the Glorified indicates: ﴿Indeed they are filth﴾. This is explicit that the intended turning away is either avoidance of them because of the spiritual uncleanness that is understood from it, or leaving off reforming them by ceasing the dealings whose purpose is purification through urging them toward repentance. These people are filth that does not accept purification. It has also been said that ﴿so that you may turn away﴾ is in the sense of "lest you turn away," and that the turning away in it is also a turning away of abhorrence. It is not hidden that this is a strained interpretation that is not needed. As for His words the Exalted: ﴿and their refuge is Hell﴾, it is either part of the reasoning, since their being among the people of the Fire is one of the motives for avoiding them and for abandoning the effort to reform them through blame and reproach; or it is an independent reason, meaning: the Fire suffices them as reproach, in the manner of the saying "their reproach is the sword and their admonition is the slap," so you should not burden yourselves with that. ﴿Recompense﴾ is put in the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) emphasizing a verb implied from its own root, occurring as a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: they will be repaid with a recompense; or it emphasizes the content of what precedes it, since that implies the meaning of requital, as if it were said: they will be repaid with a recompense. ﴿For what they used to earn﴾ 95, meaning for what they habitually earn of various kinds of evil deeds in this world, or for their continuous earning of that.

It is also permitted that it be a object of purpose (maf'ul lahu) and a circumstantial clause (hal) from the predicate, according to those who hold that view.

ۭ﴿They swear to you﴾ is a substitute (badal) for what preceded, and the object of the oath is omitted because it is evident, as mentioned earlier; that is, they swear by Allah, Exalted is He, to what they have offered as excuses. ﴿So that you may be pleased with them﴾ by their oath, and that you would continue doing to them what you were doing. ﴿But if you are pleased with them﴾ according to what they requested, ﴿then indeed Allah is not pleased with the defiant people﴾ (96). That is, your being pleased with them yields them no benefit, because Allah, Exalted is He, is angry with them, and there is no effect to the pleasure of anyone when Allah, Exalted is He, is displeased.

Some have permitted that "being pleased" (al-rida) is a metaphor (kinaya) for deception (al-talbis), meaning: if they are able to deceive you with false oaths so that they please you, they cannot deceive Allah, Exalted is He, with that so that He is pleased with them, and so He does not expose their concealed matters nor humiliate them. This is contrary to the apparent meaning.

The phrase "the defiant people" (al-fasiqin) is placed in the position of their pronoun, to record against them their departure from obedience, which necessitates what has befallen them. The intended meaning of the verse is the prohibition of the addressees from being pleased with them and from being deceived by their false excuses, in the most emphatic and forceful manner, for being pleased with one with whom Allah, Exalted is He, is not pleased is something that hardly issues from a believer.

The verse was revealed, as narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, concerning Jadd ibn Qays, Mu'attib ibn Qushayr and their companions from among the hypocrites, who were eighty men. When they returned to Medina, the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded the believers not to sit with them or speak to them, and they complied. And it is narrated from Muqatil that it was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, who swore to the Prophet (ﷺ) that he would never stay behind from him, and sought that he be pleased, but he did not do so (ﷺ).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 97:

﴿Al-A'rab﴾ is a plural form, but it is not the plural of "Arab" according to what is reported from Sibawayh, so that it would not follow that the plural is more specific than the singular. The Arabs are this well-known lineage in general, while the A'rab (Bedouins, the dwellers of the desert) are those among them who live in the desert. For this reason, the relative adjective is formed on its form, so one says "A'rabi" (a Bedouin). It has also been said that "Arab" refers to the dwellers of cities and villages, while "A'rab" refers to the dwellers of the desert from this lineage, or their clients (mawali). In that case the two are distinct. The singular and plural are differentiated by the letter ya' in both, so one says for the singular "'Arabi" and "A'rabi," and for the collective "'Arab" and "A'rab," and likewise "a'arib." This is like saying the singular "majusi" and "yahudi," and then the ya' is dropped in the plural, so one says "al-majus" and "al-yahud," meaning the people of the desert. ﴿Are more intense in disbelief and hypocrisy﴾ than the people of the settled areas who are disbelievers and hypocrites, because of their wildness, the hardness of their hearts, their not mixing with people of wisdom, and their being deprived of hearing the Book and the Sunnah. They are the most like animals. In a hadith from al-Hasan, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "Whoever dwells in the desert becomes harsh, whoever follows game becomes heedless, and whoever goes to the ruler falls into temptation." It has also come: "Three of the major sins," and he counted among them "ta'arrub" after the migration (hijrah), which is to return to the desert and live with the A'rab after having been a muhajir. Whoever returned to his place after the hijrah without an excuse, they regarded as an apostate. This was because evil predominates among the dwellers of the desert, and "the nature is a thief," or because of distance from the gatherings of knowledge and the people of goodness, and it leads to much evil. The judgment on the A'rab with what has been mentioned is by way of describing a genus with the description of some of its individuals, as in His saying: ﴿And man is ever ungrateful﴾, since not all of them are as mentioned. This is indicated by His saying, which follows: ﴿And among the A'rab is one who believes﴾, etc. Ibn Sirin, as Abu al-Shaykh reported from him, used to say: "If one of you recites this verse, let him recite the next verse," meaning by it what we have pointed out. The verse mentioned, as reported from al-Kalbi, was revealed concerning Asad and Ghatafan, but the lesson is drawn from the generality of the wording, not from the specificity of the occasion of revelation.

﴿Wa-ajdar﴾ means more entitled and more fitting, and it is, as al-Tabarsi said, derived from "jadr al-hA'it" (the foundation of a wall) with a sukun on the dal, which is its root and base. It is construed with the letter ba', so His saying ﴿alla ya'lamu﴾ is with the implied "bi-an ya'lamu" (that they should know) ﴿the limits of what Allah has revealed to His Messenger﴾.

These, as Abu al-Shaykh reported from al-Dahhak, are the obligations and what they were commanded regarding jihad. Some included the Sunan within the limits, but the well-known view is that they are specific to the obligations or the commands and prohibitions, based on His saying: ﴿These are the limits of Allah, so do not transgress them﴾ and ﴿These are the limits of Allah, so do not approach them﴾. Perhaps this is by way of predominance, and there is no distance in it, for the A'rab are more likely not to know all of that because of their distance from those from whom knowledge is acquired. It has also been said that the intended meaning, by the indication of the context, is His threat against opposing the Messenger (ﷺ) in jihad. And it has been said: the measures of the obligations. ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing﴾, He knows the states of each of the people of the camel-hair tents and the people of the cities, ﴿All-Wise﴾ regarding what He will inflict upon their wrongdoers and their good-doers of punishment and reward.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 98:

﴿And among the Bedouin﴾ i.e., of their kind, who are described by the description of some of their individuals. And it has been said: of the group mentioned previously. ﴿Are those who take﴾ i.e., consider ﴿what they spend﴾ i.e., expend in the way of Allah the Exalted and give in charity, as the context requires, ﴿as a loss﴾ i.e., a penalty and a ruin, from al-gharam, meaning destruction. And it has been said: from al-ghurm, which is the befalling of a calamity upon wealth without any wrongdoing; and its root is from constant obligation, and from it each of two debtors is called a gharim (creditor/debtor). They regard it as such because they do not spend it seeking reward and hoping for the reward of Allah the Exalted, so that it might be a gain for them; rather they spend it out of taqiyya (dissimulation) and to be seen by people, so it is purely a penalty. What is in the form of the verb "ittakhadha" of the meaning of choosing and benefiting by what is taken is only with regard to the purpose of the spender, namely showing off and taqiyya, not with regard to the nature of the expenditure itself, I mean its being a penalty. ﴿And they wait for misfortunes to befall you﴾ i.e., they await for you the vicissitudes of time and its calamities that encompass a person, so that your affair may be overturned by them and your state changed, and so that they may be freed from what they have been afflicted with. ﴿Upon them is the misfortune of evil﴾ — a supplication against them with something like what they wait for upon you; and it is a parenthetical statement between two speeches, as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿And the Jews say, "The hand of Allah is chained." Their hands are chained, and they are cursed for what they said﴾, etc. It is also permitted that the sentence be a report of the occurrence of what they wait for upon them. The word "dā'ira" is a name for a calamity, and it is originally a verbal noun like "āfiya" and "kādhiba," or an active participle from "dāra yadūru"; its full discussion has been given before. And "al-sū'" is originally also a verbal noun; then it was applied to every harm and evil, and it was originally an attribute of "dā'ira," then it was made a genitive construction with it, so the genitive is of the type of a described noun with its attribute, as in your saying: "rajul ṣidq" (a man of truth), and there is in it what there is of emphasis. Upon this is His saying the Exalted: ﴿Your father was not a man of evil﴾. And it has been said: the meaning of "dā'ira" entails the meaning of "sū'," so the genitive is for explanation and emphasis, as they say: "shams al-nahār" (the sun of the day) and "liḥyā ra'sihi" (the beard of his head). Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read (al-Sū'a) here and in the second occurrence with a fatha, with a damma; and it is then a noun meaning punishment, not a verbal noun like the fathah form. Al-Farra' distinguished between them on this basis. Abu al-Baqa' said: "al-Sū'" with a damma is harm, and it is in reality a verbal noun; one says: "su'tuhu su'an wa masā'atan wa masā'iyyatan"; and with a fatha it is corruption and badness. He seems to say that each of them is in reality a verbal noun, as al-Shihab understood from his words. Makki said: the one with a fatha means corruption, and the one with a damma means defeat and harm. Its apparent meaning, as it has been said, is that both are nouns. ﴿And Allah is All-Hearing﴾ of their shameful statements at the time of spending, ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of their corrupt intentions, among which is that they wait for misfortunes to befall you. And in this is what is not hidden of the severity of the warning.

"And among the Bedouins" means of their kind in general, "are those who believe in Allah and the Last Day" in the manner commanded, "and take" by way of choosing and preferring, "what they spend" in the way of Allah Most High, "as means of nearness" (qurubat). Qurubat is the plural of qurbah, meaning taqarrub (drawing near). It is the second object of yattakhidh (take). The meaning is taking that expenditure as a means of drawing near, either through metonymy in the attribution or through an implied term. Qurbah may also be used for that by which one draws near, and the first interpretation is the choice of the majority. The plural is in view of the kinds and the individuals. His words, "with Allah" ('inda Allah), are either an adjective of qurubat or an adverbial complement of yattakhidh.

Abu al-Baqa' permitted it to be an adverbial complement, so that qurubat means "bringing near" (muqarrabat) with Allah Most High. His words, "and the prayers of the Messenger" (wa salawat al-Rasul), are conjoined to qurubat, meaning "and a means for his supplication," peace be upon him, for he (ﷺ) used to invoke good and blessing upon those who gave charity and to seek forgiveness for them. Therefore it is recommended (yusann) for the one who receives charity to supplicate for the giver when he takes his charity. However, he is not permitted to send salah (prayers of blessing) upon him. They said: prayers are not offered upon anyone other than the prophets and angels, peace be upon them, except by way of following, because in salah there is a greatness not found in other supplications, and it is for the increase of mercy and nearness to Allah Most High. It is therefore not fitting for one who may be subject to faults and sins. It was permitted upon him only as a follower, due to what this involves of honoring the one who is followed.

It is disputed whether this is makruh (disliked) as prohibitively disliked, or as lesser disliked, or as contrary to what is preferable (khilaf al-awla). Al-Nawawi, in al-Adhkar, corrected the second view. But in the introduction of the Sharh al-Ashbah of al-Biri: whoever sends prayers upon others sins and it is disliked, and this is the sound view. As for what the Six (compilers of hadith) other than al-Tirmidhi narrated of his saying (ﷺ): "O Allah, send prayers upon Abu Awfa," it is not a proof against the one who prohibits this. That, as stated in al-Mustasfa, is his (ﷺ) right, so he may bestow it upon whomever he wills initially, and others are not like that.

As for salam (peace), al-Laqqani, in his commentary on Jawharat al-Tawhid, reported from Imam al-Juwayni that it has the meaning of prayer. Therefore it is not used for an absent person, nor is it singled out for anyone other than the prophets and angels, peace be upon them. So one does not say, "Ali alayhi al-salam," but rather "radiya Allahu ta'ala 'anhu" (may Allah be pleased with him). This applies equally to the living and the dead, except for the present, where one says "al-salam," or "salamun 'alayka," or "'alaykum." This is agreed upon. End of quotation.

I say: perhaps from the present category is "al-salamu 'alayna wa 'ala 'ibad Allah al-salihin" and "salamun 'alaykum dara qawmin mu'minin"; otherwise the matter is problematic. The apparent reason for prohibiting salam is what al-Nawawi said regarding the reason for prohibiting salah: that it is the distinctive mark (shi'ar) of the people of innovation (ahl al-bid'a), and that in the language of the early generations it is specific to the prophets and angels, peace be upon them, just as our saying "'azza wa jall" (Mighty and Majestic) is specific to Allah the Glorified. Therefore one does not say "Muhammad 'azza wa jall," even though he is mighty and exalted (ﷺ).

Then al-Laqqani said: Qadi Iyad said: "What the scholars (al-muhaqqiqun) have adopted, and to which I incline, is what Malik and Sufyan said, and what many jurists and theologians have chosen: that it is obligatory to restrict the Prophet (ﷺ) and all the prophets, peace be upon them, to salah and salam, just as Allah the Glorified is specified when He is mentioned with sanctification and transcendence, while others are mentioned with forgiveness and good pleasure, as He, Most High, said: ﴿Allah is well pleased with them, and they are well pleased with Him﴾, and ﴿They say: Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith﴾." He also said: "Moreover, that practice regarding those other than those mentioned did not exist in the first era. Rather, the Rafidah (Shi'a rejectors) introduced it concerning some of the imams, and resembling the people of innovation is forbidden, so opposing them is obligatory." End of quotation.

It is not hidden that the Hanbali school permits this for others than the prophets and angels independently, acting upon the apparent meaning of the hadith mentioned above. The disliking of resembling the people of innovation is also established in our school, but not absolutely; rather it applies to what is blameworthy and to what is intended as imitation of them, as al-Haskafi mentioned in al-Durr al-Mukhtar. So understand.

Then, the mention of the attribute of faith in Allah and the Last Day regarding this group, although the thrust of the speech is to clarify the difference between the two groups in showing the status of taking what they spend, both in present state and in outcome, and that the mention of taking it as a means of nearness and prayers suffices, without explicit statement of that, due to the complete care for their faith and the showing of their being characterized by it, and the increased concern to establish the distinction from the outset. As for the first group, their characterization with disbelief and hypocrisy is known explicitly from the context of the noble verse.

It is also permitted to conjoin ﴿and the prayers﴾ to "what he spends," and Abu al-Baqa' restricted himself to this: he takes what he spends and the prayers of the Messenger, peace be upon him, as means of nearness.

﴿Surely it is a nearness for them﴾: a testimony to them from the presence of Allah Most High of the soundness of what they believed, and a confirmation of their hope. The pronoun (ha') refers either to the expenditure known from what preceded, or to "ma" (what), which is in its meaning, so it returns to that by meaning, which is why it is feminine; or it is for observing the predicate. Ibn al-Khazin permitted its return to the prayers, but most scholars take the first view. The tanwin (indefiniteness marker) of qurbah is for magnification, dispensing with the plural: a nearness whose reality cannot be fully comprehended. In making the sentence nominal and using the two particles of alerting and affirmation (inna and ala), there is an eloquence that is not hidden.

The restriction to showing that it is a nearness for them is because it is the ultimate goal, and the prayers of the Messenger, peace be upon him, are among its means. It was also read as qurubatan, with a damma on the ra' for the sake of following (the vowel of the preceding word).

﴿Allah will admit them into His mercy﴾: a promise to them of the encompassing of His mercy, Glorified is He, as the particle fi, which indicates containment, suggests. It stands in contrast to the threat for the earlier group, referred to by His words, ﴿Allah is Hearing, Knowing﴾. Within it is also an explanation of the nearness. The sin (lam) of al-sin (the particle sa-) is for confirmation and emphasis, since it has been said that it is affirmative in contrast to lan (will not), which is negative.

﴿Indeed Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾: a confirmation of what preceded, serving as evidence for it.

The verse, as Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh and others narrated from Mujahid, was revealed concerning Banu Muqarrin of Muzayna. Al-Kalbi said it was revealed concerning Aslam, Ghifar and Juhayna. It was said that the preceding verse was revealed concerning Asad, Ghatafan and Banu Tamim, and this verse concerning Abd Allah dhi al-Bijadayn ibn Nahm al-Muzani, may Allah be pleased with him.

The commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 100:

﴿And the foremost, the first of the Emigrants and the Helpers﴾ is an explanation of the virtues of the noblest of the Muslims, following an explanation concerning a group of them. By them is meant, as has been narrated from Sa'id, Qatadah, Ibn Sirin and a group, those who prayed toward the two qiblahs. 'Ata' ibn Rabah said: they are the people of Badr. Al-Sha'bi said: they are the people of the Pledge of al-Ridwan, which took place at al-Hudaybiyah. It was also said: they are those who embraced Islam before the Hijrah. And the Helpers (al-Ansar) are the people of the First Pledge of al-'Aqabah, which took place in the eleventh year of the Prophethood, and they were, according to some narrations, seven men; and the people of the Second Pledge of al-'Aqabah, which took place in the twelfth year, and they were seventy men and two women. And those who embraced Islam when Abu Zurarah Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr ibn Hashim ibn 'Abd Manaf came to them before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had sent him with the people of the Second 'Aqabah, to teach them the Qur'an and instruct them in the religion. ﴿And those who followed them in goodness﴾, i.e., while embodying it. The intended meaning is every good quality. They are those who follow the foremost of the two groups, on the reading that "min" is partitive, or ﴿those who followed them in goodness﴾ with faith and obedience until the Day of Resurrection. Thus by the foremost is meant all the Emigrants and the Helpers, may Allah be pleased with them. The meaning of their being foremost is that they are first in relation to all the rest of the Muslims, and many people have gone to this view.

It has been narrated from Humayd ibn Ziyad that he said: One day I said to Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi: "Will you not inform me about the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning what occurred among them of the strife?" He said to me: "Indeed Allah the Exalted has forgiven all of them, and has made Paradise obligatory for them in His Book, both their good doers and their wrongdoers." I said to him: "In what place has He made Paradise obligatory for them?" He said: "Glory be to Allah! Do you not read His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And the foremost, the first﴾, the verse, so that you know that He, the Exalted, made Paradise and the good pleasure (of Allah) obligatory for all the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), and He stipulated a condition for the Successors?" I said: "And what is that condition?" He said: "He stipulated upon them that they follow them in goodness, which is that they emulate them in their good deeds and do not emulate them in other than that. Or it is said: it is that they follow them in goodness in speech, and that they do not speak ill of them, and that they do not direct criticism at what they undertook." Humayd ibn Ziyad said: "It was as if I had never read this verse at all." And on this (reading) the verse includes, concerning the virtue of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, what it does not include on the first interpretation.

Al-Qutb objected to the earlier interpretations of "the foremost of the Emigrants" on the grounds that praying toward the two qiblahs, witnessing Badr and the Pledge of al-Ridwan are shared between the Emigrants and the Helpers. It was answered that the intention of those who specified their precedence is their companionship and emigration to him (ﷺ), over others of that category. Al-Imam (al-Razi) chose that by the foremost of the Emigrants is meant those foremost in the Hijrah, and by the foremost of the Helpers those foremost in the support (nusrah), and he claimed that this is the correct view according to him. He argued for it by saying that He, glory be to Him, mentioned their being foremost but did not explain in what they were foremost, so the word remained general; yet when He described them as Emigrants and Helpers, it became known that the intended precedence is precedence in the Hijrah and the support, removing the generality from the word. Also, each of the Hijrah and the support, being an act difficult upon the soul, is a great act of obedience, so whoever undertakes it first becomes an example to others in this obedience. This strengthens the heart of the Messenger (ﷺ) and is a cause for the removal of loneliness from his noble mind (ﷺ). Therefore Allah the Exalted praised everyone who was foremost in both, and established for them what He established. And how could it not be so, when they believed while the Muslims in Makkah and Madinah were few and weak; so Islam was strengthened through them, the number of Muslims increased by their embracing Islam, and his heart (ﷺ) was strengthened by their entry into Islam and the emulation of others of them. So their state in this was like the state of one who establishes a good tradition, and in the report: "Whoever establishes a good tradition, he has its reward and the reward of whoever acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection." And it is not hidden that this is good.

It is permissible in my view that by the foremost is meant those who preceded to faith in Allah and the Last Day and to taking what they spend as acts of nearness, and the indication for this is clear. In any case, ﴿the foremost﴾ is the subject, and its predicate is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Allah is pleased with them﴾, i.e., by accepting their obedience and approving their deeds, ﴿and they are pleased with Him﴾ by what they attained of the magnificent blessings. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that the predicate be ﴿the first﴾ or ﴿of the Emigrants﴾, and that ﴿the foremost﴾ be in conjunction with ﴿whoever believes﴾, i.e., and among them are the foremost. What we have mentioned is the most apparent of the views. It is narrated from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he recited "wal-Ansaru" with a nominative case, on the basis that it is conjoined to ﴿the foremost﴾.

Abu 'Ubaydah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and others recorded from 'Amr ibn 'Amir al-Ansari that 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, used to recite by omitting the waw from ("wal-ladhina ittaba'uhum"), so that the relative clause would be a description of the Helpers, until Zayd said to him: "It is with the waw." So he said: "Bring me Ubayy ibn Ka'b." He came to him and asked him about that, and he said: "It is with the waw," and 'Umar followed him.

Abu al-Shaykh recorded from Abu Usamah and Muhammad ibn Ibrahim al-Taymi, both of whom said: "'Umar ibn al-Khattab passed by a man reciting ﴿wal-ladhina﴾ with the waw, and he said: 'Who taught you this?' He said: 'Ubayy.' So he took him by the hand to him and said: 'O Abu al-Mundhir, this man informed me that you taught him it thus.' Ubayy said: 'He is right, and I received it thus from the mouth of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).' 'Umar said: 'You received it thus from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)?' He said: 'Yes.' So he repeated it to him, and he said a third time, while angry: 'Yes, by Allah, Allah sent it down to Jibril, peace be upon him, and Jibril sent it down upon the heart of Muhammad (ﷺ), and the Khattab and his son were not consulted about it.' So 'Umar went out raising his hands while saying: Allah is greatest, Allah is greatest."

In a narration also recorded by Abu al-Shaykh from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, that Ubayy, may Allah be pleased with him, said to 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: "The confirmation of this verse is at the beginning of al-Jumu'ah: ﴿and others of them﴾, and in the middle of al-Hashr: ﴿and those who came after them﴾, and at the end of al-Anfal: ﴿and those who believed after [them]﴾, etc." His intention, may Allah be pleased with him, was that these verses indicate that the Successors are other than the Helpers.

And in it, that 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "I used to think that we were raised to a rank that no one after us would reach," and he intended the restriction of precedence to the Emigrants. The apparent mention of the Emigrants before the Helpers indicates that they are more excellent than them, and this is what the incident of the Saqifah indicates. Innumerable reports concerning the virtue of the Helpers have come, and among them what al-Shaykhan and others recorded from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The sign of faith is love of the Helpers, and the sign of hypocrisy is hatred of the Helpers."

Al-Tabarani recorded from al-Sa'ib ibn Yazid that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) distributed the spoils which Allah had granted him at Hunayn among the people of Makkah from Quraysh and others, so the Helpers became angry. He came to them and said: 'O assembly of the Helpers, news has reached me of your talk concerning these spoils with which I gave preference to some people in order to win them over to Islam, so that they may witness after today; and Allah the Exalted has entered Islam into their hearts.' Then he said: 'O assembly of the Helpers, did Allah not bestow upon you the favor of faith, and single you out with honor, and name you with the best of names, the Helpers of Allah the Exalted and the Helpers of His Messenger, peace be upon him? Were it not for the Hijrah I would have been a man of the Helpers. And if people were to travel a valley and you were to travel a valley, I would travel your valley. Are you not pleased that the people should go away with these spoils, the camel and the sheep, while you go away with the Messenger of Allah?' They said: 'We are pleased.' So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Answer me in what I have said.' They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, you found us in darkness, and Allah brought us out to the light through you; you found us on the brink of a pit of the Fire, and Allah rescued us through you; you found us astray, and Allah the Exalted guided us through you. So we are pleased with Allah the Exalted as Lord, and with Islam as religion, and with Muhammad (ﷺ) as Prophet.' Then he, peace be upon him, said: 'If you had answered me with other than this statement, I would have said: You have spoken truly. If you had said: Did you not come to us as one expelled, and we sheltered you? And as one denied, and we affirmed you? And as one forsaken, and we supported you? And we accepted what the people rejected from you? You would have spoken truly.' They said: 'Rather, to Allah the Exalted and to His Messenger belong the favor and the grace upon us and upon others.'" So observe how the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) spoke to them and how they answered him, may Allah be pleased with them.

﴿And He has prepared for them gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾, i.e., He prepared that for them in the Hereafter. Ibn Kathir read "min tahtiha" (from beneath them), and most of what comes in the Qur'an agrees with this reading. ﴿Abiding therein forever﴾, without end. ﴿That is the great success﴾, i.e., the success beyond which there is no success. And the meaning of distance in "dhalika" (that) has been said to be for indicating the distance of their rank in excellence and the greatness of their degree from among the believing Bedouins. And it is not hidden that this can hardly be correct except with some forcing, if by ﴿those who followed them﴾ is intended a category other than the Companions, because the apparent meaning is that the believing Bedouins are Companions, and no one who is not a Companion excels a Companion, as is indicated by his saying (ﷺ): "Do not revile my Companions, for if one of you were to spend gold equal to Mount Uhud, it would not reach a mudd of one of them, nor half of it." And his saying (ﷺ): "My community is like the rain; it is not known whether its first is better or its last." This is from the mode of hyperbole.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 101:

﴿And among those around you of the Bedouins are hypocrites﴾ This begins the explanation of the hypocrites of the people of Medina and those around it of the Bedouins, after the explanation of the state of the people of the desert among them. That is: and among those around your city are hypocrites. The intended referents of the relative clause, as Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ikrimah, are Juhaynah, Muzaynah, Ashja', Aslam and Ghifar, whose dwellings were around Medina. A group of exegetes went to this view, such as al-Baghawi, al-Wahidi, Ibn al-Jawzi and others. This was questioned on the ground that the Prophet (ﷺ) praised these tribes and supplicated for some of them. al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and others reported from Abu Hurayrah, from him (ﷺ), that he said: "Quraysh, the Ansar, Juhaynah, Muzaynah, Ashja', Aslam and Ghifar are the clients (mawali) of Allah and His Messenger, they have no clients other than Him." And there also came from him (ﷺ) that he said: "Aslam, may Allah keep them safe, and Ghifar, may Allah forgive them. Indeed I did not say it, rather Allah the Exalted said it." It is answered that this is in consideration of the majority of them. ﴿And from the people of Medina﴾ is a conjunction upon (﴿among those around you﴾), so it functions as a predicate for "hypocrites" in the same way as the item conjoined to it, as if it were said: "The hypocrites are from a people around you and from the people of Medina." This is conjunction of a singular upon a singular. The phrase of His, glorified is He, ﴿they persisted (maradu) in hypocrisy﴾ would then be a resumptive clause with no place in i'rab (grammatical analysis), brought to explain their excess in hypocrisy after explaining their being characterized by it. Or it is a description of "hypocrites." Abu Hayyan considered this unlikely, because it involves separating the description from what it describes. He also permitted that (﴿from the people of Medina﴾) be a fronted predicate, with the subject after it omitted, its description taking its place. The estimate is: "And from the people of Medina are a group who persisted." Omitting the described noun and placing its description in its stead, when it is part of a noun governed by min or fi that precedes it, is analogical and common, as in "Some of us stayed and some of us departed." Otherwise it is either a necessity of poetry or rare. An example is the verse of Suhaym:

"I am the son of Jala, and the climber of the summits; when I put down the turban, you will know me."

This is according to one of the interpretations of it. The root of maradu (persisting), as Ali ibn Isa mentioned, is smoothness, and from it comes "a smooth (mumarrad) palace." The beardless youth (amrad) is one without hair on his face, and "al-marda'" is a sandy stretch that grows nothing. Ibn Arafa said: its root is manifestness, and from it is their saying "a marda' tree" when its leaves have fallen and its branches have become exposed. In the Qamus: "maradha, like nasara and karuma, marudan, murudatan and maradatan; so he is marid, marid and mutamarrid," meaning he advanced and became insolent, or it is that he reached the extreme by which he emerges from the whole category of that kind. They explained it as habituation and training in a matter until one becomes skilled in it. This is close to what is mentioned in the Qamus about reaching the extreme. It is hardly used except for evil.

It encompasses both groups on the first two interpretations, according to the scope of hypocrisy. On the last interpretation it is specific to the hypocrites of the people of Medina. This is what was given preference. It was said that this is the most suitable with the mention first of the hypocrites of the people of the desert, then the hypocrites of the neighbouring Bedouins, then the hypocrites of the people of Medina. It remains on this view that he did not state the rank of the neighbours in hypocrisy, unlike the case if it encompasses both groups. Moreover, it is not hidden that if persisting in hypocrisy implies greater intensity in it, then there is a problem with their exegesis of the superlative in His, glorified is He, ﴿The Bedouins are more intense in disbelief and hypocrisy﴾ compared with the people of the settled towns. Perhaps the intention is to prefer the collective over the collective, or one must commit to the view that it does not imply this.

His, exalted is He, saying ﴿You do not know them﴾ is an explanation of their persistence, that is: you do not recognize them by the title of their hypocrisy. That is, they have reached such skill in hypocrisy and such refinement in observing dissimulation (taqiyyah) and avoiding places of suspicion that their state is hidden from you, despite your complete intelligence and true insight. In attaching the negation of knowledge of them, although it relates to their state, there is exaggeration in this, and an indication that what they are upon of the attribute of hypocrisy, through its deep rootedness and firm establishment in them, has become like their essential qualities or defining features, such that one who does not recognize them by that attribute is not considered to have knowledge of them. There is no need in this meaning to take knowledge as transitive with two objects and to estimate the second object as "you do not know them as hypocrites." It was said: the intention is "you do not recognize them individually, even if you know them in general." What we have mentioned, because of the exaggeration in it, is better. Its summary is: you do not recognize their hypocrisy. ﴿We know them﴾, that is, we recognize them by that title. Attributing knowledge in the sense of recognition to Him, exalted is He, is not something one should hesitate about, and whoever has doubts about it is mistaken, especially when this comes in the manner of mushakalah (rhetorical correspondence of wording). Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, explained knowledge here as recognition, as reported from him by Abu al-Shaykh.

Yes, there is no prohibition in taking it in its more obvious meaning, just as there is no prohibition in taking it in that sense in what preceded. But this requires an estimate, and not estimating is better than estimating.

The sentence is a confirmation of what preceded of their skill in hypocrisy, that is: no one comprehends their inner secrets fixed within them except one from whom nothing is hidden, because of how intensely they are concerned with nullifying disbelief and displaying sincerity. The matter of attaching knowledge here is like the matter of attaching its negation in what passed. It has been inferred from the verse that one should not venture to claim hidden matters of the heart's actions and the like. Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir and others reported from Qatadah that he said: "What is the matter with people who presume over others, saying: So-and-so is in Paradise and so-and-so is in Hell? When you ask one of them about himself, he says: I do not know. By my life, you know more about yourself than about the deeds of people, and you have presumed something that no Prophet presumed. Noah, peace be upon him, said: ﴿And I have no knowledge of what they were doing﴾ and Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, said: ﴿And I am not a guardian over you﴾, and Allah the Exalted said to Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿You do not know them; We know them﴾." These verses and their like are the strongest proof in refuting those who claim unveiling and access to the unseen by mere purity of heart and the stripping of the soul from preoccupations. Some of them are extremely lax in this matter.

﴿We will punish them﴾, and it is necessary, to realize what is required of them customarily, ﴿twice﴾. Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani in al-Awsat and others reported from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood on a Friday delivering a sermon and said: 'Stand up, so-and-so, and go out, for you are a hypocrite. Go out, so-and-so, for you are a hypocrite.' He expelled them by their names and exposed them. Umar ibn al-Khattab had not attended that Friday prayer because of a need he had. He met them as they were leaving the mosque, and he hid from them out of shame that he had not attended the Friday prayer, and he thought that the people had dispersed. They too hid from him and thought that he had learned of their affair. He entered the mosque and found that the people had not dispersed. A man said to him: 'Rejoice, O Umar, for Allah the Exalted has exposed the hypocrites today.' This is the first punishment, and the second punishment is the punishment of the grave." In the narration of Ibn Mardawayh from Ibn Mas'ud al-Ansari: "He (ﷺ) stood on the pulpit that day and expelled thirty-six men."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid that he explained the "two punishments" as hunger and killing. Perhaps what is meant by it is their fear and anticipation of it. It was said: it is conditional, if they manifest hypocrisy. In another narration from him, they were punished with hunger twice. From al-Hasan: the first punishment is the taking of zakat and the second is the punishment of the grave. From Ibn Ishaq: the first is their rage at the people of Islam and the second is the punishment of the grave. Perhaps the repetition of their punishment is because of the disbelief accompanied by hypocrisy, or the hypocrisy emphasized by their persistence in it.

It is permitted that "twice" be understood as multiplicity, as in His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿Then turn your gaze again, twice﴾, in view of His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿Do they not see that they are tested every year once or twice?﴾ ﴿Then they will be returned﴾ on the Great Day of Resurrection ﴿to a mighty punishment﴾ 101. This is the punishment of the Fire. The change in style, as has been said, is that the punishment mentioned earlier is attributed to the plural of majesty (nun of greatness), in keeping with the attribution of the knowledge mentioned before it, while the return to the later punishment is attributed to themselves. This signals that the two differ in state: the first is specific to them in occurrence and time, and Allah, glorified and exalted, undertakes it, while the second is general to the disbelievers in general in occurrence and time, though the levels of their punishment differ. It is not hidden that if the mighty punishment is interpreted as the punishment of the lowest level of the Fire, it would not include all the disbelievers. Yes, it includes only the hypocrites in general. It may be said: in the construction of ﴿they will be returned﴾ in the passive voice there is a degree of magnification that fits the mighty punishment, and therefore the composition was changed to it. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 102:**

﴿And others﴾ is an explanation of the state of a group of Muslims who were weak in resolve regarding the matter of the religion, and they were not hypocrites according to the sound view. It has been said: they were a group of the hypocrites, except that they were granted success in repentance, so Allah accepted their repentance. It has been said that it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate (khabar) is the clause ﴿they mixed﴾, which is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) with the implied ﴿qad﴾, and the predicate is the clause ﴿it may be that Allah﴾ etc. But the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun) hold that it is conjoined (ma'tuf) to ﴿hypocrites﴾, meaning: and among them, i.e., among those around you or among the people of Madinah, are others, a people ﴿who have admitted﴾, i.e., acknowledged with knowledge, ﴿their sins﴾, which are their staying behind from the military campaign, preferring ease over it,
[Page 12]
and their contentment with the evil company of the hypocrites. They did not offer the false excuses, confirmed with false oaths. They were, as al-Bayhaqi related in al-Dala'il and others, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both): "Ten men stayed behind from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the expedition of Tabuk. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was about to return, seven of them tied themselves to the pillars of the mosque. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) used to pass by them in the mosque when he returned. When he saw them he said: 'Who are these who have tied themselves?' They said: 'This is Abu Lubabah and his companions, who stayed behind from you, O Messenger of Allah, and they have sworn that they will not release themselves until you are the one who releases them.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'And I swear by Allah, I will not release them nor excuse them until Allah is the One who releases them.' So Allah revealed the verse. The Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) then sent to them, and he released them and excused them."

In another narration from him, they were three. Ibn Abi Hatim related from Zayd that they were eight. It has also been narrated that they were five. The narrations agree that Abu Lubabah ibn 'Abd al-Mundhir was among them. ﴿They mixed a righteous deed﴾, namely going out to fight with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), ﴿and another evil one﴾, namely staying behind from him (peace and blessings be upon him). This was related from al-Hasan and al-Suddi. And from al-Kalbi: the first is repentance and the second is sin. It has been said: the righteous deed encompasses all righteousness and obedience, and the evil deed is whatever is its opposite. The verb *khalata* (to mix) is the act of blending, and it requires something mixed and something it is mixed with. The first here is the first, and the second is the second, according to some. The *waw* (and) is with the meaning of *ba'* (with), as was related from Sibawayh in their saying: *ba'tu al-shah shatan wa-dirhaman* (I sold the sheep for a sheep and a dirham). This is of the category of metaphor, because *ba'* indicates attachment and *waw* indicates conjunction, and they are from one valley. The commentator of al-Lubab related from Ibn al-Hajib that the original form of the example is *ba'tu al-shah shatan bi-dirham*, meaning "together with a dirham." Then this usage became common, so the *ba'* of accompaniment was replaced by *waw*, and therefore what follows it must take the same case-ending as what precedes it, as in their saying: *kull rajulin wa-day'atuhu* (every man and his property). The excessive artificiality in this is not hidden.

Al-Zamakhshari mentioned that each of the two conjoined items is both mixed and that with which something is mixed, because the meaning is that each of them was mixed with the other, as in your saying: *khalatu al-ma'a wa-al-laban* (I mixed the water and the milk), meaning: I mixed each of them with its companion. In this there is something that is not in your saying: *khalatu al-ma'a bi-al-laban* (I mixed the water with the milk), because you have made the water the mixed item and the milk the thing mixed with. When you say it with *waw* and make the water and the milk both mixed items and things mixed with, it is as if you said: "I mixed the water with the milk and the milk with the water." The summary is that the thing mixed with in each of the two acts of mixing is the thing mixed in the other, because mixing, once it requires something mixed with, that is either the other or something else, and the second is ruled out by the basic meaning and by the context of the speech. When one says: "I mixed this and that," it means that each of them is mixed and that with which it is mixed, and this is more eloquent than saying "I mixed one of them with the other," because the latter has one act of mixing, whereas the *waw* has two acts of mixing.

It is objected that mixing one of two things with the other entails mixing the other with it, so in both the *waw* and the *ba'* there are two acts of mixing, and therefore there is no difference. It is answered that the *waw* explicitly indicates the two acts of mixing, unlike the *ba'*, so the difference is established. This answer concedes the premise of entailment. But it is not hidden that there is confusion in it, since it did not distinguish between mixing (*khalt*) and intermixing (*ikhtilat*). The truth is that the intermixing of one of two things with the other entails the intermixing of the other with it. As for mixing one of them with the other, it does not entail mixing the other with it, because mixing water with milk means that one intends the water first and makes it mixed with the milk. It is clear that this does not entail that one intends the milk first; rather, it negates it. On this basis, the meaning of mixing a righteous deed with an evil one is that they first did a righteous deed and then followed it with an evil one, and the meaning of mixing an evil deed with a righteous one is that they first did an evil deed and then followed it with a righteous one. To this the words of al-Sakkaki point, where he took the wording of the verse to be: "They mixed a righteous deed with an evil one and another evil deed with a righteous one," i.e., at one time they obeyed and nullified the obedience by a grave sin, and at another time they disobeyed and made up for the disobedience by repentance. This clearly indicates that the righteous deed
[Page 13]
and the evil deed in one of the two acts of mixing are other than those in the other act of mixing. The words of al-Zamakhshari clearly indicate that they are one and the same, and there is what there is in that. For this reason he preferred what al-Sakkaki went to. However, what he mentioned about nullification leans toward the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah (a theological school that held that grave sin nullifies good deeds). Some have claimed that what is in the verse is a type of rhetorical embellishment (badi') called *ihtibak* (concealment by implication), and the original would be: "They mixed a righteous deed with another evil one, and they mixed something with a righteous deed." But this is contrary to the apparent meaning.

Ibn al-Munir preferred that *khalt* (mixing) is here implicitly containing the meaning of *'amal* (doing), and that the change from *ba'* was for this reason, as if it were said: "They did a righteous deed and another evil one." I choose that *khalt* here means gathering (*jam'*). If the context and the occasion of revelation are taken into account, the intended meaning of the righteous deed is the acknowledgment of sins, namely the staying behind from the military campaign and what accompanied it. The evil deed is those sins themselves. The intended object of gathering, which is first in the sense of being joined (*al-muttawajjah ilayhi awwalan*), is the acknowledgment, and the expression of this by *khalt* is to indicate that this acknowledgment occurred in its complete form, so that it is as if it penetrated the sins and changed their character. If the occasion of revelation is not taken into account, it is permissible that by the righteous deed is meant acknowledgment of sins in general, and by the evil deed the sins in general, and the rest of the discussion stands as it is. It is also permissible that by the righteous deed and the evil deed is meant the good and bad actions that proceeded from them in general. Probably the intended object is preferable on this view as well, so that the righteous deed is included, because by adding it the door of goodness is opened. In a report: "Follow the evil deed with a good deed and it will erase it." Some have interpreted the good deed in this report in its general sense.

Ibn Sa'd related from al-Aswad ibn Qays, who said: "One day al-Hasan ibn 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with them both) met Habib ibn Maslamah and said: 'O Habib, how many a journey you have made not for the obedience of Allah!' He said: 'As for my journey to your father, it is not of that kind.' He said: 'Yes, but you obeyed Mu'awiyah for a small, passing worldly gain. So if he has stood by you in your worldly life, he has certainly sat you down in your religion. And if, when you did evil, you had done good, that would have been as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They mixed a righteous deed and another evil one﴾. But you are as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Nay, rather, what they used to earn has rusted over their hearts﴾.'" The expression by *khalt* at that time may be because of the alteration it contains as well. Perhaps by *khalt* is meant mere gathering without considering any priority between them. The expression by *khalt* is perhaps only to give notice of intermingling, since mere gathering does not require it. This interpretation is also suggested by what Abu al-Shaykh and al-Bayhaqi related from Mutarrif, who said: "I lie down at night on my bed and reflect on the Qur'an, and I present my deeds to the deeds of the people of Paradise. Their deeds are so exacting: they were few in the night who slept, they spent the night before their Lord prostrating and standing: ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing…﴾. Then I do not see myself among them. So I present myself to this verse: ﴿What has brought you into Saqar?﴾ ﴿They will say: 'We were not of those who prayed'﴾ up to His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and we used to deny the Day of Judgment﴾. Then I see the people as deniers, and I do not see myself among them. Then I pass by this verse: ﴿And others have admitted their sins﴾ etc., and I hope that I and you, O brothers, will be among them." Similarly, what they both and others related from Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi, who said: "There is no verse in the Qur'an dearer to me for this community than His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And others﴾ etc."

The apparent meaning is that the repentance of these others was not understood from it. Rather, the ruling understood from His saying, glorified is He: ﴿it may be that Allah will accept their repentance﴾ was established for them absolutely. Otherwise, this verse and many of the verses on this subject are equal. And more hopeful to me than these is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah; indeed Allah forgives all sins﴾. The well-known view is that the verse is understood to mean that, because repentance from Allah, glorified is He, means the acceptance of repentance, and this requires that it proceed from them. So it is as if it were said: "And others have admitted their sins; they mixed a righteous deed and another evil one; so they repented; it may be that Allah…" etc.

Some scholars made the admission an indication of repentance, probably because of the necessary connection between them by custom. Al-Shihab said: "Because it is repentance when it is accompanied by remorse and the resolve not to return." But in this there is the claim that this is a matter of the general and the specific, and they have mentioned that the general does not indicate the specific by any of the three kinds of indication. The word ﴿it may be﴾ (*'asa*) is for expressing hope, and it comes from the most generous of the generous. It is an obligation, and what an obligation!

﴿Indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ is a reason for what it implies of the obligation of acceptance. It is not the obligation that the Mu'tazilah speak of, as is not hidden. That is, He, exalted is He, is abundant in forgiveness and mercy, He overlooks the one who repents, and He bestows His favor upon him.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 103:

﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾ Ibn al-Mundhir and others reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that when they were released they set out and came with their wealth, saying: "O Messenger of Allah, these are our possessions; give charity from them on our behalf and seek forgiveness for us." Upon him be prayers and peace, he said: "I was not commanded to take anything from your wealth," and then the verse was revealed, and the Prophet, may Allah's prayers and peace be upon him, took a third of it, as occurs in some of the narrations.

The charity here is not the obligatory charity, I mean zakah, since he was commanded to take it. Rather, it is, as has been said, an expiation for their sins, as His words, Mighty and Majestic, indicate: ﴿to purify them﴾, that is, from the filth of staying behind with which they had defiled themselves. Al-Jubba'i reported that what is meant is zakah, and that he, upon him be prayers and peace, was commanded to take it here to remove the suspicion that they were linked with some of the hypocrites, for it was not accepted from them, as you know. The matter of purification is easy. In any case, the pronoun in "their wealth" refers to these who acknowledged their wrongdoing. It has been said that, on the second view, it refers to the owners of wealth in general. The plural "wealth" indicates that what is taken is from all kinds of property. The prepositional phrase "from their wealth" is connected to "take", and it may also be connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial qualifier of "charity". The "ta" in "tutahhiruhum" is for the second person address. It was also read with the jussive, on the basis that it is the answer to the imperative, and with the nominative, on the basis that the clause is a circumstantial qualifier of the subject of "take", or an attribute of "charity" with the implied "bi-ha" (by it), since what follows indicates it, or it is a resumptive clause, as Abu al-Baqa' said. It was also permitted, on the attributive reading, that the "ta" be for the third person and the feminine pronoun refer to "charity", in which case there is no need for "bi-ha". It was read as "tutahhiruhum" from "atharahu", with the meaning of "tahharahu". ﴿And purify them thereby﴾ with the affirmation of the "ya", and it is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the clause is a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun in the imperative or in its answer. It has been said that it is a resumptive clause, meaning: "And you purify them thereby", that is, you increase by that charity their good deeds and their wealth, or you exert yourself in purifying them. That the meaning is the elevation of their ranks from the ranks of the hypocrites to the ranks of the righteous and sincere is evident in that the people were hypocrites, while the correct view is otherwise. This is on the reading of the jussive in "tutahhiruhum". As for the reading of the nominative, "watuzakkihim" is conjoined to it. The apparent meaning of what is in al-Kashshaf indicates that the "ta" here is for the second person address and nothing else, because of His, glorified be He, words: "thereby". Taking it to mean that charity itself purifies them is far from the eloquence of the revelation. Maslamah ibn Muharib read "tuzakkihim" without the "ya". ﴿And pray for them﴾, that is, supplicate for them and seek forgiveness. The verb is transitive with "ʿala" because it implies the sense of bending over them, since it derives from the two prayers. Taking the lexical meaning here is what comes first to mind, and taking it to mean the funeral prayer is far-fetched, even though it was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. For this reason the verse is cited as evidence for the recommendation of supplicating for one who gives charity. Al-Shafiʿi recommended in its wording that one say to the giver: "May Allah reward you for what you have given, make it a purification for you, and bless what you have kept." Some said: it is obligatory for the imam to supplicate when he takes it. It was also said: it is obligatory in obligatory charity and recommended in voluntary charity. It was also said: it is obligatory for the imam and recommended for the poor. The correct view is that it is recommended in all cases. ﴿Indeed, your prayer is a comfort for them﴾ is a justification for the command to pray. "Sakan" means tranquility, and also that to which the soul finds rest, such as family and homeland, for example. On the first view, prayer itself is made the tranquility and assurance, as an intensification. On the second view, the meaning is to compare his prayer, upon him be prayers and peace, in being resorted to, with a dwelling place of rest. The first is preferable, that is: your supplication is one to which their souls find rest, and their hearts are reassured by it to the utmost, and they are confident that He, glorified be He, has accepted them.

Some of the seven readers read "ṣalawatika" in the plural, in consideration of the multiplicity of those for whom prayer is made. ﴿And Allah is All-Hearing﴾, who hears the acknowledgment of sin, the repentance, and the supplication. ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of what is in their hearts of regret and grief over what was neglected, and of sincerity in repentance and supplication.
Page 15

Or: All-Hearing, who answers your supplication for them; All-Knowing of what wisdom requires. The sentence in that case is a closing phrase that confirms the justification and establishes its content. On the first view, it is a closing phrase for the preceding two verses, confirming what is in them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 104:

﴿Did they not know﴾ The pronoun may refer to those who are forgiven, and the purpose is to establish the acceptance of their repentance in their hearts and to count their charities (ṣadaqāt) as valid. Or it may refer to others, and the purpose is to urge (taḥḍīḍ) them to repentance and charity and to encourage (targhīb) them toward both.

It has been read as (taʿlamū) with the letter tāʾ. On the first reading this is an iltifāt (shift of address), and on the second it is with the implied qul (say). It is also permitted that the pronoun refers to both the penitents and others, with the aim being only establishment and urging. Some scholars chose that it refers only to others, because it is narrated that when the repentance of these penitents was revealed, those among the rear-guard (mukhallafīn) who had not repented said: "These were with us yesterday; they were not spoken to nor sat with, so what is their situation today?" Then this was revealed. The practice of the majority indicates a preference for the first view, and this is what the context of the verse requires. As for the report, we have not found a chain of narration for it on which one can rely.

That is, did these penitents not know ﴿that Allah, He is the One who accepts repentance﴾ that is sound and sincere ﴿from His servants﴾ who are sincere in it? The transitive use of "accepts" with ʿan (from) is because it includes the sense of overlooking and pardoning, i.e., He accepts it while overlooking their sins from which they repented. It has been said that ʿan here means min (from), and the pronoun is either for emphasis, or the first part with the restriction means that Allah, glorified is He, accepts repentance and no other, i.e., He definitely does this, since the separating pronoun (ḍamīr al-faṣl) and the present-tense verb in its proper place convey this. Some scholars made the restriction relative to the Messenger (ﷺ), meaning that He, exalted is He, accepts repentance and not His Messenger (peace be upon him), because the frequency of people's returning to him could give rise to the assumption of that. The "servants" are either those penitents, and the use of the apparent noun in place of the pronoun indicates the cause implied by acceptance, or it is all of the servants, who enter into this by primary inclusion.

﴿And He takes the charities﴾ i.e., He accepts them as one accepts something in order to give back its equivalent. Here "taking" is a metaphor for accepting. It is also permitted that attributing "taking" to Allah, the Exalted, is a loose figurative usage (majāz mursal). It has been said that the attribution of taking to the Messenger in His words "Take (khudh)," then its attribution to His own Self, exalted is He, indicates that the Messenger's taking (peace be upon him) stands in place of Allah's taking, honoring the status of His Prophet (ﷺ), as in His words: ﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you, they are only pledging allegiance to Allah﴾. So it is in its literal sense. This is a good meaning, except that claiming literal sense involves what is not hidden. The preferred view according to me is that by taking charities is meant giving attention to their matter and their being placed by Him in a good position, and in the expression with it there is, as is not hidden, encouragement.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq narrated from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah, exalted is He, accepts charity when it is from good (wholesome) earnings, and He takes it with His right hand, and indeed a man gives in charity the like of a morsel, and it is nurtured for him just as one of you nurtures his foal or his colt, until it becomes like Uhud."
