Al-Daraqutni in al-Afrad narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Give charity, for indeed one of you gives a morsel or a thing, and it falls into the hand of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, before it falls into the hand of the beggar," then he recited this verse. Some narrations indicate that there is no literal taking: Ibn al-Mundhir and others narrated from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, no servant gives a charity of good earnings, and Allah accepts only what is good, and nothing good ascends to heaven but that it is placed in the right, and it is as if he places it in the hand of the Most Merciful, and He nurtures it for him just as one of you nurtures his foal or his colt, until the morsel or the date comes on the Day of Resurrection like a great mountain."

The confirmation of this in the Book of Allah, the Exalted, is His words: ﴿Did they not know that Allah accepts repentance...﴾ (the verse). The "al" in "al-ṣadaqāt" may be a replacement (ʿiwaḍ) for the pronoun of possession, i.e., "their charities," or it may be for the genus, i.e., the genus of charities into which their charities fall by primary inclusion, and this is what the apparent sense of the report requires.

﴿And that Allah, He is the Accepter of Repentance, the Most Merciful﴾ 104. This is an emphasis for what was conjoined to it, and an addition of affirmation to what it affirms, with an added meaning not in it. That is, did they not know that He, glorified is He, is the One specifically possessing, uniquely, the ultimate reach of acceptance of repentance and mercy, and that this is one of His affairs and a constant custom of His? Other views have been stated. The two clauses are in the accusative position governed by "ya'lamū," each of them filling the place of its two objects.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 105:

﴿And say: Work﴾ whatever deeds you wish, ﴿and Allah will see your deed﴾, whether good or evil. The sentence is a causal explanation (ta'lil) of what precedes it, or an emphasis (ta'kid) of what is derived from it of encouragement (targhib) and warning (tarhib). The sin (the letter س) is for emphasis, as we have established. That is, Allah, exalted is He, will certainly see it. ﴿And His Messenger and the believers﴾ is a conjunction (ʿatf) with the Majestic Name. The delay of the mention after the object is to indicate the difference between the two kinds of seeing. The meaning of seeing the deed, according to the majority, is to be informed of it and to know it with clear knowledge. Attributing this to the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, and to the believers is on the basis that Allah does not conceal that from them and informs them of it, either by revelation or by other means.

Ahmad and Ibn Abi al-Dunya in al-Ikhlas narrated from Abu Sa'id, from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who said: "If one of you were to work on a solid rock that has no door and no window, Allah would bring out his deed to the people, whatever it may be." The specification of the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, and the believers by mention in this respect is because they are the ones whom the addressees care to have informed about it. Some have interpreted "the believers" as the angels who record the deeds, but this is nothing. Similar to it, and even more calamitous and bitter, is what some of the Imamiyyah (Imami Shi'a) claimed: that they are the pure Imams. They narrated that the deeds are presented to them every Monday and Thursday after being presented to the Prophet ﷺ.

Some verifiers (muhaqqiqun) allowed that knowledge here may be a metonymy (kinayah) for requital, and that this is specific to the worldly, such as the display of praise and honor, for example, and not to the bad. It has been said that it is permissible to keep the seeing on what is understood from it. It has been objected that this entails the claim of seeing meanings, which is a strain, although with respect to Allah, exalted is He, it is not far-fetched. You know that among deeds are some that are customarily seen, such as movements, and there is no need for the aforementioned claim of entailment. Moreover, that entailment on the side of the conjoined element is not hidden in what it contains.

Ibn Abi Shaybah and others narrated from Salamah ibn al-Akwa' that "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited (fa-sayura Allahu ʿamalakum)," meaning: so He will make it manifest. ﴿And you will be returned﴾, that is, after death, ﴿to the Knower of the unseen﴾, and of it is what you will see of deeds, ﴿and the witnessed﴾, and of it is what you make apparent. In the mention of this title there is an amplification of the matter and an education in awe that is not hidden.

﴿Then He will inform you﴾, after the return, which is an expression for the extended affair, ﴿of what you used to do﴾ before that in the world. The informing (inba') is a figurative usage (majaz) for requital, or a metonymy (kinayah), that is, He will requite you according to that: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil. So in the verse there is a promise and a warning.

[Verse 9:106] "And others [are] deferred (wa-ākharūna) — a conjunction with the preceding "others" (ākharūna), meaning: and among them are other people, not the ones who confessed who were mentioned, [who are] deferred (murjawna), i.e., postponed, and their affair is left in suspense (mawqūf amruhum) li-amri Allāh — i.e., until the command of God Most High regarding them becomes manifest."

The people of Madina and Kufa, except Abu Bakr, read (murjawna) without hamza, and the rest read (murji'ūna) with hamza. Both are dialectal variants (lughatān): one says arja'tuhu and arjaytuhu, like a'taytuhu. It is possible that the yā' is a substitute for the hamza, as in their saying qara'tu and qaraytu, and tawaḍḍa'tu and tawaḍḍaytu, which is frequent in their speech. On the basis that it is an original root, it is from the y-root; and it has been said that it is from the w-root. From this root comes al-Murji'a (the Murjiʼa, Murjiah), one of the sects of the People of the Qibla, and it has come with both the hamza and its omission. They were named thus because they postponed (ta'khīrihim) sin from consideration in deserving punishment, since they said: there is no punishment with faith, so sin has no effect in their view. In al-Mawāqif they were named Murjiʼa because they defer action from intention (yarjūna al-'amal 'ani al-niyya), i.e., they postpone it in rank from it and from belief; or because they give hope (al-rajā') in their saying: no sin harms along with faith. End of quotation.

On the first two interpretations, it may be read with or without the hamza. As for the third, it should be said Murjiʼa with a fatha on the rā' and a shadda on the jīm. The intended referents of "those deferred," as in the two Ṣaḥīḥs, are Hilāl ibn Umayya, Ka'b ibn Mālik, and Murāra ibn al-Rabī', and this is related from Ibn ʻAbbās and the great Companions, may God be pleased with them all. They had stayed behind from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for a certain matter, with the intention of joining him (peace be upon him), but it was not possible for them, and their staying behind was not from hypocrisy — far be it from them, for they were among the sincere. When the Prophet (ﷺ) returned, and what happened among those who stayed behind happened, they said: "We have no excuse except our error," and they did not offer excuses to him (ﷺ), and they did not do as the people of the pillars did. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) ordered that they be shunned and made the matter severe upon them, as you will know, God willing, until there was revealed His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Certainly God has turned in forgiveness to the Prophet and the Emigrants and the Helpers﴾ etc. Their affair had been suspended for fifty nights, not knowing what God Most High would do with them. ﴿Either He punishes them or He turns in forgiveness to them﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: from among them, these are either punished or made subject to forgiveness.

It has been said: the predicate of (ākharūna) is that it is a subject (mubtada') and murjawna is its attribute; but the first is more apparent. As for "immā" being for classification (lil-tanwī') in the sense that their matter lies between these two affairs; and it has been said: for alternation (lil-tardīd) in view of corruption, and the meaning is: let their affair be with you between hope and fear. The intent is to commit that to the will and volition of God Most High, since it is not obligatory upon Him, glory be to Him, to punish the disobedient or to forgive the penitent. He was severe with them despite their sincerity, because jihad is a communal obligation (farḍ kifāya). This is what is related from Ibn Baṭṭāl in al-Rawḍ al-Unuf, and he approved it: that jihad was, for the Helpers specifically, an individual obligation (farḍ ʻayn), because they pledged allegiance to the Prophet (ﷺ). Do you not see the verse of their rajaz-poet at the Trench:

"We are those who pledged allegiance to Muhammad, to wage jihad as long as we live forever."

And these were among their noblest, so their staying behind was a grave matter. It is related from al-Ḥasan that this verse is about the hypocrites, and in that case "the others" does not refer to those we mentioned, since they are as you know; rather it refers to other hypocrites. On this view, the statement of the one who said regarding ﴿either He punishes them﴾ — i.e., if they persist in hypocrisy — should be the case, and you know that this contradicts what is in the two Ṣaḥīḥs. Carrying "hypocrisy" in the words of the speaker to what resembles it is far-fetched and an assertion without evidence.

﴿And God is Knowing﴾ of their conditions, ﴿Wise﴾ regarding what was done to them of deferment (al-irjā'). In the reading of ʻAbd Allāh: (Forgiving, Merciful).

[p. 18]

**﴿And those who took a mosque﴾** is coordinated (*'atf*, grammatical conjunction) with what precedes it, meaning: **﴿And among them are those who﴾**. It is also permitted that it be a subject (*mubtada'*, the topic of the sentence), whose predicate (*khabar*) is **﴿Is he then who founded﴾**, and the returning pronoun (*'a'id*) is omitted because it is known, meaning: *among them*. Or the predicate is omitted, meaning: *among those We have described*. And it is also permitted that it be in the accusative, governed by an implied verb, as in *"I condemn"* or *"I mean"*.

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read it without a *waw* (the conjunction "and"). In that reading the possibilities mentioned earlier apply, except coordination. It may also be a substitute (*badal*) for **﴿others﴾** according to the less preferred interpretation.

His words, glorified is He, **﴿harm﴾** (*diraran*) are an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*, the accusative of reason), and so is what follows it. It has also been said that it is a verbal noun (*masdar*) in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*), or a second object of **﴿took﴾**, on the basis that it means "made" (*sayyaru*). Or it is an absolute object (*maf'ul mutlaq*) of an implied verb, meaning: *they harm the believers by it, a harming*. And *dirar* is the seeking of harm and attempting it.

Ibn Jarir and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that a group of the Ansar were told by Abu 'Amir: "Build a mosque, and gather as much strength and weapons as you can, for I am going to Qayşar, king of the Romans, and I will bring an army of Romans and expel Muhammad (ﷺ) and his companions." When they finished their mosque, they came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "We have finished building our mosque, and we would love for you to pray in it and invoke blessing." Then this was revealed.

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayra (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "The people of the Mosque of Harm came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was preparing for Tabuk, and they said: 'O Messenger of Allah, we have built a mosque for the sick, the one in need, and the nights of rain and cold. We would love for you to come to us and pray in it for us.' He (ﷺ) said: 'I am on the verge of a journey and in a state of preoccupation,' or as he (ﷺ) said, 'If we return, if Allah wills, we will come to you and pray for you in it.' When he (ﷺ) returned from his journey and alighted at Dhu Awan, a town between him and Madinah, an hour into the day, news of the mosque reached him. He summoned Malik ibn al-Dukhshum, brother of Bani Salim ibn 'Awf, and Ma'n ibn 'Adiyy, and his brother 'Asim ibn 'Adiyy, one of Bal'ajan, and said: 'Go to this mosque whose people are wrongdoers, demolish it and burn it.' So they set out quickly until they reached Bani Salim ibn 'Awf, the kin of Malik. Malik said to his companion: 'Wait for me until I bring you a fire from my family.' He went into his household, took palm fronds, lit a fire in them, then they both came out running until they entered the mosque, while its people were inside. They burned it and demolished it, and they scattered away from it. And there was revealed concerning them what was revealed of the Qur'an."

The builders were twelve men: Khudham ibn Khalid of Bani 'Ubayd ibn Zayd, one of Bani 'Amr ibn 'Awf, and from his house the mosque was brought out; 'Abbad ibn Hunayf, also of Bani 'Amr ibn 'Awf; Tha'laba ibn Hatib; Wadi'a ibn Thabit, both of Bani Umayya ibn Zayd, the kin of Abu Lubaba ibn 'Abd al-Mundhir; Mu'attib ibn Qushayr; Abu Habiba ibn al-Az'ar; Harith ibn 'Amir and his two sons Mujammi' and Zayd; Nabil ibn al-Harith; Nijad ibn 'Uthman; and Bajdah of Bani Dubay'a.

Al-Baghawi mentioned, from a narration that al-Tha'labi mentioned, as al-'Iraqi said, without a chain of transmission, that after the mosque was burned and demolished, the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered that it be made a dumping ground where carrion, filth, and refuse would be thrown, as a humiliation to its people because they had taken it for harm.

**﴿and disbelief﴾**, meaning: *so that they might disbelieve in it*. Some scholars supplied the word "strengthening," meaning: *and the strengthening of the disbelief they conceal*. It was objected that disbelief is suitable as a cause by itself, so what is the need for the supplied word? It was answered that this may be because taking it was not itself disbelief, but what was said in it and what it contained was disbelief. So reflect.

**﴿and dividing the believers﴾**. They are, as al-Suddi said, the people of Quba', for they used to pray together in their mosque, so these people, out of envy, wanted them to split and their word to be divided.

**﴿and as an outpost﴾**, meaning: *a waiting and lying in ambush*. **﴿for whoever had warred against Allah and His Messenger﴾**, and this is Abu 'Amir, father of Handhala, "the washed one of the angels," may Allah be pleased with him. He had been a monk in the pre-Islamic period, wore woolen garments, and had become a Christian. When the Prophet (ﷺ) came to Madinah, Abu 'Amir said to him: "What is this religion you have brought?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The pure, white *hanifiyya*, the religion of Ibrahim (peace be upon him)." He said: "I am upon it." He (ﷺ) said to him: "You are not upon it." He said: "Yes, but you have introduced into it what is not part of it." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I have not done so, but I have come with it pure and white." Abu 'Amir said: "May Allah cause the liar among us to die alone and exiled." So the Prophet (ﷺ) said amen, and the people named him Abu 'Amir the Liar. The Prophet (ﷺ) named him the Corrupt. When the day of Uhud came, he said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "I find no people fighting you except that I fight you with them." He remained so until the day of Hunayn. When Hawazin were routed that day, he fled to al-Sham, and he sent to the hypocrites urging them to build a mosque, as we mentioned earlier from the scholar. They built it and remained waiting for his arrival, so that he could pray in it and prevail over the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Then it was demolished as has passed. Abu 'Amir died alone at Qinnasrin, and what they had concealed remained as regret in their hearts.

**﴿from before﴾** is related to *harab* (warred), meaning: *warred against Allah and His Messenger (peace be upon him) before this taking*. Or it is related to **﴿took﴾**, meaning: *they took it before they became hypocrites by staying behind, since they had built it before the Battle of Tabuk, as you have heard*. The purpose is to emphasize the condemnation.

**﴿And they will surely swear, "We intended only﴾**, meaning: *we did not intend by building this mosque* **﴿except the good﴾**, meaning: *except the good quality, which is prayer, the remembrance of Allah, and providing space for those who pray*. So *husna* is the feminine of *ahsan* (best), and originally it is an adjective of the quality, and it has come as an object of **﴿intended﴾**. It is also permitted that it stands in place of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: *the good intention*.

**﴿And Allah bears witness that they are indeed liars﴾**, concerning what they swore to.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 9, verse 108:**

﴿Do not stand﴾, i.e., for prayer, ﴿in it﴾, i.e., in that mosque, ﴿ever﴾. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that the explanation of ﴿do not stand﴾ is "do not pray", the standing being used metaphorically for prayer, as in their saying: "So-and-so stands the night (in prayer)." And in a hadith: "Whoever stands (in prayer) during Ramadan out of faith and seeking reward, his past sins will be forgiven."

﴿A mosque founded﴾, i.e., whose foundation was laid, ﴿on piety﴾, i.e., the piety of Allah, the Exalted, and obedience to Him. The particle ʿalā ("on") is used in its apparent sense. The emphasis in making piety itself the foundation is not hidden. It has also been said that ʿalā here means maʿa ("with"), and it has been said that it indicates causation, given the consideration of it in what preceded regarding the act of taking (the mosque as a place of harm). The lām (in *la-masjidun*) is either the lām of inception or the lām of oath, i.e., "By Allah, a mosque..." In either case, *masjidun* is the subject (mubtada'), and the clause after it is its description (sifah). The words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿from the first day﴾ are connected to *ussisa* ("was founded"), and *min* here indicates the starting point of time, as is the apparent meaning. In this there is evidence for the Kufans, who hold that *min* can indicate the starting point in general, not restricted to place. The Basrans disagreed, and they prohibited its use with time, restricting it to *mudh* and *mundhu*. They interpreted the verse as having an omitted noun (muḍāf), meaning "from the founding of the first day." Al-Zajjaj objected to this, and Abu al-Baqa' followed him, saying that this interpretation is weak, because the implied "founding" is not a place, so *min* could not indicate the starting point of a place in it. It is answered that their purpose in the interpretation was to avoid the view that it indicates the starting point of time, and that this has been achieved by that assumption. Nothing in their statements indicates that it indicates the starting point only in place. Al-Radi said: "I do not see in the verse and its like the meaning of starting point, because the intended sense of it is that the action is something extended, like travel or walking, and the noun governed by *min* is the starting point (as in: 'I traveled from Basra'), or that it is the origin of something extended (as in: 'I went out from the house'), since going out is not extended, and founding is neither extended nor the origin of something extended, but rather they are two events occurring after (*min*), and this is the meaning of *fi* ("in"). And *min* in adverbials often occurs with the meaning of *fi*." End of quotation.

Regarding the claim that founding is not the origin of something extended, there is clear objection. Yes, al-Allama al-Thani went to the possibility that it is an adverbial (zarfiyyah), and he has a point; in that case the argument is nullified, and the verse is not evidence for the Kufans. The truth is that many verses and Arabic speech bear witness to their view, and insisting on interpreting all of that is an unnecessary strain.

The words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿it is more worthy that you stand in it﴾: the predicate (khabar) of the subject, and *ahaqqu* is an elative (ism tafḍīl). The thing it is compared to is every mosque, or the mosque of harm (on the assumption), or the meaning is "it is, according to their claim." It has also been said that *ahaqqu* means *ḥaqīq* ("worthy"), i.e., that mosque is worthy that you pray in it. There is disagreement about what is meant by it. From Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak, it is the Mosque of Quba'. Reports have come about the merit of praying in it. Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Tirmidhi, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and Ibn Majah narrated from Usayd ibn Zuhayr, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said:
"Prayer in the Mosque of Quba' is like an 'umrah (lesser pilgrimage)." Al-Tirmidhi said: "We do not know anything from Usayd other than this hadith." Similar in meaning is what Ahmad and al-Nasa'i narrated from Sahl ibn Hunayf. Ibn Sa'd narrated from Zuhayr ibn Rafi' al-Harithi, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Whoever prays in the Mosque of Quba' on Monday and Thursday returns with the reward of an 'umrah."

A group held that it is the Mosque of Madinah, the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). They used as evidence what Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, al-Nasa'i and others narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "Two men disagreed about the mosque that was founded on piety. One of them said: 'It is the Mosque of Quba'.' The other said: 'It is the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).' So they came to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) and asked him about it. He said: 'It is this mosque of mine (ﷺ).' And he said: 'In it there is much good,' meaning the Mosque of Quba'." In several narrations it has come that he (peace be upon him) was asked about this and said: "It is my mosque, this one."

The first view was supported by saying that it is the more suitable in terms of context (siyaq) and what follows (liḥāq), and that it was built before the mosque of Madinah. Al-Sharif al-Samhudi combined the reports, and al-Suhayli preceded him in that, saying: "Each of the two mosques is intended, because each of them was founded on piety from the first day of its founding." The secret in the Prophet's (ﷺ) answer to the question with what is in the hadith is to remove what the questioner imagined, that this applied exclusively to the Mosque of Quba', and to highlight the distinction of this one over that. But after this combination it is not hidden that the apparent meaning of the hadith narrated by the group from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri is far from it. For this reason some of the researchers chose the second view and supported it by saying that the Mosque of the Prophet (ﷺ) is more worthy of the description of being founded on piety from the first day, and that the expression of "standing" for prayer in the words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿it is more worthy that you stand in it﴾ requires persistence, and this is reinforced by the emphasis of the prohibition with the words ﴿ever﴾. The Messenger's (peace be upon him) persistence in prayer was found only in his noble mosque (peace be upon him).

As for what al-Tirmidhi and Abu Dawud narrated from Abu Hurayrah, that the words of Allah, the Majestic and Exalted, ﴿in it are men who love to purify themselves﴾ were revealed concerning the people of Quba', who used to cleanse themselves with water, it does not contradict the explicit text of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). As for what Ibn Majah narrated from Abu Ayyub, Jabir and Anas, that "when this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'O assembly of the Ansar, Allah, the Exalted, has praised you well concerning purification. What is this purification of yours?' They said: 'We perform ablution for prayer and we bathe from impurity.' He said: 'Is there anything beyond that?' They said: 'No, except that when one of us goes out to relieve himself, he loves to cleanse himself with water.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'That is it, so keep to it.'" This does not indicate the exclusivity of the people of Quba', nor does it preclude interpreting it as referring to the people of his mosque (ﷺ) from among the Ansar.

I say: The reports concerning the revelation of this verse about the people of Quba' are numerous. Ahmad, Ibn Khuzaymah, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Hakim narrated "from 'Uwaym ibn Sa'idah al-Ansari that the Prophet (ﷺ) came to them in the Mosque of Quba' and said: 'Allah, the Exalted, has spoken well of you concerning purification in the story of your mosque. What is this purification with which you purify yourselves?' They mentioned that they wash their posteriors after relieving themselves."

Ahmad, Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Bukhari in his *Tarikh*, al-Baghawi in his *Mu'jam*, Ibn Jarir and al-Tabarani narrated similar from Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Salam, from his father. 'Abd al-Razzaq and al-Tabarani narrated from Abu Umamah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to the people of Quba': 'What is this purification with which you were singled out in this verse: ﴿in it are men who love to purify themselves﴾?' They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, none of us goes out from relieving himself except that he washes his place.'"

'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Harith ibn Nawfal something similar, along with other reports. The view that the verse was revealed concerning the people of Quba' is also reported from a group of the Companions and others, such as Ibn 'Umar, Sahl al-Ansari, 'Ata' and others. As for the reports indicating that the mosque mentioned in the verse is the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), they are also numerous, and likewise those who hold this view are numerous. In my view, combining the reports and the statements is impossible. I have nothing better than investigating the condition of those narrations, in terms of soundness and weakness. Whenever the strength of one of them over the other becomes evident, the stronger is relied upon.

The apparent meaning of some scholars' words suggests that the stronger narration is the one indicating that the intended mosque is the Mosque of the Messenger (peace be upon him). The meaning of its being founded on piety from the first day is that its foundation on that was from the first day of its existence, not something that arose after it. And it is impossible that "the first day" be taken in an unrestricted sense, by necessity. Yes, those who held that the mosque is the Mosque of Quba' said that "the first day" means the first days of the Hijrah and the entry into Madinah.

Al-Suhayli said: "From the verse is derived the correctness of what the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all, agreed upon with 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, when he consulted them about the calendar. Their opinion agreed that it should begin from the year of the Hijrah, because it was the time in which Allah honored Islam, the period in which the Prophet (ﷺ) was secured, the mosques were built, and Allah was worshipped as He should be. So their opinion agreed with the apparent meaning of the revelation. And we now understand from their transmission that the words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿from the first day﴾ mean that this day is the first day of the calendar by which we now date. If the Companions took it from this verse, then that is what we presume of them, because they are the most knowledgeable of people about the interpretation of the Book of Allah, the Exalted, and the most understanding of what it contains of allusions. And if that was by opinion and effort (ijtihad), then Allah, the Exalted, knew it and indicated its correctness before it was done, since it is not understood that someone says 'I did it on the first day' except with reference to a known year, a known month, or a known date. There is no reference here in meaning except to this known date, due to the absence of indicators pointing to anything else, whether by verbal or circumstantial context. So reflect on it; in it is a lesson for whoever takes heed, and knowledge for whoever sees with the eye of the heart and gains insight." End of quotation.

It is not hidden from one who is knowledgeable in history that what occurred was by ijtihad, and that his statement "there is no reference here..." etc. is open to question. It is also derived from the verse, as has been said, the prohibition against praying in mosques built for boasting, showing off, reputation, or for a purpose other than seeking the Face of Allah, the Exalted. Every mosque built with impure wealth is also included in this.

It is reported from Shaqiq what supports this. It is also reported from 'Ata' that when Allah opened the cities to 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, he ordered the Muslims to build mosques, and not to take two mosques in one city, one of which harms the other.

Whoever understands the purification in it as what the earlier reports have spoken of says: From it is derived the recommendation (sunnah) of cleansing with water (istinja' bil-ma'). A report from al-Bazzar explains it as combining water and stone, which is better than limiting oneself to one of them. Some explained it as purification from sins and blameworthy qualities, which is a metaphorical meaning for it. And when it is explained as including purification from major impurity and filth, and freedom from sins and the like, there is much praise in it.

Regarding the clause ﴿in it are men﴾, three possibilities have been allowed: that it is a new independent clause explaining the worthiness of standing in that mosque by way of the situation (ḥāl), after explaining the worthiness by way of the place; or that it is a description of the subject (mubtada'), coming after its predicate; or that it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in *fīhi* ("in it"). In every case, it contains confirmation and establishment of the entitlement to standing in it. And it was read as *an yaṭṭahharū* with idgham (assimilation of the two identical letters).

﴿And Allah loves those who purify themselves﴾ 108: i.e., He is pleased with them, honors them, and magnifies their reward. This is what is meant by Allah's love according to the Ash'aris and their followers. They mention that true love cannot be attributed to Him, the Glorified, and some of them interpreted the expression of love here as a case of *mushakala* (rhetorical correspondence). The intended meaning of "those who purify themselves" is either those men, or the category, and they include them in it.

﴿Is he who laid the foundation of his building﴾, i.e., its structure (*mabniyyahu*). It is a verbal noun (*masdar*) like *al-ghufran* (forgiveness), used in the sense of the passive participle. It is reported from Abu 'Ali that *al-bunyan* is a plural whose singular is *bunyanah*. Perhaps he meant that it is a collective noun (*ism jins jam'i*) whose singular is what has been mentioned; otherwise it is nothing. *Al-ta'sis* (laying the foundation) is placing the *asas* (foundation), which is the base and beginning of the building. It is also used in the sense of making firm (*al-ihkam*), and some have interpreted it here in this sense. Others preferred the first interpretation because of the use of *'ala* (upon) in His words, exalted is He, ﴿upon piety from Allah and approval﴾, since the apparent connection is that it is linked to it. It has been permitted that it be linked to an omitted element that serves as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the implicit pronoun in *assasa*, but this is contrary to the apparent meaning, as is not hidden. The meaning of *al-ridwan* (approval) is seeking it through obedience, metaphorically. If you wish, you may assume an elided genitive (*mudaf*) so that the two conjoined items are both deeds of the servant. The interrogative *hamzah* is for denunciation, and the *fa'* is for coordination with an omitted element, as they said about its counterparts, meaning: "Is it so far from what is known of their state that he who laid the foundation of his building upon piety and fear of Allah, the Exalted, and sought His good pleasure through obedience..."

﴿is better, or he who laid the foundation of his building upon the brink of a crumbling bank?﴾ i.e., its edge. From this comes *ashfa 'ala al-halak*, meaning he came to the edge of destruction. *Shafa al-mari*d (the sick man recovered) because he came to the edge of recovery and safety. It is dual as *shafawan*. *Al-jurf* with two *dammas* is a well that has not been lined with masonry. It is said that it is a precipice and what the flood carries away from the valleys, because the water erodes it, i.e., eats it and removes it. Abu Bakr, Ibn 'Amir and Hamzah read ﴿jurfin﴾ with the lighter pronunciation, and this is a dialectal variant of it. ﴿Crumbling﴾ means split, overhanging, on the verge of falling. It is said: fallen. It is an adjective of *jurf*. Its original form is *hawirun* or *hayirun*, so it is inverted (*maqlub*), and its pattern is *fali'*. It is said that its middle radical was elided irregularly (*i'tibatan*), so its pattern is *fal*, and its inflection is on its *ra'*, like *bab*. It is said that there is neither inversion nor elision in it, and its origin is *hawrun* or *hayrun*, on the pattern *fi'l* with a kasra on the middle radical, like *katif*. When the weak letter became vocalized and the letter before it was vowelled with a fatha, it was changed to an *alif*. The apparent point is that the brink of the precipice was placed in opposition to piety in the preceding part. Here there is an explicit, actual metaphor (*isti'arah tasrihiyyah tahqiqiyyah*), in that falsehood and hypocrisy were likened to the brink of a crumbling precipice in their lack of stability, and then this was borrowed for that. The opposing indicator is present. His words, exalted is He, ﴿so that it collapsed with him into the fire of Hell﴾, are a supporting element (*tarshih*). The *ba'* in *bihi* is either for transitivity or for accompaniment. The brink was placed in opposition to good pleasure to alert that the foundation of that is on a matter that protects its holder from what he fears and conveys him to what is the least of its requirements, Paradise. The foundation of this on what is on the verge of falling into the Fire, moment by moment, and then the inevitable return to it, is what is intended. The metaphor in what precedes is implicit (*makniyyah*), in that piety was likened to the foundations of construction, a likeness hidden in the mind, indicated by what is among its attendants and concomitants, namely laying the foundation and the building. Several scholars have chosen that the meaning of the verse is: "Is he who laid the foundation of the building of his religion upon a firm base, which is piety, and sought approval through obedience, better, or he who laid it upon the weakest and most slack of bases, which led him, because of its frailty and his lack of firm grip, to fall into the Fire?" It is said that this interpretation was chosen because it is more suitable for describing the people of the mosque of harm (*masjid al-dirar*) as causing harm to the Muslims, disbelief, division and ambush, and for describing the people of the mosque of piety as those who love to purify themselves. This is based on the view that the intended purification is from sins and blameworthy traits, because the requirement, according to some, is the love of Allah, exalted is He, not the purification mentioned in the reports. The matter of the metaphor according to this interpretation is in the same manner as in the first interpretation. It has been permitted that in the first clause there is an allegory (*tamthil*) for the state of one who is sincere to Allah, exalted is He, and performs righteous deeds, by the state of one who built a firm building in which he dwells and by which he is protected. It has also been permitted that *al-bunyan* is an original metaphor (*isti'arah asliyyah*) and *al-ta'sis* a supporting element (*tarshih*) or a subordinate metaphor (*tab'iyyah*). Likewise, an allegory has been permitted in the second clause, and its application there is evident after considering its application to its counterpart. The subject of *inhara* (collapsed) is either the pronoun referring to the building, with the pronoun in *bihi* referring to the one who laid the foundation, or it refers to the brink, with the pronoun in *bihi* referring to the building. The apparent meaning of the exegesis mentioned just above inclines to the latter.

The apparent meaning of the reports is that when that mosque collapsed, it fell into the Fire. Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Qatadah that he said about the verse: "By Allah, it did not stop short of falling into the Fire. It was reported to us that a patch of ground in it was dug, and smoke was seen rising from it."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated the like of it from Ibn Jurayj. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi that he said concerning it: "It proceeded, when it was swallowed up, into the Fire." And from Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah: it is said that it is a patch of the fire of Hell.

You know that I, praise be to Allah, Exalted, believe in His power, glorified is He, in the most perfect manner, and that He, may His majesty be exalted, is the doer of whatever He wills. But I do not believe in such outward reports unless there comes a sound report from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Nafi' and Ibn 'Umar read ﴿ussisa﴾ in the passive voice in both places. It was also read as *asasu bunyanihi* and *ussu bunyanihi* in the genitive construction. This is attributed to 'Ali ibn Nasr. It was read as *asas* with fathas, and this is attributed to 'Asim. It was read as *isas* with a kasra. It has been said that all three are plurals of *ussun*, but this is open to question. In *al-Sihah* it is stated: *al-ussu* is the base of a building, and so is *al-asas*, and *al-asas* is a shortened form of it. The plural of *al-ussu* is *asas*, like *'ussun* and *'issas*. The plural of *al-asas* is *ussus*, like *qadhal* and *qudhul*. The plural of *al-ussus* is *asas*, like *sabab* and *asbab*, end of quotation.

It has been permitted that *ussus* in ﴿ussusin﴾ is a verbal noun. 'Isa ibn 'Amr read ﴿wa-taqwan﴾ with tanwin. Ibn Jinni explained this by saying that the *alif* is for lengthening (*ilhaq*), as in *arta* which was lengthened to match *ja'far*, not for feminization, like the *alif* in *tatra* in *ra'a*. Otherwise its tanwin would not be permitted. Ibn Mas'ud read: ﴿so that its foundations collapsed with him into the fire of Hell﴾. ﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ (108), i.e., to their own detriment, or those who place things in other than their proper places. That is, He guides them to what is good for them with guidance that is necessarily effective.

[Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 110 (part 1 of 2):]

﴿Their building which they built will never cease to be a cause of doubt in their hearts.﴾ That is, their building (bina'uhum) which they built. Here al-bunyan is a verbal noun (masdar, the infinitive form of the verb) used in the sense of the object built, as has already been explained. He described it with a singular form, which conflicts with the claim that it is a collective noun (jam'iyyah). Likewise, the predicate about it in His words, glorified is He, ﴿a doubt in their hearts﴾, has the same problem. Taking the noun as having an implied genitive construction (taqdir mudaf), or making the adjective and likewise the predicate refer to a noun understood from it, goes against the apparent meaning. Yes, it has been said: the statement that it is "a doubt" does not prove that it is not a collective noun, because one says: "The walls are collapsed (munhadimah) and the mountains are firmly fixed (rasiyah)." Some scholars allowed that al-bunyan remains a verbal noun, with ﴿which﴾ (alladhi) as its object, and that al-rayba (doubt) is a noun derived from al-rayb, meaning suspicion (al-shakk). Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, explained it this way. What is meant is their doubt about his prophethood (ﷺ), which is hidden within their hearts, and this is the very hypocrisy (nifaq). The building itself has been made to be the doubt, for the sake of emphasizing that it is the cause of it. Al-Imam (al-Razi) said: There are several explanations for this:

First: The hypocrites greatly rejoiced in its construction. When he (ﷺ) commanded its destruction, it weighed heavily upon them, their rage increased, and their doubt about the prophethood of the Prophet (may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him) grew.

Second: When he (ﷺ) commanded its destruction, they thought that this was out of envy, so their sense of security regarding him (ﷺ) was lost, and their fear increased. They doubted whether they would be left in their state or whether an order would be given to kill them and seize their wealth.

Third: They believed that they had done good in building it, so when he (ﷺ) was ordered to destroy it, they remained in doubt and uncertainty about the reason for which he was commanded to do so.

The correct view is the first.

It is possible, as the scholar al-Tibi said, to prefer the second view by understanding al-rayba in its original meaning, and what is meant by it is the restlessness (qalaq) and agitation of the soul.

The meaning in summary: The demolition of their building, which they built, will not cease to be a cause of restlessness, agitation, and fear in their hearts. He described their building with what He described it with in order to indicate the manner in which they built it and founded it, according to what it is founded upon, as you know, and to point to the reason for the ruling. It has also been said: It was described in this way to show that what is meant by "the building" is the thing that is actually built, and not the plans they devised, since the word "builder" (banna') is sometimes used for planning and arranging a matter. This is as in their saying: "I build (kam abni) and you demolish," and in the line of verse:

When will the building ever be completed? When you build it while another demolishes it.

The summary is that the description serves to emphasize, and its purpose is to block a figurative reading (majaz). This is similar to what they said about His words, glorified is He: ﴿And Allah spoke to Moses directly﴾. There is some discussion about this.

The exception in His words, the Exalted: ﴿unless their hearts are cut to pieces﴾ is either from the most general of times or the most general of states, and what follows it is in the accusative position as an adverb of time (zarf). That is: their building will continue to be a doubt at every time except the time when their hearts are cut to pieces, or in every state except the state of their being cut, that is, their being separated and removed from the capacity to perceive. This is a metaphor (kinayah) for the firm establishment of doubt in their hearts, which are the seat of perception and of concealing polytheism, such that it does not leave them as long as they are alive, unless their hearts are cut and separated, and at that point the doubt leaves them and disappears. This is stated as an image and a hypothetical assumption. It has been said: What is meant by the cutting is what happens at death, namely the separation of the parts of the body in actuality, and this was related from some of the early generation (salaf). Ibn al-Mundhir and others transmitted from Ayyub who said: 'Ikrimah used to recite: "Unless their hearts are cut to pieces in their graves." It has also been said: What is meant is: unless they repent and feel a great remorse that breaks their hearts and their livers apart, so the cutting is a metaphor or figurative expression for intense regret. Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted this from Sufyan. The verb "taqatta'a" is from the form (tafa''ala) with one of the two taa's (the second one is removed), and the verb is in the active voice, that is, "tatqatta'a." It is also read as "tuqatta'a," in the passive voice of the intensive form (tafil), and as an active form of the same intensive verb, on the basis that the address is to the Messenger (ﷺ), meaning: unless you (ﷺ) cut their hearts by killing them. It is also read in the passive voice from the triliteral form, both with a masculine and feminine subject.

Al-Hasan read "ila an taqta'a" with the address form. In the reading of 'Abd Allah (ibn Mas'ud): "wa law quttti'at qulubuhum," with the verb in the passive voice attributed to their hearts. From Talhah: "wa law qatta'ta qulubahum," with the address to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It is also valid to take the address as directed to every addressee. Likewise, the pronoun in "taqatta'a" with the accusative "qulubahum" may be taken as referring to the doubt. Allah is All-Knowing of all things, among which is what has been mentioned of their states, ﴿All-Wise﴾ in all His acts, among which is His command, glorified is He, which was revealed concerning them.

* * *

Furthermore, from the sphere of allusive interpretation (ishara) regarding the verses: ﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah: "If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity and surely be among the righteous."﴾ This is an allusion to the description of the deluded ones who have not tasted the flavor of love, and upon whom the breeze of gnosis (irfan) has not blown. For this reason they set their own standards for their actions and said: "We will surely give charity." ﴿But when He gave them of His bounty, they became stingy with it﴾, that is, they broke the covenant as soon as what they had asked for appeared to them. Stinginess, as Abu Hafs said, is abandoning generosity at the time of need for it. ﴿Do they not know that Allah knows their secret﴾, which is what they do not know about themselves, ﴿and their private conversation﴾, that is, what they know of it apart from the people. It has been said: The secret is what only the Knower of secrets is aware of, and private conversation is what the guardian angels are made aware of. ﴿And they said: "Do not go out in the heat." Say: "The Fire of Hell is far more intense in heat."﴾ They intended to discourage the believers by explaining some hardships of military campaigns, and they did not realize that the lover finds bitterness sweet in seeking union with the beloved, sees sorrow as easy, and finds hardships to be delights in that pursuit. There is no good in one whom heat or cold prevents. He answered them by saying that by opposing the Messenger they chose the Fire, which is far more intense in heat. The hypocrites in this discouragement resemble the idle people who discourage travelers on the spiritual path from journeying by explaining the hardships of the path and the loss of worldly pleasures. ﴿But the Messenger and those who believed with him strove with their wealth and their selves﴾, so they spent all of that in seeking their Lord, may His majesty be exalted. ﴿And for them are the good things﴾, the direct witnessings (mushahadat), the unveilings (mukashafat), and the nearnesses (qurubat). ﴿And they are the successful﴾, those who attain the desired goal.

﴿There is no blame upon the weak﴾, that is, those whom the burden of love has weakened, ﴿nor upon the sick﴾ with the illness of longing, to the point that their bodies have melted,

[Page 25]

from the heat of disbelief and the hardships of spiritual discipline (riyadah), ﴿nor upon those who find nothing to spend﴾, and they are those who are stripped of the worlds of existence (akwan), ﴿there is no fault (haraj)﴾, meaning sin, in remaining behind from the lesser struggle (jihad al-asghar), ﴿when they are sincere to Allah and His Messenger﴾ by guiding the creation to the truth. ﴿And among the Bedouin are those who regard what they spend as a loss﴾, a penalty and a ruin. It has been said: Everyone who considers possession to belong to himself will regard what he spends as a loss, and everyone who considers things to belong to Allah, the Exalted, and that they are on loan to him, will regard what he spends as a gain. ﴿And the foremost, the first (al-sabiqun al-awwalun)﴾, that is, those who preceded to unity from among the people of the first category, ﴿among the Emigrants (muhajirin)﴾, and they are those who abandoned the dwelling places of the soul, and the Helpers (ansar), and they are those who supported the heart with true knowledge against the soul. ﴿And those who followed them﴾ in taking on the attributes of the Truth, ﴿in good conduct (bi-ihsan)﴾, that is, with a witnessing among the witnessings of beauty and majesty. ﴿Allah is pleased with them﴾ for what He gave them of His ultimate goal and His success, ﴿and they are pleased with Him﴾ by accepting what He commanded, glorified is He, and by spending their wealth and their lives in His way, may His dignity be exalted. ﴿And He has prepared for them gardens﴾ from the gardens of acts and attributes, ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾, and these are the rivers of the sciences of trust in God (tawakkul) and contentment (rida) and the like. Beyond these shared gardens among those who are linked together lies the Garden of the Essence (jannat al-dhat), which is specific to the foremost.

﴿And others have acknowledged their sins﴾, and they are those in whom the disposition of sin has not taken firm root, and in whom the light of readiness (isti'dad) remains. For this reason their obstinacy was softened, they acknowledged their sins, and they saw their ugliness. As for one in whom the disposition of sin has taken firm root, and whom the darkness has overcome, he sees none of the foul deeds he commits except as good. ﴿They mixed a righteous deed with another evil one﴾, since they were at the level of the self-reproaching soul (al-nafs al-lawwamah), whose connection with the heart has not yet become a disposition for it, and whose illumination by its light has not yet become a settled state. For this reason it sometimes obeys the heart and does righteous deeds, which happens when the heart has gained control over it, and at other times it turns away from the heart and commits evil deeds when it is veiled from the heart by its own darkness. It remains always between this and that until its connection with the heart grows strong, and this becomes a disposition for it. At that point its state becomes sound and it is saved from transgressions. Perhaps His words, glorified is He: ﴿Perhaps Allah will turn to them in forgiveness﴾ are an allusion to this. Yet the dark dispositions may pile up upon it, so it regresses, its readiness disappears, it is veiled from the lights of the heart, and it plunges down into the prison (sijjin) of nature, and perishes along with the perishing. The tipping of one side over the other comes about through companionship. If success overtakes it, it accompanies the righteous, is adorned with their characteristics, does their deeds, and becomes one of them. If abandonment overtakes it, it accompanies the corrupters and mixes with them, becomes stained by their qualities, and does their deeds, and becomes one of the losers. May Allah protect us from that. How excellent is the saying of the one who said:

Hold fast to the masters of hearts, for whoever comes to be attached to the masters of hearts becomes a leader.
And beware lest you be content with the companionship of one deficient, for you would fall in rank from your height and be belittled.
So from that point Abu Mazzamil's lowering rose high, clarifying my words, urging and warning.

The inclination toward the side of connection may also come about through other causes, as His words, glorified and exalted is He, indicate: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them and cause them to grow﴾. This is because wealth is the material of desires. So He commanded the Prophet (ﷺ) to take from it, so that the first state of theirs would be detachment, in order that the powers of the soul be broken, its desires and attributes weakened, and it be purified from the dark dispositions and cleansed from the filth of sins and the impurity of the promptings of Satan. ﴿And pray for them﴾ by supporting their resolve and pouring out the lights of companionship. ﴿Indeed, your prayer is a source of tranquility for them﴾, that is, a cause for the descent of serenity (sakinah) upon them. They explained serenity as a light that settles in the heart, by which one remains steadfast in turning toward the Truth and is freed from frivolity. ﴿A mosque founded on piety from the first day is more worthy that you stand in it﴾, because the soul is affected in it by the purity of the time, the goodness of the state, and the taste of ecstatic feeling (wijdan), unlike when it is built upon the opposite of that, for then the soul is affected in it by turbidity, division, and constriction.

The root of this is that the world of dominion (ʿālam al-mulk, the visible world) is under the control and subjugation of the world of the unseen realm (ʿālam al-malakūt, the invisible world). Therefore, the intentions and dispositions of souls must have an effect on the deeds they perform. Do you not see how the Kaʿba was honored and magnified, and made a place of blessing, because it was built by the hand of the Friend of God (Khalīl Allāh), upon him be blessings and peace, with a sincere intention and a noble soul? We also find the effect of purity and inner unity (jamʿiyyah) in some places and locales, and the opposite in others. I mean only that this is found by those with sensitive, pure souls. Otherwise, wicked souls find the matter the reverse of what the possessors of those souls find. The person with bile disorder (al-ṣafrāwī) finds sugar bitter, and the dung beetle (al-juʿl) finds the scent of the rose foul. Hence, the hypocrite in the mosque is like the fish on dry land, and the sincere believer in it is like the fish in water. ﴿In it are men who love to purify themselves﴾, that is, people of will and effort in purifying themselves from sins. This is an indication that the companionship of the righteous has a great effect. What is derived from this and what precedes it is an indication that one should observe both the place and the companions in attaining inner unity. The scholars (al-qawm, i.e., the Sufis) have also said that one must observe this together with observing the time in attaining what has been mentioned. ﴿And God loves those who purify themselves﴾. If His love for them were not so, they would not love that.

From Sahl: purity has three aspects: the purity of knowledge from ignorance, the purity of remembrance from forgetfulness, and the purity of obedience from disobedience. Another of them said: purity has many divisions. So: the purity of the secret (al-isrār) from passing thoughts (al-khaṭarāt), the purity of the spirits from heedlessness, the purity of the hearts from desires, the purity of the intellects from ignorances, the purity of the souls from disbelieving tendencies, and the purity of the bodies from slips. Another said: complete purity is the purity of the secret from the defilement of other-than-God.

And God, Exalted, is the One who guides to the straight path.

[Page 27]

﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their properties, for that they will have Paradise﴾ etc. This is an exhortation to the believers to engage in jihad, by describing the state of those who stay behind from it. And, as al-Shihab (al-Khafaji) relates, there is no more excellent or eloquent exhortation to jihad than what is in this verse, because it is presented in the form of a contract whose party is the Lord of Majesty, may His majesty be exalted, and whose price is "what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived." He did not make the object of the contract merely their being killed, but also their being killers, for the exaltation of Allah's word and the victory of His religion, glory be to Him. He also made it recorded in the heavenly books, and what a deed (ṣakk, a written document) that is. He made His promise a truth, and none is more faithful to his promise than the One who makes it. Thus His deferred payment is stronger than the cash payment of others. He also pointed to the profit and great success in it. This is a metaphorical allegory (istiʿāra tamthīliyya, a metaphor in which a whole scene is depicted).

He depicted the believers' jihad, their spending of their wealth and their lives in it, and Allah's rewarding them for that with Paradise, in terms of buying and selling. He said, glory be to Him, ﴿they fight﴾ etc., as an explanation of the place of handing over, which is the battlefield. To this refers the saying of the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him: "Paradise is under the shade of the swords." Then He confirmed it, may His majesty be exalted, by saying ﴿That is the great triumph﴾. From here the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, gave great attention to the meaning of this verse. Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, who said: This verse, ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased﴾ etc., was revealed to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, while he was in the mosque. The people gathered in the mosque, and a man from the Ansar came, folding the two ends of his cloak over his shoulder, and said: "O Messenger of Allah, has this verse been revealed?" He said: "Yes." The Ansari said: "A profitable sale; we will not cancel it nor ask to cancel it."

Some people explained the aspect of the emphasis (of this verse) thus: He, glory be to Him, expressed His acceptance from the believers of their lives and their properties, which they spent in His cause, and His rewarding them by setting Paradise as their price through the image of buying, by way of an indirect metaphor (istiʿāra tabaʿiyya, a metaphor in which the verb or its root is borrowed). Then He made the object sold, which is the main purpose and goal of the contract, the believers' lives and properties, and the price, which is the means in the transaction, Paradise. He did not reverse this by saying: "Allah has sold Paradise to the believers in exchange for their lives and properties," to show that the purpose of the contract is Paradise, and what the believers spend in exchange for it is a means to it, with the utmost care for them and their wealth. Then, He, exalted be He, did not say "for Paradise," but said, may His dignity be exalted, ﴿for that they will have Paradise﴾, to emphasize the arrival of the price to them and its being specifically theirs, as if it were said: "[Their price is] Paradise, which is established for them and specifically theirs." From here it is known that this reading is more eloquent than the reading of al-Aʿmash. It is also attributed to ʿAbd Allah (ibn Masʿud), may Allah be pleased with him, with "for that they will have Paradise," because it accords better with the occasion of revelation.

Ibn Jarir related from Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi and others that they said: "ʿAbd Allah ibn Rawaha said to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him: 'Stipulate for your Lord and for yourself whatever you wish.' He said: 'I stipulate for my Lord that you worship Him and not associate anything with Him, and I stipulate for myself that you protect me from what you protect yourselves and your wealth from.' They said: 'And what is for us?' He said: 'Paradise.' They said: 'A profitable sale; we will not cancel it nor ask to cancel it.' Then ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased﴾ was revealed, to the end of the verse."

It has also been said: He expressed it thus to praise the believers, that they spent their lives and their properties merely on the basis of the promise, out of their complete trust in His promise, may He be exalted. And the completion of the metaphor depends on this, for if it had said "for Paradise," it could have been understood that the purchase is in its literal sense, since Paradise is fit to be a counter-value, unlike a promise of it. This was objected to: The basis for the indication of the promise in the sublime composition is not that it is a circumstantial clause introduced by "that" (an), for that has nothing to do with indicating the future. Rather, it is Paradise, whose existence in the world is impossible. Even if it were granted that the counter-value is the Paradise promised, not the promise itself, the claim that the purchase could be literal if it were said "for Paradise" is also open to question, as has been said, because the literal sense of buying is not valid for Him, exalted be He, since He is the Owner of all things, and buying is only from one who does not own. Hence the jurists said: "Seeking to buy invalidates the claim of ownership." Yes, it may not invalidate it in some cases, such as when a father buys a house for his young son from himself, and the son grows up without knowing, then the father sells it and hands it to the buyer, then the son asks to buy it from him, and then he learns what his father did and claims the house. His claim is accepted, and that request does not invalidate it, as the words of al-Astrushani imply. But this does not harm us in what we are discussing.

Some scholars explained the indication of the promise in the noble composition by saying that it necessarily implies, by its explicit meaning, the absence of handing over, and that is the very promise. For when you say, "I bought from you such-and-such for such-and-such," it may mean cash payment. Unlike when you say, "for you is such-and-such," which means "such-and-such is owed by me and in my liability." The lām here is not for ownership, since it would not fit to buy what is already his own with his own property, like the dowry in the case of one of the two servants (a saying meaning the dowry is an obligation). So it is for entitlement, and it implies that there is no receipt.

As for the completion of the metaphor depending on this, it also has a basis, since the intended metaphor is the allegorical metaphor (istiʿāra tamthīliyya). For otherwise it would be valid to make "buying" a figure for "exchange," for example, which is not worth considering, given that the allegory achieves eloquence and subtle meanings, as is well known. However, you should know that the discussion here is still not free from examination. From what we have pointed out of the excellence of allegory, it is known that the view which takes the metaphor or the metonymy (majāz mursal) in "purchased" alone is inferior, as some have held.

As for His saying, ﴿they fight in the cause of Allah﴾: it has been said that it explains the place of handing over, as indicated above, because the sale was completed, as al-Tibi and others said. It has also been said that it explains what the purchase was for, as if, when He said ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased﴾ etc., it was asked: "Why did He do that?" and it was answered: "So that they fight in His cause." It has also been said that it explains the sale which the purchase mentioned requires, as if it were asked: "How do they sell their lives and properties for Paradise?" and it was answered: "They fight in His cause, glory be to Him, and that is a giving of their lives and properties toward Him, and an exposing of them to destruction."

It has also been said that it explains the purchase itself. And it has been said that it mentions some of what the preceding statement included, for its importance. The meaning of that is that He purchased from the believers their lives by spending them in righteous deeds, and their properties by giving them up in what pleases Him. In all of this, it is a report in form and meaning, and it has no place in the grammatical structure (i'rab). It has also been said that it is in the sense of a command, like His saying, ﴿and strive with your wealth and your lives﴾. This is justified by saying that the present tense is used after the past tense to indicate continuity, as if it were said: "I purchased from you your lives in eternity, and I gave their price, Paradise, so hand over the object sold and continue in fighting." What is in some of these views of examination is not hidden. Consider whether there is an obstacle to making the sentence in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), as if it were said: "He purchased that from them while they are fighting in His cause." I have not found anyone who explicitly stated this, although it is the most suitable of the views for the allegorical metaphor. Reflect.

His saying, glory be to Him, ﴿so they kill and are killed﴾, is an explanation that fighting in the cause of Allah, Exalted, is giving up one's life, and that the fighter in His cause gives it up, even if he remains safe and victorious. For the attribution in the two verbs is not by way of requiring that both be combined, nor by way of requiring that one of them must definitely occur. Rather it is by way of ascribing the state of some to all, for fighting is realized from all, whether both acts occur, or one of them occurs from them or from some of them. Indeed, it is realized even if neither of them occurs from them, as when there is striking (in battle) but no killing from either side. The words of some of them imply that jihad is realized by mere determination, by setting out, and by increasing the numbers, even if there is no striking. This is not far-fetched, since it also involves exposing oneself to destruction. And apparently the rewards of the mujahidin differ in quantity and quality, even if there is a common measure among them. In Sahih Muslim, the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, said: "No raiding party that raids in the cause of Allah and obtains booty fails to receive two-thirds of its reward in this world, while one-third remains for them. And if they obtain no booty, their reward is complete for them." In another narration: "No raiding party or detachment that raids and returns safely fails to have received two-thirds of its rewards in advance, and no raiding party or detachment that is struck down and wounded fails to have its rewards completed."

Some claimed that they are equal in reward, and that their reward is not diminished by booty. They based this on what is in the two Sahihs, that the mujahid returns with what he gained of reward and booty, and on the fact that the people of Badr obtained booty and they were who they were. This is answered by saying that the report in the two Sahihs is unrestricted, while the report of Muslim is restricted, so the unrestricted must be read in light of the restricted. Also, no text has come concerning the people of Badr that, had they not obtained booty, their reward would have been of the same measure as theirs, and they only obtained booty. And that they were who they were does not necessarily mean that there is no rank beyond their rank that is higher than it. The claim that in the chain is Abu Hani', who is unknown, so his report should not be relied upon, is a gross error, for he is a well-known trustworthy narrator from whom al-Layth ibn Saʿd, Hayway, Ibn Wahb and many other imams related. His reliability is sufficiently established by Muslim's citing him in his Sahih. Similar to this is what al-Qadi related from some of them, that the hastening of two-thirds of the reward is only in booty taken in an improper manner, for if it were so, there would not be a third of the reward. Likewise is what has been said, that the hadith is to be understood as referring to one who went out with the intention of both fighting and booty, for that certainly reduces his reward. The correct view, therefore, is that the reward of one who did not obtain booty is greater than the reward of one who did, in accordance with what we have mentioned, which agrees with the explicit well-known sound hadiths from the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them.

From this it is known that the reward of one who is killed is greater than that of one who kills, because the former is among the martyrs and the latter is not. The apparent meaning of what Muslim related from Abu Hurayrah is: "Whoever is killed in the cause of Allah, Exalted, is a martyr, and whoever dies in the cause of Allah, Exalted, is a martyr." That is, being killed in the cause of Allah and dying in it are equal in reward. This accords with the meaning of His saying, Exalted: ﴿And whoever leaves his home emigrating to Allah and His Messenger, then death overtakes him, his reward has already become due from Allah﴾. Some scholars also argued for this with other things that do not indicate it, as al-Nawawi, may Allah have mercy on him, explicitly stated. The placing of the state of being killers before the state of being killed in the verse is to signal that there is no difference between them in being instances of giving up one's life in fighting. The verb of the passive form was read by Hamza and al-Kisa'i with the passive verb placed first (﴿they are killed and kill﴾), in observance of the fact that martyrdom is well established in this domain, and to signal that they are not concerned with death in the cause of Allah, but rather that it is dearer to them than safety, as Kaʿb ibn Zuhayr said about them:

They do not rejoice when their spears attain a people,
though they are not captives (or: though they are not pursued).
When they are attacked, the spear strikes only their chests,
and for them there is no cry of lamentation at the watering places of death.

[Continuing from part 1]

It is also said that this indicates their boldness, in that they did not break down because some of them were killed. Some people answered the question by saying that the order is not observed in this reading, since the particle *wa* (and) does not require order. This was objected to on the grounds that this does not help, because placing first what should come later in eloquent speech does not happen merely for the safety of the commander, as is well known. ﴿A promise binding upon Him﴾ (*wa'dan 'alayhi*) is an emphatic infinitive (*maṣdar mu'akkid*) confirming the meaning of the sentence, because the sense of the purchase, that for them is Paradise, is a promise to them of it in return for striving in the way of Allah, glorified is He. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿truly﴾ (*ḥaqqan*), is a qualifier of it, and ﴿'alayhi﴾ (upon Him) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) relating to ﴿truly﴾, because it precedes it. His saying, glorified is He: ﴿in the Torah, the Gospel and the Qur'an﴾ is connected to an omitted element that stands as a qualifier of *wa'dan* as well, meaning: a promise established in the Torah and the Gospel just as it is established in the Qur'an. The purpose is to join what is not known to what is known, since it is known that this ruling is established in the Qur'an. Then, what is in the two Books is either that Allah, exalted is He, purchased from the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) their selves and their wealth in exchange for that, or that whoever strives with his self and his wealth has that reward. In both matters there is an established ruling consistent with what is in the Qur'an. It is also permitted for the preposition phrase to be connected to *ishtarā* (He purchased), *wa'dan* (a promise), and *ḥaqqan* (truly).

﴿And who fulfils his covenant better than Allah?﴾ is a parenthetical interjection confirming the content of what precedes it, regarding the reality of the promise. What is intended by such a construction, by custom, is the negation of equality, meaning: no one is like Him, exalted is He, in fulfilling His covenant. This is like saying: "There is no one in Medina more knowledgeable in jurisprudence than so-and-so," for it conveys, by custom, that he is the most knowledgeable of its people. There is no hiding what is implied by making the promise a covenant and a binding pact, in terms of giving great attention to its matter.

﴿So rejoice﴾ is a shift to the second-person address to them, for added honour. *Istibshār* (rejoicing) is the manifestation of their joy. The *sīn* in it is not for requesting (*ṭalab*), and the *fā'* (so) is for the sequence of it, or the sequence of the command to it upon what precedes it, meaning: since it is so, then show your joy in what you have attained of Paradise. He, glorified is He, said ﴿in your bargain﴾ (*bi-bay'ikum*) even though the delight in it is in view of its leading to Paradise, because the purpose is to encourage them to striving, which He expressed as a sale. The contract was not mentioned under the heading of a purchase because that comes from Him, glorified is He, and not from them, and encouragement, as is said, is only complete in what comes from them. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿which you have contracted﴾ (*alladhī bāya'tum bihi*) is for added emphasis on their sale, and to indicate its distinction over others, for it is the sale of the perishable for the everlasting. Also, both exchanges belong to Him, glorified and exalted is He. For this reason, al-Ḥasan (al-Baṣrī) used to say when he recited the verse: "Selves, which He created; and wealth, which He provided."

﴿And that﴾, i.e., the sale which you were commanded to make, ﴿is the great triumph﴾ (111), than which there is no greater triumph. What is in that of distance indicates the distance of the rank of what is referred to, and the loftiness of its status in perfection. The sentence is an elevating confirmation that establishes the content of the preceding command. It is also possible that it is an elevating comment on the noble verse, and a reference to Paradise, which was made the price in exchange for what they expended of their selves and wealth. In that is the magnification of the price, and from it the state of the thing priced is known.

It is transmitted from al-Aṣma'ī that he recited for al-Ṣādiq, may Allah be pleased with him, [poetry]:

I barter with the precious self, its Lord (its owner),
for there is none in all creation equal to it (in value).
I buy with it the Gardens, if I sell it
for something other than it—indeed that is a loss.
If my self departs for a worldly thing I have obtained,
then it has departed from me, and the price has departed too.

It is well known from him, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Your bodies have no price except Paradise, so do not sell them except for it." This clearly indicates that the thing sold is the bodies. Some eminent scholars also stated this in their glosses on the commentary of al-Bayḍāwī (d. 685 AH), where he said: "Allah, exalted is He, purchased from the believer, who is an expression for the enduring substance, whose body is its vehicle and instrument." The apparent meaning is that by the enduring substance he meant the specific immaterial substance, namely the rational soul. But it is not hidden that the majority of theologians hold the denial of immaterial substances and the rejection of the rational soul, and that the human being is this sensible frame. On this basis, some eminent later scholars among the recent learned men refuted the view of the creation of acts, because of what it entails: that the agent and the recipient would be one, and they have held that the unity of the two is impossible. The fair position is to affirm something distinct from the body and from the sensible frame in the human being. The thing sold is either that, and the meaning of selling it is exposing it to perils and removing it from its specific attachment to the body; or it is the body, and the meaning of selling it is apparent, except that one may claim that what is understood from "self" is other than that, as is not hidden from those of pure souls.

[Page 30]

**Ruh al-Ma'ani** of al-Alusi, commentary on Surah 9, verse 112:

﴿The ones who repent﴾ is a qualifying description (*na't*) of "the believers," or a case of *qat'* (a shift in grammatical case) for the purpose of praise. That is, they are "the ones who repent." This is supported by the reading of Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) and Ubayy (ibn Ka'b), *al-ta'ibin* with a *ya'* (the genitive/accusative plural form), which indicates that it is either accusative for praise or genitive as a qualifier of "the believers."

It is also permitted that *al-ta'ibun* be the subject (*mubtada'*) with an omitted predicate (*khabar*), meaning: "They too are among the people of Paradise, even if they did not fight, because of His saying, ﴿And to each Allah has promised the best [reward]﴾, for *kullan* (each) is general, and *al-husna* means Paradise."

It has also been said that the predicate is His saying, ﴿the worshippers﴾, and what follows it is a predicate after a predicate. It has also been said that its predicate is ﴿those who enjoin good﴾. And it has been said that it is an apposition (*badal*) of the pronoun in ﴿they fight﴾. The first view is the most apparent, except that under it, the one promised Paradise is the fighter who possesses these attributes, not every fighter. This is indicated by what Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he said: "The martyr is the one who has the nine characteristics," and he recited this verse.

It has been objected that this contradicts what is authentically reported in the hadith of Muslim, that "whoever is killed in the way of Allah, while he is patient, seeking reward, advancing and not turning his back, his sins are expiated, except for debt." For this shows that the fighter may not possess all the qualities mentioned in the verse; otherwise there would be no sense in the expiation of sins. It is perhaps from here that al-Zajjaj chose that it is a subject with an omitted predicate, as you have heard, since in the verse according to this view there is good news for all fighters in general of what has been mentioned, which is what is understood from the apparent meanings of the reports. Indeed, many of them indicate that the merit mentioned concerning the fighters is specific to those who fight so that the word of Allah may be supreme, and that whoever fights for worldly gain and reputation deserves the Fire. Sahih Muslim contains what implies this, so let it be understood.

The intended meaning of "the repentant," as reported by Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and others from al-Hasan and Qatadah, is those who repented from polytheism and did not behave hypocritically. Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from al-Dahhak that they are those who repented from polytheism and sins. This is supported by the fact that "the repentant" is in the sense of "those who repent," which is a general expression that encompasses every repentant person, so restricting it to one who repents from some sins is arbitrary. It is answered that mentioning them after the mention of the hypocrites clearly indicates that repentance is taken to mean repentance from disbelief and hypocrisy. Also, if repentance were taken to mean repentance from sins, the attributes mentioned afterwards would not be of complete benefit, especially since the one who possesses these attributes is apparently one who avoids sins.

The intended meaning of "the worshippers" is those who perform worship in its proper manner. Al-Hasan said: "They are those who worship Allah at all times.
