By Allah, it is not a month or two months, nor a year or two years, but as the righteous servant said: ﴿and He has enjoined upon me prayer and zakah as long as I remain alive﴾." Qatadah said: "They are a people who took from their bodies in their night and their day."

﴿The ones who praise﴾, i.e., those who praise Allah in every state, as has been reported from more than one of the early generations. So *al-hamd* (praise) here means describing Him with beauty in general. It has been said that it means gratitude, so it would be in contrast with a blessing, i.e., "those who are grateful for His blessings." You know that praising Him in every state is better, and in it there is emulation of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Ibn Mardawayh, Abu al-Shaykh and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* reported from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "The first to be called to Paradise will be the praisers, who praise (Allah) in times of ease and hardship." It has also come from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "When something came to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, that pleased him, he would say: 'Praise be to Allah, through whose blessing good deeds are completed.' And when something came to him that he disliked, he would say: 'Praise be to Allah in every state.'"

﴿The ones who travel﴾, i.e., those who fast. Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with them, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked about it and he answered with what has been mentioned. A large number of the Companions and Successors also adopted this view.

It has come from Aisha: "The travelling of this community is fasting." This is a metaphor, because fasting restrains one from desires, just as travel generally prevents them. Or it is because it is a spiritual discipline through which much of the states of the dominion and the kingdom of the unseen are revealed. So the attainment of these is likened to the attainment of distant lands and places, since the disciplined ascetic continually progresses from station to station and enters from cities of knowledge to one city after another upon the steeds of thought. Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Zayd that the travellers are the emigrants, and there is no travelling in the community of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, except emigration.

He and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ikrimah that they are seekers of knowledge, because they travel the earth to seek it. It has also been said that they are the fighters, based on what al-Hakim reported and authenticated, and al-Tabarani and others reported from Abu Umamah, that "a man asked the permission of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to travel, and he said: 'The travelling of my community is struggle in the way of Allah.'" The preferred view is the one previously mentioned, as we indicated. The travelling was not interpreted in its well-known sense because it is a type of monasticism (*rahbaniyyah*), which is forbidden, and it was, as Ibn Jarir reported from Wahb ibn Munabbih, among the Children of Israel.

﴿The ones who bow and prostrate﴾, i.e., in the obligatory prayers, as reported from al-Hasan. So bowing and prostration are in their literal meaning. Some have made them an expression for prayer, since they are its greatest pillars, so it is as if it were said: "those who pray."

﴿Those who enjoin good﴾, i.e., faith, ﴿and forbid evil﴾, i.e., polytheism, as reported from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, concerning both matters. If the wording of the sublime text were left in its general sense, it would have a valid meaning. Indeed, it has been said that this is preferable. The conjunction here, according to what is in *al-Mughni*, is due to the fact that enjoining and forbidding, as such, are opposites, unlike the rest of the attributes, because the one who enjoins good also forbids evil, and evil is the abandonment of good, and the one who forbids evil also enjoins good. So attention is drawn to the importance of each of the two qualities, and that what is achieved within the other is not sufficient for it. Its summary, as it has been said, is that the conjunction is due to the opposition between them, or to remove ambiguity.

Some scholars explained this by saying that there is a mutual implication between them in mind and in external reality, because commands include prohibitions, and an opposition apparently, because one is a demand for an action and the other a demand for abstention. So they were between perfect connection and separation, which calls for conjunction, unlike what precedes them.

It has also been said that the conjunction is to indicate that they are in the status of one single quality, as if it were said: "those who combine the two attributes." This is refuted by its literal sense, since ﴿the ones who bow and prostrate﴾ are also in the status of one single quality, so conjunction should have been used for them too, since its meaning is "those who combine bowing and prostration." This is answered with slight consideration.

As for the conjunction in His glorified saying: ﴿and those who guard the limits of Allah﴾, i.e., in what He has explained and specified of realities and laws, it has been said that it is for signalling that the count has been completed with the seventh, since seven is the complete number, and the eighth is the beginning of another count joined to it. For this reason it is called the *waw al-thamaniyah* (the conjunction of eight). Abu al-Baqa and others who affirmed the *waw al-thamaniyah* inclined to this view, but it is a weak opinion that the grammarians did not accept, as Ibn Hisham explained in detail. Its verification will come, if Allah the Exalted wills. It has also been said that it is to alert to the fact that what precedes is a detailed list of virtues, and this is its summary, meaning that it is a mention of a general matter encompassing what precedes it and other things. Something like this is introduced with conjunction, as in: "Zayd, Amr and all his tribe are generous." Because of the difference between summary and detail, and between generality and specificity, it was conjoined to it. It has also been said that it is conjoined to what precedes it, the commanding and forbidding, because whoever's deeds do not confirm his words, his commands are of no benefit, and his prohibitions are not an effective restraint.

Some scholars said: The intended meaning of guarding the limits is its apparent sense, which is the establishment of the prescribed punishment, such as retaliation, upon the one who deserves it. The earlier attributes, up to His glorified saying "those who enjoin," are praiseworthy qualities of the person in himself, while these are for him in relation to others. Therefore the expression of the two categories differs: the conjunction is omitted in the first category and used in the second. And since the first must be united in one thing, the conjunction was omitted in them due to the strength of their connection, unlike these, since it is permissible for their doers and those they relate to to differ. This is the motive for parsing ﴿the ones who repent﴾ as a subject described by what follows it, with ﴿those who enjoin﴾ as its predicate. It is as if it were said: "They are the perfect in themselves, who perfect others." The first is placed first because the one who perfects others is not able to perfect them unless he is perfect in himself. By this the composition aligns most fittingly without strain. This is a sound reason for the conjunction in some items and its omission in others. However, what is transmitted from the early generations, such as Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and others, is interpreting "those who guard the limits of Allah" as "those who uphold His obedience, glorified is He," and this contradicts what is in this explanation. Perhaps the matter here is easy, and Allah the Exalted knows best what He means.

﴿And give good news to the believers﴾ (112), i.e., to those described by those sublime attributes. Placing "the believers" in the place of their pronoun is to alert that the criterion of the matter is faith, and that the complete believer is the one who is like this. The omission of what the good news is about is an indication that it is a sublime matter that the scope of explanation cannot encompass.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 113:

﴿It was not [fitting]﴾: that is, it was not valid in the judgment and wisdom of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and it was not proper, ﴿for the Prophet and those who believe﴾ in Allah, the Exalted, in the manner commanded, ﴿to ask forgiveness for the polytheists﴾ before Him, glorified is He, ﴿even though they be near relatives﴾: that is, the polytheists are relatives of theirs. The answer to (law, "even if") is omitted, because of what precedes it indicating it, and the clause is conjoined to another clause before it that is omitted by a regular ellipsis, meaning: "even if they were not near relatives, and even if they were such." ﴿After it has become clear to them﴾: that is, to the Prophet, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, and to the believers, ﴿that they﴾ (that is, the polytheists) ﴿are the companions of the Blazing Fire﴾ (113), by their dying in disbelief, or because revelation came down that they are sealed upon their hearts and will never believe at all. In this is evidence for the validity of asking forgiveness for those of them who are still living, about whom there is no certainty of their hearts being sealed. What is meant by it, concerning them, is the request for their being granted success in faith. It was said that it necessarily implies this by way of implication, so it should not be said that there is no benefit in seeking forgiveness for an unbeliever. According to the sound view, the verse was revealed concerning Abu Talib, for Ahmad, Ibn Abi Shaybah
Page 33
al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il, and others narrated from al-Musayyab ibn Hazn, who said: "When death approached Abu Talib, the Prophet, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, entered upon him, and with him were Abu Jahl and Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayyah. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: 'O uncle, say: There is no god but Allah, so that I may plead for you with it before Allah.' Abu Jahl and Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayyah said: 'O Abu Talib, will you turn away from the religion of Abd al-Muttalib?' The Messenger of Allah, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, kept presenting it to him, while Abu Jahl and Abd Allah kept repeating that statement to him. Abu Talib said, as the last thing he said to them: 'He is upon the religion of Abd al-Muttalib,' and he refused to say: 'There is no god but Allah.' The Prophet, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, said: 'I will certainly ask forgiveness for you as long as I am not forbidden from you.' Then it was revealed: ﴿It was not [fitting] for the Prophet﴾," and the verse.

Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl found this unlikely, since the death of Abu Talib was about three years before the Hijrah, while this surah is among the last of what was revealed at Medina. al-Wahidi said: This unlikelihood is itself unlikely. What harm is there in saying that he, peace be upon him, kept asking forgiveness for Abu Talib from that time until the revelation of the verse, for severity toward the disbelievers appeared only in this surah? A similar view was mentioned by the author of al-Taqrib. According to this, his words "then it was revealed" in the report do not mean that the revelation came immediately after the statement, but rather that this was the cause of revelation, so the fa' in it indicates causation, not sequence. Many of the eminent scholars relied on this interpretation, and it is a sound interpretation, except that it is troubled by what Ibn Sa'd and Ibn Asakir narrated: "From Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, who said: I informed the Messenger of Allah, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, of the death of Abu Talib, and he wept. He said: 'Go, wash him, shroud him, and bury him; may Allah forgive him and have mercy on him.' I did so, and the Messenger of Allah, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, kept asking forgiveness for him for days and did not leave his house until Gabriel, peace be upon him, descended to him with this verse: ﴿It was not [fitting] for the Prophet﴾," and so on. For this clearly indicates that the revelation was before the Hijrah, since the not leaving the house is limited by it. Unless it is said that the hadith is weak, but we have not seen anyone address it. The better answer to the basic unlikelihood is to say: that this surah is among the last revealed in terms of the majority is as mentioned before, and so it does not preclude that some of it was revealed at Medina. And the verse according to this is evidence that Abu Talib died a disbeliever, which is the well-known position of the People of the Sunnah and the Community.

Ibn Ishaq narrated in his Sirah, from al-Abbas ibn Abd Allah ibn Ma'bad, from some of his family, from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, in a long report: "That the Prophet, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, said to Abu Talib during his final illness, when he was hoping for him: 'O uncle, say it, that is, there is no god but Allah, so that I may use it to gain intercession for you on the Day of Resurrection.' He, peace be upon him, urged him to this. He said: 'By Allah, O nephew, were it not for the fear of reproach upon you and upon the sons of your father after me, and that Quraysh would think I said it out of fear of death, I would have said it, and I say it only to delight you with it.' When death drew near to Abu Talib, al-Abbas looked at him moving his lips, so he leaned his ear to him and said: 'O nephew, my brother has said the word that you ordered him to say.' The Prophet, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, said to him: 'I did not hear it.'" He relied on this and similar verses of his poetry, which contain acknowledgment of the truth of what he, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, brought, his intense tenderness toward him, and his support for him, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace. The Shi'ah, who hold that he died a believer, relied on this, and they said: "This is what is narrated from the People of the House, and the People of the House know best." You know the strength of the proof of the Community. So relying on what is narrated from Ibn Abbas to the exclusion of it is something that would make the bereaved laugh. The verses, in their chains of transmission, are cut off, and in them there is no uttering of the two testimonies, which is the axis around which faith revolves. Intense tenderness and support are things no one denies, but they are far from what we are discussing. The reports of the Shi'ah from the People of the House are weaker than a spider's house, and indeed it is the weakest of houses. Yes, it is not fitting for a believer to delve into this, just as one should not delve into the rest of the disbelievers of Quraysh, such as Abu Jahl and his like,

Page 34

for he has a distinction over them through the noble deeds he did with the Messenger of Allah, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace. It has been narrated that this benefited him in the Hereafter; will it not benefit him in this world through restraint from him and not treating him as one treats other disbelievers? From Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, that he heard the Messenger of Allah, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, say, when his uncle was mentioned in his presence: "Perhaps my intercession will benefit him on the Day of Resurrection, so that he will be placed in a shallow fire." It has come in another report that "it was said to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace: 'Your uncle Abu Talib used to protect you and support you; will that benefit him?' He said: 'Yes, I found him in the depths of the Fire and brought him out to a shallow fire.'" Reviling him is, in my view, very blameworthy, especially if it harms some of the 'Alawis, for it has been reported: "Do not harm the living by reviling the dead," and "Part of the goodness of a person's Islam is leaving what does not concern him."

Some claimed that the verse was revealed concerning something else. For al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il and others narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "One day the Prophet, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, went out to the graves, and came until he sat by one of them, and he conversed with it for a long time, then wept, so we wept at his weeping. Then he stood and prayed two rak'ahs. Umar came to him and called him, then called us, and said: 'What made you weep?' We said: 'We wept at your weeping.' He said: 'The grave I sat beside is the grave of Aminah, and I asked my Lord for permission to visit her, and He permitted me; and I asked Him for permission to ask forgiveness for her, and He did not permit me, and He revealed to me: ﴿It was not [fitting] for the Prophet﴾,' and so on. So I was seized by what a child feels for his mother of tenderness, and that is what made me weep." It is not hidden that the sound view regarding the cause of revelation is the first. Yes, the report about seeking permission to ask forgiveness for his mother, peace be upon him, and that permission was not granted, comes in a sound narration, but there is nothing in it that this was the cause of revelation. Muslim, Ahmad, Abu Dawud, Ibn Majah, and al-Nasa'i narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, came to the grave of his mother and wept, and made those around him weep. Peace be upon him, he said: 'I asked my Lord for permission to ask forgiveness for her, and He did not permit me; and I asked permission to visit her grave, and He permitted me. So visit the graves, for they remind you of death.'" Some used this report and similar ones as evidence that his mother, peace be upon him, is among those for whom forgiveness is not sought. There is a well-known dispute among the scholars about this, and perhaps the discussion will lead to establishing the truth in it, God willing.

The commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 114 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Nor was the plea for forgiveness by Abraham for his father﴾ Azar, by his saying: ﴿"And forgive my father"﴾, meaning: by his asking that He grant him guidance to faith and guide him to it, as is indicated by the reason given in His saying: ﴿"Indeed, he was among the misguided"﴾. The sentence is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) to confirm what preceded and to dispel what appears, on the surface, to be a contradiction. Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn 'Asakir narrated, through the chain (tariq) of Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna, from 'Amr ibn Dinar, who said: "When Abu Talib died, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: 'May Allah have mercy on you and forgive you. I will not cease to ask forgiveness for you until Allah forbids me.' So the Muslims began to ask forgiveness for their dead who had died while they were polytheists. Then Allah revealed: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists﴾ — the verse. They said: 'Abraham asked forgiveness for his father.' So He, glory be to Him, revealed: ﴿Nor was the plea for forgiveness by Abraham for his father except because of a promise﴾."

Talha recited: (wa-ma istaghfara) and, on his authority, (wa-ma yastaghfiru), as a narration of a past state. It does not mean that the seeking of forgiveness will occur after the Day of Resurrection, as might be supposed from what will come, if Allah wills.

The exception (istithna') is "detached" (mufarragh) from the most general category of causes: that is, his, peace be upon him, seeking forgiveness for his father did not arise from anything except a promise (mawi'dah). ﴿He had promised him﴾, that is, Abraham (peace be upon him) had promised ﴿him﴾, that is, his father, by his saying: ﴿"I will surely ask forgiveness for you"﴾, and his saying: ﴿"I will ask my Lord to forgive you"﴾. Thus the promise came from Abraham, peace be upon him.

This is supported by what was narrated from al-Hasan, Hammad al-Rawiya, Ibn al-Sumayqa, Ibn Nahik and Mu'adh al-Qari, that they recited (wa-'adaha abahu) with the single letter ba' (b). This was counted among the three letters which Ibn al-Muqaffa' altered in the Qur'an, [Page 35] which is not to be heeded after the recitation of more than one of the early generations (salaf) with it, even though it is irregular (shadhdha).

The overall meaning of the verse: "It was not for you to ask forgiveness after it had become clear. Abraham's seeking forgiveness, peace be upon him, was only because of a promise made before it became clear." Its implication is that Abraham's seeking forgiveness, peace be upon him, took place before it became clear. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿So when it became clear to him﴾, that is, to Abraham, peace be upon him, ﴿that he﴾, that is, his father, ﴿was an enemy of Allah﴾, that is, persistent in his enmity toward Allah, may He be exalted, and his non-belief in Him. This happened by revelation to him, peace be upon him, that he was obstinate in disbelief.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and a group narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that this clarification came through his father's death in disbelief, and Qatada held this view. It has been said that the more fitting interpretation, given the description of enmity, is the first, though the matter is not critical.

﴿He disassociated himself from him﴾, that is, he cut off the bond between himself and him. The intended meaning is that he kept himself far from seeking forgiveness for him and withdrew from him entirely. In this there is an emphasis that is not present in merely leaving it or similar expressions. ﴿Indeed, Abraham was a man of much supplication (awwah)﴾, that is, he was greatly given to sighing (ta'awwuh). According to a group, this is a metaphor (kinaya) for perfection of tenderness and softness of heart.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and others narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn Shaddad, who said: "A man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what is the awwah?' He said: 'The humble one, who is submissive and frequently supplicates.'"

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam that it is "the one who supplicates, humbling himself before Allah, like the sick man groaning from his illness," and this is close to what preceded. It was also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, Mujahid, Qatada, 'Ata', al-Dahhak and Ikrima that it means "the certain one" (al-muqin) in the language of Abyssinia (al-Habasha). From 'Amr ibn Shurahbil, it is "the merciful" in that language. Ibn Mas'ud gave an unqualified interpretation of it as this. From al-Sha'bi, it is "the one who glorifies (al-musabbih)". Al-Bukhari, in his Tarikh, narrated that it is "the one whose heart is attached to Allah, may He be exalted". Al-Bayhaqi, in Shu'ab al-Iman, and others narrated from Ka'b that Abraham was described as awwah because whenever he mentioned the Fire, he would say: "Uff (awwah) from the Fire!"

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Abu al-Jawza' something similar. When the interpretation of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of it is authentic, it is not proper to deviate from it. Yes, what the majority held is not inconsistent with it, and its relevance to our subject is evident, as is clear. Many have stated explicitly that awwah is an intensive form (fa''al for mubalagha) from ta'awwuh, and that the analogous form of its verb would be triliteral, because the patterns of intensive nouns are generally derived from it. Qutrub related for it a triliteral verb, saying: "It is said: 'Ah (ah) yu'uh (ya'uh), like qama yaqum, uhan (uhan).'" Others denied this against him and said: "It is only said awwaha and ta'awwaha." Al-Muthaqqab al-'Abdi said: "When I rise, saddling her in the night, she groans (ta'awwaha) the groan (ahat) of a sorrowful man." The root of ta'awwuh is the utterance "ah" and similar words that the grieving person says. In al-Durra by al-Hariri, it is stated that the most eloquent form is to say, for ta'awwuh: "awwih," with a kasra, damma or fatha on the ha', and the kasra is the most common. On this is the poet's saying: "So groan (awwih) for her remembrance whenever you recall her, though between us are a land and a sky." Some doubled the waw and sukūn the ha', saying "awwah," and some changed the waw into an alif, saying "ah." Among them is one who omitted the ha' and kasra'd the waw, saying "awi." Then he mentioned that the conjugation of the verb from this is awwaha and ta'awwaha, and that the verbal noun is ahah and ahhah, and that al-Muthaqqab's saying cited above is among this.

﴿Forbearing (halim)﴾ (114), that is, patient with harm, forgiving of offence. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "It was part of his forbearance, peace be upon him, that if a man of his people harmed him, he would say to him: 'May Allah guide you.'" That its interpretation as "the lord (sayyid)," as narrated from the rabbi (al-Habr), is metaphorical. The sentence is a resumptive clause explaining what moved him, peace be upon him, to the promise of seeking forgiveness for his father, despite his father's harshness toward him and bad conduct with him, as is indicated by the saying of the one who was peace be upon him:

[Page 36] ﴿"If you do not desist, I will surely stone you, and leave me for a long time."﴾

It has been said that it is a resumptive clause explaining what moved him to seek forgiveness. An objection has been raised to it: that it suggests on its surface that Abraham's, peace be upon him, seeking forgiveness for his father was out of abundant mercy and increased forbearance, and this contradicts the beginning of the verse, which indicates that it was only because of a promise. Perhaps the intended meaning is that the cause of seeking forgiveness was nothing but the promise arising from what was mentioned, and so there is no difficulty. In this there is also an emphasis on the obligation to avoid him after it became clear. It is as if it were said: he, peace be upon him, disassociated himself from him after it became clear, while he was in the utmost tenderness of heart and forbearance; so others must be even more inclined to avoid and disavow him.

Some have allowed that the subject of wa'ada (promised) be the father, and the pronoun (iyyahu) refer to Abraham, peace be upon him, meaning: "except because of a promise which his father had made to Abraham," and that is the promise of faith.

The shaykh of our shaykhs, Sibghat Allah Afandi al-Haydari, said: "Perhaps this is the more evident interpretation, for the apparent context is that this verse is a response to what might be an objection to the first verse, namely, Abraham's seeking forgiveness for his unbelieving father. Mere mention of his being in his father's lifetime suffices for this, since it is taken to mean a request for forgiveness for him through guidance to faith, as was established earlier, without any need for the matter of the promise. Thus ﴿except because of a promise he had made to him﴾ becomes superfluous on the first interpretation of the two pronouns. By contrast, on this interpretation, its sense is that Abraham's seeking forgiveness does not pose a counterexample to what we have said, since it only came from him, peace be upon him, on account of his faith, since his promise to him had preceded, peace be upon him, so he supposed that he had fulfilled the promise and acted in accordance with the covenant, and so he asked forgiveness for him. Then, when it became clear to him that he would neither fulfil it nor ever believe, or he did not fulfil it and did not believe, he disassociated himself from him."

It is possible that mention of the promise may also be justified on the first interpretation, by saying: "Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, intended to include in the answer that this seeking of forgiveness was during the lifetime of the one for whom forgiveness was sought, and interpreting it as the request mentioned yields another benefit: that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), out of his extreme firmness in religion and intense zeal for certainty, did not seek forgiveness for him, though it was permissible. Yet he showed patience and forbearance, and so he sought forgiveness for him, fulfilling the promise he had made to him. So reflect." End.

And you know that on the second interpretation, what they said about the resumptive clause, that it explains what moved him, does not hold, and it would have been necessary to mention the reason for it. Also, the saying of its author, may Allah be exalted in his mercy, in explaining the benefit, "but he showed patience and forbearance," where he attributed forbearance to Abraham, peace be upon him, in the reflexive form (tafa''ul), while He, exalted, described him, peace be upon him, as "forbearing," is a slip that is not to be ascribed to its author. Carrying that on the basis of figurative correspondence (mushakala) while intending an act that does not suit his purpose and the flow of his speech is untenable. The truth that should be relied upon is the first interpretation of the verse, which is what is required by what was narrated from al-Hasan and others of the early generations of the Ummah, may Allah be pleased with them. He mentioned the hadith of the promise to explain the actual state of affairs, together with what it contains of an indication to the emphasis on avoidance and the strengthening of the distinction, as if it were said: "There is a clear distinction between the seeking of forgiveness you were forbidden from and the seeking of forgiveness by Abraham, peace be upon him, for his seeking was before it became clear and was out of a promise which the abundance of his compassion and forbearance prompted him to make, whereas what you were forbidden is not like that."

It remains that this verse is contradicted by the apparent meaning of what al-Bukhari narrated in his Sahih from Abu Hurayra, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Abraham, peace be upon him, will meet his father on the Day of Resurrection, and on his face will be darkness and dust. Abraham, peace be upon him, will say: 'Did I not tell you: do not disobey me?' His father will say: 'Today I will not disobey you.' Abraham, peace be upon him, will say: 'O Lord, You promised me that You would not disgrace me on the day they are resurrected. What disgrace could be greater than my father, the most distant?' Allah, may He be exalted, will say: 'I have forbidden Paradise to the disbelievers.' Then it will be said: 'O Abraham, what is under your feet?' He will look, and behold, there is a male hyena (dhih) covered in filth. It will be seized by its legs and thrown into the Fire." Another narrator added: "Then he will disown him (fa-yatabarra'u minhu)."

For the verse clearly indicates the severing of Abraham's, peace be upon him, hope that his father would become a believer, and his certainty that he would not be forgiven. For this reason he disowned him and abandoned seeking forgiveness for him, since seeking forgiveness for him while being certain that he would not be forgiven is something that cannot be conceived of from a knower of Allah (arif), especially one like the Friend (Khalil) of Allah, peace be upon him. They have explicitly stated that seeking forgiveness for a polytheist is a request that contradicts Allah, glory be to Him, in His own declaration. The hadith clearly indicates that he, peace be upon him, asks this for him on the Day of Resurrection, and he does not despair of his salvation until after the transformation (maskh); when he is transformed, he despairs of him and disowns him.

Ibn Hajar (al-Hafiz) answered the objection with two answers, which some of the learned men of Rum examined. It is strange that he said in the second answer: Ibrahim, upon him be prayer and peace, did not become certain that his father died in disbelief, because it is possible that he had believed inwardly and that the Prophet (peace be upon him) did not know about that, and that the time of his disavowal of him was after the state that occurred in the hadith. This is clearly contrary to what is understood from the verse, that both the manifestation (of enmity) and the disavowal took place in this world. That [scholar] answered this by saying: We do not concede a contradiction between the verse and the hadith. Such a contradiction would exist only if the hadith indicated that Ibrahim asked forgiveness for his father and sought intercession for him. But it does not. His saying "O Lord, You promised me..." etc. was intended by him, upon him be prayer and peace, as a pure inquiry into the reality of the situation, for there arose in his noble breast the thought that this condition befalling his father was a disgrace to him, and that the father's disgrace is the son's disgrace, which would lead to the breaking of the promise referred to in his words: "You promised me that You would not disgrace me on the Day they are raised." You know that the report is clear regarding intercession, and intercession is a form of seeking forgiveness, as the words of the scholars in that context indicate.

This is further clarified by what al-Hakim narrated from Abu Hurayrah as well, and he authenticated it, saying it meets the condition of Muslim: that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "A man will meet his father on the Day of Resurrection, and he will say: O father, what kind of son was I to you? He will say: The best of sons. He will say: Will you obey me today? He will say: Yes. He will say: Take hold of my garment. He will take hold of his garment, then he will set off until he reaches Allah, Exalted is He, who is judging between the creatures. He will say: O My servant, enter by whichever gates of Paradise you wish. He will say: O Lord, and my father with me? For You promised me that You would not disgrace me. He said: Then his father will be transformed into a hyena, and he will fall into the Fire. He will take hold of his nose, and He, Glorified is He, will say: O My servant, this is your father. He will say: No, by Your might."

Al-Hafiz al-Mundhiri said: It is in Sahih al-Bukhari, except that he said: "Ibrahim will meet his father," and he mentioned the story. From this it is understood that the man in the hadith of al-Hakim is Ibrahim, upon him be prayer and peace, and his request for forgiveness for his father and his entry into Paradise is more evident in it than in the hadith of al-Bukhari. What al-Zamakhshari mentioned is, it is said, contrary to what is commonly reported from the Mu'tazilah: that the impermissibility of seeking forgiveness for the disbeliever is known through revelation, not through reason, because reason allows that Allah, Exalted is He, might forgive the disbeliever. Do you not see the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him) to Abu Talib: "I will certainly seek forgiveness for you as long as I am not forbidden"? This would serve this purpose only if it were combined with Ibrahim, upon him be prayer and peace, not knowing that through revelation until the Day of Resurrection, and that is something a rational person would hardly undertake, let alone a virtuous one.

Some contemporary scholars answered that Ibrahim, upon him be prayer and peace, knew of his father's disbelief and was certain that Allah, Exalted is He, does not forgive that He be associated with, but that natural compassion and tenderness overcame him when he saw his father on the plains of the Day of Resurrection, with dust upon his face, so he could not control himself and made the request he made. A similar example in some respects is the saying of Nuh, upon him be prayer and peace, to his Lord, Glorified is He: ﴿My Lord, indeed my son is of my family, and indeed Your promise is true﴾. It is not hidden that this is deeply corrupt. Similar to it is what was said: that he assumed the exception of his father from the generality of ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that He be associated with﴾, because Allah had promised him that He would not disgrace him, so he proceeded to intercede for him. By my life, none would proceed to this except one ignorant of his own ignorance.

As for the first, it is because the prophets, upon them be peace, are too exalted in rank for their souls to overcome them so as to undertake what involves the denial of Allah's own word. As for the second, it is because if there were any basis for that assumption, he, peace be upon him, would not have disavowed him in this world after it became clear to him that he was an enemy of Allah, and he was the one who is "al-Awwah, the forbearing."

It has also been said: the best answer is to hold that what is in the two reports is not from intercession at all. It is said that Ibrahim, upon him be peace, thought that his father's disgrace was equivalent to disgrace for himself, so, by the ruling of Allah's promise to him that He would not disgrace him, he sought to rescue him from that as much as possible, so He rescued him from it by transforming him into a dhib (male hyena). Perhaps that is something Ibrahim, upon him be peace, regarded as a rescue for him from disgrace, due to the difference in species and because those who knew his father did not recognize that he was his father anymore, as if the fatherhood had been cut off between them. This is indicated by the fact that after the transformation, He, Glorified is He, takes him by the nose and says to him, peace be upon him: "O My servant, this is your father?" He says: "No, by Your might." Perhaps the intended meaning of the disavowal in the earlier report, in the first hadith, is this statement. The mention of the hadith about the prohibition of Paradise for the disbelievers is not because Ibrahim, peace be upon him, was seeking to have his father entered into it, but rather to show the impossibility of this way of rescue, to dishearten his father and to inform him of the magnitude of what he had done. His saying, upon him be peace, in the report of al-Hakim, when it is said to him, "O My servant, enter by whichever gates of Paradise you wish," "O Lord, and my father with me?" may be understood as: "Shall I enter while my father is standing with me?" The meaning is: I will not enter with my father in this condition, but I will enter when it has changed. His saying, upon him be peace, "For You promised me that You would not disgrace me," serves as a reason for the negation implied by the presumed interrogative. In that case the matter returns to a request for rescue from what he considered disgrace for him as well, and so he is transformed into a hyena for that. It is not objected that rescue is possible by means other than the stated transformation, because we say: perhaps the choice of that transformation over the other possible matters, apart from entry into Paradise, is for a wisdom known only to Him, Glorified is He. They have mentioned that the wisdom of his transformation into a hyena rather than other animals is that the hyena is the most foolish of animals, and from its foolishness it neglects what it must be alert to. For this reason Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, said: "I will not be like the hyena that hears the sound of a hunter and goes out to it until it is hunted." And Azar, when he did not accept the advice of the one most compassionate toward him at a time when benefiting from it was possible, and took hold of his garment when that benefited him nothing, was most like the hyena among creatures, so he was transformed into a hyena rather than other things for that reason. They did not mention the wisdom in choosing the transformation over other things, and it is not free of wisdom, and ignorance of it does no harm. End of quote.

It is not hidden what artificiality is in this answer. More preferable than it is to hold that the subject of "wa'd" (promised) is the father's pronoun, and the pronoun in "iyyahu" refers to Ibrahim, upon him be prayer and peace, and that the manifestation and disavowal took place in the Hereafter as the two preceding reports contain. Then it is not far-fetched that Ibrahim was seeking forgiveness for his father after his promise to him of faith, asking Paradise for him, thinking that he had fulfilled his promise, so that he would be transformed into a dhib. But the apparent meaning of the verse does not support this, nor does the transmitted report from the early generations of this community, even if it is valid that the verse is applied to it as a response to the objection that also arises against the first verse by way of contrast, through a stretch of interpretation. Perhaps the least burdensome of the answers is that what Ibrahim, upon him be prayer and peace, intended by that dialogue which took place from him in that station was to show his excuse before his father and others in the most complete manner, not to seek forgiveness in reality. This is like what the Mu'tazilah said regarding Musa's, upon him be peace, request to see Allah, Exalted is He, while knowing its impossibility in their assumption. And the view that the people of the plain, the prophets, upon them be prayer and peace, and others among the believers and disbelievers, are equal in knowing that forgiveness for a polytheist, for example, is in the realm of prohibition, and perhaps the non-equality is claimed based on the apparent request of the disbelievers for pardon and removal from the Fire and the like. Indeed, in the two preceding reports there is what indicates that the father did not know the reality of the situation, and that he would not be forgiven. So reflect on that, and Allah, Glorified is He, will take charge of your guidance.

It also remains that an objection was raised to the view that Ibrahim's seeking forgiveness for his father until it became clear to him that he was an enemy of Allah was during his lifetime, based on the verse in Surat al-Mumtahanah: ﴿There has been for you a good example in Ibrahim﴾ up to His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿except the saying of Ibrahim to his father: "I will surely ask forgiveness for you"﴾, where he was prohibited from following him in that. Had it been during his lifetime, he would not have been prohibited from it, because seeking forgiveness in the sense of seeking faith for living polytheists is permissible. It is answered that he was prohibited only from following its outward meaning, and [he] thought

﴿And Allah would not let a people go astray﴾ means: it is not befitting of the grace and bounties of Allah the Exalted that He should describe a people as having strayed from the path of truth, blame them, and apply His rulings to them ﴿after He had guided them﴾ to Islam ﴿until He has made clear to them﴾ through revelation, explicitly or by indication, ﴿what to fear﴾, meaning what must be guarded against among the prohibitions of the religion, so that they would not refrain from what they were forbidden. It seems to be a consolation for those who sought forgiveness for the polytheists before the clarification, since it indicates that it is not part of Allah's grace, exalted is He, to blame the believers and hold them accountable for seeking forgiveness before He makes clear that it is impermissible for one whose polytheism is established. But He, glory be to Him, does blame and hold accountable those who seek forgiveness for them after that. According to what is related from al-Hasan, the verse was revealed when some Muslims died before the obligations were revealed, and their brothers said: "O Messenger of Allah, our brothers who died before the revelation of the obligations, what is their station and how is their condition?" And from Muqatil and al-Kalbi: a people came to the Prophet (ﷺ) before the prohibition of wine and the turning of the qibla toward the Ka'bah, then returned to their people. Afterward wine was prohibited and the qibla was changed, but they had not acted accordingly until they came to Madinah after some time and learned of this. They said: "O Messenger of Allah, you were upon a religion and we were upon other than it, so we are in error." Then Allah the Exalted revealed the verse. Taking "leading astray" in it to mean what we have mentioned is the apparent meaning, and it has nothing to do with Mu'tazilism (the Mu'tazilah, a rationalist theological school) as is imagined. Perhaps for this reason al-Wahidi departed from it, claiming that the meaning is: Allah would not have caused error to fall into their hearts. He took from it as evidence that the heedless person, who has not heard the text or the scriptural evidence, is not accountable. The Mu'tazilah restricted that to what is not known by reason, such as truthfulness in reports and the returning of a deposit, which according to them is not dependent on revelation. This is a branch of the principle of rational good and evil (al-husn wa'l-qubh al-'aqliyyan), on which the People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah) have a position.

﴿Indeed Allah is Knowing of all things﴾ (115) is a causal explanation of what preceded: Allah the Exalted knows all things, among which is their need for clarification, so He makes it clear to them. It was also said that it is a resumption to emphasize the threat understood from what precedes. Likewise His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Indeed, to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾, with no partner in it, ﴿He gives life and causes death, and you have not besides Allah any guardian or helper﴾ (116).

Others said: when He forbade them from seeking forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they were of near kin, and this included the obligation of total disavowal of them, He made clear that Allah, glory be to Him, is the owner of every existing thing, the one who manages its affairs and dominates it, and that no guardianship or help is possible for them except from Him, exalted is He. So they should turn to Him, exalted is His majesty, with their whole selves, disavowing whatever is other than Him and intending none but Him.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 117:

﴿Indeed, Allah turned in forgiveness toward the Prophet and the Emigrants and the Helpers.﴾ The scholars of meanings (aṣḥāb al-ma'ānī) said: The intended meaning is the mention of the repentance (tawbah) toward the Emigrants and the Helpers, except that the Prophet (ﷺ) was included in that for the sake of honouring them and magnifying their station. This is like what they said regarding the mention of Him, exalted is He, in His saying: ﴿So that for Allah is one-fifth of it and for the Messenger﴾ etc. That is, He, glorified is He, pardoned them for the lapses that had preceded from them on the Day of Uhud and the Day of Ḥunayn. It was also said: The intended meaning is the mention of the repentance toward him (ﷺ) and toward them, and the sin, in relation to him (ﷺ), is of the category of what is less than the best (khilāf al-awlā), in view of his lofty station. It is explained here, according to what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, as the permission given to the hypocrites to stay behind, and in relation to them, may Allah be pleased with them, there is no barrier to its being literal, since there is no infallibility (ʿiṣmah) for anyone other than the Prophets, peace be upon them, according to us. And it may be explained by what was explained first.

It is also permitted that it is of the category of what is less than the best, based on what was said: Their sin was the inclination to remain behind from the expedition of Tabuk, since it took place at a harsh time. Repentance may also be explained as freedom from sin and preservation from it, metaphorically, since there is no blame in every case; and the apparent meaning of the unrestricted expression is the literal sense. In the verse there is what is not hidden of exhortation and urging to repentance for all people ﴿who followed him﴾ and did not lag behind him (ﷺ) ﴿in the hour of hardship﴾, that is, in the time of severity and straitness. Expressing it as "the hour" is for greater specification of it. That severity was their condition in the expedition of Tabuk, for they were in severe heat, ten men taking turns on a single camel; and in severe want of provisions, they took dates infested with worms, barley infested with weevils, and rancid fat; the hardship reached the point that two men shared a single date, and sometimes a group would suck it so that they might drink water after it, as narrated from Qatadah; and in severe want of water, until they slaughtered the camels and squeezed their dung, as narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him; and in a time of severe heat, dearth and famine. From here that expedition was named the Expedition of Hardship (ghazwat al-ʿusrah), and its army the Army of Hardship (jaysh al-ʿusrah).

The description of the Emigrants and the Helpers with following (al-ittibā') in this hour is to indicate that they are deserving that Allah should turn to them for that; and in it also is an emphasis on the matter of the preceding exhortation. ﴿After the hearts of a group of them had nearly swerved﴾ is an explanation of the extreme severity and its reaching its utmost limit, and it is the approach of some of them to inclining toward staying behind the Prophet (ﷺ). It was also said: It is the approach of some of them to inclining away from steadfastness in faith, and that was understood as mere concern and whisperings. It was also said: It was an inclination from their weak ones and those recently converted to Islam. In kāda, the pronoun is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n), and ﴿qulūb﴾ is the subject of ﴿yazīgh﴾, and the clause is in the position of the predicate of kāda, and it needs no connecting pronoun since it is a predicate of the pronoun of the matter; this is what is transmitted from Sibawayh. The implicit matter (iḍmār al-sha'n), according to what is transmitted from al-Radi, is not well known in verbs of approximation except in kāda, and in the defective verbs except in kāna and laysa. It is also permitted that the subject of kāda is a pronoun for the people, and the clause is also in the position of the predicate, and the connecting pronoun for it is the pronoun in ﴿minhum﴾. This is on the reading ﴿yazīgh﴾ with the yā' (third person), which is the reading of Ḥamzah, Ḥafṣ and al-A'mash. As for the reading (tazīgh) with the tā' (second person), which is the reading of the rest, it is possible that ﴿qulūb﴾ is the subject of kāda and (tazīgh) its predicate, and in it there is a pronoun returning to its subject; this does not hold on the first reading, because of the masculine pronoun of ﴿yazīgh﴾ and the feminine of what it refers to. This possibility was mentioned by Muntakhab al-Din al-Hamdani, Abu Talib al-Makki and others, and al-Kashf objected to it, saying that making qulūb the subject of kāda departs from its established form, which requires that its subject precede its predicate, as mentioned by Shaykh Ibn al-Ḥājib in his commentary on al-Mufaṣṣal. In al-Baḥr it is said that placing the predicate of kāda before its subject is based on permitting the construction "kāna yaqūmu Zayd", and there is a difference of opinion on it, and the sounder view is prohibition. One of the learned men of Rum answered that Abu 'Ali permitted that, and that is sufficient as proof; and also that Ibn Malik's statement in al-Tashil, and likewise the statements of its commentators, including Abu Hayyan, follow it; and he also followed it in his al-Irtishaf. The opposition to it in al-Baḥr is not to be heeded, since the basis of that is analogy with the chapter of kāna, and that does not contradict the explicit text from Abu 'Ali. Moreover, that Abu Hayyan is among the people of analogy is clearly a point of prohibition; so the truth is permissibility. It is also possible that the subject of kāda is a pronoun returning to the collective of the Emigrants and the Helpers, meaning: after the collective had nearly... And Ibn 'Atiyyah took the referent of the pronoun to be "the people", meaning: after the people had nearly..., and this is weak, because a pronoun is implied in kāda that returns only to an imagined referent, and because its predicate would then be in the nominative by way of causation, whereas they have said that it raises only a pronoun returning to its subject; and likewise the predicate of its sister verbs other than 'asā, according to one opinion. This objection also applies to the two possibilities for the first reading, though the matter is easy on the first possibility. Al-Radi permitted interpreting the verse as a case of tanāzu' (contention between two governors), which is clear on the second reading; and in that case it is necessary to make the first governor operative, for if the second were made operative it would have been necessary to say in the first "kādat" as Ubayy, may Allah be pleased with him, read it. It is not permitted to say kāda except in the view of al-Kisa'i, for he deletes the subject. It seems al-Radi did not mind what follows from this interpretation of the predicate of kāda preceding its subject, since you have known that it is not an impermissible matter according to what is correct. Abu Hayyan held that ﴿kāda﴾ is superfluous (zā'idah) while its meaning is intended, like kāna, and it has no governance over any subject or predicate, so as to be free from debate. It is supported by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: (mimba'di mā zāghat) with the deletion of kāda. The Kufans held that it is superfluous in such expressions as lam yakad, even though it is both governing and governed; so this is preferable.

Al-A'mash read (tuzīgh) with a ḍammah on the tā'. According to Ibn Mas'ud's reading, they took the pronoun to refer to those who stayed behind, whether they were hypocrites or not, like Abu Lubabah. ﴿Then He turned to them in forgiveness﴾ is a repetition for emphasis, based on the view that the pronoun refers to the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Emigrants and the Helpers, may Allah be pleased with them. Emphasis may be connected with "then" (thumma), as the grammarians explicitly state, even if the statement of the people of meanings appears to contradict it. In it is an alert that His turning in forgiveness is in return for what they bore of hardships, as indicated by the conditioning with the relative clause. It is also possible that the pronoun refers to the group, and the meaning is that He turned to them because of their near-deviation and their closeness to swerving, since that is a crime requiring repentance for it; so there is no repetition of what preceded. His saying: ﴿Indeed He is to them Compassionate, Merciful﴾ is a resumptive explanatory clause, for the attributes of compassion and mercy are among the motives for repentance and pardon. It is also permitted that the first refers to the removal of harm and the second to the bestowal of benefit, or that one of them pertains to past matters and the other to what follows.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 9, verse 118 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And upon the three﴾ is a conjunction with ﴿the Prophet﴾. It has also been said that ﴿accepted repentance﴾ is implied in the structure of the speech, because this repentance differs from the earlier repentance, though this view is open to question. That is: and He accepted the repentance of the three ﴿who were left behind﴾. That is, their matter was deferred (khalafa amruhum), and it was postponed (ukhkhira) from the matter of Abu Lubabah and his companions, since He did not accept from them an excuse like theirs, nor was it rejected, and He did not decide anything concerning them until the revelation descended regarding them. Thus the attribution to them is either metaphorical (majaz) or by means of an implied genitive (taqdir mudaf) in the noble wording. The transitive may also be interpreted as intransitive, meaning: those who stayed behind from the expedition (al-ghazw). They were Ka'b ibn Malik of the Banu Salimah, Hilal ibn Umayyah of the Banu Waqif, and Murarah ibn al-Rabi' of the Banu Amr ibn Awf. It is also said of him: Ibn Rabi'ah. In Muslim and others he is described as al-Amiri, but many of the scholars of hadith have corrected this to al-Umari instead.

Ikrimah, Razin ibn Hubaysh and Amr ibn Ubayd read (khalafu) with a fatha on the kha and the lam, lightened, meaning: they remained behind the fighters in Madinah, or they became corrupt, from al-khalifah (the one left behind) and khuluf al-fam (staleness of the mouth). Ali ibn al-Husayn, Muhammad al-Baqir, Ja'far al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with them, and Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read (khalafu) with a different reading (khalafu). Al-A'mash read: (wa ʿala al-mukhallafina).

The apparent meaning of His words, ﴿until, when the earth became constricted for them despite its vastness﴾, is that it is an end point (ghayah) for the deferment, in the sense of postponing the matter, meaning: their matter was delayed until the earth became constricted for them ﴿despite its vastness﴾, that is, despite its breadth and extent, because people turned away from them and did not sit with them or converse with them, in obedience to the Prophet's (ﷺ) command to them in this regard. It is a metaphor for extreme bewilderment. The meaning is that they did not settle in this world despite its breadth, as has been said:
It is as if the lands of Allah, though spacious, are for the fearful pursued a loop for the snarer.

﴿And their souls became constricted for them﴾, that is, their hearts; he expressed it this way metaphorically, because the existence of the selves is by them, and the meaning of their constriction is their grief and sorrow, as if they could not contain joy because of their constriction. In this there is an ascent from the constriction of the earth upon them to the constriction within their own souls, and it is of the utmost eloquence. ﴿And they thought that there is no refuge from Allah except in Him﴾, that is, they knew that there is no refuge from His wrath except by seeking His forgiveness and repenting to Him, glorified is He. Interpreting "thought" as "knew" is because that suits them. ﴿Then He accepted their repentance﴾, that is, He enabled them to repent. ﴿That they might repent﴾; or He sent down the acceptance of their repentance in the Qur'an and informed them of it, so that the believers would count them among the repentant; or He returned to them with acceptance and mercy time after time, so that they would remain steadfast in repentance and continue upon it. It has also been said: repentance is not itself what is accepted, and the meaning is: He accepted their repentance from having stayed behind, so that they would repent in the future, since a lapse had come from them, and so that they would not despair of His generosity, glorified is He. ﴿Indeed Allah is He, the Accepter of repentance﴾, the one who exceeds in accepting repentance from whoever repents, even if he returns a hundred times in a day. ﴿The Merciful 118﴾, the one who bestows upon them favours of every kind, despite their deserving the various forms of punishment.

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Muslim and al-Bayhaqi related through the route of al-Zuhri, who said: Abd al-Rahman ibn Abd Allah ibn Ka'b ibn Malik informed me that Abd Allah ibn Ka'b ibn Malik, who was the guide of Ka'b from among his sons when he became blind, said: I heard Ka'b ibn Malik narrate his account of when he stayed behind from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the expedition of Tabuk. Ka'b said: "I never stayed behind from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in any expedition he undertook, except the expedition of Tabuk, though I had stayed behind from the Battle of Badr, and he did not punish anyone who stayed behind from it. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out only seeking the caravan of Quraysh, until Allah brought them together with their enemy without prior arrangement. I was present with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the night of al-Aqabah, when we pledged ourselves to Islam, and I would not wish to have it in exchange for the Battle of Badr, though Badr is more remembered among people and more famous. The account of my situation when I stayed behind from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the expedition of Tabuk is that I was never stronger or more well-off than when I stayed behind from him in that expedition. By Allah, I had never before gathered two riding beasts until I gathered them in that expedition. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rarely intended an expedition without concealing it with another destination, until that expedition, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out in it in intense heat, faced a long journey and deserts, and faced a numerous enemy. So he made clear to the Muslims their matter so that they could prepare the preparation for their enemy, and informed them of the direction in which he intended to go. The Muslims with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were numerous and no written register held them, meaning the diwan." Ka'b said: "Few men wished to absent themselves without thinking that it would remain hidden for them, so long as no revelation from Allah, mighty and majestic, had come down concerning it. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out on that expedition when the fruits were ripe and the shade was pleasant, and I was then the least of them. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made his preparations for it, and the believers were with him. I began to go out in the morning in order to prepare with them, but I would return without having accomplished anything, and I would say to myself: I am able to do so whenever I wish. This continued with me until the people became serious, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set out in the morning, and the Muslims with him, while I had accomplished nothing of my equipment. I said: I will prepare a day or two after him, then I will catch up with him. So I went out on the day they departed to prepare, but I returned without accomplishing anything of my equipment. Then I went out and returned without accomplishing anything. This continued with me until they reached their destination and the expedition had gone far ahead. I resolved to set out and catch up with them, and I wish I had done so, but that was not decreed for me. I began, when I went out among the people after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), to be grieved that I saw none but a man openly accused of hypocrisy, or a man whom Allah had excused. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not mention me until he reached Tabuk, and then he said while he was sitting among the people at Tabuk: 'What has Ka'b ibn Malik done?' A man from the Banu Salimah said: 'O Messenger of Allah, his two cloaks and his gazing at his own sides have held him back.' Then Mu'adh ibn Jabal said to him: 'What an evil thing you have said! By Allah, O Messenger of Allah, we know nothing of him but good.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) fell silent. When it reached me that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had turned back, returning from Tabuk, something came to my mind, and I began to think of falsehood, saying: 'By what means can I escape his anger tomorrow?' I sought help in that from every man of judgement among my family. When it was said: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has drawn near, arriving,' falsehood left me, and I knew that I would never escape from him by anything at all. So I resolved upon truthfulness. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) arrived in the morning, and when he returned from a journey he would begin with the mosque, pray two rak'ahs, then sit for the people. When he did that, those who had stayed behind came and began to give excuses to him and to swear oaths to him. They were eighty-some men. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) accepted their outward profession, asked forgiveness for them, and left their inner states to Allah, until I came. When I greeted him, peace be upon him, he smiled the smile of one who is angry, then said to me: 'Come here.' I came walking until I sat before him. He said to me: 'What held you back? Had you not bought your mount?' I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, if I had sat before anyone else among the people of this world, I would have thought to escape his anger with an excuse. I have indeed been given eloquence in argument, but by Allah, I know that if I told you today a false account with which you were pleased with me, Allah would surely soon bring your anger upon me. And if I tell you a true account with which you find fault with me, I hope in it for the reward from Allah, the Exalted. By Allah, I had no excuse. By Allah, I was never more free of obligation or more well-off than when I stayed behind from you.'" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "As for this one, he has spoken the truth. Stand up until Allah decides concerning you." So I stood up, and men from the Banu Salimah hurried after me and followed me, saying to me: "By Allah, we did not know that you had committed any sin before this. You were unable not to have offered an excuse to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) as the others who stayed behind offered. The Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) seeking forgiveness for you would have sufficed you for your sin?" He said: "By Allah, they did not cease to reproach me until I wanted to return and call myself a liar. Then I said: 'Has anyone else met with this along with me?' They said: 'Yes, two men met it with you, and each said what you said, and each was told what you were told.' I said: 'Who are they?' They said: 'Murarah ibn al-Rabi' and Hilal ibn Umayyah.' They mentioned to me two righteous men who had both witnessed Badr, in whom I had an example. So I went on when they mentioned them to me." He said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade speaking to us, the three of us, from among all who had stayed behind. The people avoided us and changed toward us, until the earth became strange to me within myself; it was not the earth I had known. We remained in that state for fifty nights. As for my two companions, they grew feeble and sat in their houses. As for me, I was the strongest and most steadfast of the people. I would attend the prayer with the Muslims and walk through the markets, but no one spoke to me. I would come to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was in his assembly after the prayer, greet him, and say to myself: 'Did he move his lips to return the greeting or not?' Then I would pray near him and steal glances at him. When I turned to my prayer he would turn toward me, and when I turned toward him he would turn away. Until, when this long avoidance by the Muslims became burdensome for me, I walked until I scaled the wall of the garden of Abu Qatadah, who was my cousin and the most beloved of people to me. I greeted him, but by Allah, he did not return my greeting. I said to him: 'O Abu Qatadah, I adjure you by Allah: do you know that I love Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ)?' He was silent. I returned and adjured him again, and he was silent. I returned and adjured him, and he said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' My eyes overflowed, and I turned away until I scaled the wall. While I was walking in the market of Madinah, behold, a Nabataean from the Nabataeans of Syria, one of those who had come with food to sell in Madinah, was saying: 'Who will guide me to Ka'b ibn Malik?' The people began to point him to me, until he came and handed me a letter from the king of Ghassan. I was a writer, and in it was: 'To proceed: we have heard that your companion has forsaken you. Allah has not made you a dwelling of humiliation or of loss. So join us, and we will console you.' When I read it I said: 'This too is one of the trials.' So I took it to the oven and set it alight."

فَسَجَرْتُهُ فِيها حَتّى إذا مَضَتْ أرْبَعُونَ لَيْلَةً مِنَ الخَمْسِينَ إذا بِرَسُولِ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صَلّى اللَّهُ تَعالى عَلَيْهِ وسَلَّمَ يَأْتِينِي فَقالَ: إنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صَلّى اللَّهُ تَعالى عَلَيْهِ وسَلَّمَ يَأْمُرُكَ أنْ تَعْتَزِلَ امْرَأتَكَ. قُلْتُ: أُطَلِّقُها أمْ ماذا أفْعَلُ؟ قالَ: بَلِ اعْتَزِلْها ولا تَقْرَبْها وأرْسَلَ إلى صاحِبَيَّ مِثْلَ ذَلِكَ فَقُلْتُ لِامْرَأتِي: الحَقِي بِأهْلِكِ لِتَكُونِي عِنْدَهم حَتّى يَقْضِيَ اللَّهُ تَعالى في هَذا الأمْرِ فَجاءَتِ امْرَأةُ هِلالِ بْنِ أُمَيَّةَ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صَلّى اللَّهُ تَعالى عَلَيْهِ وسَلَّمَ فَقالَتْ: يا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ إنَّ هِلالًا شَيْخٌ ضائِعٌ ولَيْسَ لَهُ خادِمٌ فَهَلْ تَكْرَهُ أنْ أخْدُمَهُ؟ فَقالَ: لا ولَكِنْ لا يَقْرَبَنَّكِ. قالَتْ: وإنَّهُ واللَّهِ ما بِهِ حَرَكَةٌ إلى شَيْءٍ واللَّهِ ما زالَ يَبْكِي مِن لَدُنْ أنْ كانَ مِن أمْرِهِ ما كانَ إلى يَوْمِهِ هَذا فَقالَ لِي بَعْضُ أهْلِي: لَوِ اسْتَأْذَنْتَ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صَلّى اللَّهُ تَعالى عَلَيْهِ وسَلَّمَ في امْرَأتِكَ فَقَدْ أذِنَ لِامْرَأةِ هِلالٍ أنْ تَخْدُمَهُ. فَقُلْتُ: واللَّهِ لا أسْتَأْذِنُ فِيها رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صَلّى اللَّهُ تَعالى عَلَيْهِ وسَلَّمَ وما أدْرِي ماذا يَقُولُ إذا اسْتَأْذَنْتُهُ وأنا رَجُلٌ شابٌّ قالَ: فَلَبِثْتُ عَشْرَ لَيالٍ فَكَمُلَ لَنا خَمْسُونَ لَيْلَةً مِن حِينِ نَهى عَنْ كَلامِنا ثُمَّ صَلَّيْتُ صَلاةَ الفَجْرِ صَباحَ خَمْسِينَ لَيْلَةً عَلى ظَهْرِ بَيْتٍ مِن بُيُوتِنا فَبَيْنا أنا جالِسٌ عَلى الحالِ الَّتِي ذَكَرَ اللَّهُ تَعالى عَنّا قَدْ ضاقَتْ عَلَيَّ نَفْسِي وضاقَتْ عَلَيَّ الأرْضُ بِما رَحُبَتْ سَمِعْتُ صارِخًا أوْفى عَلى جَبَلِ سَلْعٍ يَقُولُ بِأعْلى صَوْتِهِ: يا كَعْبُ بْنَ مالِكٍ أبْشِرْ فَخَرَرْتُ ساجِدًا وعَرَفْتُ أنْ قَدْ جاءَ فَرَجٌ فَآذَنُ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صَلّى اللَّهُ تَعالى عَلَيْهِ وسَلَّمَ بِتَوْبَةِ اللَّهِ تَعالى عَلَيْنا حِينَ صَلّى الفَجْرَ فَذَهَبَ النّاسُ يُبَشِّرُونَنا وذَهَبَ قِبَلَ صاحِبَيَّ مُبَشِّرُونَ ورَكَضَ إلى رَجُلٍ فَرَسًا وسَعى ساعٍ مِن أسْلَمَ وأوْفى عَلى الجَبَلِ فَكانَ الصَّوْتُ أسْرَعَ مِنَ الفَرَسِ فَلَمّا جاءَنِي الَّذِي سَمِعْتُ صَوْتَهُ يُبَشِّرُنِي نَزَعْتُ لَهُ ثَوْبِي وكَسَوْتُهُما إيّاهُ بِبِشارَتِهِ واللَّهِ ما أمْلِكُ غَيْرَهُما يَوْمَئِذٍ فاسْتَعَرْتُ ثَوْبَيْنِ فَلَبِسْتُهُما فانْطَلَقْتُ أؤُمُّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صَلّى اللَّهُ تَعالى عَلَيْهِ وسَلَّمَ فَتَلَقّانِي النّاسُ فَوْجًا بَعْدَ فَوْجٍ يُهَنِّئُونَنِي بِالتَّوْبَةِ يَقُولُونَ: لِيَهْنِكَ تَوْبَةُ اللَّهِ تَعالى عَلَيْكَ حَتّى دَخَلْتُ المَسْجِدَ فَإذا رَسُولُ اللَّهِ ﷺ جالِسٌ في المَسْجِدِ حَوْلَهُ النّاسُ فَقامَ إلَيَّ طَلْحَةُ بْنُ عُبَيْدِ اللَّهِ يُهَرْوِلُ حَتّى صافَحَنِي وهَنَّأنِي واللَّهِ ما قامَ إلَيَّ رَجُلٌ مِنَ المُهاجِرِينَ غَيْرُهُ قالَ: فَكانَ كَعْبٌ لا يَنْساها لِطَلْحَةَ قالَ كَعْبٌ: فَلَمّا سَلَّمْتُ عَلى رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صَلّى اللَّهُ تَعالى عَلَيْهِ وسَلَّمَ قالَ وهو يَبْرُقُ وجْهُهُ مِنَ السُّرُورِ: أبْشِرْ بِخَيْرِ يَوْمٍ مَرَّ عَلَيْكَ مُنْذُ ولَدَتْكَ أُمُّكَ. قُلْتُ: أمِن عِنْدِكَ يا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ أمْ مِن عِنْدِ اللَّهِ؟ قالَ: لا بَلْ مِن عِنْدِ اللَّهِ تَعالى وكانَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلّى اللَّهُ تَعالى عَلَيْهِ وسَلَّمَ إذا سُرَّ اسْتَنارَ وجْهُهُ حَتّى كَأنَّهُ قِطْعَةُ قَمَرٍ فَلَمّا جَلَسْتُ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ قُلْتُ: يا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ إنَّ مِن تَوْبَتِي أنْ أنْخَلِعَ مِن مالِي صَدَقَةً إلى اللَّهِ تَعالى ورَسُولِهِ صَلّى اللَّهُ تَعالى عَلَيْهِ وسَلَّمَ. قالَ: أمْسِكْ بَعْضَ مالِكَ فَهو خَيْرٌ لَكَ. قُلْتُ: إنِّي أُمْسِكُ سَهْمِي الَّذِي بِخَيْبَرَ. وقُلْتُ: يا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ إنَّما نَجّانِي اللَّهُ تَعالى بِالصِّدْقِ وإنَّ مِن تَوْبَتِي أنْ لا أُحَدِّثَ إلّا صِدْقًا ما بَقِيتُ، فَواللَّهِ ما أعْلَمُ أحَدًا مِنَ المُسْلِمِينَ أبْلاهُ اللَّهُ تَعالى في الصِّدْقِ بِالحَدِيثِ مُنْذُ ذَكَرْتُ ذَلِكَ لِرَسُولِ اللَّهِ صَلّى اللَّهُ تَعالى عَلَيْهِ وسَلَّمَ أحْسَنَ مِمّا أبَلّانِي اللَّهُ تَعالى، واللَّهِ ما تَعَمَّدْتُ كَذِبَةً مُنْذُ قُلْتُ ذَلِكَ إلى يَوْمِي هَذا وإنِّي لِأرْجُوَ أنْ يَحْفَظَنِي اللَّهُ تَعالى فِيما بَقِيَ قالَ: وأنْزَلَ اللَّهُ تَعالى ﴿لَقَدْ تابَ﴾ الآيَةَ فَواللَّهِ ما أنْعَمَ اللَّهُ تَعالى عَلَيَّ مِن نِعْمَةٍ قَطُّ بَعْدَ أنْ هَدانِي اللَّهُ سُبْحانَهُ لِلْإسْلامِ أعْظَمَ في نَفْسِي مِن صِدْقِي رَسُولَ اللَّهِ عَلَيْهِ الصَّلاةُ والسَّلامُ يَوْمَئِذٍ أنْ لا أكُونَ كَذَبْتُهُ فَأهْلِكَ كَما هَلَكَ الَّذِينَ كَذَّبُوهُ فَإنَّ اللَّهَ تَعالى قالَ لِلَّذِينِ كَذَّبُوهُ حِينَ نَزَلَ الوَحْيُ شَرَّ ما قالَ لِأحَدٍ فَقالَ: ﴿سَيَحْلِفُونَ بِاللَّهِ لَكم إذا انْقَلَبْتُمْ إلَيْهِمْ لِتُعْرِضُوا عَنْهم فَأعْرِضُوا عَنْهُمْ﴾ إلى قَوْلِهِ سُبْحانَهُ: ﴿الفاسِقِينَ﴾»
وجاءَ في رِوايَةٍ «عَنْ كَعْبٍ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ تَعالى عَنْهُ قالَ: نَهى رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلّى اللَّهُ تَعالى عَلَيْهِ وسَلَّمَ عَنْ كَلامِي وكَلامِ صاحِبَيَّ فَلَبِثْتُ كَذَلِكَ حَتّى طالَ عَلَيَّ الأمْرُ وما مِن شَيْءٍ أهَمَّ إلَيَّ مِن أنْ أمُوتَ فَلا يُصَلِّيَ عَلَيَّ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلّى
[p. 45]
اللَّهُ تَعالى عَلَيْهِ وسَلَّمَ أوْ يَمُوتَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلّى اللَّهُ تَعالى عَلَيْهِ وسَلَّمَ فَأكُونَ مِنَ النّاسِ بِتِلْكَ المَنزِلَةِ فَلا يُكَلِّمُنِي أحَدٌ مِنهم ولا يُصَلِّي عَلَيَّ فَأنْزَلَ اللَّهُ تَعالى تَوْبَتَنا عَلى نَبِيِّهِ صَلّى اللَّهُ تَعالى عَلَيْهِ وسَلَّمَ حِينَ بَقِيَ الثُّلُثُ الأخِيرُ مِنَ اللَّيْلِ ورَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلّى اللَّهُ تَعالى عَلَيْهِ وسَلَّمَ عِنْدَ أُمِّ سَلَمَةَ وكانَتْ مُحْسِنَةً في شَأْنِي مُعِينَةً في أمْرِي فَقالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلّى اللَّهُ تَعالى عَلَيْهِ وسَلَّمَ: يا أُمَّ سَلَمَةَ تِيبَ عَلى كَعْبِ بْنِ مالِكٍ. قالَتْ: أفَلا أُرْسِلُ إلَيْهِ أُبَشِّرُهُ؟ قالَ: إذًا تُحَطِّمُكُمُ النّاسُ فَيَمْنَعُونَكُمُ النَّوْمَ سائِرَ اللَّيْلِ حَتّى إذا صَلّى صَلّى اللَّهُ تَعالى عَلَيْهِ وسَلَّمَ صَلاةَ الفَجْرَ آذَنَ بِتَوْبَةِ اللَّهِ تَعالى عَلَيْنا»
هَذا وفي وصْفِهِ سُبْحانَهُ هَؤُلاءِ بِما وصَفَهم بِهِ دَلالَةٌ وأيَّةُ دَلالَةٍ عَلى قُوَّةِ إيمانِهِمْ وصِدْقِ تَوْبَتِهِمْ وعَنْ أبِي بَكْرٍ الوَرّاقِ أنَّهُ سُئِلَ عَنِ التَّوْبَةِ النَّصُوحِ فَقالَ: أنْ تَضِيقَ عَلى التّائِبِ الأرْضُ بِما رَحُبَتْ وتَضِيقَ عَلَيْهِ نَفْسُهُ كَتَوْبَةِ كَعْبِ بْنِ مالِكٍ وصاحِبَيْهِ

The verse: ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah﴾ regarding what He does not approve, ﴿and be with the truthful﴾ (119). That is, be like them in their truthfulness. Ibn al-Anbari (Ibn al-Anbari) related from Ibn Abbas that he used to recite (And be among the truthful). Similarly, al-Bayhaqi and others related from Ibn Mas'ud that he used to recite it in this way. It has been said that the address is to those among the People of the Book who believed, and this was related from Ibn Abbas. Accordingly, the truthful refers to those who were true in their faith and in their covenant with Allah the Exalted and His Messenger (ﷺ) to obey. It is also permissible that the address is general, to them and to others, so the truthful refers to those who were true in their religion in intention, speech and action. It is also possible that it is specific to those who stayed behind and tied themselves to the pillars. Therefore, the most fitting interpretation is that the truthful refers to the three, meaning: be like them in truthfulness and sincerity of intention.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Jarir related from Nafi' that the verse was revealed concerning the three who were left behind. The truthful here refers to Muhammad (ﷺ) and his companions, and Ibn Umar interpreted it this way, as related by Ibn Abi Hatim and others. It is also related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that the meaning is: be with Abu Bakr and Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both.

Ibn Asakir and others related from al-Dahhak that he said: "They were commanded to be with Abu Bakr and Umar and their companions." Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Asakir related from Abu Ja'far, that the meaning is: be with Ali, may Allah honour his face. Some of the Shi'a used this to argue for his right to the caliphate. Its invalidity, even if the report were authentic, is clear. Al-Suddi interpreted it as referring to the three, without addressing the address.

The apparent meaning is the generality of the address, and it includes those who repented, initially. Likewise, the object of (fear) is general, and it initially includes dealing with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in matters of the military campaigns. Likewise the generality of (the truthful) is also intended, referring to those mentioned earlier, on the assumption of the generality of the address.

The verse contains clear praise of truthfulness. Al-Jalal al-Suyuti said that it has been used as evidence by those who do not permit lying in any situation, neither explicitly nor by indirection (ta'ridh). Several have related from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "Lying is not fitting in earnest or in jest, nor that one of you promises his child something and then does not fulfil it," and he recited the verse and the many hadiths condemning it, more than can be counted. The correct position, however, is that it is permissible in certain situations. Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ahmad related from Asma' bint Yazid, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "All lying is written against the son of Adam, except a man who lies in deception during war, or in reconciling two people, or a man who speaks to his wife to please her."

Likewise, the permissibility of indirect speech (ma'arid, speech that implies one meaning while intending another without outright falsehood). Ibn Adi related from Imran ibn Husayn, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, in indirect speech there is a sufficient alternative to lying."

﴿It was not⦆ (i.e., it was not proper or fitting) ﴿for the people of Madinah and for those of the Bedouins around them﴾ such as Muzaynah, Juhaynah,
[p. 46]
Ashja', Ghifar, Aslam, and their like, ﴿to stay behind from the Messenger of Allah﴾ when he set out for battle, peace and blessings be upon him, ﴿nor to prefer themselves over his self﴾. That is, they should not hold their selves back from his noble self, nor spare themselves from what he did not spare himself from; rather, they should endure what he endures of hardships. Its underlying sense is: they should not raise themselves above his self by disliking for themselves the hardships while not disliking them for him, peace and blessings be upon him. Rather, they must reverse the matter. The words of al-Wahidi point to this, where he said: "It is said, 'I preferred myself over this matter,' meaning I rose above it." In al-Nihayah (of Ibn al-Athir) it is said: "I preferred so-and-so over this matter," meaning I disliked that for him.

It is also permitted that ﴿yarghabu﴾ be in the accusative, being conjoined to ﴿yatakhallafu﴾, which is in the accusative due to ﴿an﴾, with the repetition of (lā) to emphasize the negation and reinforce it. This is the apparent reading. It may also be jussive, as a prohibition, which is the intended meaning of the speech, except that it was expressed in the form of a negation for emphasis. The people of Madinah were specifically mentioned because of their closeness to him, peace and blessings be upon him, and their knowledge of his departure. The apparent meaning of the verse is that mobilization (nafir) is obligatory when the Messenger of Allah, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace, goes out personally to battle.

Some scholars mentioned that the verse has been cited as evidence that jihad was an individual obligation (fard ʿayn) in his time, peace and blessings be upon him. Ibn Battal said this as well, and he gave the reason that they had pledged allegiance to him, peace and blessings be upon him. Therefore, mobilization is not obligatory alongside any of the caliphs unless the enemy attacks and its repulsion is not possible without it. Some scholars supposed in the verse an added term referring to the Messenger of Allah, meaning: "that they should not stay behind from the judgment of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace."
